pinneapple_analysis.proof.graph.doc:
Proof graphs: a mathematical argument as a graph of assumptions, definitions, lemmas, theorems and conjectures,
each with machine checks, and a status that only rises as far as its evidence and its dependencies allow.

The same discipline as the physics audit, applied to mathematics: every claim says what supports it.

=================  ==========================================================================================
status             meaning
=================  ==========================================================================================
``ASSUMED``        an assumption or definition: taken as given, stated explicitly
``PROVED``         every check is exact (symbolic identity, exhaustive enumeration over a finite set, a
                   symbolic degree or sign argument) and passed, and every dependency is PROVED or ASSUMED
``ARGUED``         the exact checks passed but part of the argument is a written proof step the machine did not
                   check (``argument=...`` without a check covering it), or a dependency is only ARGUED
``SUPPORTED``      only numerical evidence (random tests, counterexample searches that found nothing): evidence,
                   not proof
``REFUTED``        a check found a counterexample: the claim is false as stated
``OPEN``           no check, or a symbolic check that could not be decided
=================  ==========================================================================================

pinneapple_analysis.proof.pt_chains.doc:
Does the no-go theorem for linear exceptional-point tuning extend from PT dimers to longer chains?

The dimer theorem (Zenodo 23287622): with a reciprocal polynomial coupling b(lam), gamma_EP^2 = |b(lam)|^2 has
degree 2 deg(b) and a positive leading coefficient, so it can never be the linear target
l(lam) = J^2 + lam J G (G != 0). The paper leaves open (Q2 / Conjecture 2) whether chains obey the same restriction.
Uniform chains do, by scaling. This graph attacks the first non-uniform case, the PT tetramer

    H = [[ i gamma, b1, 0, 0 ], [ b1*, 0, b2, 0 ], [ 0, b2*, 0, b3 ], [ 0, 0, b3*, -i gamma ]]

with the couplings polynomials in a real control lam, where the inner and outer bonds can be modulated
independently. Lemmas, checked by sympy (exact) and numerically:

* PT symmetry (P = exchange) holds iff b3 = b1; b2 is free;
* the characteristic polynomial depends only on A = |b1|^2 and B = |b2|^2:
  E^4 + (gamma^2 - 2A - B) E^2 + (A^2 - B gamma^2);
* the PT-breaking threshold lies on branch I (an E^2 root reaches 0: gamma^2 = A^2 / B) or on branch II (two E^2
  roots collide: (gamma^2 - 2A + B)^2 = 4 A (A - 2B)), the region of real spectrum being bounded by these two
  curves (argued, and checked numerically against the matrix);
* branch I cannot be linear: A^2 = B l would need an even degree (4 deg b1) to equal an odd one (2 deg b2 + 1);
* branch II cannot be linear: it squares to (B + l)^2 = 4 A (l - B), whose two sides have leading coefficients of
  opposite sign when …

pinneapple_analysis.reproduction.doc:
Neutral tools for reproducing published numbers: one evaluator for the error metrics papers report, seed
statistics, and the status rule fixed before any run (examples/paper_reproductions).

Every metric takes ``pred`` and ``ref`` on the same points (flattened); none of them knows which method produced
``pred``, so all methods in a comparison are scored by the same code.

Metric definitions (each cites where the definition comes from, never a paper's numbers):

- ``rel_l2``  ``||pred - ref||_2 / ||ref||_2`` (Raissi et al. 2019, Lu et al. 2021 and most PINN papers);
  identical to PINNsFormer's "rRMSE" (``sqrt(sum (u - u_hat)^2 / sum u^2)``, official notebook
  ``demo/convection/convection_pinnsformer.ipynb``, cell 6, variable ``rl2``).
- ``rmae``    ``sum |pred - ref| / sum |ref|`` (PINNsFormer's "rMAE", same cell, variable ``rl1``).
- ``max_abs`` / ``mean_abs``  maximum and mean absolute error (X-TFC tables report absolute errors).
- ``mse``     mean squared error (MeshGraphNets / GNS rollout RMSE is ``sqrt(mse)``, see ``rmse``).

The status rule (``status``) is the one in the reproduction protocol: "reproduced" when our median is inside the
paper's reported spread or, with no spread, within a factor ``2`` of the paper's error (same order of magnitude
when the paper's error is below ``1e-6``); "partially reproduced" when the qualitative ordering against the
paper's baseline holds but the number is outside that band; "not reproduced" otherwise. Reduced-scale runs and
runs …

A real, local, embedding-based semantic index over a
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.retrieval.corpus.Document` corpus.

Deliberately a small numpy cosine-similarity index, not a dedicated
vector database (chromadb/faiss) -- at this corpus's real current size
(tens to low hundreds of documents), brute-force cosine similarity over

embedding API dependency. Requires the ``retrieval`` extra
(``pip install pinneapple[retrieval]``); importing this module without
it installed raises a clear ``ImportError`` naming the extra, not a

lognormal, triangular). The estimators are checked against the exact indices of the Ishigami and G functions …

pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.effects.doc:
Effect curves, local derivatives and the "which parameters can be frozen" decision.

- :func:`effect_curves`: partial dependence (the main effect: output averaged over the other inputs while one input
  sweeps its range; Friedman 2001) and individual conditional expectation curves (ICE; Goldstein et al. 2015). ICE
  curves that are not parallel reveal interactions.
- :func:`local_derivatives`: the Jacobian at a nominal point, by automatic differentiation when a torch function is
  given, otherwise by central finite differences; also scaled by each input's range (output change across the range,
  linearised) and as elasticities.
- :func:`freeze_recommendation` + :func:`verify_freeze`: an input can be frozen at its nominal value when the upper
  confidence bound of its total Sobol index is below a threshold for every output; the recommendation is then checked
  directly by re-running the model with those inputs frozen and comparing output variance and pointwise change.

pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.morris.doc:
Morris elementary effects: a cheap screening of which inputs matter, ``r (d + 1)`` evaluations.

Each of ``r`` trajectories starts at a random point of a ``levels``-level grid of the unit hypercube and moves one
input at a time by ``delta = levels / (2 (levels - 1))``, in random order (Morris 1991, Technometrics 33:161). The
elementary effect of input ``i`` is the output change per unit of its *normalised* range (the unit hypercube, mapped
to each distribution through its inverse CDF; for an unbounded distribution the unit interval covers the
0.5 %-99.5 % quantiles). Per input: ``mu`` (mean effect), ``mu_star`` (mean absolute effect, Campolongo et al. 2007:
the importance measure) and ``sigma`` (spread: nonlinearity or interactions), with a bootstrap interval on
``mu_star`` over trajectories.

pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.sobol.doc:
Variance-based (Sobol) sensitivity indices with bootstrap confidence intervals.

Design: two independent quasi-random matrices ``A`` and ``B`` (a scrambled Sobol sequence in ``2 d`` dimensions,
mapped to each input's distribution through its inverse CDF) and the matrices ``AB_i`` (``A`` with column ``i`` from
``B``); for second-order indices also ``BA_i``. Estimators:

- first order ``S_i``: Saltelli et al. (2010), Comput. Phys. Commun. 181:259, eq. (b) of table 2,
  ``mean(f(B) (f(AB_i) - f(A))) / V``;
- total ``ST_i``: Jansen (1999), ``mean((f(A) - f(AB_i))^2) / (2 V)``;
- second order ``S_ij``: Saltelli (2002), Comput. Phys. Commun. 145:280,
  ``mean(f(BA_i) f(AB_j) - f(A) f(B)) / V - S_i - S_j``;

with ``V`` the variance of ``[f(A), f(B)]``. Confidence intervals: percentile bootstrap over the rows of the design
(Archer et al. 1997). Cost: ``N (d + 2)`` model evaluations, ``N (2 d + 2)`` with second order.

:func:`first_order_given_data` estimates first-order indices from an existing sample (a dataset, a campaign's runs)
without a designed experiment, by the correlation-ratio estimator on equal-count bins.

pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.testfunc.doc:
Benchmark functions with closed-form Sobol indices, to check a sensitivity estimator against the exact answer.

- Ishigami & Homma (1990): ``f = sin x1 + a sin^2 x2 + b x3^4 sin x1`` on ``[-pi, pi]^3``; indices from Sobol &
  Levitan (1999), also tabulated in Saltelli et al. (2008), *Global Sensitivity Analysis: The Primer*, sec. 4.9.
- Sobol' G function: ``f = prod (|4 x_i - 2| + a_i) / (1 + a_i)`` on ``[0, 1]^d``; partial variances
  ``V_i = 1 / (3 (1 + a_i)^2)`` (Saltelli & Sobol' 1995).

pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kal.doc:
Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) for
sequential state estimation / data assimilation.

Relocated from ``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py``
(a single-file implementation tightly coupled *by location*, not by
API, to ``DigitalTwin``) so it can be used standalone -- fuse a plain
physics model with a stream of sensor observations -- without building
a full ``DigitalTwin``. The implementation already operated purely on
plain ``np.ndarray`` state/observation vectors and user-supplied
transition/observation callables ``f``/``h``; it never referenced
``DigitalTwin``, ``SystemState``, or ``Observation``, so no API
generalization was needed for the move -- this is the same code,
verbatim, at a general-purpose home.

``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py`` now contains
a thin re-export shim pointing back here (the same convention as
``pinneapple_models/registry.py``), so every existing caller
(``DigitalTwin._build_default_filter`` included) keeps working
unchanged.

This is classic sequential/recursive *state* filtering (predict ->
observe -> update, repeated over a time series) -- not to be confused
with ``pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.ensemble_kalman``'s
``EnsembleKalmanInversion`` / ``IteratedEKI`` (EKI/TEKI), which are
derivative-free *parameter* estimation methods that iterate an
ensemble to a converged parameter estimate rather than filtering a
state through time.

pinneapple_analysis.study_contracts.doc:
The shared data contracts (:mod:`pinneapple_data.contracts`) for uncertainty and sensitivity studies.

- :func:`space_from_contract` / :func:`space_to_contract`: a ``ParameterSpace`` is bounds per parameter; a study needs
  a distribution per parameter. A continuous or integer parameter becomes uniform on its bounds unless
  ``metadata["distributions"][name]`` gives another distribution (``{"dist": "normal", "mean": .., "std": ..}``)
  (integer parameters are sampled as continuous: the model must accept non-integer values);
  a constant parameter is held at its value; categorical and log-scaled parameters are refused (no ordering /
  no log-uniform sampling here) rather than silently treated as uniform.
- :func:`model_from_ref` / :func:`model_to_ref`: ``ModelRef`` <-> :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.study_models.StudyModel`
  (``zoo:<name>`` URIs, or ONNX bytes supplied with the reference).
- :func:`uncertainty_result` / :func:`sensitivity_result`: a ``StudyResult`` from the dicts of
  :func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.study.uncertainty_study` and
  :func:`pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.study.sensitivity_study`, with the checks that actually ran.

pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.doc:
Surrogate models from simulation results: select, compare at equal budget, measure on unseen data, package.

>>> from pinneapple_analysis import surrogate
>>> data = surrogate.examples.airfoil_rans()                 # OpenFOAM RANS campaign, Cl and Cd
>>> study = surrogate.run_study(data, budget=5.0, seeds=2)   # every applicable method, same splits and budget
>>> study.best, study.ranking("test"), study.trust["decision"]
>>> study.model.predict({"T0": 0.15, ..., "alpha_deg": 4.0})  # outputs + per-row OOD assessment
>>> study.model.save("model_dir")

Modules: ``data`` (tables and arrays -> ``SurrogateData``), ``splits`` (held-out and distribution-shift splits),
``methods`` (ridge, gp, gbt, mlp, fno, deeponet, pinn and when each applies), ``pde`` (declared equations for the
PINN), ``limits`` (validity bounds, OOD gate, error concentration), ``model`` (``SurrogateModel``), ``study``
(``run_study``), ``examples`` (datasets that need no download), ``contracts`` (``DatasetSpec``, ``ModelRef``,
``StudyResult`` of ``pinneapple_data.contracts``; imported on use). Needs ``pip install "pinneapple[surrogate]"``
(scikit-learn; Parquet, HDF5 and ONNX support).

Checks map ``supports`` / ``contradicts`` / ``not_run`` to ``PASS`` / ``FAIL`` / ``NOT_RUN``; a check is only

``SurrogateData`` holds the arrays a surrogate is trained on; ``read_table`` reads CSV, Parquet, JSON, HDF5 and NPZ
(from a path or bytes) and ``from_table`` picks the input and output columns. A field is a set of output columns
``<name>_<i>`` (or ``<name>[i]``) ordered by ``i``, reshaped to ``grid_shape``; NPZ/HDF5 can carry ``X``, ``Y`` and
``coords`` arrays directly.

pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.examples.doc:
Example surrogate datasets that need no download.

``airfoil_rans``  the zoo dataset ``airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6``: OpenFOAM RANS (k-omega SST, Re = 4e6) of CST airfoils;
                  inputs the six CST coefficients and the angle of attack, outputs Cl and Cd (Cm is not recorded);
                  group = the shape (whole airfoils can be held out). Its train and test splits are pooled (the
                  study re-splits); unsteady runs of the train split, recorded at the final iteration rather than
                  time-averaged, are left out.
``burgers_fields`` viscous Burgers ``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx`` on x in [-1, 1], u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x), u(+-1, t) = 0,

                  for ``n`` viscosities log-uniform in ``nu_range``; output the field u(x, t) on an ``nx`` x ``nt``
                  grid, t in [0, t_max]. Small viscosities form a steep front at x = 0 (a near-discontinuity); the
                  recommended shift split holds out the smallest viscosities.

                  Latin-hypercube designs over height H, width W and load angle) as a field dataset on its

pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.limits.doc:
Where a surrogate may be used: validity bounds, an out-of-distribution gate, and where its errors concentrate.

``OODGate`` is the batched form of ``pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.Envelope`` (same rule, vectorised): a query is out of distribution when an input is
outside the training range, or when its nearest training sample is farther than ``knn_limit`` times the typical
training spacing (standardised inputs, log10 for positive inputs), i.e. inside the box but in a hole of the data.

``limitations`` measures, on held-out samples only: the error inside and outside the gate, the error per input
quartile (where the error concentrates), the worst samples, the extrapolation ratio (shift error / test error) and,
for fields, where on the grid the error is largest.

functions.doc1: ``X_eval`` / ``err``: held-out samples (test and shift) and their per-sample error; ``sets``: name -> boolean mask over them. ``field_err``: (n_eval, n_points) pointwise absolute error, for the error map.

pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.model.doc:
A trained surrogate packaged for use: predict with the OOD gate, save / load, export, model card.

``SurrogateModel.save(dir)`` writes ``model.pkl`` (the fitted candidate, pickled) and ``card.json`` (inputs,
outputs, validity bounds, OOD gate, held-out metrics, limitations, trust report, dataset hash, the model file's
sha256). ``load`` verifies that hash before unpickling. Unpickling runs code: load only models you produced
(the gateway stores the ones it publishes; it never unpickles an upload).

``export(path, "torchscript" | "onnx")`` writes a self-contained graph of the PyTorch candidates (mlp, fno,
deeponet, pinn) that takes raw inputs ``(n, d)`` and returns raw outputs ``(n, p)`` (normalisation included); the
scikit-learn and XGBoost candidates have no such export here.

pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.pde.doc:
PDE declarations for physics-informed surrogates: which residual a PINN candidate adds to its data loss.

A declaration names the equation, maps its coordinates to the field's coordinate names and its coefficients to
input columns (or constants)::

    {"type": "burgers", "coords": {"x": "x", "t": "t"}, "coefficients": {"nu": "nu"}}

Supported equations (``u`` the scalar field):

========== =============================== ==================
type        residual                        coords / coefficients
========== =============================== ==================
heat        u_t - alpha u_xx                x, t / alpha
burgers     u_t + u u_x - nu u_xx           x, t / nu
advection   u_t + c u_x                     x, t / c
poisson_1d  k u_xx + f                      x / k, f
laplace_2d  u_xx + u_yy                     x, y / -
========== =============================== ==================

The PINN candidate is only offered when a declaration is given: without a PDE there is no physics loss.

pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.study.doc:
Surrogate study: train every applicable candidate on the same data and budget, measure on unseen data, pick one.

``run_study(data, ...)``

1. splits once (``make_splits``): train / validation / held-out test, plus a distribution-shift set never seen in
   training (whole groups, the edge of the input space, or one end of an input);
2. lists every candidate with the reason it does or does not apply (fields vs scalars; PINN only with a declared
   PDE; GP sample limit);
3. trains each applicable candidate for each seed under the same ``ComputeBudget``
   (``pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget``) and measures, in physical units, the held-out and shift errors,
   training time, inference time per query, parameter count and model size;
4. selects the method with the lowest **validation** error (the test and shift sets never choose), and packages it
   as a ``SurrogateModel`` with its limitations (validity bounds, OOD gate, where errors concentrate) and a trust
   report (``pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport``) whose checks all ran on held-out data.

Error metrics: scalars, ``nrmse`` = RMSE / standard deviation of the training targets, per output then averaged;
fields, ``rel_l2`` = ||pred - true|| / ||true|| per sample, averaged.

pinneapple_analysis.trust.field_card.doc:
Trust card of a field on a grid: the physics checks a result must pass before anyone uses it.

``trust_card`` takes a field sampled on a tensor-product grid (from any source: a PINN, a solver, a file written
by another code) and checks it with NumPy only:

* sanity: finite values, values inside the physical range;
* PDE residual: ``laplace(u) = f`` (``"laplace"`` / ``"poisson"``) or ``u_t = alpha laplace(u) + f`` (``"heat"``),
  by finite differences on the interior of the grid;
* boundary conditions: Dirichlet values on named faces (``"x_min"``, ``"y_max"``, ...);
* conservation: the divergence theorem, net flux through the boundary against the integral of the source
  (steady problems);
* maximum principle (steady problems without a source): no interior value outside the boundary range;
* reference: relative L2 error against a reference field or a closed form;
* applicability (OOD): the grid, or the query points, inside the bounds the model was trained on.

The checks feed two existing views: the six questions of the lab trust card
(``pinneapple_lab.curation.trust_stages``) and the deploy decision of ``TrustReport`` (``APPROVED``, ``REVIEW``,
``REJECT``; a failing critical check rejects).

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.trust.field_card import trust_card
>>> x = y = np.linspace(0, 1, 41)
>>> X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing="ij")
>>> u = np.sin(np.pi * X) * np.sinh(np.pi * Y) / np.sinh(np.pi)
>>> card = trust_card({"x": x, "y": y}, u, …

pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_gate.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_gate — ``TrustGate``: pre-consumption
trust scoring of a trained model's own prediction, before it is allowed
to feed a live digital twin.

Distinct from two existing, adjacent mechanisms — this is neither of them:

- ``pinneapple_llm.guardrail.PhysicsGuardrail`` verifies a *problem spec*
  an LLM proposed (residual re-check, dimensional analysis, conservation)
  before training even starts.
- ``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.monitoring.anomaly.MahalanobisDetector``
  scores a live sensor *innovation vector* against a running Kalman
  filter's state covariance, continuously, once a twin is already
  running.

``TrustGate`` scores one specific prediction from an already-trained
model, combining up to three independent [0, 1] sub-scores:

- an out-of-distribution (OOD) score: the fraction of query points whose
  Mahalanobis distance to the model's training-coordinate distribution has
  a chi-squared p-value (``scipy.stats.chi2.sf``) of at least ``ood_level``
  (default 0.01: the point lies inside the 99 % region of a Gaussian with
  the training mean and covariance). Each point is tested on its own -- the
  same Mahalanobis-distance +
  chi-squared concept ``MahalanobisDetector`` already uses, reimplemented
  here (rather than called directly) because it fits once from a static
  training sample instead of updating per Kalman step, a different call
  shape;
- a residual score: re-evaluating a PDE residual on the model's own
  prediction (any …

pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report — relatório de confiança para decidir o deploy de um modelo.

Junta checagens independentes (acurácia contra referência, consistência física, OOD, calibração de
incerteza, comparação com dado experimental) numa decisão única: APPROVED, REVIEW ou REJECT. Cada
checagem usa o mesmo vocabulário das provas do E11 do PINNeAPPle-CFD:

- ``supports``: a checagem passou no critério;
- ``contradicts``: a checagem falhou no critério;
- ``not_run``: a checagem não foi executada (com o motivo). Não entra no score, mas conta na cobertura.

Regras (escolhas de projeto, documentadas e revogáveis, não normas):

1. Qualquer checagem ``critical`` com ``contradicts`` → REJECT.
2. Qualquer outra ``contradicts`` → REVIEW.
3. Cobertura (checagens executadas / total) abaixo de ``min_coverage`` → REVIEW.
4. Score (média ponderada das checagens executadas) abaixo de ``min_score`` → REVIEW.
5. Caso contrário → APPROVED.

``from_trust_score`` converte o ``TrustScore`` do ``TrustGate`` (OOD, resíduo, ensemble) em checagens.
pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report.doc1: pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report — relatório de confiança para decidir o deploy de um modelo.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.doc:
pinneapple_uq — Uncertainty Quantification for physics-informed neural networks.

This module provides a unified, PyTorch-native toolkit for estimating and
evaluating predictive uncertainty in PINNs and related surrogate models.

Uncertainty types
-----------------
``AleatoricHead`` / ``aleatoric_nll_loss``
    **Aleatoric (data) uncertainty** — irreducible noise in the data.
    The model learns both mean μ(x) and log-variance log σ²(x).
    Optimized via heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL.

``MCDropout`` / ``EnsembleUQ``
    **Epistemic (model) uncertainty** — reducible uncertainty from limited data
    or model capacity.  MC Dropout runs *n* stochastic forward passes;
    ensembles aggregate multiple independently-trained models.

``decompose_uncertainty``
    **Decomposition** — splits total variance into aleatoric + epistemic
    components from *n* stochastic passes of an AleatoricHead model.

``ConformalPredictor``
    **Conformal prediction** — distribution-free coverage guarantees via a
    held-out calibration set.

Quantile regression
-------------------
``QuantileHead`` / ``QuantileLoss``
    Learn conditional quantiles via pinball loss; also accessible from
    ``pinneapple_timeseries.uncertainty``.

Calibration utilities
---------------------
``CalibrationMetrics``
    Static methods for ECE, coverage, sharpness, and Gaussian NLL.

Resampling
----------
``block_bootstrap`` / ``group_bootstrap`` / ``skill_score`` / ``jackknife``
    Confidence intervals for …

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.aleatori.doc:
Aleatoric (data) uncertainty via heteroscedastic NLL regression.

The model predicts both a mean μ(x) and a log-variance log σ²(x).
Loss = 0.5·log σ² + 0.5·(y − μ)²·exp(−log σ²)  — Gaussian NLL, numerically stable.

This captures *irreducible* uncertainty: noise in the data that no model can remove.
For reducible (epistemic) uncertainty use MCDropout, EnsembleUQ, or decompose_uncertainty.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import AleatoricHead, aleatoric_nll_loss

    base = MyModel()
    model = AleatoricHead(base, out_dim=1, in_dim=2)
    # model(x) → (mean, log_var), both shape (N, out_dim)

    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for x_batch, y_batch in loader:
        mean, log_var = model(x_batch)
        loss = aleatoric_nll_loss(mean, log_var, y_batch)
        loss.backward(); optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Inference
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        result = model.predict_with_uncertainty(x_test)
    # result.aleatoric_std  →  predicted noise std

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.applicab.doc:
Where is a model's prediction reliable? Applicability gates on the inputs and a routing rule that sends the cases
the model cannot answer to the high-fidelity solver.

:class:`ApplicabilityDomain` is fitted on the model's reference data (its training or calibration inputs) and tells,
for every query point:

- ``outside``: an input lies outside the validity range (the declared bounds, or the range of the data);
- ``sparse``: inside the range, but the nearest reference points are farther than for ``level`` of the reference
  points themselves (k-nearest-neighbour distance in standardised inputs, leave-one-out on the reference): the model
  interpolates across a hole in its data;
- ``inside``: in range and as close to the data as the data are to each other.

The Mahalanobis p-value of :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustGate` is reported as well (it flags points far from
the bulk of a roughly Gaussian cloud; the k-NN test also catches holes inside the range).

:func:`route_cases` combines the gate with the prediction interval: a case goes to the high-fidelity solver when it is
outside or sparse, when its interval is wider than the accuracy the decision needs, or when the interval straddles a
decision limit (the surrogate cannot tell on which side the case falls).
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.applicab.doc1: Where is a model's prediction reliable? Applicability gates on the inputs and a routing rule that sends the cases the model cannot answer to the high-fidelity solver.

Learning Using Calibrated Regression*. ICML.

Levi, D. et al. (2022). *Evaluating and Calibrating Uncertainty Prediction in
Regression Tasks*. Sensors, 22(15).

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conforma.doc:
Split Conformal Prediction for regression.

Split conformal prediction provides *distribution-free*, *finite-sample* valid
coverage guarantees without making any assumptions about the data-generating
process.

References
----------
Vovk, V., Gammerman, A. & Shafer, G. (2005). *Algorithmic Learning in a
Random World*. Springer.

Angelopoulos, A. N. & Bates, S. (2022). *A Gentle Introduction to Conformal
Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification*.
arXiv:2107.07511.

classes.name: ConformalPredictor
classes.doc1: Split conformal predictor for regression tasks.

functions.doc1: The split-conformal quantile of any array of non-conformity scores (NumPy, list or tensor): the ``ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha))``-th smallest score, clipped to the largest (see ``_conformal_quantile``).

functions.name: conformal_quantile_valid
functions.doc1: True when ``n`` calibration scores are enough for the finite-sample guarantee at level ``alpha`` (``n >= ceil(1 / alpha) - 1``); otherwise the quantile is clipped to the largest score and the guarantee does not hold.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conforma.doc:
Split-conformal prediction intervals for any model's predictions (NumPy), with the coverage *measured* on a
held-out test split that the calibration never saw.

:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal.ConformalPredictor` wraps a torch model; this module works on
predictions alone, so it serves a zoo model, an ONNX graph, a solver-trained surrogate or a column of predictions in
a CSV file alike::

    study = conformal_study(y_cal, pred_cal, y_test, pred_test, alpha=0.1)
    study.coverage, study.coverage_ci        # fraction of held-out targets inside their interval, Wilson interval
    lo, hi = conformal_interval(pred_new, study.q)

Scores are absolute residuals ``|y - pred|`` (constant width) or, when a per-point scale is given (an ensemble
standard deviation, a predicted sigma), normalised residuals ``|y - pred| / scale`` (width proportional to the
scale: locally adaptive). The guarantee is marginal coverage of at least ``1 - alpha`` for exchangeable data
(Vovk et al. 2005; Angelopoulos & Bates 2022, arXiv:2107.07511); it says nothing about a region the calibration
data do not cover, which is why the coverage is also reported per group.
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conforma.doc1: Split-conformal prediction intervals for any model's predictions (NumPy), with the coverage *measured* on a held-out test split that the calibration never saw.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.decompos.doc:
Variance decomposition: total predictive uncertainty = aleatoric + epistemic.

Theory
------
Given *S* stochastic forward passes of a model that returns ``(μ_i, log σ²_i)``:

  Predictive mean   μ̄  = E[μ_i]
  Aleatoric var        = E[σ²_i]       (average predicted data noise)
  Epistemic var        = Var[μ_i]      (spread of the predicted means)
  Total var            = aleatoric + epistemic

For purely deterministic models (ensemble / MC-dropout *without* a variance head),
only epistemic variance can be estimated; set ``has_aleatoric=False``.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import AleatoricHead, MCDropoutWrapper, MCDropoutConfig
    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import decompose_uncertainty

    # 1) Build a model that outputs (mean, log_var)
    aleatoric_model = AleatoricHead(my_base_model, out_dim=1, in_dim=2)

    # 2) Wrap with MC Dropout to activate stochasticity
    mcd = MCDropoutWrapper(aleatoric_model, MCDropoutConfig(n_samples=50))

    # 3) Decompose
    result = decompose_uncertainty(mcd, x_test, has_aleatoric=True, device="cuda")
    print("aleatoric:", result.aleatoric_std.mean().item())
    print("epistemic:", result.epistemic_std.mean().item())

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.drift.doc:
Drift monitoring of a deployed surrogate: accuracy, calibration, input shift and residual trend in one report.

A surrogate trained on one input distribution degrades silently when the operating point moves. Given a batch of new
predictions with their measured (or high-fidelity) truth, :func:`assess_drift` computes

* the normalised RMSE ``sqrt(mean(r^2)) / std(y_true)`` and the bias ``mean(r)`` of the residuals
  ``r = y_pred - y_true``, with a t-type test of ``bias = 0``;
* the empirical coverage of the central Gaussian interval ``y_pred +- z sigma`` at ``level``, compared with the
  binomial standard error ``sqrt(level (1 - level) / n)`` (Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery 2007);
* per input feature, the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and p-value between the reference (training) inputs
  and the new inputs (``scipy.stats.ks_2samp``; Massey 1951), Bonferroni-corrected over the features;
* the fraction of new inputs outside the training box ``bounds``;
* a Mann-Kendall trend test of the residuals against their order of arrival (Mann 1945; Kendall 1975), computed as
  Kendall's tau between the time index and the residual (``scipy.stats.kendalltau``).

The decision is a screening heuristic, not a statistical guarantee; every threshold is a field of
:class:`DriftThresholds`. A *flag* is raised by each of: a significant bias, an nRMSE above ``nrmse_review``, an
interval coverage more than ``coverage_z`` binomial standard errors below ``level``, a KS p-value …
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.drift.doc1: Drift monitoring of a deployed surrogate: accuracy, calibration, input shift and residual trend in one report.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.margin.doc:
Does a design that passes at its nominal dimensions still pass with its manufacturing tolerances? Monte Carlo
margin study against an upper limit, with checks on the study itself.

``margin_study(fn, nominal, tolerances, limit)`` draws ``n`` designs within the tolerances
(:func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate`, uniform by default: with no process-capability data
there is no basis for a narrower normal), evaluates the model on each and reports the distribution (mean, standard
deviation, min, max, the nearest-rank 95th percentile, the fraction under the limit with its Wilson interval) and a
verdict on the p95: ``FRAGILE`` (p95 above the limit), ``MARGINAL`` (p95 within ``marginal_fraction`` of the limit)
or ``ROBUST``.

Six checks of the result, each PASS / WARNING / FAIL with its number:

1. every sample is finite;
2. p95 stability: an independent batch of the same size gives a p95 within half the p95 margin (at least
   ``min_drift``) of this one;
3. p95 with fewer samples: an independent batch of ``n_small`` gives a p95 within the same band;
4. the hottest sample drawn against the limit;
5. corner stack-up (:func:`corner_stackup`): every tolerance at an end of its band at once, a deterministic method
   independent of the sampling (exact worst case for a model monotone in each input);
6. p95 against the limit (the verdict).

The checks are also given as a :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport` (FAIL of 4-6 is critical; WARNING is a
non-critical …
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.margin.doc1: Does a design that passes at its nominal dimensions still pass with its manufacturing tolerances? Monte Carlo margin study against an upper limit, with checks on the study itself.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.pce.doc:
Polynomial chaos expansion by least squares: output mean, variance and Sobol indices from one regression.

Every input is written as ``x_i = F_i^-1((xi_i + 1) / 2)`` with ``xi_i`` uniform on [-1, 1] (the inverse-CDF map of
:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.distributions`), and the output is fitted on the orthonormal Legendre
polynomials of the ``xi`` of total degree ``<= degree``. With orthonormal terms the mean is the constant
coefficient, the variance the sum of the other squared coefficients, and the Sobol indices are sums of squared
coefficients (Sudret 2008, Reliab. Eng. Syst. Saf. 93:964). The fit is only as good as its leave-one-out error
(``loo_q2``, computed exactly from the hat matrix); a low Q2 means more samples or a higher degree, or a model that
is not smooth enough for this expansion. It is cheap for a few inputs and a low degree: the number of terms is
``C(d + degree, degree)``.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.posterio.doc:
Posterior-matching metrics for generative / probabilistic inverse solvers (PosteriorBench).

A solver whose posterior *mean* is right can still have the wrong posterior: too narrow (the
classic MC-dropout failure), too wide, or with the wrong spatial texture. PosteriorBench
(neuraloperator/PosteriorBench, MIT; Wang et al., "PosteriorBench: From Point Estimates to
Posterior Matching in Evaluating Generative Inverse Solvers", NeurIPS 2026, arXiv:2609.20794)
compares predicted and reference posterior *ensembles* of 2D fields with:

- relative L2 of the mean and of the pointwise standard deviation;
- MMD with a multi-scale Gaussian kernel (bandwidths 0.2..5 x the median cross distance);
- sliced Wasserstein distance with Gaussian-random-field projection directions (smooth
  directions, drawn in the DCT domain) instead of isotropic white-noise directions;
- geometric mean of the relative error of the radially averaged power spectrum.

The implementation follows ``posteriorbench/evaluation/metrics.py`` (MIT, Copyright the
PosteriorBench authors); all quantities accept weighted ensembles (e.g. importance-sampled
reference posteriors). Its datasets are on the Hugging Face Hub (``pinneapple_catalog``:
``posteriorbench``).
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.posterio.doc1: Posterior-matching metrics for generative / probabilistic inverse solvers (PosteriorBench).

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.quantile.doc:
Quantile (distribution-free) uncertainty estimation.

Provides pinball-loss training for quantile regression models and a general
QuantileHead that wraps any point-prediction model.

Unlike conformal prediction, quantile regression *learns* conditional quantiles
from data rather than relying on post-hoc calibration.  Use
:class:`~pinneapple_uq.conformal.ConformalPredictor` when distribution-free
coverage guarantees are required.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import QuantileHead, QuantileLoss, QuantileConfig

    cfg  = QuantileConfig(quantiles=(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
    head = QuantileHead(base_model, cfg)
    loss = QuantileLoss(cfg.quantiles)

    for x_batch, y_batch in loader:
        y_pred = head(x_batch)          # (B, H, Q)
        metrics = loss(head, y_pred, {"y": y_batch})
        metrics["total"].backward()
        ...

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.reachabi.doc:
RESEARCH ONLY -- set-based encounter feasibility for relative motion (collision risk, rendezvous).

Inspired by the set-based view of PRISM (A. Enayati, "PRISM: Predictive Reachability-Intercept
Set Model for Relative Motion and Intercept Kinematics", Zenodo 22979350, CC BY 4.0): instead of
propagating two point states and checking a miss distance, each body is a *region* of possible
positions that grows with state uncertainty, velocity uncertainty, information latency and
bounded acceleration; two bodies can meet at time t only if their regions overlap.

Scope of this module (deliberately): the generic, dual-use kinematics for civilian questions --
"could these two objects come into contact within T?" (collision screening for satellites,
drones, vehicles) and "can a chaser reach a target region within T?" (rendezvous / docking
feasibility). It contains no targeting, no guidance law and no engagement planning, and none
will be added: those would turn it into weapon-system tooling. It is marked research only:
a ResearchOnlyWarning is emitted on use and PINNEAPPLE_COMMERCIAL_MODE=1 refuses it.

Model: a body with nominal position p0, velocity v0, position uncertainty radius r_p, velocity
uncertainty radius r_v, control latency tau and acceleration bound a_max (free space, no
gravity -- use relative coordinates, e.g. Clohessy-Wiltshire, when that matters) can be anywhere
in the ball
    B(t) = { p0 + v0 t + e :  |e| <= r_p + r_v t + 0.5 a_max max(t - tau, 0)^2 },
which is exact …

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.resampli.doc:
Resampling confidence intervals for dependent data: moving-block and group bootstrap, skill scores, jackknife.

Forecast errors are rarely independent: consecutive time steps are autocorrelated and the cases of one event (a
storm, an experiment, a sequence) move together. Resampling single cases then gives confidence intervals that are
too narrow. The functions here resample whole blocks or whole groups instead. NumPy only.

* :func:`block_bootstrap` -- moving-block bootstrap (Kunsch 1989) for a statistic of a time series.
* :func:`group_bootstrap` -- cluster bootstrap that resamples whole groups (Davison & Hinkley 1997, sec. 3.8).
* :func:`skill_score` -- ``1 - E|e_model| / E|e_ref|`` with a paired bootstrap interval (blocks, groups or iid).
* :func:`jackknife` -- delete-one-block jackknife standard error (Efron & Tibshirani 1993, ch. 11).

Every bootstrap returns ``(estimate, lo, hi)``: the statistic on the full sample and the equal-tailed percentile
interval at ``level`` (Efron & Tibshirani 1993, ch. 13). Non-finite entries are dropped before resampling.

References
----------
Kunsch, H. R. (1989). The jackknife and the bootstrap for general stationary observations. *Annals of Statistics*
17(3), 1217-1241.

Efron, B. & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*. Chapman & Hall.

Davison, A. C. & Hinkley, D. V. (1997). *Bootstrap Methods and their Application*. Cambridge University Press.
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.resampli.doc1: Resampling confidence intervals for dependent data: moving-block and group bootstrap, skill scores, jackknife.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.residual.doc:
Residual-to-error calibration (#699): turn the PDE residual of a prediction, which needs no true answer, into an
error bound an engineer can use ("the error is below X with 90 % confidence").

Two routes, both reported:

**Theory (linear elliptic problems).** For a discrete problem ``A u = f`` with ``A`` symmetric positive definite and
``A >= c L`` for a reference operator ``L`` (both SPD), the error of any candidate ``u`` against the discrete solution
``u_h`` obeys

    ||u_h - u||_A  <=  ||r||_{L^-1} / sqrt(c),     r = f - A u,

because ``A^-1 <= L^-1 / c``. For Darcy and steady heat conduction, ``-div(k grad u) = f``, in the cell-centred
finite volumes of ``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` (:func:`darcy_problem`), ``L`` is the same operator with ``k = 1``
and ``c = min k`` (every face coefficient is a harmonic mean, never below ``min k``). The bound is guaranteed and
needs no data; it can be loose when the coefficient contrast is large.

**Calibration (any problem).** :class:`ResidualErrorCalibrator` learns the map residual -> error on a calibration set
with split conformal prediction (the finite-sample quantile of ``uncertainty.conformal``): the score is
``error / g(residual)`` with ``g`` the identity (``mode="ratio"``) or a power law fitted on a separate set
(``mode="power"``), and the bound of a new query is ``q * g(residual)``. Coverage is guaranteed for queries
exchangeable with the calibration set; under an input shift it is measured and reported, not …

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.study.doc:
One uncertainty study of one model output: is the prediction reliable here, and which cases need the solver?

:func:`uncertainty_study` composes the pieces of :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty`:

1. split-conformal intervals calibrated on ``(X_cal, y_cal)`` with their coverage **measured** on ``(X_test, y_test)``
   (never used to calibrate), plus the coverage of the raw ensemble interval when the model has a spread;
2. an applicability gate fitted on reference inputs (the training inputs when known) and the declared validity range;
3. screening of ``cases`` (scenarios, a batch of designs): prediction, interval, gate, route, and optionally the
   high-fidelity answer for the routed cases (or all), which shows whether the rule sent the right cases;
4. propagation of uncertain inputs around a nominal operating point (MC / LHS / Sobol, and polynomial chaos when
   cheap), with the probability of meeting the limits with and without the model's own error, and the share of the
   propagated samples that leave the region where the model was checked.

Every number in the returned dict comes from these runs; nothing is assumed.

pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.toleranc.doc:
Monte-Carlo propagation of input (manufacturing, operating) tolerances through any model.

Each input ``i`` is drawn independently around its nominal value ``x0_i``:

* ``"normal"``: ``x_i ~ N(x0_i, t_i^2)`` -- the tolerance ``t_i`` is the standard deviation;
* ``"uniform"``: ``x_i ~ U(x0_i - t_i, x0_i + t_i)`` -- the tolerance is the half-width, variance ``t_i^2 / 3``
  (``(b - a)^2 / 12`` with ``b - a = 2 t_i``).

The model is evaluated once on the ``(n, d)`` sample matrix and the output statistics are the sample mean, standard
deviation and percentiles (JCGM 101:2008, "Propagation of distributions using a Monte Carlo method"). The
probability of meeting the specification limits ``lo <= y <= hi`` (jointly over the outputs and per output) comes
with the Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion (Wilson 1927; Brown, Cai & DasGupta 2001), which stays
inside [0, 1] and keeps its coverage when the proportion is close to 0 or 1 -- the usual case for a yield.

References
----------
JCGM 101:2008. *Evaluation of measurement data -- Supplement 1 to the GUM -- Propagation of distributions using a
Monte Carlo method*. BIPM.

Wilson, E. B. (1927). Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference. *JASA* 22(158),
209-212.

Brown, L. D., Cai, T. T. & DasGupta, A. (2001). Interval estimation for a binomial proportion. *Statistical
Science* 16(2), 101-133.
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.toleranc.doc1: Monte-Carlo propagation of input (manufacturing, operating) tolerances through any model.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.doc:
Red team / blue team for validation (#707): adversarial generators of wrong-but-plausible cases against the
checks, and a loop that hardens them.

Built on the fault library of :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection` (#697)::

    from pinneapple_analysis.validation import arena
    rep = arena.run_arena("darcy_2d", budget="small", alpha=0.05)     # or arena("darcy_2d", ...) / pp.validate.arena
    print(rep.to_markdown())          # escapes, false alarms, mutation score, ROC/AUC, minimal detectable magnitude
    rep.save_cases("darcy_cases.json")    # replayed in CI by `pinneapple check --arena-cases darcy_cases.json`

Modules: :mod:`.search` (differential evolution, CMA-ES, L-BFGS-B on the unit box), :mod:`.generators` (mutation
operators and physics-consistent attacks), :mod:`.red` (evasion and false-alarm search, mutation score),
:mod:`.blue` (split-conformal combined test, hardening), :mod:`.cases` (regression cases, replay), :mod:`.loop`
(rounds and report). The module itself is callable: ``arena(problem, checks, budget=...)`` is ``run_arena``.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.doc1: Red team / blue team for validation (#707): adversarial generators of wrong-but-plausible cases against the checks, and a loop that hardens them.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.__m.doc:
``python -m pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena``: run the arena on Darcy 2-D and Burgers 1-D.

Writes ``arena_<problem>.md`` and ``arena_<problem>.json`` into ``--out`` and the regression cases into
``--cases`` (``<problem>.json``; the files shipped with the library live in ``arena/cases/``). Exit 1 when the
acceptance of #707 fails after the last blue round.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.__m.doc1: ``python -m pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena``: run the arena on Darcy 2-D and Burgers 1-D.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.blu.doc:
Blue team: calibrated thresholds with a stated false-alarm rate, one combined test, and hardening.

**Defence.** A set of checks with a threshold each; a case is rejected when any check exceeds its threshold. Round
0 of the arena is the hand-set tolerances of the checks (``Defence.from_checks``).

**Calibration** (``calibrate``). The checks are combined into one statistic so that false alarms do not grow with
the number of checks. With the clean calibration cases split in two halves A and B:

1. each check's scale ``s_j`` is the split-conformal quantile of its values on A
   (``pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal.conformal_quantile``), at least 1 % of the check's own tolerance;
2. the combined statistic of a case is ``T = max_j value_j / s_j``;
3. its threshold ``q`` is the split-conformal quantile of ``T`` on B at level ``alpha_cal``.

``T`` is a fixed function of a case once A is used, so for a new clean case exchangeable with B,
``P(T > q) <= alpha_cal`` (Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer 2005; Angelopoulos & Bates 2022, arXiv:2107.07511) for the
whole family of checks at once: the family-wise false-alarm rate. The guarantee needs
``ceil((n_B + 1)(1 - alpha_cal)) <= n_B``; ``Defence.alpha_guaranteed`` says whether that holds. ``alpha_cal`` is
``safety * alpha`` (default ``safety = 0.5``) so that the rate measured on a finite held-out set stays below the stated
``alpha``. The combined test is the same as per-check thresholds ``q s_j``, which the reports list.

**Hardening** …
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.blu.doc1: Blue team: calibrated thresholds with a stated false-alarm rate, one combined test, and hardening.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.cas.doc:
Stored regression cases of the arena and their replay (``pinneapple check --arena-cases``).

A cases file holds the problem (name and options), the hardened defence (check names and thresholds) and every
escape and false alarm the red team found, each as a few numbers: the seed and variation of the correct case, and
the generator with its parameters. Replaying regenerates each case, runs the stored defence and requires every
escape to be rejected and every false alarm to pass. A file is JSON::

    {"format": "pinneapple-arena-cases/1", "problem": "darcy_2d", "options": {...},
     "defence": {"checks": [...], "thresholds": {...}, ...},
     "cases": [{"kind": "escape", "seed": 123, "variation": {}, "generator": "coefficient_field",
                "params": {...}, "true_error": 0.14, ...}, ...]}
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.cas.doc1: Stored regression cases of the arena and their replay (``pinneapple check --arena-cases``).

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.gen.doc:
Red-team generators: parametrised families of wrong-but-plausible outputs that the evasion search explores.

A generator maps a correct case and a parameter vector to ``(faulty_case, correct_field)``. Parameters are named,
with bounds; the search works on the unit box and ``Generator.params`` maps back. Families:

* ``mutant``: the mutation operators of the fault library combined (bias, scale, smoothing, noise), the model-side
  operators of mutation testing for deep learning (DeepCrime, Humbatova et al. 2021; MuFF, arXiv:2501.09846).
* ``smooth_modes``: a smooth distortion that keeps the boundary or initial condition exactly (Darcy: sine modes
  vanishing on the boundary; Burgers: periodic modes growing from zero at t = 0).
* physics-consistent attacks, outputs that solve a nearby problem exactly, so the PDE residual stays small:
  Darcy ``coefficient_field`` (a smooth change of log a) and ``source_field`` (a smooth change of f); Burgers
  ``viscosity`` (another nu), ``hard_ic_evolution`` (the exact initial condition at t = 0, then the evolution of a
  smoothed and rescaled one, what a hard-constrained PINN with spectral bias returns) and ``time_warp``
  (u(x, s t)).
* ``fault:<name>``: one fault of the fault library at a given magnitude (escapes found by the mutation score are
  stored with these).
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.gen.doc1: Red-team generators: parametrised families of wrong-but-plausible outputs that the evasion search explores.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.loo.doc:
The arena loop: rounds of red team then blue team, and the report.

``run_arena(problem, checks=None, budget=...)``:

* **Round 0 defence**: ``checks`` with their own tolerances (default: ``default_checks(problem)``, what users run
  today).
* **Red** (each round): the mutation score of the defence on the fault library (and the mutants that matter but
  pass), evasion searches with every generator on ``n_bases`` correct cases, and the false-alarm search over correct
  cases. Escapes (true relative error >= ``min_error`` and accepted) and false alarms (correct and rejected) are
  stored as regression cases.
* **Blue** (each round): split-conformal calibration of the combined test on clean calibration cases, hardened with
  checks from ``check_library(problem)`` until every stored escape is rejected; stored false alarms pass.
* **Evaluation** (each round): false-alarm rate on a held-out clean set, stored escapes rejected, stored false
  alarms accepted, mutation score after the round, and per check the detection rate, false-alarm rate, ROC AUC over
  fault magnitude and minimal detectable magnitude (from the fault-injection matrix).

Everything is seeded; ``ArenaReport.save_cases`` writes the regression cases replayed by
``pinneapple check --arena-cases``.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.loo.doc1: The arena loop: rounds of red team then blue team, and the report.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.red.doc:
Red team: search for escapes (wrong but passing) and false alarms (right but rejected) against a defence.

* ``evasion_search``: for one generator and one correct case, maximise the true error of the generated output
  (against the reference solver) while every check stays under its threshold. Objective (minimised on the unit box):
  ``-min(error, 2) + 10 * sum_j max(0, margin_j + 0.02)``, ``margin_j = value_j / threshold_j - 1``; the best
  point that the defence accepts is the escape, if its error is at least ``min_error`` (10 % by default).
* ``false_alarm_search``: over correct cases (the problem's ``variation_space``: coefficient contrast, feature size,
  amplitude, viscosity, solver resolution, for several random fields), maximise the largest margin of the defence:
  the most suspicious-looking correct case, a false alarm when its margin is positive.
* ``mutation_score``: the share of the fault library's mutants that matter (true error >= ``min_error``) which the
  defence rejects, from a fault-injection detection matrix; the mutants that pass are escapes too.

Every search is seeded; a finding carries what it needs to be regenerated (case seed and variation, generator and
parameters).

pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.sea.doc:
Black-box minimisers on the unit box for the red team: differential evolution (SciPy), CMA-ES and a
finite-difference L-BFGS-B (a gradient method for objectives that are smooth in the fault parameters).

CMA-ES is written from N. Hansen, "The CMA Evolution Strategy: A Tutorial" (arXiv:1604.00772, 2016): weighted
recombination, cumulative step-size adaptation, rank-one and rank-mu covariance updates with the default constants
of the tutorial's Table 1. Box constraints are handled by evaluating the projection of each sample onto the box.

Every minimiser takes an evaluation budget, a seed, and returns the best point and value and the number of
evaluations used; all are deterministic for a given seed.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.sea.doc1: Black-box minimisers on the unit box for the red team: differential evolution (SciPy), CMA-ES and a finite-difference L-BFGS-B (a gradient method for objectives that are smooth in the fault parameters).

pinneapple_analysis.validation.error_map.doc:
Where is a field wrong? Pointwise error of a prediction against a reference on the same points, the regions where
it concentrates, and a short text that compares them with the global number.

    from pinneapple_analysis.validation.error_map import error_map
    em = error_map(points, pred, ref, regions={"clamp": clamp_nodes, "tip": tip_nodes})
    em.error                # |pred - ref| per point (vectors: norm of the difference)
    em.hotspots             # clusters of the largest errors: centre, extent, max, share of the squared error
    em.regions              # per named region: share of the squared error against its share of the points
    em.summary()            # "Relative L2 error 3.9 % ... 41 % of the squared error is in clamp (10 % of the points)"

Every number comes from the arrays given: nothing is estimated or interpolated here (map the reference onto the
prediction's points first when the meshes differ). ``weights`` (cell volumes, nodal areas) make the shares integrals
instead of point counts.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_inj.doc:
Fault injection: measure how often each validation check catches known model and data defects (#697).

A "pass" from a check carries no stated power until the check has been run against defects of known size. This
package injects a library of controlled faults into correct cases of problems with a verified reference solver and
records every check's response::

    from pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection import run_fault_injection
    rep = run_fault_injection("darcy_2d", n_cases=50)
    print(rep.to_markdown())            # detection matrix, false alarms, minimal detectable magnitudes
    assert rep.passed                   # every fault caught at its documented magnitude, <= 1 % false alarms

Modules: :mod:`.problems` (Darcy 2-D and Burgers 1-D cases from ``operator_benchmarks``), :mod:`.checks` (the
checks under test, as ``physics_audit.monitor.ValidityCheck``), :mod:`.faults` (the fault library), :mod:`.matrix`
(the detection matrix and its report). The adversarial arena (:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena`) is
built on these.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_inj.doc1: Fault injection: measure how often each validation check catches known model and data defects (#697).

pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_inj.doc:
``python -m pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection``: regenerate the detection matrix (check power).

Writes ``check_power.md`` (the Markdown tables) and ``check_power.json`` per problem into ``--out``, prints the
acceptance verdict and exits 1 when a fault is not caught at its documented magnitude or a check exceeds 1 % false
alarms. ``--small`` is the CI size (a few cases, seconds per problem).

The checks under test, as ``physics_audit.monitor.ValidityCheck`` objects scoring a :class:`~.problems.Case`.

A check is ``fn(field, case) -> value`` with a tolerance; it flags a case when ``value > tolerance`` (or the value is
not finite). The values are continuous, so the same check can be thresholded by hand (the defaults here), calibrated
(:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena`) or attacked (an optimiser sees how close a case is to being flagged).

Building blocks reused, not reimplemented: the finite-difference provider and relative residual of
:mod:`pinneapple_check.numerics` (``GridD``, ``rel_rms``), the conservative Darcy operator of the verified solver
(``operator_benchmarks.darcy_operator``) and its Burgers integrator (``burgers_1d``), the spectral shells of
``validation.field_metrics``, the Darcy consistency and the duplicate and leakage detectors of the dataset audit
(``pinneapple_data.audit``), and the bounds and training-envelope checks of ``pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.monitor``.

Two check sets per problem:

* ``default_checks(problem)``: what a user would run today (a finite-difference PDE residual, boundary and bounds
  checks, the training envelope), with hand-set tolerances. This is round 0 of the arena.
* ``check_library(problem)``: every check available, including stronger ones (the conservative residual on the
  solver's own stencil, a one-step re-integration, conservation, spectral content, invariants). The blue team of
  the arena picks …

pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_inj.doc:
The fault library: controlled defects of a model's output or of a dataset, each with a magnitude.

A model fault turns a correct :class:`~.problems.Case` into what a defective model would return for the same
question, and gives the correct field it should be compared with (a fault that changes the inputs, such as
out-of-range use, changes the correct answer too). A data fault turns a correct :class:`~.problems.Dataset` into
what a defective datapipe would hand to training.

Model faults (#697): ``bias``, ``scale``, ``noise`` (high frequency), ``smoothing`` (spectral bias),
``wrong_boundary``, ``source_sign_flip``, ``out_of_range`` (a model used outside its input range), ``stale_model``
(trained on an older physics configuration, as in the rover zoo v1.0 case).

Data faults: ``coefficient_drift`` (a discretisation coefficient off by a constant factor, modelled on the Darcy2D
datapipe report NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036), ``duplicates`` and ``low_diversity`` (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035),
``leakage`` (test samples copied from training), ``unit_mixup`` (outputs in mm instead of m), ``swapped_channels``.

Each fault has a ladder of magnitudes and a ``documented`` magnitude: the one the detection matrix promises to catch
with at least one check (the acceptance test of #697).
pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_inj.doc1: The fault library: controlled defects of a model's output or of a dataset, each with a magnitude.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_inj.doc:
Benchmark problems with a verified reference solver, as sources of correct cases for the fault-injection suite.

A :class:`Case` is one input/output pair of an operator-learning problem: the inputs the model is given, the field it
returned on a fixed grid, and the parameters of the equation. The two problems wrap the verified solvers of
:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.operator_benchmarks` (checked in ``tests/test_operator_benchmarks.py``):

* :class:`DarcyProblem`: ``-div(a grad u) = f`` on the unit square, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, ``a`` a thresholded
  Gaussian random field (Li et al. 2021); the field is ``u`` at the ``n x n`` cell centres.
* :class:`BurgersProblem`: ``u_t + (u^2/2)_x = nu u_xx`` on the periodic interval [0, 1); the field is the space-time
  solution ``u(t_k, x_j)`` at ``n_t`` snapshots from 0 to ``t_end`` (what a space-time PINN or an autoregressive
  operator returns).

Every case is reproducible from its ``seed`` and its ``variation`` (the knobs of the false-alarm search: coefficient
contrast, feature size, amplitude, viscosity, solver resolution), so a stored regression case is a few numbers.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_inj.doc1: Benchmark problems with a verified reference solver, as sources of correct cases for the fault-injection suite.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.field_met.doc:
PDEBench-style error metrics for gridded fields (NumPy, no torch).

Given a prediction and a reference on the same regular grid, report the
error the way neural-operator / surrogate benchmarks do, so a PINNeAPPle
model can be compared with published PDEBench numbers:

``rmse``      root-mean-square error over space, averaged over the rest
``nrmse``     ``rmse / rms(target)`` per sample/channel/time, then averaged
``max_error`` worst absolute pointwise error
``crmse``     error of the spatial *mean* (conserved-quantity error)
``brmse``     RMSE restricted to the boundary faces of the box
``frmse``     RMSE split into low / mid / high radial-wavenumber bands
``vrmse``     RMSE / std(target) -- The Well's headline metric (variance-scaled)
``pearson``   spatial Pearson correlation between prediction and target

Definitions follow PDEBench (Takamoto et al., NeurIPS 2022 Datasets &
Benchmarks; code ``pdebench/models/metrics.py``, MIT), adapted:

- **Full spectrum.** PDEBench's 2-D/3-D Fourier metric accumulates only the
  ``i, j < n/2`` quadrant of the FFT (negative frequencies are skipped), so
  half (2-D) or three quarters (3-D) of the spectral error is ignored. Here
  every FFT coefficient is binned by its integer radial wavenumber
  ``floor(|m|)``, with ``m`` the signed mode index, so nothing is dropped and
  Parseval holds: the shell energies sum to ``rmse^2`` (tested).
- **Normalisation.** ``frmse`` is reported per shell in the same units as
  ``rmse`` …
pinneapple_analysis.validation.field_met.doc1: PDEBench-style error metrics for gridded fields (NumPy, no torch).

pinneapple_analysis.validation.gallery.doc:
The ending every example in ``examples/validation/`` shares (#705): the validation report of a good model, the
trust card, the outputs ``pinneapple check`` reads in CI, and one real failure the checks catch on a broken variant.

:func:`conclude` compares the two reports, requires the expected check to fail on the broken model and not on the
good one, writes ``report.json`` / ``trust_card.json`` / ``report.sarif`` / ``failure.json`` and returns a
:class:`GalleryResult`. The gallery test runs every example at smoke size and checks these results.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.gallery.doc1: The ending every example in ``examples/validation/`` shares (#705): the validation report of a good model, the trust card, the outputs ``pinneapple check`` reads in CI, and one real failure the checks catch on a broken variant.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorph.doc:
Metamorphic tests for surrogates: relations between inputs and outputs that physics guarantees whatever the true
answer is, so a model can be tested where no reference solution exists (NumPy only; any callable model).

A relation transforms a sampled input, runs the model on both, and measures how far the outputs are from what the
relation requires, relative to the output scale. The worst sample is kept as the counterexample.

Relations
---------
``Symmetry``
    ``f(T x) = S(x, f(x))``: reflect or rotate the input field or geometry, and the output transforms accordingly
    (``reflect_field``, ``rotate_field`` build ``T``/``S`` for gridded fields).
``Similarity``
    Dimensionless groups unchanged, so the dimensionless output is unchanged: ``g(T x, f(T x)) = g(x, f(x))`` (same
    Reynolds number at another size or speed, same Biot or Fourier number, Darcy with ``a`` and ``f`` scaled
    together).
``Invariance``
    A change that must not move the output at all (``f(T x) = f(x)``), e.g. the thermal resistance of a linear
    conduction-convection model under a change of power.
``Monotonicity``
    More of an input gives no less (or no more) of an output: more heat input, no lower peak temperature; more air
    speed, no higher thermal resistance; larger permeability, no larger pressure drop.
``Superposition``
    Linear problems (Darcy with a fixed coefficient, linear elasticity, heat conduction):
    ``f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)`` (with ``f(0)`` subtracted for affine maps) …
pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorph.doc1: Metamorphic tests for surrogates: relations between inputs and outputs that physics guarantees whatever the true answer is, so a model can be tested where no reference solution exists (NumPy only; any callable model).

pinneapple_analysis.validation.physics_l.doc:
Physics learning verification: has a model learned the physics, or only a low loss?

A low physics loss (the residual on the model's own collocation points) and a low held-out error (on the training
distribution) do not show that a model responds to causes as the physics does. This verifier tests the *learned
relations* themselves, independently of the training loss:

``intervention:*``
    Change one cause (power, source location, a conductivity, the cooling, a contact resistance the model was
    never given) and compare the model's response with the reference solver's response to the same change, at
    informative points and on the peak temperature: magnitude and sign. The expected responses are solved, not
    hand-written rules.
``residual``, ``interface_flux``, ``boundary:*``, ``energy_balance``
    The governing equation inside each layer, continuity of heat flux across each interface, the boundary
    conditions, and the global heat balance -- on the model's own field, at points chosen by the verifier.
``symmetry``, ``scaling``
    The mirror image of the source gives the mirror field; twice the power gives twice the temperature rise
    (linear conduction).
``neighbour_consistency``
    Inside a layer the field is harmonic, so its value equals the mean over a small circle around the point
    (mean-value property): a stencil-free consistency test between a point and its neighbours.
``sufficiency``
    For each informative point, does the model's *input* set contain …

pinneapple_analysis.validation.physics_l.doc:
Verification case for :mod:`.physics_learning`: a cross-section of a die, TIM and lid heated at the junction.

Steady conduction in ``(x, z)`` per unit depth (W/m, temperature rise above ambient):

* die (silicon, 100 um, ``k_die``), TIM (30 um, ``k_tim``), lid (copper, 500 um, ``k_lid``), ``L = 2 mm`` wide;
* a Gaussian line source of ``P`` W/m at the bottom of the die, centred at ``x_s`` (fraction of ``L``), width
  ``sigma`` (fraction of ``L``);
* Robin cooling ``h`` on the top of the lid, adiabatic sides and bottom;
* an optional contact resistance ``R_c`` (m^2 K / W) on the die/TIM interface.

The reference is the cell-centred finite-volume scheme of :mod:`pinneapple_condense.fv` on a fine grid (milliseconds
per solve), so every expected response of the verifier comes from solving the physics, not from a rule.

``theta`` is a dict over :data:`PARAMS`; :data:`TRAIN_BOX` is the domain the models under test were built for.
:func:`defective_models` builds the deliberately defective models of the report (low loss and low mean error, wrong
in one physical respect each) and :func:`good_models` the controls.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.pinn.doc:
PINN validation (#703): the residual at points never used in training, detectors for the known failure modes, the
exact-solution gate and a training-time monitor.

A PINN's training loss is measured on its own collocation points and mixes the residual with boundary and initial
terms, so a low loss says little about the solution. :func:`validate_pinn` evaluates a trained network on fresh points
and names what went wrong:

``pinn.residual``
    The PDE residual on a dense uniform grid, on fresh random points and on adaptive points (the neighbourhood of the
    largest residuals of a large random sample): RMS and maximum, normalised by the problem's residual scale; the map
    on the grid is in the evidence.
``pinn.trivial``
    Near-trivial solution: the spread and the gradient energy of the field against the exact solution's (or the
    problem's expected scale). A network that stopped near its initial, nearly constant state fails here.
``pinn.causality``
    Propagation failure in time (compare Wang, Sankaran & Perdikaris 2022, "Respecting causality is all you need"):
    the residual concentrated at late times, or -- with an exact solution -- an error that grows in time while the
    residual stays small (a solution of the PDE that did not come from the initial condition).
``pinn.boundary`` / ``pinn.initial``
    Boundary and initial conditions on fresh points, against the solution scale. When they fail while the residual
    passes, the condition was traded off against the …

pinneapple_analysis.validation.report_ar.doc:
The validation report as an artifact (#706): a versioned JSON schema, provenance hashes, the difference between two
reports (what a new model version lost), a section for a Hugging Face model card, a badge, and signatures.

``REPORT_SCHEMA``

pinneapple_analysis.validation.rollout.doc:
Rollout validation of autoregressive surrogates (#701): invariant drift, energy spectrum over the horizon,
divergence time ("trust horizon") and long-run statistics without a reference trajectory.

An autoregressive model can look accurate for a few steps and then drift, lose energy, blur or blow up. Given a
rollout ``pred`` of shape ``(T, ...)`` (time first, then any leading axes, then ``ndim`` spatial axes) and,
optionally, the reference trajectory ``ref`` from the same initial state:

``invariant_series`` / ``invariant_drift``
    Conserved or slowly varying quantities (mass, energy, enstrophy, momentum, or any callable) along the rollout:
    their drift rate (least-squares slope relative to the initial value) and, with a reference, the largest relative
    deviation from the reference's own series (decaying turbulence loses energy; the model must lose it at the same
    rate).
``spectral_drift``
    The high-wavenumber energy ratio (``validation.spectral``) at every horizon, against the reference at that time
    or against the training statistics (a reference spectrum). Spectral blurring is a falling ratio.
``divergence_time``
    The first horizon where the pointwise error, the spectral bias or an invariant deviation crosses its tolerance;
    the trust horizon is the earliest of them.
``long_run_statistics``
    For chaotic systems, where pointwise error is meaningless after a few Lyapunov times: the histogram of the field
    (Wasserstein-1 distance), the temporal …

pinneapple_analysis.validation.schema.doc:
The vocabulary of a validation report, in one place: statuses, credibility factors and levels, and the stable check
IDs used by ``pp.validate`` (``pinneapple_analysis.validation.validate``), the trust card and ``pinneapple check``.

Other modules map their own results onto these IDs; new checks add an entry here (the report refuses unknown IDs).

Statuses
    ``pass``, ``warn``, ``fail``, ``not-applicable``. A check that cannot apply (no reference, no PDE stated, a
    tabular model asked for a spectrum) is reported as ``not-applicable`` with the reason, never silently skipped.

Credibility factors
    Modelled on NASA-STD-7009A (credibility assessment) and ASME V&V 40 (credibility factors): the evidence for a
    model is grouped by what it supports. The levels are this library's own reading of those standards, not a
    certification under them.

Credibility levels (per factor)
    0 no evidence (every check not applicable), 1 evidence contradicts the model (a critical check failed), 2 passes
    with warnings (a non-critical check failed or warned) or only qualitative evidence, 3 passes quantitative checks,
    4 passes against an independent reference or a guaranteed bound.
pinneapple_analysis.validation.schema.doc1: The vocabulary of a validation report, in one place: statuses, credibility factors and levels, and the stable check IDs used by ``pp.validate`` (``pinneapple_analysis.validation.validate``), the trust card and ``pinneapple check``.

pinneapple_analysis.validation.spectral.doc:
Spectral fidelity of a predicted field: energy spectra, high-wavenumber bias, phase error, coherence, structure
functions and gradient-based errors (NumPy only, no torch).

Relative L2 error rewards smooth predictions: a blurred field can have a small L2 error and still miss the small
scales that carry heat transfer, mixing or loads. The metrics here measure what L2 hides.

``energy_spectrum``
    Radially binned spectrum ``E(k)`` of a field on a regular grid, integer shells ``k = rint(|m|)`` (``m`` the signed
    mode index), shell-summed so that ``sum_k E(k) = mean(u^2)`` (Parseval). Leading axes (samples, time, channels)
    are averaged. Non-periodic fields are mean-removed and multiplied by a Hann window normalised to unit mean square,
    so the windowed spectrum keeps the field's energy on average.
``spectral_comparison``
    Prediction against reference per shell and per band: energy ratio, phase error and coherence. The **high-wavenumber
    bias** is ``E_pred / E_ref - 1`` summed over the high band: about ``-1`` for a field with its small scales smoothed
    away, ``0`` for the reference against itself, positive for added noise. Bands are fractions of the *resolved*
    range: the shells where the reference has energy above ``floor * max(E_ref)``, so a dealiased reference (exact
    zeros above ``n / 3``) does not divide by zero.
``structure_functions``
    ``S_p(r) = <|u(x + r) - u(x)|^p>`` along each grid axis (averaged over the axes), the signed third-order …

pinneapple_analysis.validation.validate.doc:
``pp.validate``: one call, one validation report for a Physics AI model (#696).

``validate(model, problem, data=None, reference=None, level="standard", query=None)`` picks the checks that apply to
the model and the problem from the existing modules, runs them, and returns a :class:`ValidationReport`: per-check
evidence and a pass / warn / fail status, a credibility level per factor (``schema.FACTORS``) and a deploy decision.
A check that cannot apply is reported as not applicable with the reason.

Models: a zoo model (``pp.zoo.load(...)`` or its name), a ``torch.nn.Module`` (PyTorch, PhysicsNeMo), an ONNX file
(``.onnx``, run with onnxruntime) or any callable. Problems: a zoo model's own card (``problem=None``), ``"darcy_2d"``
(or ``{"pde": "darcy", "f": 1.0}``: field operators ``a -> u`` on the cell-centred grid of
``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d``), or a small spec ``{"valid_range": {...}, "relations": [...]}`` for a tabular
callable.

``quick``          applicability (validity range, training envelope), solution verification (guaranteed residual
                   bound, flux balance), reference error, the zoo gate, the method's catalog status

pinneapple_analysis.verification.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.verification -- Physics verification building blocks.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``physics_verification_engine`` product
(``core/*.py``) so any code can import it; the HTTP service over these
modules is ``apps/verified_physics``.

Sub-modules
-----------
dimensional_analysis
    Real, first-principles dimensionless-number calculations (Reynolds,
    Prandtl, Peclet, Mach, Froude, Weber, Damkohler, a Nusselt
    correlation when its validity range is satisfied) plus a
    geometry-aware flow-regime classifier.

mesh_intelligence
    Mesh-quality assessment: per-triangle aspect ratio / equiangular
    skewness (real, computed from the mesh's own geometry), an
    explicitly-labeled y+-driven required-first-cell-height ESTIMATE,
    and a structured ``MeshQualityReport`` of what failed and why.

causal_discrepancy
    Two independent tools: ``run_intervention``, a causal/intervention
    engine ("what happens if I change parameter X?") that retrains and
    re-verifies real runs and reports real percentage changes; and
    ``fit_discrepancy_model``, a Kennedy & O'Hagan (2001) model-form
    discrepancy correction (``y(x) = physics_model(x) + delta(x)``) fit
    by ordinary MSE regression on a held-out split.

knowledge_graph
    A real Physics Knowledge Graph (Phenomenon -> Equation ->
    Parameters -> Preset -> Reference -> VerificationMethod), rebuilt
    at call time from PINNeAPPle's own live preset registry and
    AST-scanned validation test …

pinneapple_analysis.verification.archite.doc:
Adversarial review of a proposed Physics-AI architecture/pipeline
design -- "assume the role of a Principal Engineer trying to prove this
architecture is wrong" as a structured, checked-menu LLM tool, not free-
form commentary.

Why a fixed checklist instead of an open-ended "critique this" prompt:
the whole point of an adversarial review is to catch failure modes the
architecture's OWN author didn't think to ask about -- an open-ended
prompt tends to just restate whatever the author already emphasized. This
module forces the LLM to produce a verdict for EVERY category in
``FAILURE_MODE_CHECKLIST`` (data leakage, shortcut learning, dimensional
inconsistency, identifiability, extrapolation failure, unstable training,
bad benchmark design, misleading metrics, malformed physics constraints,
excessive simulator/solver dependency, deployment risk) -- the same
"checked menu, reject anything outside it, reject an incomplete response"
anti-hallucination pattern already used throughout this codebase
(``pinneapple_llm.cad_draft``/``geometry_draft``, and this package's own
``geometry_intelligence._llm_assign_semantics``).

This is explicitly a STRUCTURED PROMPT for a general-purpose LLM, not a
new trained classifier -- it does not (and cannot) guarantee the LLM's
critique is correct; it guarantees the critique's SHAPE is complete and
checkable (every category addressed, every verdict/severity value drawn
from a fixed vocabulary, an invented category name or verdict outside
that …

Which PINNeAPPle neural architecture to reach for FIRST, given a
