solver can generate more, whether the model needs to generalize across
parameters/geometry, and whether the target is a forward or inverse

pinneapple_analysis.verification.causal_.doc:
Two roadmap points from the product README's honest 21-point scope table:

Point 15 -- Causal / intervention engine
-----------------------------------------
"What happens if I increase pressure 20%?" -- ``run_intervention`` re-runs
the ``pipeline.analyze`` pipeline once as a baseline, then
once per requested parameter value with that one parameter overridden in
the drafted preset's kwargs, and reports REAL percentage changes (final
training loss, the guardrail's re-computed PDE residual, and the trained
model's own prediction at a fixed query point for every field the preset
produces) -- never a fabricated number, and never a percentage change
presented as reliable when the guardrail marked that run (or the
baseline itself) NOT TRUSTWORTHY.

``draft_problem`` is only ever invoked once (inside the single baseline
:func:`pinneapple_analysis.verification.pipeline.analyze` call); every
perturbed run below repeats just the execution + verification steps
(``pinneapple_physics.get_preset``/``solve_pde`` and
``pinneapple_llm.PhysicsGuardrail``) with one kwarg overridden.

Cost note / future optimization (not built here): every intervention
value in this module currently retrains a PINN from scratch. A real
deployment would want to cache/reuse the baseline-trained model as a
warm start (or freeze/fine-tune) when the architecture and epoch budget
are unchanged between the baseline and the perturbed run, rather than
paying the full training cost per intervention value. Kept out of …

Grid-convergence / mesh-independence study automation.

Public API
----------
    richardson_extrapolate(
        f_coarse, f_medium, f_fine, r, *,
        p_assumed=None, safety_factor=1.25, asymptotic_tolerance=0.10,
    ) -> ConvergenceResult

    mesh_independence_study(
        solve_fn, resolutions, quantity_extractor, *,
        refinement_ratio=None, p_assumed=None, safety_factor=1.25,
        asymptotic_tolerance=0.10,
    ) -> MeshIndependenceStudyResult

This closes the gap flagged in the capability audit: PINNeAPPle has a real
mesh-*quality* module (``mesh_intelligence.py``, geometric aspect
ratio/skewness/y+ estimates from a single mesh) and real numerical solvers
with configurable resolution (``pinneapple_simulation/numerical_solvers/
fdm.py``, ``fem.py``, ``lbm.py``, etc.), but nothing that runs a solver at
several systematically-refined resolutions and asks the orthogonal
question "is the SOLUTION converging as resolution increases, and can we
estimate the discretization error and the resolution-independent 'exact'
answer from that trend?" -- i.e. mesh-*independence*, not mesh-*quality*.

This module is deliberately solver-agnostic: it never imports anything
from ``pinneapple_simulation`` and knows nothing about FDM/FEM/LBM
specifics. ``mesh_independence_study`` takes an arbitrary ``solve_fn(resolution)``
callable and an arbitrary ``quantity_extractor(solution)`` callable, so any
solver that can be re-run at different resolutions (or any external
tool wrapped …

Real, first-principles dimensionless-number calculations + a simple,
honestly-scoped flow-regime classifier.

This is genuinely new (not previously in PINNeAPPle) and is the concrete
implementation of the user's own architectural point 3
("Dimensional analysis / scaling... o sistema deveria automaticamente
calcular e raciocinar sobre Reynolds, Prandtl, Peclet, Mach, Nusselt,
Damkohler, Fourier, Weber, Froude"). Every formula below is a standard,
textbook dimensionless group -- cited in each function's docstring --
computed directly from the physical parameters the caller supplies, not
guessed or LLM-generated. This is the layer that lets the engine
"reason automatically" about which physical regime a problem is in
*before* deciding which PDE closure/solver family is appropriate, e.g.
Stokes flow (Re << 1) needs no turbulence closure at all, while Re >
4000 in a pipe needs one.

Regime classification is DELIBERATELY simple and honestly caveated: real
transition thresholds depend on geometry (external flow past a sphere
transitions at different Re than internal pipe flow), so
``classify_flow_regime`` documents exactly which geometry its thresholds
assume, rather than presenting one universal answer as if it always
applies. This is the same "state precisely what was and wasn't checked"
ethic as the rest of this codebase.

pinneapple_analysis.verification.forecas.doc:
Forecast skill against a reference forecast, with confidence intervals that respect serial correlation.

Forecasts verified from many start times along one or a few trajectories are not independent: two starts 20 time
units apart share most of their future. The intervals here come from a **moving-block bootstrap** over the start
times (Kuensch 1989), with blocks about as long as the correlation time of the errors.

    from pinneapple_analysis.verification.forecast_skill import skill_vs_lead
    res = skill_vs_lead(err_model, err_persistence, leads, block=10)   # errors: (starts, leads)
    res.horizon                     # last lead up to which the model is better with 95 % confidence
    res.skill_score[:, 0]           # 1 - E_model / E_ref per lead (lo / hi in columns 1, 2)

Statistics of time series from a simulation (time means and their intervals) use **batch means**
(:func:`batch_means_ci`), the usual estimator for correlated samples in turbulence statistics.

``GeometryOODGuardrail`` -- flags when an input geometry is
out-of-distribution (OOD) relative to the geometries a model/preset was
actually designed and validated against.

Why this module exists
-----------------------
PINNeAPPle's verification/trust stack (``pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_gate
.TrustGate``, ``pinneapple_analysis.verification.physics_confidence_score``,
``pinneapple_analysis.verification.evidence_graph``) already scores several
independent trust signals for a prediction: coordinate-space OOD
(``TrustGate``'s own Mahalanobis-distance check on *where in the domain* a
query point sits), PDE-residual re-evaluation, ensemble variance, guardrail
checks, numerical convergence, UQ calibration, and benchmark agreement. None
of these ask a different, equally important question: **is the input
geometry itself the kind of shape this model/preset was ever trained or
validated on?** ``pinneapple_analysis.verification.geometry_intelligence``
sounds adjacent but solves a different problem entirely -- semantic
region/BC classification of a mesh's surfaces, not "is this whole shape
anomalous". This module closes that specific, real gap.

ported)

pinneapple_analysis.verification.nozzle_.doc:
Rocket nozzle screening by two methods that do not share code: a PINN and the ideal 1-D isentropic nozzle.

:func:`screen_nozzle` runs, on the same inputs,

1. :func:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.rocket_nozzle.nozzle_performance` (exit Mach, pressure, temperature,
   C_F, Isp of an ideal nozzle), and
2. a PINN on the ``rocket_nozzle_cfd`` preset (axisymmetric compressible Euler), trained with
   :func:`pinneapple_physics.solve_pde` on the preset's own tagged geometry
   (:func:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets.tag_geometry.build_tag_batch`: the divergent cone from the
   throat to the exit, no invented chamber), re-checked by :class:`pinneapple_llm.PhysicsGuardrail`, and read
   at the exit plane (section average over the radius),

then reports the relative difference of exit Mach number and exit pressure and whether the two agree within a
tolerance. Disagreement is the expected outcome today, not a failure of this function: the preset's residual is
in raw SI units (pressure ~1e6 Pa next to velocity ~1e3 m/s; the source app measured residuals of 1e22-1e26
against the guardrail's 1e-2 threshold and 73-4764 % disagreement), its wall condition is no-slip on inviscid
equations, and its domain box extends past the cone. The network output is rescaled per field
(:func:`scaled_field_head`) so each field starts at its physical magnitude; that changes units, not physics, and
does not make a short run converge.

``PhysicsConfidenceScore``: a transparent, componentized aggregate score
built ONLY from real, already-executed checks -- never a black-box number.

Why this module exists, and why it is not a contradiction of this repo's
anti-fabrication design
------------------------------------------------------------------------
This repo has an explicit, deliberate anti-hallucination principle, stated
outright in ``saas/physics_verification_engine/core/uncertainty_inverse.py``
(now living at ``pinneapple_analysis/verification/``, alongside this
module): :class:`~saas.physics_verification_engine.core.uncertainty_inverse.UncertaintyReport`
is documented as "a structured UQ report distinguishing uncertainty
*types*, not a single opaque confidence score", and
``quantify_uncertainty``'s own docstring says its numbers come from real
PINNeAPPle UQ classes "-- never a fabricated confidence number." A prior
capability audit flagged "no aggregate physics confidence score exists" as
a **deliberate** choice, not a gap, for exactly that reason: collapsing
several independent, differently-scoped signals into one opaque number
invites exactly the false confidence this repo's whole verification stack
(``PhysicsGuardrail``, Richardson/GCI convergence, calibration metrics,
benchmark comparison) exists to prevent.

This module honors that principle rather than overriding it. It is a
**transparent aggregator over real checks a caller already ran** -- never
a check-running black box, and never a source of …

pinneapple_analysis.verification.pipelin.doc:
Problem description -> dimensional analysis -> LLM-drafted preset -> PINN training -> guardrail -> selection.

``analyze(description, ...)`` runs one natural-language physics problem through the library calls that already
exist, in order:

1. :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.dimensional_analysis.compute_dimensionless_numbers` and
   :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.dimensional_analysis.classify_flow_regime` on the caller's physical
   parameters (context for the record; they do not choose the preset);
2. :func:`pinneapple_llm.draft_problem` picks a registered preset and its kwargs (an unknown preset or kwarg name
   is rejected by that function, not trusted);
3. :func:`pinneapple_physics.get_preset` + :func:`pinneapple_physics.solve_pde` train one PINN per candidate
   architecture;
4. :class:`pinneapple_llm.PhysicsGuardrail` re-evaluates each trained model on fresh points;
5. :func:`rank_key` picks the winner: a trustworthy candidate beats any untrustworthy one, then the smaller
   re-computed PDE residual wins, and only then the training loss;
6. a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.provenance.ProvenanceRecord` records the run.

What this does not check: whether the drafted preset is the right one for the description. The guardrail
re-checks the physics of the preset that was chosen, not the choice (a heat-conduction request drafted as Burgers
can come back trustworthy). Read ``provenance.drafted_preset`` and ``provenance.draft_reasoning``.

pinneapple_app.backend.core.physics_adap.doc:
Physics adapters: turn a ``ProblemDefinition`` into a trainable physics loss.

The experiment runner used to call ``compile_problem``'s loss with the wrong
arguments (``physics_fn(model, x_col, {})``), which raised inside a bare
``try/except`` every epoch -- so no physics loss was ever applied -- and it
replaced every boundary condition with ``u = 0``. Custom problems got a
``(pred ** 2).mean() * 0.0`` placeholder. This module is the replacement:

* :class:`PresetPhysics` builds the batch ``compile_problem`` actually expects
  (``x_col``, ``x_bc``/``n_bc``/``x_ic`` and one ``mask_<condition>`` per
  condition), with boundary/initial points placed exactly on the faces of the
  preset's box domain so the presets' own selectors and value functions apply.
* :class:`CustomPhysics` compiles user equations such as ``"u_xx + u_yy"``
  through :class:`pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.SymbolicPDE` and enforces
  Dirichlet/Neumann boundary and initial conditions.

Anything that cannot be applied (e.g. a ``"tag"`` condition naming real
geometry such as ``"fin_surfaces"``) is listed in ``unresolved`` instead of
being silently dropped, so the report can flag it.

pinneapple_app.backend.core.surrogate_re.doc:
Surrogate quality report: the "can I trust this model?" section of a run.

Every section is computed from held-out data or from points the model never
trained on, and every number states what it was measured against:

* ``error``          -- relative/absolute error vs the reference solution on a
                        held-out test split (never on training points).
* ``convergence``    -- did the loss actually settle, diverge or stall.
* ``generalization`` -- train vs held-out error, and training vs unseen-point
                        PDE residual.
* ``variables``      -- inputs, outputs, predicted ranges vs expected ranges,
                        and input sensitivity.
* ``weights``        -- loss-term weights, each term's share of the final
                        loss, and network parameter health.
* ``uncertainty``    -- snapshot-ensemble spread and, when reference data
                        exists, split-conformal intervals with measured
                        coverage.
* ``physics_checks`` -- governing-equation residual, boundary/initial
                        conditions, mass conservation, energy balance and
                        physical bounds, each with pass/warn/fail.

A check that cannot be computed says so (``status="n/a"`` with a reason); it
is never reported as passing.

pinneapple_arena.doc:
pinneapple_arena — YAML/JSON-driven multi-model physics benchmark runner.

Features
--------
  * ALL pinneapple_neural models via ModelRegistry.build() (~80+ architectures)
  * pinneapple_physics compiled losses (when physics_preset is set)
  * pinneapple_data datasets (DatasetConfig)
  * pinneapple_analysis inverse problems (InverseConfig.enabled=True)
  * pinneapple_analysis UQ (UQConfig.enabled=True)

Quick start
-----------
    from pinneapple_arena import Arena

    arena = Arena.from_yaml("my_benchmark.yaml")
    arena.run()

    # programmatic:
    from pinneapple_arena import ArenaConfig
    cfg = ArenaConfig.from_dict({
        "problem": {"name": "kovasznay_ns", "params": {"re": 40.0}},
        "models": [
            {"name": "VanillaPINN", "type": "vanilla_pinn",
             "network": {"hidden": [128, 128, 128, 128]},
             "training": {"epochs": 2000, "lr": 5e-4}},
            {"name": "FNO-2D", "type": "fno2d",
             "training": {"epochs": 600, "lr": 1e-3}},
            {"name": "MeshGraphNet", "type": "meshgraphnet",
             "training": {"epochs": 600, "lr": 1e-3}},
        ],
        "output": {"dir": "outputs/", "prefix": "benchmark"},
    })
    Arena(cfg).run()

pinneapple_arena.autoresearch.doc:
Autoresearch mode: an automated experiment loop over a single training script.

Pattern from karpathy/autoresearch (MIT, ``ROADMAP.md`` §11): a fixed-time-budget training script,
one metric, and a proposer that edits the script between runs; changes that improve the metric are
kept, the others reverted, and every trial is logged. Here, adapted to physics AI:

- ``program.md`` holds the research instructions and the physics context for the proposer.
- ``train.py`` is the only file that changes. It must print ``METRIC <name>=<value>`` (lower is
  better, e.g. relative L2 against a closed form) and respect ``PINNEAPPLE_TIME_BUDGET`` seconds.
- Edits are limited to the ``# >>> TUNABLE`` ... ``# <<< TUNABLE`` block (``NAME = value`` lines),
  which keeps each proposal small, reviewable and safe to apply automatically.
- Proposers: :class:`RandomSearchProposer` (no LLM, reproducible) and :class:`LLMProposer`
  (any provider of ``pinneapple_llm``, or your own ``llm_call(prompt, system=...) -> str``).

Every trial goes to ``results.tsv``; the best script so far is kept as ``best_train.py``.

    from pinneapple_arena.autoresearch import AutoResearch, RandomSearchProposer, init_workdir
    init_workdir("runs/poisson")  # program.md + train.py (1D Poisson PINN, rel-L2 vs sin(pi x))
    AutoResearch("runs/poisson", RandomSearchProposer({"LR": [1e-3, 3e-3, 1e-2], "WIDTH": [16, 32, 64]}),
                 budget_s=60).run(max_trials=20)

pinneapple_arena.config.doc:
ArenaConfig — structured configuration for PINNeAPPle Arena benchmarks.

Supports loading from YAML, JSON, or direct Python construction.

Example YAML
------------
problem:
  name: kovasznay_ns
  physics_preset: ns_incompressible_2d_default   # optional: use pinneapple_physics preset
  params:
    re: 40.0
  grid_n: 40
  n_col: 2000
  n_bc: 500

models:
  - name: VanillaPINN
    type: vanilla_pinn
    network:
      hidden: [128, 128, 128, 128]
      activation: tanh
    training:
      epochs: 2000
      lr: 5.0e-4
      grad_clip: 1.0

  - name: FNO-2D
    type: fno2d
    network:
      width: 32
      modes: 12
      layers: 4
    training:
      epochs: 600
      lr: 1.0e-3

  - name: MeshGraphNet
    type: meshgraphnet
    network:
      hidden_dim: 128
      n_message_passing: 6
    training:
      epochs: 600
      lr: 1.0e-3

# Optional: load a pinneapple_data dataset instead of a built-in problem
# dataset:
#   dataset_id: navier_stokes_2d
#   input_fields: [x, y]
#   output_fields: [u, v, p]
#   n_train: 1000

# Optional: inverse problem mode
# inverse:

#   params: [re]

#   noise_std: 0.01

#   n_iters: 2000

#   enabled: true
#   budget: 2                 # at most 2 models are trained
#   thresholds: {rel_l2: 0.05, residual: 1.0e-3}
#   evidence_path: outputs/decision_evidence.json

# Optional: …

pinneapple_arena.custom_builder.doc:
High-level API for defining custom physics problems.

The user provides:
  - equation name and description
  - coordinate names and bounds
  - field names (unknowns)
  - PDE as a string (e.g. ``"eps * u_xx - k * u + f"``)
  - boundary/initial conditions as simple dicts
  - optional analytical solution for metrics

Everything else (loss generation, data sampling, Arena pipeline) is automatic.

Derivative notation in PDE strings
-----------------------------------
``u_x``  → ∂u/∂x       ``u_xx`` → ∂²u/∂x²
``u_t``  → ∂u/∂t       ``v_xy`` → ∂²v/∂x∂y
``p_yy`` → ∂²p/∂y²     etc.

All coordinate names and param names are available in the expression.
Math functions available: ``sin``, ``cos``, ``exp``, ``sqrt``, ``tanh``, ``log``,
``abs``, ``pi``, ``e``.

Examples
--------
1-D reaction-diffusion::

    from pinneapple_arena import define_problem
    import numpy as np

    prob = define_problem(
        name="reaction_diffusion",
        description="eps·u'' − k·u = f  on [0,1],  u(0)=u(1)=0",
        coords={"x": (0.0, 1.0)},
        fields=["u"],
        pde="eps * u_xx - k * u + (eps * pi**2 + k) * sin(pi * x)",
        bcs=[
            {"type": "dirichlet", "at": "x_min", "field": "u", "value": 0.0},
            {"type": "dirichlet", "at": "x_max", "field": "u", "value": 0.0},
        ],
        params={"eps": 0.1, "k": 1.0},
        analytical=lambda x, eps=0.1, k=1.0: {"u": np.sin(np.pi * x)},
    )
    prob.solve(models=["VanillaPINN", "SIREN"], epochs=3000)

pinneapple_arena.dataset_bench.doc:
dataset_bench.py -- High-level benchmark API using pinneapple_data datasets.

Every dataset registered in ``pinneapple_data`` has a recommended preset here
(input/output fields, model list, training config, mode).  The public surface
is intentionally minimal:

  * :data:`DATASET_PRESETS`        -- full preset table, keyed by dataset_id
  * :func:`benchmark_dataset`      -- one-liner: load preset, build Arena, run
  * :func:`list_benchmarks`        -- show available presets (with category filter)
  * :func:`get_benchmark_preset`   -- retrieve a preset dict for inspection

Usage
-----
::

    from pinneapple_arena.dataset_bench import benchmark_dataset

    # Simplest usage -- all defaults from preset
    benchmark_dataset("burgers_1d", output_dir="outputs/burgers/")

    # Override epochs and model list
    benchmark_dataset(
        "kovasznay_ns",
        models=["VanillaPINN", "SIREN"],
        epochs=3000,
        mode="pinn_data",
        output_dir="outputs/kovasznay/",
    )

    # Regression dataset
    benchmark_dataset("airfoil_noise", output_dir="outputs/airfoil/")

    # List everything available
    from pinneapple_arena.dataset_bench import list_benchmarks
    list_benchmarks()
    list_benchmarks(category="pde")

pinneapple_arena.dataset_problems.doc:
DatasetProblem — ArenaProblem backed by a real pinneapple_data dataset.

Converts any dataset registered in ``pinneapple_data`` into a first-class
Arena problem, handling:

  * **PDE datasets** (burgers_1d, heat_1d, kovasznay_ns …)
    Structured spatial/temporal grids are properly flattened into
    ``(N, in_dim)`` training arrays without losing coordinate alignment.

  * **Timeseries datasets** (lorenz63, spring_mass, van_der_pol …)
    Direct time→state regression, or sliding-window sequences.

  * **Regression datasets** (airfoil_noise, concrete_strength …)
    Standard feature-matrix → target, no spatial structure assumed.

  * **Geometry datasets** (naca0012, cylinder_2d …)
    Interior/boundary point arrays surfaced as collocation data.

  * **Physics-hybrid mode**  (``mode="pinn_data"``)
    Combines a supervised data loss (from the dataset) with an autograd
    physics residual for any dataset that maps to a known PDE type.

Usage
-----
::

    from pinneapple_arena.dataset_problems import DatasetProblem

    prob = DatasetProblem.from_dataset(
        "burgers_1d",
        input_fields=["x", "t"],
        output_fields=["u"],
        mode="supervised",       # or "pinn_data" for PINN hybrid
        Nx=256, Nt=101,          # kwargs forwarded to load_dataset()
    )
    # prob is a fully registered ArenaProblem — use it in any Arena config
    Arena(ArenaConfig.from_dict({
        "problem": {"name": prob.name},
        "models": [...],
    })).run()

pinneapple_arena.decision_mode.doc:
Arena as a decision laboratory: the decision engine picks which models to train.

Default Arena mode trains every configured model and ranks them. Decision mode
(``Arena.run_decision(budget=...)`` or ``decision: {enabled: true}`` in the
config) instead runs the ``pinneapple_decision`` loop over the configured
models::

    DECIDE   which configured model to train next  (PhysicsChoice "arena_model";
             options = model names; constraints: geometry support, budget,
             not already trained in this session)
    EXECUTE  Arena._train_one + Arena._evaluate_one  (ArenaExecutor)
    VALIDATE ThresholdVerifier on rel_l2 (mean relative L2 over fields) and, for
             PINN-family models, residual (final PDE residual); any Verifier works
    LEARN    EvidenceStore; the next decision reads the verification tags and
             penalizes the family of a model that failed

and stops when a result passes verification (``stop_when_passed``) or after
``budget`` trained models. Models that were never chosen are not trained.

The engine decides *which experiment to run*; the metrics come from the Arena's
own training and evaluation against the problem's reference data. A metric the
Arena did not produce (e.g. ``residual`` for a supervised model) is a check that
did not run, not a pass.

pinneapple_arena.external.doc:
External model catalog: references to third-party physics-ML libraries and the glue that runs them.

Every entry (`ModelSpec`) is a reference: name, organisation, repository URL, licence (with where it was read),
citation and install instructions. No third-party code is copied here: each runner in
``pinneapple_arena.external.runners`` imports the real library at run time, builds a minimal instance, runs one
forward pass or simulation on a small synthetic input (``demo_datasets``) and reports a ``ModelResult`` whose
``status`` says what really happened:

========================== ===============================================================================
``ok``                     the library was imported and a real call ran; the output is genuine
``not_installed``          pip-installable, not installed here (the result carries the pip command)
``skipped_heavy``          GPU / heavy dependency, run only with ``include_heavy=True``
``manual_install``         no pip package (git-only, Julia, C++); the result carries the clone/build steps
``failed``                 it ran and raised; the exception is in ``error``
``finetune_not_supported`` no fine-tune / reconfigure routine for this library
========================== ===============================================================================

A result is never invented. Datasets (The Well) have their own catalog (``DATASETS``) and a ``probe`` action that
loads one real sample through the dataset's own loader.

pinneapple_arena.external.__main__.doc:
Command line for the external model catalog (``python -m pinneapple_arena.external``).

This is what the
external-catalog API points you at when it can't run a model itself in this
process (heavy GPU dependency, or a git-only research repo) — install the
dependency yourself, then run the same demo the "Run inference" / "Fine-tune"
actions would run, from your own machine.

Usage
-----
    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --list
    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --list --category pinn
    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --list --domain fluids

    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --model deepxde --action infer
    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --model deepxde --action finetune --epochs 300 --lr 0.001
    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --model mace --action infer --include-heavy

    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --category pinn --action infer --json report.json
    python -m pinneapple_arena.external --action infer --json report.json --csv report.csv   # whole catalog

pinneapple_arena.external.finetune.doc:
Fine-tuning / retraining runners — one per pip-installable model in the
catalog (light or heavy; manual-install-only repos have nothing to run
in-app regardless, same as for inference).

Three different things happen under one "fine-tune" action in the UI,
distinguished by `ModelResult.metrics["mode"]`:

  - "finetune"    — a real, short (CPU, seconds) gradient-based training or
                    variational-optimization loop on the model's own
                    learnable parameters.
  - "reconfigure" — the model has no learnable weights (it's a physics
                    solver/engine, not a trained network) or the weights
                    require a real dataset+checkpoint this demo can't
                    provide, so "retraining" means re-running the same
                    solver with user-supplied parameters instead, or (for
                    checkpoint-only frameworks) re-confirming a real import
                    with an honest note about what a full fine-tune needs.
                    Either way it's a genuine run, just not gradient descent
                    on a loss.

Every model without a pip package (git-only repos, non-Python tools) has no
entry here — `run_finetune()` falls back to the same manual-install status
inference already reports for them, since nothing changes about whether the
app can execute their code.

pinneapple_arena.nas.doc:
Architecture + hyperparameter search over the existing model catalog.

**What this is**: a *search-based* joint selection of (architecture family,
architecture hyperparameters, learning rate) over a fixed, already-registered
catalog (``pinneapple_neural.architectures.ModelRegistry``), driven by the
same Optuna TPE-sampler-with-median-pruner / random-search-fallback
machinery that ``pinneapple_neural.trainer.adaptive_sweep`` already uses.
Each Optuna "trial" both picks an architecture *and* samples that
architecture's hyperparameters (architecture choice is treated as just
another categorical hyperparameter — a flat search space, exactly the shape
``AdaptiveSweepConfig.param_space`` already expects), builds it via
``ModelRegistry.build()``, trains it for a small number of epochs on a real
``ArenaProblem`` via the real ``pinneapple_arena.trainer.train_pinn`` path,
and scores it from the real evaluation metrics (+ optionally the real
``TrainResult.physics_residual``).

**What this is not**: this is *not* a differentiable / weight-sharing NAS
(no DARTS-style supernet, no shared weights across candidates, no gradient
w.r.t. architecture choice). Every trial trains an independent model from
scratch. That is a deliberate scope decision — a true weight-sharing NAS
would be a much larger undertaking than the existing infrastructure (a
fixed architecture catalog + a black-box Optuna sweep) naturally supports,
and "search over the catalog + its hyperparameters" is what is …

pinneapple_arena.pointwise.doc:
Pointwise field benchmarks: the problems, reference data, losses, model adapters and training protocol of the
PINNeAPPle Arena app (``apps/pinn_arena``).

An arena problem is a field regression on coordinates: ``(N, in_dim)`` points in, ``(N, out_dim)`` field values
out. For each of the 34 catalog problems (``PROBLEMS_CATALOG``) a reference dataset comes from an analytic or
numerical solution (``DatasetGenerator``), the PDE residual from a PINNeAPPle preset or a native autograd residual
(``PhysicsLossGenerator``), and any registry architecture (``ARCHITECTURES_CATALOG``) is built through
``pp.build_model`` and, if it expects grids or sequences, wrapped so each point is its own sample (``adapters``).
``training`` trains one architecture under the arena protocol (data loss + warmed-up, magnitude-balanced PDE
residual on separate collocation points, cosine LR, early stopping on a validation split, best weights restored)
and scores it on a held-out split; ``leaderboard.aggregate`` ranks architectures over many experiments.

    from pinneapple_arena import pointwise as pw

    gen = pw.DatasetGenerator("burgers_1d", {})
    ref = gen.generate(n_samples=2000)                     # coords (N, 2) = (x, t), solution (N, 1)
    loss_fn = pw.PhysicsLossGenerator("burgers_1d", {}).compile_losses()
    model = pw.instantiate_model("vanilla_pinn", 2, 1)     # ArchitectureUnavailable if the registry can not build it

This differs from ``pinneapple_arena.Arena`` (YAML-driven runs of …

pinneapple_arena.pointwise.adapters.doc:
Input adapters between the arena's pointwise data and PINNeAPPle architectures.

Every arena problem is pointwise field regression: a batch of coordinates
X of shape (N, in_dim) maps to field values of shape (N, out_dim), and the
physics loss differentiates u(x_i) with respect to x_i by autograd. Many
PINNeAPPle architectures, however, take grids or sequences — channels-first
(B, C, L) for FNO / conv1d, (B, C, H, W) for conv2d, (B, H, W, C) for AFNO,
(B, T, D) for transformers, RNNs, TCNs and reservoirs. Handed a flat (N, d)
tensor they either crash or silently treat the N points as one sample.

The adapters below treat every point as its own sample of spatial / temporal
extent 1. That keeps each prediction a function of its own point only (no
mixing across points, independent of point order), which is exactly what the
autograd physics residual requires.

Three groups:
- PointwiseAdapter  — gradient-trained models; reshape in, flatten out.
- ClosedFormAdapter — models whose readout is solved in closed form via
  fit(X, y) (ELM, hybrid RBF, ESN readouts); trained by the pipeline's
  closed-form path instead of gradient descent.
- NOT_APPLICABLE    — unsupervised trajectory / snapshot models (Koopman/EDMD,
  POD, DMD, HAVOK, ARIMA). Their fit() takes a time series or snapshot matrix
  and no target, so a coordinates→field regression cannot train them.

pinneapple_arena.pointwise.leaderboard.doc:
Global ranking of architectures over many arena experiments (the PINNeAPPle Arena leaderboard).

``aggregate(experiments)`` takes completed experiments (``{"id", "winner", "problem_id", "model_results"}``, the
``model_results`` as written by the arena pipeline) and returns one entry per architecture: mean relative L2, MAPE,
RMSE, R2, max error, training time, convergence rate (relative L2 below 0.1), PDE evaluations, peak memory and
inference time, ranked by mean relative L2 (lower is better), plus 0-100 scores per objective:

- ``accuracy`` is absolute: ``(1 - mean relative L2) * 100``, floored at 0;
- ``training_cost``, ``memory`` and ``inference_speed`` are relative to the other entries of the same call
  (min-max), so they depend on the hardware and on which architectures ran;
- ``convergence`` is the convergence rate in percent.

The mean relative L2 pools experiments on different problems; filter ``experiments`` to one problem (or one domain)
for a like-for-like ranking.

pinneapple_arena.pointwise.losses.doc:
PDE-residual losses of the arena problems, ``(model, {"X": collocation points}) -> (loss, info)``.

Loss lookup order for each problem:
  1. Native PyTorch autograd residual of this module, built with the experiment's parameters (nu, alpha, c, ...)
  2. The PINNeAPPle preset's compiled PDE residual (``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compile_problem``) via the
     explicit preset_key, then via problem_id; it uses the preset's own parameters, and only its ``pde`` term is
     used (boundary and initial conditions come in through the data). The preset's coordinate order must match
     the arena data (e.g. ``(x, t)`` for Burgers).
  3. None  (supervised-only training)

The source arena tried the preset first, but called it with an outdated signature, so every preset loss raised
and was skipped silently; the wrapper below adapts it, and the native residual (parameter-aware) comes first.
pinneapple_arena.pointwise.losses.doc1: PDE-residual losses of the arena problems, ``(model, {"X": collocation points}) -> (loss, info)``.

pinneapple_arena.pointwise.training.doc:
Training and scoring of one architecture on a pointwise field problem (the PINNeAPPle Arena protocol).

Every arena problem is a field regression: coordinates ``(N, in_dim)`` in, field values ``(N, out_dim)`` out. A
model is built from the PINNeAPPle registry (``pp.build_model``) and, when it takes grids or sequences, wrapped by
``pinneapple_arena.pointwise.adapters``. It is trained on reference samples with an optional PDE residual on
separate collocation points (``pinneapple_arena.pointwise.losses``), early-stopped on a validation split, and
scored on a held-out test split (``field_metrics``, ``prediction_quality``).

No stand-in is ever trained under an architecture's name: when the registry cannot build an architecture for this
data, ``instantiate_model`` raises ``ArchitectureUnavailable`` (or ``ArchitectureNotApplicable``) and the caller
reports the architecture as failed, with the reason.

    from pinneapple_arena.pointwise import training as T
    in_dim, out_dim = T.problem_dims("burgers_1d")
    model = T.instantiate_model("vanilla_pinn", in_dim, out_dim)
    out = T.train_torch_model(model, X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val, X_col, loss_fn, n_epochs=200, lr=1e-3, device="cpu")
    metrics = T.field_metrics(T.predict(model, X_test), y_test)

pinneapple_arena.problems.doc:
Arena physics problem registry.

22 problems across 8 physics domains:

  Fluid Mechanics         kovasznay_ns, stokes_2d, lid_driven_cavity_ns
  Diffusion / Heat        heat_1d, heat_2d, convection_diffusion_1d, darcy_flow_2d
  Elliptic                poisson_2d, laplace_2d, biharmonic_2d, helmholtz_2d
  Transport               advection_diffusion_1d
  Waves                   wave_1d, klein_gordon_1d, nls_1d
  Nonlinear / Solitons    burgers_1d, kdv_1d
  Reaction-Diffusion      allen_cahn, fisher_kpp_1d, fitzhugh_nagumo_1d
  Structural / Finance    linear_elasticity_2d, black_scholes_1d

Each problem exposes:
  - analytical(x, y, **params) -> dict[str, ndarray] | None
  - pinn_residuals(net, xy_int, xy_bc, uv_bc, **params) -> (res_loss, bc_loss)
  - supervised_data(n_train, n_bc, grid_n, **params)
        -> (X_int, Y_int, X_bc, Y_bc, X_eval, Y_eval, field_names)
  - compiled_losses(**params) -> dict | None   (via pinneapple_physics)
  - physics_preset: Optional[str]
  - description, input_dim, output_dim

classes.name: Stokes2D
classes.doc1: 2D Stokes (Poiseuille) flow: u = 1-y², v = 0, p = -2x.

classes.name: Heat1D
classes.doc1: 1D heat: u_t = alpha*u_xx,  u = exp(-alpha*pi^2*t)*sin(pi*x).

classes.name: Heat2D
classes.doc1: 2D heat: u_t = alpha*(u_xx+u_yy).

classes.name: ConvectionDiffusion1D
classes.doc1: Steady 1D convection-diffusion: c*u_x = eps*u_xx. Analytical: u = (exp(c*x/eps) - 1)/(exp(c/eps) - 1) on [0,1], u(0)=0, u(1)=1.

classes.name: DarcyFlow2D
classes.doc1: 2D Darcy: -Δp = f,  p = sin(πx)sin(πy),  f = 2π²sin(πx)sin(πy).

classes.name: Laplace2D
classes.doc1: 2D Laplace: Δu = 0,  u = sin(πx)sinh(πy)/sinh(π).

classes.name: Poisson2D
classes.doc1: 2D Poisson: Δu = -2π²sin(πx)sin(πy),  u = sin(πx)sin(πy).

classes.name: Helmholtz2D
classes.doc1: 2D Helmholtz: u_xx + u_yy + k²u = f,  u = sin(πx)sin(πy).

classes.name: Biharmonic2D
classes.doc1: 2D Biharmonic (thin plate): Δ²u = f, u = sin(πx)sin(πy), f = 4π⁴*u.

classes.name: AdvectionDiffusion1D
classes.doc1: 1D advection-diffusion: u_t + c*u_x = nu*u_xx. Analytical: u = exp(-nu*pi²*t)*sin(pi*(x - c*t)).

classes.name: Wave1D
classes.doc1: 1D wave: u_tt = c²u_xx,  u = sin(πx)cos(πct).

classes.name: KleinGordon1D
classes.doc1: 1D Klein-Gordon: u_tt - u_xx + m²u = 0. Analytical: u = cos(kx)cos(ωt),  ω² = k² + m².

classes.name: NLS1D
classes.doc1: 1D NLS bright soliton: |ψ(x,t)| = A*sech(A*(x-vt)). We solve for (u, v) = (Re ψ, Im ψ) using the real/imaginary split. Solves i*psi_t + psi_xx + 2*|psi|^2*psi = 0 (nonlinearity coefficient 2).

classes.name: Burgers1D
classes.doc1: 1D Burgers: u_t + u*u_x = nu*u_xx, u(x,0) = -sin(pi*x), u(-1,t)=u(1,t)=0.

classes.name: KdV1D
classes.doc1: 1D KdV: u_t + 6u*u_x + u_xxx = 0. Soliton: u = -2c*sech²(sqrt(c)*(x - 4c*t)).

classes.name: AllenCahn
classes.doc1: 1D Allen-Cahn: u_t = eps²u_xx + u - u³.  Tanh interface.

classes.name: FisherKPP1D
classes.doc1: 1D Fisher-KPP: u_t = D*u_xx + r*u*(1-u). Exact Ablowitz-Zeidler traveling wave: u = [1/(1+exp(w*(x-v*t)))]^2 with v = 5*sqrt(D*r/6) and w = sqrt(r/(6D)).

classes.name: FitzHughNagumo1D
classes.doc1: 1D FitzHugh-Nagumo excitable media (two fields: v, w). v_t = v_xx + v(1-v)(v-a) - w + I,  w_t = eps*(v - gamma*w).

classes.name: LinearElasticity2D
classes.doc1: 2D plane-strain linear elasticity (manufactured solution). Displacement: u = sin(πx)sin(πy), v = 0. Body force computed from Lamé equations.

classes.name: BlackScholes1D
classes.doc1: 1D Black-Scholes PDE for a European call option. V_t + r*S*V_S + sigma^2*S^2/2*V_SS - r*V = 0. Analytical via BS formula (evaluated on (log-price, time) grid).

pinneapple_arena.regimes.doc:
Regime arena: which method works best for a physical problem, per data regime, under one protocol.

``run_regime_arena(data, ...)`` trains every candidate of ``pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.methods`` that applies to
the data, with

* **equal data**: one split (fixed seed) shared by every method and every model seed;
* **equal compute**: the same ``ComputeBudget`` for every iterative method (``train_within_budget``), one-shot fits
  report the time they used;
* **the same stopping rule**: budget spent, best of ten validation checkpoints (iterative methods);
* **several seeds**: the model seed varies, the data does not; every number has its spread across seeds;

and measures, on data no method trained on, per regime:

==================  =============================================================================================
interpolation       random held-out samples inside the training distribution
few_data            the same held-out samples, training on ``few_data_fraction`` of the training samples
extrapolation       the distribution-shift set: one end of an input, or the edge of the input space
geometry_change     whole groups (geometries, cases) held out, when the data has groups
steep_fronts        fields: the held-out samples with the steepest gradients (top quartile of max |grad u|): a
                    proxy for discontinuities
==================  =============================================================================================

plus training …

pinneapple_arena.showcase.doc:
Four contrasting PINN architectures trained on the same viscous Burgers problem, ranked by accuracy and by
Arena's physics-aware view.

Problem: ``burgers_1d`` (u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx, u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x) on [-1, 1], nu = 0.01/pi; Raissi, Perdikaris &
Karniadakis 2019, J. Comput. Phys. 378), reference by the Cole-Hopf solution inside the problem class. A steep front
forms near x = 0 around t ~ 0.3 and persists to t = 1.

The run uses Arena's own pieces (:func:`~pinneapple_arena.model_factory.build_model`,
:func:`~pinneapple_arena.trainer.train_pinn`, :func:`~pinneapple_arena.trainer.evaluate_model`,
:func:`~pinneapple_arena.arena.rank_by_accuracy`, :func:`~pinneapple_arena.arena.physics_aware_rank`), one model at
a time so a caller can report progress. ``physics_aware_rank`` never reorders the accuracy ranking; it flags models
whose PDE residual is an outlier of the group (median + n_std * std) and, when ``residual_threshold`` is given,
above that absolute value too. The relative test alone can miss models that are all bad together: with four
models, a model with a residual far above the others raises the group std with it (see the app README for a
measured case).

Per-architecture budgets (``DEFAULT_ARCHITECTURES``) were tuned in the source project for convergence on the front:
Vanilla PINN 4x64 for 12,000 epochs, SIREN 3x64 with omega_0 = 15 for 4,000, PIELM (frozen random hidden layer,
trained output layer) 128 features for 5,000, XTFC (constrained basis, trained output …

pinneapple_autolab.doc:
pinneapple_autolab -- the Autonomous Physics Lab: an AI that manages evidence to make engineering decisions.

Two layers, shared by every mission:

* the agent loop (:mod:`.core`): a mission in plain language -> a plan of controlled library calls -> evidence
  (``Tool``, ``Toolbox``, ``Step``, ``TemplatePlanner``, ``LLMPlanner``, ``execute``); the physics of each mission
  lives in its domain package (e.g. :mod:`pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling`);
* the scientific cycle on a costly reference simulator (:mod:`.lab`): plan -> build (geometry and boundary-condition
  checks) -> simulate -> learn (surrogate families compared on held-out data, with uncertainty) -> optimise (NSGA-II
  on the surrogate) -> assess every candidate (validated domain, probability of meeting the limits, expected field
  error where the decision is made) -> choose the next simulation by what is still unknown -> verify -> deliver (a
  simulated design, its trust report and the ledger).

    from pinneapple_autolab import AutonomousLab
    from pinneapple_autolab.domains.racecar import RaceCarAero, flagship_mission

    lab = AutonomousLab(flagship_mission(), RaceCarAero(), "runs/aero", critical_region="diffuser")
    summary = lab.run()

Only the ledger's runs are evidence; predictions are labelled as predictions until a simulation confirms them.
pinneapple_autolab.doc1: pinneapple_autolab -- the Autonomous Physics Lab: an AI that manages evidence to make engineering decisions.

pinneapple_autolab.agent.doc:
The lab driven by an agent: a mission in words -> a Mission -> tool calls on the lab -> an audited answer.

    from pinneapple_autolab.agent import run_agent
    res = run_agent("Find a lower-drag design at 70 m/s. Preserve the downforce ... 24 CFD runs.", sim, "runs/agent",
                    domain=racecar_domain())                        # deterministic planner
    res = run_agent(text, sim, folder, domain=..., provider="anthropic")   # an LLM decides each step (needs a key)

The agent decides one step at a time (:func:`pinneapple_autolab.core.act`): :class:`LabPlanner` (deterministic, no
network) or :class:`~pinneapple_autolab.core.LLMStepPlanner` (a language model), over the same toolbox
(:func:`lab_toolbox`): a closed set of :class:`~pinneapple_autolab.core.Tool` with declared inputs. There is no tool
to change the operating conditions, the bounds, the limits or the solver settings; a step with an argument a tool
does not declare is refused and the refusal is recorded as evidence. Every number a tool returns
comes from the lab's ledger or from a surrogate prediction labelled as such. The final answer is audited
(:func:`audit_claims`): every number in it must appear in what the tools returned, and the recommended run must be a
successful simulation that meets every limit; otherwise the answer is marked unsupported.

:func:`interpret_mission` turns the text into a :class:`~.mission.Mission` from a domain description
(:class:`MissionDomain`): a deterministic reading of …

pinneapple_autolab.core.doc:
Mission -> plan -> controlled tool calls -> evidence: the agent loop of the Autonomous Physics Lab.

The agent never runs code of its own. It picks steps from a :class:`Toolbox` of library calls registered for one
kind of mission, with arguments checked against each tool's declared inputs, and every call is logged as
:class:`Evidence` (arguments, a short summary of the result, wall time, error). Two planners share one interface:

* :class:`TemplatePlanner`: deterministic, the steps a mission kind always needs (no network, no API key);
* :class:`LLMPlanner`: asks a language model (``pinneapple_llm.call_llm``: Anthropic / OpenAI / Ollama) for a JSON
  plan over the same toolbox; any unknown tool, unknown argument or failure falls back to the template plan and the
  reason is recorded in the plan.

    box = Toolbox("board_cooling"); box.add(Tool("simulate", fn, "...", {"design": "..."}))
    plan = TemplatePlanner([Step("simulate", {"design": "baseline"})]).plan("cool this board", box)
    run = execute(plan, box)            # run.state: outputs by tool name; run.evidence: one entry per call

pinneapple_autolab.dashboard.doc:
The lab's dashboard: four synchronised areas over the real state of a session.

    from pinneapple_autolab.dashboard import build_dashboard, serve
    build_dashboard("runs/aero", "runs/aero/dashboard", scenes={"baseline": sc0, "best": sc1})   # static page
    serve("runs/aero", "runs/aero/dashboard", port=8120)            # live: the page polls /state.json

* **Geometry**: the original and the optimised design in 3-D (the studio viewer, skin Cp, streamlines, slices) and
  the variables that changed.
* **Physics**: drag and downforce per component (CFD of both designs), the force history of a run with its averaging
  window and iteration noise, the aero balance.
* **Models**: every surrogate family's held-out error per output, cross-validated predictions against CFD with their
  95 % intervals, the error of each prediction made before its simulation.
* **Decisions**: drag x downforce (candidates, surrogate front, simulated designs), the budget, the decision
  timeline (label before -> after, rule, reason), the validation criteria and the three trust cases.

The page shows what the ledger says and nothing else: a simulation in progress is shown as running, a failed run as
failed (red), training as training; a design that was only predicted is labelled "predicted, not simulated" and is
never drawn as verified. Selecting a run anywhere (Pareto point, timeline row) selects it in every area.

pinneapple_autolab.domain.doc:
Where the surrogate has evidence: the validated domain of a set of simulated designs.

A prediction is only as good as the simulations near it. :class:`ValidatedDomain` measures, for any design in the
unit cube, the distance to the nearest simulated design in units of the typical spacing of the simulated designs
(the median nearest-neighbour distance among them). A design is inside the validated domain when

* that ratio is at most ``max_ratio`` (default 1.5: no farther from the data than the data are from each other,
  with a margin), and
* every variable lies within the range the simulations covered, widened by ``margin`` of the full range.

The reasons a design is outside are returned in words with the numbers ("rear_flap_aoa = 15.1 is below the
simulated range 17.4 to 39.0"), so a report or an agent can say why it asked for another simulation.

pinneapple_autolab.domains.racecar.doc:
The AI Aerodynamicist's simulator: a parametric open-wheel racing car in OpenFOAM, and its flagship mission.

    sim = RaceCarAero(resolution="medium")
    sim.check(params)                     # geometry and boundary-condition checks, in words
    out = sim.run(params, "cases/run001")  # snappyHexMesh + simpleFoam (k-omega SST), forces, surface Cp, cost

Design variables (:data:`VARIABLES`): front wing main-plane and flap angles, rear wing main-plane and flap angles,
diffuser angle, ride height of the floor, on :class:`~pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d.FormulaCar` (not any
team's car). The bounds keep the wing elements apart: beyond 5 deg (front) and 7.5 deg (rear) the main plane's
trailing edge cuts into the flap at low flap angles (measured with ``meshops.self_intersections``).

Outputs: drag and downforce in N at the mission's speed, CD and CL on the design's frontal area, the downforce of
each component, and the aerodynamic balance (share of the downforce on the front axle, from the moments of the
pressure and friction forces of every wall face about the rear contact patch). The surface pressure coefficient is
returned on the car's own parametric vertices (fixed count for every design), in regions ``front_wing``,
``rear_wing``, ``floor``, ``diffuser`` (the floor's ramp) and ``body``, for field surrogates.

Fixed conditions (the lab cannot change them): 70 m/s, sea-level air, road moving with the flow, half model with a
symmetry plane, steady RANS k-omega SST with …

pinneapple_autolab.ledger.doc:
The evidence ledger: every simulation the lab ran (why, with what, what it cost, what came out) and every event

The ledger is the only source the report, the dashboard and an agent may read numbers from: a value that is not in a
:class:`RunRecord` was not measured. ``Ledger.event`` appends to ``events.jsonl`` as it goes (a dashboard can tail
it); ``Ledger.save`` writes ``ledger.json`` with the runs, the environment and the budget.

pinneapple_autolab.mission.doc:
A mission as numbers: what to improve, what must hold, what may change, how much simulation it may spend.

    from pinneapple_autolab import Mission, Budget
    from pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.study import Variable, Objective

    m = Mission("Lower drag", statement="Find a lower-drag design at 70 m/s ...",
                variables=[Variable("rear_flap_aoa", 15, 40)], objectives=[Objective("drag_N", "min", "N")],
                constraints=[Limit("downforce_N", lower_frac_of_baseline=1.0, unit="N")],
                baseline={"rear_flap_aoa": 32.0}, budget=Budget(max_runs=30))
    m.resolve({"downforce_N": 4369.0})          # relative limits become absolute once the baseline is measured

A limit relative to the baseline (``lower_frac_of_baseline=1.0``: "preserve the downforce") is only a number after
the baseline has been simulated; until then :meth:`Mission.constraints` refuses to return it, so nothing can be
called feasible against a limit nobody measured.
pinneapple_autolab.mission.doc1: A mission as numbers: what to improve, what must hold, what may change, how much simulation it may spend.

pinneapple_autolab.qualification.doc:
Before a campaign: how much of the reference solver's answer is the mesh and the iteration count?

    q = solver_qualification(sim, baseline, {"coarse": {"resolution": "coarse"}, "medium": {}, "fine":
                             {"resolution": "fine"}, "medium, 1000 it": {"iterations": 1000}}, "runs/qual",
                             reference="fine", campaign="medium")

runs the same design under each variant (its own ledger, outside the mission budget) and reports, per output, the
relative difference of every variant from ``reference``. The difference between the campaign's setting and the
reference is the discretisation uncertainty every later comparison has to be read against: a design improvement
smaller than it is not resolved by the solver, and the report says so.

pinneapple_autolab.replay.doc:
A simulator that answers from a ledger of measured runs when it holds the exact design, and runs the real
simulator otherwise.

    sim = ReplaySimulator(RaceCarAero(), "examples/autolab_aero/_out/ledger.json", fields_dir="work/fields")

A replayed outcome is the recorded measurement (outputs, cost, solver metadata, fields when kept) of a run made
earlier on the same simulator settings; its ``meta["replayed_from"]`` names the ledger and run, and the time it
cost then is kept (``cost_s``) with ``meta["replay_wall_s"]`` the time it took now. A design not in the ledger
(compared to ``atol`` in every variable) is simulated for real. Nothing is interpolated.
pinneapple_autolab.replay.doc1: A simulator that answers from a ledger of measured runs when it holds the exact design, and runs the real simulator otherwise.

pinneapple_autolab.report.doc:
Figures and the engineering report of a lab session, drawn only from its snapshot (ledger runs, candidates,
model board, decisions): nothing here computes a physical number.

* :func:`fig_pareto`: every surrogate candidate (crosses) in drag x downforce, the surrogate Pareto front (circles),
  the simulated designs by purpose, the baseline and the best simulated design, the downforce limit.
* :func:`fig_models`: cross-validated prediction against the reference per output, with the 95 % intervals, and
  the score of every surrogate family.
* :func:`fig_learning`: the error of each acquisition's prediction (made before its simulation) and the best
  simulated feasible objective against the simulations spent.
* :func:`fig_field_triptych`: reference | prediction | error of a surface field (top and bottom views).
* :func:`fig_trust_cards`: three designs the lab judged differently (favourable, uncertain, out of domain), what
  was predicted, what the reference then said.
* :func:`write_report`: the Markdown report.

pinneapple_autolab.simulator.doc:
The reference simulator the lab calls: a solver run on one design, its checks before it runs, its cost after.

Any physics plugs in by implementing :class:`Simulator`:

* ``check(params) -> list[str]``: why this design cannot be simulated as asked (invalid geometry, boundary
  conditions that do not match the mission); empty when it can. The lab never runs a design with issues.
* ``run(params, workdir) -> SimOutcome``: the outputs the solver produced, whether it succeeded, its wall time and,
  optionally, fields on a fixed set of points (for field surrogates). A failed run returns ``ok=False`` with the
  reason; it never returns made-up outputs.

:class:`FunctionSimulator` wraps a Python function (tests, analytic toy problems).
pinneapple_autolab.simulator.doc1: The reference simulator the lab calls: a solver run on one design, its checks before it runs, its cost after.

classes.name: Simulator
classes.doc1: Base class: set ``name``, ``fidelity``, ``outputs`` (and ``field_names`` / ``field_points`` / ``regions`` if it returns fields), implement :meth:`check` and :meth:`run`.

classes.name: FunctionSimulator
classes.sig: (fn, outputs, *, name='function', checker=None, fail=None, field_names=(), regions=None, points=None)
classes.doc1: ``fn(params) -> {output: value}`` (optionally also ``"__fields__": {name: array}``); ``checker(params) -> list[str]``; ``fail(params) -> str | None`` makes a run fail with that message (to test failure paths).

pinneapple_autolab.surrogates.doc:
Surrogates of the reference solver, compared on data they did not see, each with an uncertainty.

Scalar models (one output at a time, inputs in the unit cube):

* :class:`GPModel`: Gaussian process, Matern 5/2 with ARD length scales (scikit-learn); predictive std.
* :class:`MLPEnsemble`: ``n`` small MLPs on bootstrap resamples (scikit-learn); std = spread of the members.
* :class:`QuadraticRSM`: ridge regression on a full quadratic basis (the classical response surface); std = the
  residual std of its own fit (homoscedastic), the honest baseline a learned model has to beat.

:func:`compare_models` scores every family by k-fold cross-validation (each fold's points held out of its fit):
RMSE, relative error, R², the fraction of held-out points inside the 95 % interval (calibration) and the fit time.
:class:`ModelBoard` keeps the table and the chosen family per output (lowest held-out RMSE).

Fields on a fixed set of points (surface pressure on a parametric shape): :class:`FieldSurrogate` = POD (SVD of the
centred snapshots) + one scalar model per retained mode; the std of the field comes from the modal stds.
Errors per region (:func:`field_errors`) say where on the shape the model is wrong.
pinneapple_autolab.surrogates.doc1: Surrogates of the reference solver, compared on data they did not see, each with an uncertainty.

pinneapple_autolab.trust.doc:
Can this prediction be used for a decision? Triage of surrogate candidates and the choice of the next simulation.

Every candidate design the optimiser proposes gets a :class:`CandidateAssessment`:

* its predicted objectives and constraints with their std (from the chosen surrogate),
* the probability that it meets every constraint, ``P(feasible) = prod Phi(margin_i / std_i)``,
* its expected improvement over the best *simulated* feasible design, weighted by ``P(feasible)`` (constrained EI),
* whether it is inside the validated domain (:mod:`.domain`), and the error the field surrogate expects in the
  region that decides the constraint (when there is one),
* a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport` built from those checks, and one of four labels:

  - ``"favourable"``: inside the domain, constraints met with >= ``p_ok`` probability, uncertainty within the
    acceptance tolerance -> worth a confirming simulation;
  - ``"uncertain"``: inside the domain, but the prediction cannot settle the decision (P(feasible) between
    ``p_drop`` and ``p_ok``, an objective std beyond tolerance, or a large expected field error in the critical
    region) -> a simulation there teaches the model where the decision changes;
  - ``"out_of_domain"``: the model is extrapolating; its numbers there are not evidence -> simulate before
    believing it;
  - ``"unlikely"``: P(feasible) below ``p_drop``; not pursued.

  After a reference run the label becomes ``"verified"``, ``"rejected by …

pinneapple_blender.blender_addon.import_.doc:
Runs INSIDE Blender's own Python (``bpy``) -- never imported by regular
PINNeAPPle code, same reasoning as ``cfd_formats/abaqus_reader.py``'s
``_abaqus_odb_export_script.py``: ``bpy`` is Blender's bundled interpreter,
not pip-installable into a normal environment, so this is launched as a
subprocess (``blender --background --python
import_pinneapple_sequence.py -- <args>``) by ``pinneapple_blender
.render.render_sequence``, not imported directly.

Imports every ``frame_XXXX.ply`` in a directory (as written by
``pinneapple_blender.export``), each into its own object, and keyframes
visibility so only frame N's object is visible at scene frame N -- the
simplest correct way to animate a sequence of separately-imported meshes
(as opposed to a single deforming mesh, which would need the point count
and topology to stay fixed across frames; a PLY-per-frame sequence makes
no such assumption, since a PINN surrogate evaluated at different
collocation samples per frame need not have a fixed point count at all).

pinneapple_blender.cycles.doc:
In-process Cycles renderer: build a small scene from NumPy arrays and render it with Blender's ``bpy`` module.

``render.py`` drives a separate Blender installation through a subprocess; this module uses the ``bpy`` Python
module directly (``pip install bpy``, which bundles Blender and Cycles), so a scene can be described from data in
the same process: surfaces from height grids, tubes along curves, point clouds, translucent planes, ribbons, text,
a camera, lights. Rendering is headless on the CPU.

    from pinneapple_blender.cycles import CyclesScene, available
    if available():
        sc = CyclesScene(resolution=(960, 540), samples=64)
        sc.add_surface(X, Y, Z, colors)               # (ny, nx) grids, colors (ny, nx, 3) in 0..1
        sc.add_plane(z=0.0, size=(10, 6), color=(0.1, 0.3, 0.6), alpha=0.35)
        sc.camera(location=(8, -9, 6), look_at=(0, 0, 0))
        sc.render("landscape.png")

``render_frames`` renders a sequence (the caller changes the scene between frames through a callback) and
``frames_to_video`` assembles them with ffmpeg.

pinneapple_blender.export.doc:
Export a PINNeAPPle result (a point cloud + one or more scalar/vector
fields, optionally over several time steps) to a sequence of ``.ply``
files Blender can import natively (built-in importer, no add-on required
just to look at one frame) -- the PINNeAPPle-side half of the Blender
bridge; ``blender_addon/`` is the other half, running *inside* Blender.

Why PLY and not Alembic
------------------------
Alembic (the usual sim-to-DCC interchange format) would need the
``alembic``/``pyalembic`` Python bindings, which are not a normal
``pip install``-able package (built against Blender's/Maya's own bundled
libraries in practice) -- adding it as a dependency here would make this
module unusable for most people who don't already have a full VFX-pipeline
Python environment. PLY (a simple, well-specified, ASCII-or-binary mesh
format supporting arbitrary per-vertex properties, including colour) is
trivially writable with nothing beyond ``numpy``, and Blender has a
built-in PLY importer -- zero extra dependencies on either side of the
bridge, at the cost of "a directory of numbered files" instead of one
Alembic cache. See ``blender_addon/import_pinneapple_sequence.py`` for how
the numbered sequence becomes a Blender animation.

Catalog of what PINNeAPPle knows about, with sources.

- ``resources``: public datasets, CAD/geometry sets, pretrained models and
  hosted benchmarks, each with a checked license and a license gate.
- ``methods``: every solver, training method, equation and problem in the
  library, with its code location, its references and its validation status.

pinneapple_catalog.methods.doc:
Every solver, training method, equation and problem in PINNeAPPle, with
its code, its references and its validation status.

IDs match the inventory of 2026-09-24 (``docs/dev/PEDIDOS_2026-09-24.md``):
S = solver, T = training method, E = physical equation, P = physical problem.

References come in two kinds, kept apart on purpose:

- ``refs_in_code``: what the module's own docstring already cites.
- ``refs_added``: the canonical source (original paper or standard textbook)
  added here because the code cites nothing. Every arXiv id in both lists
  was checked against the paper title on 2026-09-24 (that check found and
  fixed a wrong id: X-TFC cited arXiv:2005.01219, a metasurface paper, for
  Leake & Mortari; the right id is arXiv:1812.08625).

``scripts/build_method_status.py`` from ``tests/`` and stored in
``method_status.json``. An item is ``validated`` when a test that exercises
it compares against an independent reference (closed form, published
value or manufactured solution); ``tested`` when tests exist but none is a
reference comparison; ``untested`` otherwise. Anything not ``validated``
is "pending: paper + benchmark" and is left out of ``validated_methods()``.

pinneapple_catalog.resources.doc:
Catalog of public Physics AI resources: datasets, CAD/geometry sets,
pretrained models and hosted benchmarks, each with a checked license.

The evaluation behind every entry (what it is, license, size, how we use
it) lives in ``PINNeAPPle-CFD/docs/7.Recursos-publicos.md`` (research of
2026-09-23) plus the PLAID and PressNet checks of 2026-09-24. This module
turns that document into something code can query and enforce: a
component that wants a resource asks the catalog first, and the same
license gate as ``pinneapple_neural._licencas`` refuses non-commercial or
unlicensed resources when ``PINNEAPPLE_COMMERCIAL_MODE=1``.

Rules, matching the research doc:

- ``commercial`` is ``"yes"`` only when the license was read and allows
  commercial use. ``"no"`` is an explicit non-commercial / non-production
  license. ``"unverified"`` covers everything else (no license file, data
  license not declared, conflicting tags) and is treated like ``"no"``:
  a missing license means all rights reserved.
- ``paper`` is filled only with a reference whose arXiv id / DOI was
  checked against the title. Unknown stays ``None``; nothing is invented.
- ``rating`` reuses the doc's classification: ``use_now``, ``product``
  (product level, after the pilot), ``reference`` (reference / internal
  benchmark only) and ``skip`` (outside the CFD scope).

pinneapple_check.doc:
pinneapple check: a physics linter for CI.

Fails a pull request when a simulation result or a Physics-AI model violates physics: conservation, units,
boundary and initial conditions, PDE residual, bounds, out-of-distribution use, regression against a stored
reference, and integrity of the artefacts. Command line: ``pinneapple check [paths]`` (or
``python -m pinneapple_check`` / ``python -m pinneapple.check``); GitHub Action: ``action.yml`` at the root of the
repository.

From Python::

    from pinneapple_check import run
    report = run(["cases/"])
    assert not report.errors, [o.message for o in report.errors]

The package imports only NumPy at start-up (torch only to load a ``.pt`` checkpoint), and reuses the OpenFOAM and
unit readers of ``pinneapple_data``, the training envelope of ``pinneapple_physics.physics_audit``, field metrics
of ``pinneapple_analysis``, the method catalog, ``pinneapple_security`` for hashes, signatures and checkpoint scans,
and the trust-card stages of ``pinneapple_lab``.
pinneapple_check.doc1: pinneapple check: a physics linter for CI.

pinneapple_check._reuse.doc:
Load single modules of other PINNeAPPle packages without running their package ``__init__``.

Several packages (``pinneapple_data``, ``pinneapple_physics``, ``pinneapple_analysis``, ``pinneapple_catalog``)
import torch and the model zoo in their ``__init__``. The modules the checker needs from them (OpenFOAM readers,
units, the training envelope, field metrics, the method catalog) are numpy-only, so they are loaded here under a
private alias: a CI linter should start in a fraction of a second and run without torch. If the real package is
already imported, its module is used as is.

``pinneapple check [paths]``: the command line.

Exit codes (like ruff and pytest): 0 no violation (or only warnings with ``--fail-on error``), 1 violations,
2 a usage or configuration error.

The ``pinneapple`` command dispatches sub-commands: ``check`` here, and ``benchmark`` to
:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.cli` when that package is installed.

pinneapple_check.config.doc:
Configuration: ``pinneapple-check.toml`` (or ``[tool.pinneapple.check]`` in ``pyproject.toml``).

::

    [check]
    select = ["ALL"]            # ruff-style prefixes: "PC1", "PC201"
    ignore = []
    fail-on = "error"           # error | warning | never
    baseline = ".pinneapple-check-baseline.json"

    [[result]]
    path = "cases/cavity"       # OpenFOAM case, .vtu/.vtk, .npz, .h5, .csv of quantities of interest
    physics = "incompressible-flow"
    parameters = { nu = "0.01 m2/s" }
    bounds = { "alpha.water" = [0, 1] }
    [result.bc.movingWall]
    U = [1, 0, 0]

    [[model]]
    path = "models/surrogate.py:predict"
    inputs = ["x", "y"]
    outputs = ["u", "v", "p"]
    train-range = { x = [0, 1], y = [0, 1] }
    queries = "queries.csv"

Keys accept ``-`` or ``_``. Every path is relative to the configuration file. Without a configuration file the
checker discovers results under the given paths and runs the checks that need no declaration.

pinneapple_check.fields.doc:
Reading results into one structure, :class:`FieldData`, whatever the format.

Kinds:

* ``fv``: an OpenFOAM case (cell values, boundary-face values, face geometry, ``phi`` when written), read with the
  readers of :mod:`pinneapple_data.cae.foam`.
* ``grid``: arrays on a tensor-product grid. An ``.npz``/``.h5`` file with 1-D coordinate arrays (``x``, ``y``,
  ``z``, ``t``) and fields of shape ``(len(x), len(y), ...)`` (``indexing="ij"``), or a point file whose points
  happen to form such a grid.
* ``points``: a point cloud with point data (VTU/VTK through meshio, NPZ/HDF5/CSV tables through
  :mod:`pinneapple_data.cae.io`).
* ``qoi``: a CSV of quantities of interest, either long (``name,value[,unit]``) or one row with a column per
  quantity (``Cd [1]``).

pinneapple_check.fv.doc:
Finite-volume operators on an OpenFOAM mesh (Gauss theorem over the faces of each cell), and the conservative
residuals and boundary balances built on them.

Face values: linear interpolation between the two cells of an internal face; on boundary faces the value written
in the field's ``boundaryField`` (the owner-cell value where nothing is written, e.g. ``zeroGradient``). Face
fluxes come from ``phi`` when the solver wrote it, which makes the continuity check exact up to the solver
tolerance. Faces of ``empty`` patches (the front and back of a 2-D case) carry no flux.

pinneapple_check.models.doc:
Loading a model as a plain function ``(N, n_inputs) array -> {output name: (N,) array}``.

Supported ``path`` forms:

* ``models/surrogate.py:predict``: a Python function taking an ``(N, n_inputs)`` NumPy array and returning an
  ``(N, n_outputs)`` array (or a dict by output name). No torch needed: this is how to check any model, from any
  framework, behind a two-line wrapper.
* ``model.pt`` / ``model.pth`` / ``model.ckpt`` with ``architecture = "<zoo name>"`` (a name of
  ``pp.list_models()``) and ``config = {...}`` (its constructor arguments): a PINNeAPPle checkpoint
  (``BaseModel.save_checkpoint`` or a bare ``state_dict``). Its pickle stream is scanned first (rule PC803) and
  it is loaded with ``weights_only=True``. The training range is read from ``metadata.domain_bounds``.
* ``hub = "org/name"``: ``pinneapple_hub.from_pretrained``; the training range comes from the model card.
* ``zoo = "name"``: a pre-trained, verified model of ``pp.zoo`` (weights checked against the zoo manifest); inputs,
  outputs and the training range (the card's validity range) come from its model card.
pinneapple_check.models.doc1: Loading a model as a plain function ``(N, n_inputs) array -> {output name: (N,) array}``.

pinneapple_check.numerics.doc:
Derivatives of named scalar fields on three kinds of discretisation, behind one interface.

A *provider* holds scalar components by name (a vector ``U`` becomes ``u, v, w``) and gives ``val(name)``,
``d(name, axis)``, ``dd(name, a, b)`` and ``dt(name)``, plus ``interior`` (a mask of the points where the stencil is
fully inside the data) and ``where(i)`` (coordinates of point ``i`` for messages). The physics residuals in
:mod:`pinneapple_check.physics` are written once against this interface.

* :class:`GridD`: second-order finite differences (``numpy.gradient``) on a tensor-product grid, time optional.
* :class:`PointD`: weighted least-squares quadratic fit over the nearest neighbours of each point.
* :class:`ModelD`: central differences of a model's predictions at sampled points.

Finite-volume (OpenFOAM) residuals are conservative sums over faces and live in :mod:`pinneapple_check.fv`.

classes.name: PointD
classes.doc1: Weighted least-squares quadratic fit around each point (``k`` neighbours). Points whose neighbourhood is one-sided (on the hull of the cloud) are left out of ``interior``.

classes.name: ModelD
classes.doc1: Central differences of ``f`` (``(N, n_in) -> dict of (N,)``) at the points ``X``. ``axes`` are the inputs differentiated (spatial names, plus ``t`` if it is an input); other inputs are held fixed.

functions.name: components
functions.doc1: Split vector fields into named scalars: ``U`` -> ``u, v, w``, ``D`` -> ``ux, uy, uz``, another vector ``F`` -> ``F_x, F_y, F_z``; ``Ux``/``U_x`` style scalars -> ``u``... Scalars keep their names.

functions.name: rel_rms
functions.doc1: RMS of the residual over RMS of the sum of the absolute terms: 0 = exact, 1 = terms do not balance. ``floor`` bounds the denominator from below (a characteristic size of the terms), so a field whose terms all vanish (a linear profile without source) is not judged on round-off.

pinneapple_check.physics.doc:
Governing equations of the four physics, written against the derivative providers of
:mod:`pinneapple_check.numerics`, plus the parameter table (names, dimensions, defaults).

Equations (SI, any consistent units):

* ``incompressible-flow``: div u = 0 and du/dt + (u.grad)u + grad(p)/rho - nu lap(u) = 0. ``p`` is kinematic
  (OpenFOAM's incompressible solvers) unless ``rho`` is given. The time term is used when time is known.
* ``heat``: rho_cp dT/dt = k lap(T) + q. ``alpha`` (diffusivity) instead of ``k`` means rho_cp = 1.
* ``elasticity``: div(sigma) + f = 0 with sigma = lambda tr(eps) I + 2 mu eps, from ``E`` and ``nu`` (Poisson
  ratio; plane strain in 2-D). The displacement is ``D`` (OpenFOAM), ``disp``, or ``ux, uy[, uz]``.
* ``conservation``: dq/dt + div F = S for every conserved field ``q`` with its flux field ``F`` declared under
  ``flux = { q = "F" }``.
* ``maxwell``: Maxwell's equations (Gauss, Faraday, Ampere-Maxwell, continuity) and Poynting's theorem for
  field components ``Ex, Ey, Ez, Bx.. or Hx.., Dx.., Jx.., rho`` on a grid (``pinneapple_physics.maxwell_checks``),
  time-domain with a ``t`` axis or phasors (``<name>_re`` / ``<name>_im``) with ``omega``; parameters ``eps_r``,
  ``mu_r``, ``sigma``.
* ``darcy``: -div(a grad u) = f on the unit square with u = 0 on the boundary, cell-centred grid results with the
  coefficient ``a`` (or ``K``) and the solution ``u`` (or ``p``) stored side by side; checked with the finite-volume
  discretisation of the reference …

The rule table of ``pinneapple check``: every rule has an id (``PC101``), a short name, a default severity, the
trust-card stage it gives evidence for, an explanation and a fix hint.

Ids are grouped by hundreds, so ``--select PC1`` picks a whole family:

* ``PC0xx`` reading the inputs
* ``PC1xx`` conservation (mass, energy, momentum, divergence)
* ``PC2xx`` boundary and initial conditions
* ``PC3xx`` PDE residual
* ``PC4xx`` bounds and finite values
* ``PC5xx`` units
* ``PC6xx`` out-of-distribution use of a model
* ``PC7xx`` regression against a stored reference
* ``PC8xx`` integrity of artefacts (hashes, signatures, pickles)
* ``PC9xx`` method status in the catalog

pinneapple_condense.algebraic.doc:
Algebraic condensation: the method of :mod:`.substructure` for *any* assembled sparse operator.

Given a sparse matrix ``A`` (symmetric or not, saddle-point or not), the positions of its unknowns and a block
size, the unknowns are split into block interiors and a **separator**:

* every unknown gets the block that contains its position;
* of every coupled pair of unknowns (pattern of ``A + A^T``) in two different blocks, the one in the lower-numbered
  block is a separator -- so no interior unknown of one block couples to an interior unknown of another, whatever
  the stencil (finite volumes, staggered velocity-pressure, RBF-FD);
* ``primal`` (optional, per unknown) marks extra separators, e.g. one pressure per block of a saddle-point system,
  whose interior would otherwise be singular (pressure defined up to a constant).

Each block's interior is eliminated exactly: ``S = A_SS - sum_b A_SI^b (A_II^b)^-1 A_IS^b``. Blocks are compared
by **content** -- their interior and coupling submatrices in a canonical local order (positions relative to the
block, then field) -- and the factorisation and the local Schur complement of identical blocks are computed once.
Nothing is assumed about repetition: a block that differs in one entry is a new block.

**Reduced interfaces.** Separator unknowns shared by exactly two blocks form faces (keyed by the block pair and
field); unknowns shared by three or more blocks (corners) and primal unknowns stay unreduced. Each face is
projected on …

classes.doc1: Blocks of the unknowns: ``block`` per unknown (flat id), ``sep`` mask, and per block its interior and adjacent separator unknowns in canonical local order.

* :func:`configurations` -- cost to build vs cost per new power map.
* :func:`learned_study` -- learned block operators with verification vs exact per-block condensation.
* :func:`transient_study` -- Craig-Bampton transient vs the fine reference.

pinneapple_condense.exceptions.doc:
Prior field plus exception patches (track 1c): solve exactly only where a cheap prior does not hold.

1. **Prior.** A cheap field that is right in most of the package:
   ``"keff"`` -- the homogenised solution (:mod:`.homogenize`, one coarse cell per block laterally, the fine rows
   vertically), copied to every fine cell of its block and row; ``"column"`` -- every block as an isolated 1-D
   column with its own power (no lateral spreading). The Keff prior is the default: it keeps lateral spreading,
   which a 1-D column cannot (measured in the report), and costs one coarse solve.
2. **Where it does not hold.** The finite-volume residual of the prior on the fine grid, ``r = K T_prior - f``
   (one sparse product): heat created or destroyed by the prior in each cell, which is large where the prior
   misses a bump, a sub-pitch hotspot or an interface. Blocks are ranked by ``||r||`` over their cells (``select=
   "residual"``) or drawn at random (``"random"``, the baseline at the same budget).
3. **Compute exactly there.** Each selected block plus ``halo`` blocks around it is a patch; the fine problem is
   solved on the union of the patches with the prior as Dirichlet data on the cells around them.
4. **Recombine.** The patch solution replaces the prior in the selected blocks (``blend="core"``) or with a linear
   ramp across the halo (``"ramp"``, continuous). A final scalar correction ``alpha * phi`` (``phi``: the response to
   a uniform power map, one block with adiabatic …
