pinneapple_condense.flow.doc:
Steady 2-D incompressible flow and heat on a staggered (MAC) finite-volume grid, assembled as one sparse system:
the reference and the operator of the CFD falsification tests (``docs/research/condensation_falsification.md``).

Grid: ``nx x ny`` square cells of side ``h``; ``solid`` marks blocked cells (pins, fins). Unknowns: ``u`` on vertical
faces ``(nx + 1) x ny``, ``v`` on horizontal faces ``nx x (ny + 1)``, ``p`` in fluid cells. Velocities on faces of
solid cells, on the inlet and on the top/bottom walls are Dirichlet (identity rows), so every face keeps its unknown
and the continuity rows keep their pattern.

**Momentum (Oseen).** ``(a . grad) u - nu lap u + grad p = f`` with a frozen advecting velocity ``a`` (zero: Stokes;
the previous iterate: Picard for Navier-Stokes). Convection uses the hybrid scheme (central where the face Peclet
number is below 2, upwind above; Patankar, *Numerical Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow*, 1980, ch. 5).

* inlet ``x = 0``: given ``u`` profile, ``v = 0``;
* outlet ``x = L``: zero normal gradient of velocity and ``p = 0`` in the ghost cell (sets the pressure level);
* top and bottom: ``v = 0`` and either no-slip (``u`` ghost ``-u``, or ``2 U - u`` for a moving lid) or free slip
  (zero gradient), so a strip of a periodic pin array can be represented with free-slip sides;
* ``closed=True`` (cavity): walls on all four sides and one pressure fixed to zero.

**Energy / scalar.** ``rho c (u . grad T) - div(k grad T) = q`` on all cells (fluid and …

pinneapple_condense.fv.doc:
Cell-centred finite volumes for steady and transient conduction on a voxel box, and the reference solver.

``div(k grad T) + q = 0`` on a box of ``(nx, ny, nz)`` cells (uniform ``dx`` laterally, ``dz`` per z row), with

* the harmonic-mean face conductance between neighbours, plus a contact resistance ``R`` (m^2 K / W) on chosen
  horizontal faces: ``G = A / (dz_1 / (2 k_1) + R + dz_2 / (2 k_2))``;
* Robin cooling on the top and bottom faces to a zero ambient: ``G = A / (dz / (2 k) + 1 / h)``;
* adiabatic lateral faces, or *ports*: one node per lateral boundary face, joined to its cell by the half-cell
  conductance. Two boxes sharing a port node are, after eliminating the node, exactly the standard discretisation of
  the joined box; that is what makes block condensation exact (:mod:`.substructure`).

Unknown order: cells in C order ``(a, b, k)``, then ports ``x-, x+`` (each ``(b, k)``), ``y-, y+`` (each ``(a, k)``).

pinneapple_condense.hierarchy.doc:
Hierarchical (nested) condensation with reuse of identical subtrees.

The block array is split recursively in halves (the longer side first) down to single blocks. Each node of the tree
is a rectangle of blocks whose *ports* are the reduced interface dofs of its boundary faces (west, east, south,
north; ``m`` modes per face, :func:`.substructure.interface_modes`). Merging two children eliminates their shared
faces (a dense Schur complement), which is nested dissection on the reduced interfaces.

Two nodes with the same shape and the same children (recursively, the same arrangement of block variants) have the
same operator, so operators are memoised by that key: a uniform ``2^L x 2^L`` array needs ``2L`` merges whatever its
``4^L`` blocks, and an array with a few variants needs a few per level. The cost to build therefore follows the
number of *distinct* subtrees (the physical complexity of the layout), plus the dense algebra on the top separator,
whose size grows with the side of the array (sqrt of the block count).

A power map is pushed up the tree (each node condenses its children's loads with its stored elimination), the root
system is solved, and port values are pushed down; the downward pass can be limited to the path to one block
(:meth:`Hierarchy.block_ports`), which is what a point query needs.

pinneapple_condense.homogenize.doc:
Effective-conductivity (Keff) homogenisation: the baseline every condensation must beat.

Each layer with inclusions (bumps, TSVs) becomes a homogeneous anisotropic layer:

* through the layer (the inclusions are straight prisms): the parallel (Voigt) rule ``k_z = phi k_i + (1-phi) k_m``,
  exact for straight columns in one-dimensional heat flow;
* in plane: the Maxwell Garnett / Hashin-Shtrikman lower bound for aligned cylinders (Hashin and Shtrikman,
  J. Appl. Phys. 33 (1962) 3125), ``k_xy = k_m ((k_i + k_m) + phi (k_i - k_m)) / ((k_i + k_m) - phi (k_i - k_m))``.

The homogenised package is solved on a coarse lateral grid (``cells`` per block side, default 1) with the same
vertical rows, contact resistances and cooling. Its junction temperatures are block averages by construction:
whatever happens inside a block (the cooler junction above a bump, a power hotspot smaller than the pitch, the share
of heat taken by each bump) is erased, and :func:`compare` measures by how much.

pinneapple_condense.learned.doc:
Condensation with a learned block operator, error indicators and an error-driven fallback to exact condensation.

When every block differs a little (voided microbumps, a TIM contact that degrades across the die, TSV quality), the
identical-block reuse of :mod:`.substructure` is gone: each block would need its own factorisation. Here the
reduced block operator (the interface Schur complement ``S_r``, the condensed load map ``W_r`` and the observable
maps ``O_t``, ``O_p`` on ``m`` interface modes per face) is learned as a function of the block parameters ``theta``
from a few exact condensations: a POD of the operator entries (as a correction to the operator of the block at the
centre of the parameter box, so the large, parameter-independent part is exact) and a Gaussian-process regression of
the POD coefficients (:class:`pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.parametric.ParametricPOD`, which gives a predictive standard
deviation).

The learned operator is never trusted blindly. :func:`solve_adaptive`:

1. predicts every block; blocks outside the training box or with a relative predictive deviation above ``tol_std``
   are condensed exactly instead;
2. solves the global interface problem;
3. checks a set of blocks against their exact condensation *at the solved state*: the hottest blocks (the goal is
   the peak junction temperature), plus a random audit sample. The check is the junction-temperature discrepancy
   of the block (K), and the global effect of the heat-flow residual …

pinneapple_condense.meshless.doc:
Meshless solution of the chip-package benchmark (track 1b): points straight from the implicit geometry, no volume
mesh.

The package of :mod:`.package` is described implicitly: layers are z intervals, and each block's inclusion (bump,
TSV) is a square prism given by its centre and side. :func:`point_cloud` places nodes from that description only:

* a jittered lattice inside each material region, spacing ``h`` per layer (at least ``per_layer`` nodes across each
  layer), optionally ``refine`` times finer within ``refine_band`` of the inclusion walls; nodes closer than
  ``gap * h`` to a surface are dropped;
* lattices on every surface: each interface (layer planes, inclusion walls) gets a *pair* of nodes, one per side,
  and each outer boundary (top, bottom, sides) one node; surface nodes at edges are skipped.

Equations (``method``: stencils from :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.meshless.stencils`, ``rbf_fd`` or ``gfdm``):

* inside a region, ``k lap T + q = 0`` with a stencil of the nearest nodes *of the same region only*;
* top and bottom, Robin ``-k dT/dn = h T``; sides, adiabatic ``dT/dn = 0``;
* each interface pair ``(a, b)`` (normal ``n`` from ``a`` to ``b``), two equations from one-sided stencils:
  flux continuity ``k_a dT_a/dn = k_b dT_b/dn`` and the contact law ``T_a - T_b = R (-k_a dT_a/dn)``.

``interface="naive"`` drops the pairs: one node per interface point, stencils that cross materials, and the
equation of each node's own material -- the usual collocation …
pinneapple_condense.meshless.doc1: Meshless solution of the chip-package benchmark (track 1b): points straight from the implicit geometry, no volume mesh.

pinneapple_condense.meshless2d.doc:
2-D meshless (RBF-FD / GFDM) discretisations of the CFD falsification cases (``docs/research/
condensation_falsification.md``, section C), on point clouds built from the implicit geometry of a square-pin array.

* :func:`cloud` -- jittered lattice points of one unit cell (pin and fluid), replicated over the array; coordinates
  are rounded to a dyadic grid so that a block shifted by an integer has bit-identical stencil offsets (identical
  blocks then give identical matrices, which :mod:`.algebraic` detects by content);
* :func:`advection_diffusion` -- ``u . grad T - alpha lap T = q`` collocated with the stencils of
  :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.meshless.stencils`; inlet ``T = 0``, zero normal gradient elsewhere;
* :func:`stokes` -- collocated velocity-pressure Stokes on the fluid points (no-slip on the pin walls, uniform inlet,
  free-slip sides, ``p = 0`` and zero velocity gradient at the outlet);
* :func:`hybrid_conduction` -- multi-material conduction with a contact resistance on the pin walls: finite volumes
  on the cells of a band around every interface, RBF-FD on scattered points elsewhere, coupled by RBF interpolation of
  the FV cells' missing neighbours.

pinneapple_condense.package.doc:
A synthetic multilayer chip package built from one repeated unit cell (a *block*).

The package is a stack of layers (substrate, C4 bumps in underfill, silicon interposer with TSVs, microbumps in
underfill, die, TIM, copper lid) over a lateral array of identical-pitch blocks. A block is one unit cell of the
repeated structures: one C4 bump, one TSV and one microbump, all square in plan (square inclusions rasterise exactly
at every resolution, which keeps the mesh-convergence study free of staircase noise). Every layer spans the whole
array: the lid does not overhang the die in this benchmark.

Materials (W/m/K, J/m^3/K) are representative room-temperature values, not data for a real product:

* silicon k = 148, rho c = 1.63e6 (Incropera et al., *Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*, 6th ed., Table A.1);
* copper k = 401, rho c = 3.44e6 (same table);
* SAC solder k = 58, underfill k = 0.5, TIM k = 4, organic substrate k = 0.8 (typical datasheet ranges; synthetic).

A :class:`Variant` changes a block without changing its geometry: a voided microbump (conductivity factor), a
missing bump (inclusion replaced by underfill), a degraded TIM contact (contact-resistance factor). Blocks with the
same variant have the same conduction operator; that is what the condensation reuses.

Units: SI. Temperatures are rises above the ambient of the Robin boundaries.

pinneapple_condense.query.doc:
Physics queries on a chip package (track 2): the methods behind :class:`pinneapple_query.Engine` for the
package of :mod:`.package`.

Quantities (units: K for temperature *rises* above ambient, W, K/W):

* ``"T"`` at ``"die@u,v"`` (the junction cell under the point) or ``"die@u,v,w"`` (height fraction ``w`` through
  the die; needs the block's interior, rebuilt on demand);
* ``"Tj_max"`` over ``"region:die"`` or ``"region:die[i0:i1,j0:j1]"``;
* ``"q"`` through ``"ubump[I,J]"``, ``"tsv[I,J]"``, ``"c4[I,J]"``, ``"interface:die/tim"`` (optionally a block range)
  or ``"lid:top"``;
* ``"R_ja"``: peak junction temperature rise over total power.

Conditions: ``{"power": (nx, ny) W per active cell}`` (default: the package's power map).

Methods, cheapest first (each offers an expected cost and error bound; the planner of :mod:`pinneapple_query`
picks):

* ``cached`` -- the conditions were solved before: **read** the stored state (no new physics).
* ``bound`` -- *rigorous* interval from monotonicity: the conduction matrix is a nonsingular M-matrix, so
  ``K^-1 >= 0`` entrywise and ``p_min <= p <= p_max`` cell-wise brackets every temperature between the solutions for
  the uniform maps ``p_min`` and ``p_max``. For a uniform package those are one block with adiabatic sides, so the
  bound costs one block solve, ever. A **prediction** with a guaranteed interval (often wide).
* ``superposition`` -- conduction is linear in the power: if the new map is (nearly) a combination of solved …

pinneapple_condense.query_benchmark.doc:
Measured demonstration of the physics query engine on the chip package (track 2).

:func:`query_demo` builds an engine over a package, asks thousands of point, region and interface queries under the
package's own power map, under maps that are combinations of solved ones, under an unseen map and with loose
accuracy targets, and compares every answer with the fine finite-volume reference of the same conditions. It reports

the rigorous intervals contain it. Run it through :func:`pinneapple_condense.benchmark.isolated` for peak memory.

pinneapple_condense.substructure.doc:
Static condensation of repeated blocks, reduced interfaces, on-demand recovery and an error-driven refinement.

Every block of a :class:`.package.Package` is one voxel box with *port* nodes on its four lateral faces
(:func:`.fv.assemble`). Eliminating its cells gives the block's Schur complement on its ports,

    S = K_pp - K_pc K_cc^-1 K_cp,      g = W p,   W = -K_pc K_cc^-1 E,

with ``p`` the power of its active cells. Blocks with the same :class:`.package.Variant` have the same ``S``, ``W``
and the same factor of ``K_cc``: :func:`block_model` computes them once per distinct block (a cache keyed by stack
and variant), whatever the number of blocks.

The port field of each shared face is then restricted to a few *interface modes* ``Phi`` (the constant plus the
softest modes of the face's two-sided Schur complement, area weighted: characteristic constraint modes after
Castanier, Tan and Pierre, AIAA J. 39 (2001) 1182). The reduced global problem is a Galerkin restriction of the
exact one (an energy-norm best approximation over the chosen interface space; with the constant in every face basis
the global energy balance holds exactly). With ``Phi = I`` on every face it is the exact fine-grid solution.

Interior fields are never formed unless asked for: :meth:`Condensed.recover` rebuilds one block from its ports
(``T_c = Z p - Y t``), and linear observables (junction temperatures, the heat through each bump, TIM, lid) come
from precomputed per-block maps.

pinneapple_condense.transient.doc:
Transient conduction: Craig-Bampton condensation of the blocks, implicit Euler, and the fine reference.

``C dT/dt + K T = E p(t)``. Each block's cells are written as

    T_c = Psi t + Z p + Phi eta,

with ``Psi = -K_cc^-1 K_cp`` the static constraint modes (its port temperatures ``t``), ``Z p`` the static response to
its own power with the ports held (exact, so a quasi-static history is reproduced exactly), and ``Phi`` the ``k``
slowest fixed-interface modes (``K_cc Phi = C_cc Phi Lambda``, ``Phi^T C_cc Phi = I``) with amplitudes ``eta``
(Craig and Bampton, AIAA J. 6 (1968) 1313; applied here to the heat equation). A Galerkin projection with the test
space ``[Psi; I]`` and ``Phi`` gives, per block,

    [Psi^T C Psi   B^T] d/dt [t  ]   [S  0     ] [t  ]   [W p - Psi^T C Z dp/dt]
    [B             I  ]      [eta] + [0  Lambda] [eta] = [   - Phi^T C Z dp/dt ],     B = Phi^T C Psi,

and the port temperatures are restricted to the interface modes of :mod:`.substructure`. Blocks with the same
variant share all of these matrices. The global system (shared interface modes plus ``k`` amplitudes per block) is
integrated with implicit Euler at a fixed step, factorised once.

pinneapple_core.doc:
pinneapple_core: Field, Mesh, Domain and Geometry as shared primitives.

Physics AI needs tensors, geometry and topology in one object. These four are the
common vocabulary the solvers, models and datasets can build on:

- :class:`Domain`     the region (box or CSG shape): contains, sample interior/boundary
- :class:`Geometry`   a Domain with named boundaries and a mesher
- :class:`Mesh`       simplex mesh (1D/2D/3D) with exact P1 gradient/integral/interpolation
- :class:`Field`      values on a grid, mesh or point cloud
- :class:`FunctionField`  the same interface for a torch callable (PINN), by autograd

Operators (:mod:`pinneapple_core.operators`) give one function per derivative on every
representation: ``grad, div, curl, laplacian, jacobian, hessian, integrate, flux``.

Every field answers ``gradient()``, ``divergence()``, ``interpolate(x)`` and
``integrate()``, whatever it is discretised on.
pinneapple_core.doc1: pinneapple_core: Field, Mesh, Domain and Geometry as shared primitives.

pinneapple_core.backend.doc:
PhysicsBackend: one array/derivative/solve API over torch, jax and anything registered.

Code written against a :class:`PhysicsBackend` does not name an engine::

    from pinneapple_core.backend import get_physics_backend

    def energy(bk, L):                        # bk is the active backend
        x = bk.linspace(0.0, L, 101)
        return bk.integrate(bk.sin(x) ** 2, x)

    bk = get_physics_backend()
    dE = bk.grad(lambda L: energy(bk, L))(bk.asarray(2.0))

``pp.set_backend("jax")`` (or ``with use_backend("jax"):``) switches the engine, and the same function
returns the same numbers. Float64 is the default dtype so results agree across engines.

Operations: ``asarray, to_numpy, linspace, zeros, ones, eye, diag, matmul, solve, integrate`` and the
transforms ``grad, jacobian, vmap, jit`` (``jit`` is a no-op where the engine has none). Elementwise
functions (``sin, exp, sum, stack, where, ...``) live on ``bk.xp``, the engine's own numpy-like module.

Add an engine with ``register_backend("name", MyBackend)``; ``MyBackend`` subclasses :class:`PhysicsBackend`.
pinneapple_core.backend.doc1: PhysicsBackend: one array/derivative/solve API over torch, jax and anything registered.

pinneapple_core.data.doc:
Physics-native data API: ``PhysicsDataset``, ``DataLoader`` and the samplers.

One loader serves a PINN, a neural operator and an inverse problem. A loader takes *sources*, each either a
:class:`PhysicsDataset` (labelled arrays, shuffled and batched) or a :class:`Sampler` (points drawn on demand),
and yields a :class:`Batch` with one group per source::

    loader = DataLoader({"col": CollocationSampler(domain), "bc": BoundarySampler(geometry),
                         "obs": PhysicsDataset(x_obs, u_obs)},
                        batch_size={"col": 1024, "bc": 128, "obs": 16}, steps=2000)
    for batch in loader:
        x = batch["col"]["x"]                  # requires_grad already set: collocation points are differentiated
        ...

Samplers: :class:`CollocationSampler` (interior, uniform / lhs / sobol), :class:`BoundarySampler` (boundary points with
outward normals, whole boundary or a named part), :class:`MeshSampler` (nodes, cell centres or random points in cells),
:class:`TrajectorySampler` (windows of time series), :class:`AdaptiveSampler` (density follows the PDE residual) and
:class:`ActiveSampler` (picks the highest-scoring candidates by an acquisition function).
``physics_aware=True`` (the default) makes the loader set ``requires_grad`` on the points of sources that need
derivatives, convert to the model dtype and device, and attach the coordinate names to ``batch.meta``.

classes.doc1: Draws points on demand. Subclasses implement :meth:`sample` and return a dict of tensors with key ``"x"``.

classes.name: CollocationSampler
classes.doc1: Interior points for the PDE residual. ``domain``: a ``Domain``, a ``Geometry`` or ``{"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)}``. ``strategy``: ``uniform``, ``lhs`` (Latin hypercube) or ``sobol``. Every call draws fresh points, reproducibly from ``seed``.

classes.name: BoundarySampler
classes.doc1: Boundary points with outward unit normals (``"x"``, ``"normal"``). With a ``Geometry``, ``part="x_min"`` samples one named boundary. Normals are needed by Neumann conditions, so the points are differentiable by default.

classes.name: MeshSampler
classes.doc1: Points tied to a mesh: ``mode="nodes"`` (random nodes, or all when ``n >= N``), ``"cells"`` (cell centres) or ``"random"`` (uniform points inside cells, by volume). Returns ``x`` and the node or cell index.

classes.name: TrajectorySampler
classes.doc1: Windows of trajectories ``states (B, T, d)``: ``x`` is ``n_in`` consecutive states, ``y`` the next ``n_out``. For learning dynamics, one-step maps and rollouts. Returns ``x (n, n_in, d)``, ``y (n, n_out, d)``, ``t0`` (start index).

classes.name: AdaptiveSampler
classes.sig: (base, residual_fn, pool_size=20000, exponent=1.0, uniform_fraction=0.2, seed=0) -> None
classes.doc1: Residual-based adaptive sampling: a pool of candidates from ``base``; after ``update(model)`` the points are drawn with probability proportional to ``residual ** exponent`` (mixed with ``uniform_fraction`` of uniform draws so no region is abandoned). ``residual_fn(model, x) -> (P,)`` gives …

classes.name: ActiveSampler
classes.doc1: Acquisition-driven selection: draw ``n_candidates`` from ``base`` and return the ``n`` with the highest ``score_fn(model, x)`` (uncertainty, ensemble variance, expected information, ...). Use it to choose where to run the next expensive simulation or experiment. Differs from …

classes.name: DataLoader
classes.sig: (sources, batch_size=256, steps=None, shuffle=True, drop_last=False, seed=0, physics_aware=True, device=None, dtype=None) -> None
classes.doc1: Batches from datasets and samplers behind one iteration API.

pinneapple_core.domain.doc:
Domain: the region of space a problem lives on.

A :class:`Domain` is an axis-aligned bounding box, optionally cut down by a
signed distance function (negative inside). It answers the three questions a
solver asks of its region: is this point inside, give me points inside, give me
points on the boundary. Boxes work in any dimension; irregular domains come from
the CSG shapes of :mod:`pinneapple_design.geometry.csg` (2D).

>>> from pinneapple_core import Domain
>>> d = Domain.box([0, 0], [2, 1])
>>> d.volume()
2.0
>>> d.sample_interior(128, seed=0).shape
(128, 2)
pinneapple_core.domain.doc1: Domain: the region of space a problem lives on.

classes.name: Domain
classes.doc1: A region of R^d: a box, or a box cut by a signed distance function.

pinneapple_core.fem.doc:
Differentiable P1 finite elements on simplex meshes.

Everything here is written in torch, so the solution of a PDE is differentiable with respect to the
**vertex coordinates**, which is the mesh (shape) gradient. Parametrise the geometry as
``points = f(design_parameters)`` and ``loss.backward()`` returns d(objective)/d(design_parameters).
The linear solve is :func:`torch.linalg.solve`, whose backward pass is the adjoint solve.

Matrices are dense, so this is meant for meshes up to a few thousand nodes: reference cases, shape
optimisation prototypes and tests of larger solvers.

>>> import numpy as np, torch
>>> from pinneapple_core import Mesh
>>> from pinneapple_core.fem import solve_poisson
>>> m = Mesh.interval(0.0, 1.0, 20)
>>> pts = torch.tensor(m.points, dtype=torch.float64)
>>> u = solve_poisson(pts, m.cells, 1.0, m.boundary_nodes())
>>> round(float(u.max()), 4)   # -u'' = 1 on (0,1), exact max 1/8
0.125
pinneapple_core.fem.doc1: Differentiable P1 finite elements on simplex meshes.

functions.name: cell_geometry
functions.doc1: Volumes ``(M,)`` and barycentric gradients ``(M, d+1, d)`` of every cell, differentiable in ``points``.

functions.name: stiffness
functions.doc1: Dense ``(N, N)`` stiffness matrix ``K_ij = integral kappa grad(phi_i) . grad(phi_j)``.

functions.name: mass
functions.doc1: Dense ``(N, N)`` consistent mass matrix ``M_ij = integral phi_i phi_j``.

functions.name: integrate_p1
functions.doc1: Integral of the P1 interpolant of nodal ``values``, differentiable in ``points`` and ``values``.

functions.name: solve_poisson
functions.sig: (points, cells, source, dirichlet_nodes, dirichlet_values=0.0, kappa=1.0) -> Tensor
functions.doc1: Solve ``-div(kappa grad u) = source`` with ``u = g`` on ``dirichlet_nodes``; returns nodal ``u``.

pinneapple_core.field.doc:
Field: values of a physical quantity on a grid, a mesh or a point cloud.

A :class:`Field` ties values to the space they live on, so the same four calls
work on every discretisation::

    f.gradient()         # derivative, as a Field on the same support
    f.divergence()       # trace of the gradient of a vector field
    f.interpolate(x)     # values at arbitrary points
    f.integrate()        # integral over the support

Values have shape ``(N, *components)``: ``(N,)`` for a scalar, ``(N, d)`` for a
vector, ``(N, c, d)`` for a gradient of a vector. :class:`FunctionField` is the
same interface for a callable (an analytic expression or a neural network) with
derivatives from autograd, which is what a PINN needs.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pinneapple_core import Field
>>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 101)
>>> f = Field.on_grid([x], np.sin(np.pi * x))
>>> round(float(f.integrate()), 3)
0.637
pinneapple_core.field.doc1: Field: values of a physical quantity on a grid, a mesh or a point cloud.

classes.name: Grid
classes.doc1: Tensor-product grid. ``axes`` are strictly increasing 1D coordinate arrays; points are ordered with the last axis varying fastest (``indexing="ij"``).

classes.name: PointCloud
classes.doc1: Scattered points. ``weights`` are quadrature weights (they sum to the measure of the region); without them, ``integrate`` falls back to Monte Carlo over ``domain`` and assumes the points are uniform samples of it.

classes.name: Field
classes.doc1: Values on a :class:`Grid`, a :class:`~pinneapple_core.Mesh` or a :class:`PointCloud`.

classes.name: FunctionField
classes.doc1: A field defined by a torch callable ``fn((N, d) tensor) -> (N,) or (N, c)``.

pinneapple_core.func.doc:
``pp.func``: function transforms with scientific semantics, and implicit differentiation.

Two things live here.

**Transforms** wrap :mod:`torch.func` (``grad, jacobian, jacrev, jacfwd, hessian, vmap``) and add
``wrt``: the argument to differentiate, by name or position. A model written as
``model(geometry, mu)`` is differentiated with respect to its geometry with
``jacobian(model, wrt="geometry")``; several arguments return a tuple.

**Implicit differentiation** (:func:`implicit_solve`) gives gradients through a solver call
without differentiating the solver's iterations. If ``x*(theta)`` solves
``residual(x, theta) = 0``, then ``dx*/dtheta = -(dF/dx)^-1 dF/dtheta``; the backward pass is one
linear (adjoint) solve, whatever the forward solver did, including an external code.

>>> import torch
>>> from pinneapple_core import func
>>> f = lambda x, mu: (mu * x ** 2).sum()
>>> func.grad(f, wrt="mu")(torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0]), torch.tensor(3.0)).item()
5.0
pinneapple_core.func.doc1: ``pp.func``: function transforms with scientific semantics, and implicit differentiation.

functions.name: grad
functions.doc1: Gradient of a scalar-valued ``fn`` with respect to the argument(s) ``wrt``.

functions.name: jacrev
functions.doc1: Jacobian by reverse mode: cheap when ``fn`` has few outputs.

functions.name: jacfwd
functions.doc1: Jacobian by forward mode: cheap when ``fn`` has few inputs.

functions.name: jacobian
functions.doc1: Jacobian of ``fn`` with respect to ``wrt``. ``mode`` is ``"rev"``, ``"fwd"`` or ``"auto"`` (forward when the argument has fewer entries than the output has).

functions.name: hessian
functions.doc1: Hessian of a scalar-valued ``fn`` with respect to ``wrt``.

functions.name: vmap
functions.doc1: Vectorise ``fn`` over a batch dimension (``torch.func.vmap``).

functions.name: newton_solve
functions.doc1: Damped Newton iteration for ``residual(x, *params) = 0`` with a dense Jacobian.

functions.name: implicit_solve
functions.doc1: Solve ``residual(x, *params) = 0`` for ``x`` and differentiate through the solution.

pinneapple_core.geometry.doc:
Geometry: a Domain plus named boundaries and a way to mesh it.

>>> from pinneapple_core import Geometry
>>> g = Geometry.box([0, 0], [2, 1])
>>> g.boundary_names
['x_min', 'x_max', 'y_min', 'y_max']
>>> g.mesh(h=0.25).dim
2
pinneapple_core.geometry.doc1: Geometry: a Domain plus named boundaries and a way to mesh it.

classes.name: Geometry
classes.doc1: A :class:`Domain` with named boundary parts.

pinneapple_core.jsonable.doc:
JSON-safe copies of results: NumPy scalars and arrays to Python, NaN/Inf to ``None``, optional rounding.

Every service that returns a result as JSON (the apps, the MCP server, the lab, the data tools) needs the same
conversion; this is the one implementation::

    from pinneapple_core.jsonable import to_jsonable
    json.dumps(to_jsonable({"cl": np.float32(0.61), "field": np.zeros(3), "bad": float("nan")}))
pinneapple_core.jsonable.doc1: JSON-safe copies of results: NumPy scalars and arrays to Python, NaN/Inf to ``None``, optional rounding.

functions.name: round_sig
functions.doc1: ``round(x, digits)`` for ``|x| >= small``, else ``digits`` significant digits (keeps small values exact).

functions.name: to_jsonable
functions.doc1: A copy of ``obj`` that ``json.dumps`` accepts.

pinneapple_core.loss.doc:
``pp.loss``: functional loss terms and a balancer selectable by name.

Terms are plain functions returning a scalar tensor::

    pde(residual)                     mean squared PDE residual (optionally causal)
    boundary(pred, target)            boundary / initial condition mismatch
    conservation(quantity, target)    a conserved quantity or a divergence-free constraint
    energy(e, mode=...)               energy conserved, or not increasing
    symmetry(model, x, transform)     invariance / equivariance under a transformation
    supervised(pred, target, kind)    data fit: mse, mae, huber, relative_l2
    inverse(pred, observed, params)   data misfit plus a prior on the unknown parameters

``combine(terms, weights)`` sums them. For weights that change during training build a
:class:`Balancer` with a strategy name::

    total = pp.loss.combine({"pde": pde(r), "bc": boundary(u_b, g)}, {"pde": 1.0, "bc": 10.0})

    balancer = pp.loss.Balancer("gradnorm", names=["pde", "bc"], model=net)
    total = balancer({"pde": pde(r), "bc": boundary(u_b, g)}, step=i)
    total.backward()

``Balancer.strategies()`` lists the names: the fixed and learned weights, GradNorm, NTK, ReLoBRaLo,
SoftAdapt, augmented Lagrangian, inverse-Dirichlet, learning-rate annealing, PCGrad, an automatic switcher,
and ``"curriculum"`` (weights ramped over the first steps). Causal training of time-dependent residuals is
``pde(residual, t=t, causal_epsilon=...)``.
pinneapple_core.loss.doc1: ``pp.loss``: functional loss terms and a balancer selectable by name.

classes.name: Balancer
classes.sig: (strategy='fixed', names=None, model=None, weights=None, update_every=100, *, schedule=None, steps=1000, shape='linear', **options) -> None
classes.doc1: Loss weighting chosen by name. Call it with the dict of terms to get the weighted total.

functions.name: causal_weights
functions.doc1: Per-point causal weights ``exp(-epsilon * sum of the mean squared residual of earlier time chunks)`` (Wang et al. 2022), detached. ``t`` must be normalised to [0, 1].

functions.name: pde
functions.doc1: Mean squared residual. ``weights`` (one per point) gives a weighted mean ``sum(w r^2) / sum(w)``; ``t`` with ``causal_epsilon`` computes causal weights from the residual itself.

functions.name: boundary
functions.doc1: Mean squared mismatch with the prescribed boundary or initial values.

functions.name: supervised
functions.doc1: Data fit. ``kind``: ``mse``, ``mae``, ``huber`` (``delta``) or ``relative_l2`` (norm of the error over the norm of the target, over the whole batch).

functions.name: conservation
functions.doc1: Squared deviation of a conserved ``quantity`` (total mass, a flux balance, a divergence) from ``target``, divided by ``scale`` when the quantity is not O(1).

functions.name: energy
functions.doc1: Energy along time, ``e`` of shape ``(T,)`` or ``(T, ...)`` ordered in time.

functions.name: symmetry
functions.doc1: Penalty for breaking a symmetry: ``mean((f(T x) - S f(x))^2)``. ``S`` is ``output_transform`` (identity by default, which is invariance; a rotation of a vector output makes it equivariance).

functions.name: inverse
functions.doc1: Misfit to the observations plus ``reg * mean((params - prior)^2)`` on the unknown parameters (prior 0 by default).

functions.name: combine
functions.doc1: Weighted sum of named terms (weight 1 where not given). Weights for terms that are absent raise ``KeyError``: a misspelt name must not silently drop a loss term.

pinneapple_core.mesh.doc:
Mesh: simplex meshes (intervals, triangles, tetrahedra) with P1 calculus.

A :class:`Mesh` is ``points (N, d)`` plus ``cells (M, d+1)`` vertex indices.
Fields on a mesh are nodal (one value per point) and piecewise linear, so
``integrate`` is exact for P1 data and ``gradient`` is exact for linear data.

>>> from pinneapple_core import Mesh
>>> m = Mesh.structured([0, 0], [1, 1], (8, 8))
>>> m.n_cells
128
pinneapple_core.mesh.doc1: Mesh: simplex meshes (intervals, triangles, tetrahedra) with P1 calculus.

classes.name: Mesh
classes.doc1: Unstructured simplex mesh in R^d (d = 1, 2 or 3).

pinneapple_core.module.doc:
PhysicsModule: composable models and solvers, the ``nn.Module`` of physics.

Everything is a torch module with a ``kind``, so a neural network, a numerical solver and a mix of the two
compose with the same few classes::

    import torch.nn as nn
    from pinneapple_core.module import Hybrid, SolverModule

    coarse = SolverModule(coarse_fem_solve)                       # any differentiable function, or a pp.solve method
    model = Hybrid(coarse, nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 32), nn.Tanh(), nn.Linear(32, 1)), mode="residual")
    model.fit(x, y, epochs=200)                                  # trains the corrector through the solver

* :class:`PhysicsModule`  base class: ``describe()``, ``num_parameters()``, a small ``fit``.
* :class:`Sequential`     chain components, each feeding the next.
* :class:`SolverModule`   a solver as a component: ``fn`` (autograd flows through it), optional trainable
  parameters, or :meth:`SolverModule.from_method` for any ``pp.solve`` backend (not differentiable).
* :class:`Hybrid`         solver output combined with a neural correction.
pinneapple_core.module.doc1: PhysicsModule: composable models and solvers, the ``nn.Module`` of physics.

classes.name: PhysicsModule
classes.doc1: Base class for models and solvers. Subclass it and implement ``forward``.

classes.name: Lambda
classes.doc1: Wrap a plain function (no parameters) as a component.

classes.name: Sequential
classes.doc1: Chain components: the output of each is the input of the next. Accepts modules, solvers and plain functions; pass ``(name, module)`` pairs or an ``OrderedDict`` to name them.

classes.name: SolverModule
classes.doc1: A solver as a component.

classes.name: Hybrid
classes.doc1: A solver plus a neural correction.

pinneapple_core.onboarding.doc:
pinneapple_core.onboarding — the first hour with PINNeAPPle.

Everything a new user needs before writing physics code:

* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.doctor.doctor` checks the installation against a *profile*
  (``start``, ``cfd``, ``research``, ``enterprise``) and prints one fix command per problem.
* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.recommend.recommend` turns a problem described in one
  sentence, in English or Portuguese, into a preset, a method and a runnable snippet, and says why.
* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.catalog.card` prints what a preset takes, what it gives back
  and the smallest program that uses it.
* :func:`~pinneapple_core.onboarding.newproject.new_project` writes a standalone project (not an
  example inside this repository) with a case file, a runner and a README, at three levels of
  programming: ``plain`` (edit a YAML, never touch Python), ``research`` (experiment manifests and
  a notebook) and ``cfd`` (geometry and solver campaigns).

The four are also reachable from the command line as ``pinneapple doctor``, ``pinneapple
recommend``, ``pinneapple card`` and ``pinneapple new``.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> pp.doctor()                       # is this installation ready for what I want to do?
>>> pp.recommend("heat conduction in a fin")   # which preset and method should I start from?
>>> pp.card("burgers_1d")             # what does it take, what does it give back?
>>> pp.new("my_study", template="plain")       # a folder I can grow …
pinneapple_core.onboarding.doc1: pinneapple_core.onboarding — the first hour with PINNeAPPle.

pinneapple_core.onboarding.catalog.doc:
The preset catalogue: what a preset takes, what it gives back, and the smallest program that uses it.

The preset registry (``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets``) stores a factory per name and
nothing else: no description, no tags, no audience. That is fine for the solvers and useless for a
person choosing what to run. This module adds the missing half, derived from the live
:class:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.ProblemSpec` where the spec can answer and curated
by hand where it cannot:

* :func:`card` — one preset as a :class:`Card`: coordinates, fields, conditions, the method that
  runs today, and a snippet that executes as printed.
* :func:`search` — free text, English or Portuguese, to presets, with the terms that matched.
* :func:`snippet` — the smallest correct program for one preset, choosing a method that exists.

Everything here runs offline and without training. ``search`` is keyword scoring, not a model, and
it says so: every hit carries the terms that matched so the user can judge it.
pinneapple_core.onboarding.catalog.doc1: The preset catalogue: what a preset takes, what it gives back, and the smallest program that uses it.

pinneapple_core.onboarding.cli.doc:
``pinneapple doctor | recommend | card | new``: the four commands a new user needs first.

They are separate from ``pinneapple check`` (which lints results) because they answer questions
about *getting started*, not about a result. All four run offline and print plain text: no colour,
no box drawing, readable in a terminal, a log or a CI transcript.
pinneapple_core.onboarding.cli.doc1: ``pinneapple doctor | recommend | card | new``: the four commands a new user needs first.

functions.name: main
functions.doc1: ``pinneapple <doctor|recommend|card|new> ...``

pinneapple_core.onboarding.doctor.doc:
Is this installation ready for what I want to do? One check per thing, one fix per failure.

``pp.info()`` answers "what is in the library". ``pp.doctor()`` answers the question a new user
actually has, which is narrower and more useful: *for the work I intend to do, is anything
missing?* The intent is named by a profile:

=============  ==========================================================================
profile        for
=============  ==========================================================================
``start``      the first week: solve a preset, plot a field, train one small network
``cfd``        geometry to mesh to an OpenFOAM/CalculiX campaign, plus 3-D viewing
``research``   PINNs, operators, uncertainty, JAX, publication figures
``enterprise`` serving, signatures, the physics linter in CI, the hub and the MCP server
``all``        every extra the package declares
=============  ==========================================================================

Every failure prints the exact command that fixes it, and nothing is reported as fine when it was
not checked: a check that cannot run says so.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> report = pp.doctor("cfd")          # returns the report and prints it
>>> report.ok                          # True when nothing required is missing
pinneapple_core.onboarding.doctor.doc1: Is this installation ready for what I want to do? One check per thing, one fix per failure.

classes.name: Check
classes.doc1: One thing that was checked. ``ok`` is None when the check could not run.

functions.name: profiles
functions.doc1: The profiles ``doctor`` accepts, with the sentence that describes each one.

functions.name: doctor
functions.doc1: Check this installation against a profile and, with ``verbose``, print the report.

pinneapple_core.onboarding.newproject.doc:
``pp.new`` / ``pinneapple new``: a project a person can grow, outside this repository.

The repository's own scaffold (``python -m pinneapple_lab scaffold``) creates an *example* of the
library, wired into the Lab here. A user needs the opposite: a folder of their own, with no
dependency on this checkout, that runs on a clean install and survives being copied to a colleague.

Three templates, by how much Python the user wants to write:

``plain``
    The user edits ``case.yaml`` and nothing else. ``run.py`` resolves the problem (from a preset
    or from a sentence), solves it with the cheapest method that works, saves the field, a figure,
    and a one-page report. No Python is required to go from "my problem" to "a number and a plot".
``research``
    ``study.py`` solves, compares against the classical answer where one exists, records metrics
    and checks, and writes an experiment manifest the Lab can grade, next to a notebook.
``cfd``
    A campaign runner: one preset, a parameter swept over a list, the reference solver per case,
    a CSV of quantities of interest and a convergence figure, with the geometry hook written down.

Every generated file runs as written on a clean ``pip install pinneapple``; the folders the user
will fill are created; and no path depends on the directory the script was launched from.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> path = pp.new("my_study", template="plain")      # writes ./my_study and prints the next step
pinneapple_core.onboarding.newproject.doc1: ``pp.new`` / ``pinneapple new``: a project a person can grow, outside this repository.

functions.name: plan
functions.doc1: What ``new_project`` would write, without writing it. Useful for a dry run and for tests.

functions.name: new_project
functions.doc1: Write a standalone project and return its folder.

pinneapple_core.onboarding.recommend.doc:
One sentence in, a plan out: which preset, which method, which model, and why.

A new user arrives with a problem, not with a preset name. This module answers the three
questions they actually have, in the order they have them:

1. which preset is closest to my problem (and what do the near ones differ in),
2. which method gives an answer today without training anything,
3. which model to train once the problem description is right.

The ranking is keyword scoring over a curated catalogue (:mod:`pinneapple_core.onboarding.catalog`),
so it can be wrong, and it says how it decided: every recommendation carries the terms that matched
and the terms that did not. When nothing matches, it says so and routes to
``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.capabilities.suggest_problem_spec`` and to ``pp.new`` instead
of inventing a preset.
pinneapple_core.onboarding.recommend.doc1: One sentence in, a plan out: which preset, which method, which model, and why.

classes.name: Recommendation
classes.sig: (query, preset, method, model, confidence, reason, snippet, matched, alternatives, next_steps, notes, swapped_from)
classes.doc1: What to run, why this, and what to run next. ``explain()`` is the text a person reads.

functions.name: recommend
functions.doc1: Turn a problem description into a preset, a method and a model, with the reasons.

pinneapple_core.operators.doc:
Physics operators: ``grad, div, curl, laplacian, jacobian, hessian, integrate, flux``.

The ``torch.nn.functional`` of physics: one function per operator that works the same
on a continuous field (a torch callable, derivatives by autograd), on a grid, on a
simplex mesh and on a point cloud (a :class:`~pinneapple_core.Field`).

* On a :class:`Field` the operator takes no point argument and returns a ``Field``
  on the same support (``integrate`` and ``flux`` return numbers).
* On a callable or :class:`FunctionField` it takes the evaluation points ``x`` and
  returns a tensor that keeps the autograd graph.

Shape convention: ``(N,)`` scalar, ``(N, d)`` vector, ``jacobian`` is ``(N, c, d)``
with ``J[n, i, j] = d f_i / d x_j``, ``hessian`` is ``(N, d, d)``.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pinneapple_core import Field, laplacian
>>> x = np.linspace(0, 1, 41)
>>> u = Field.on_grid([x, x], lambda p: p[:, 0] ** 2 + 3 * p[:, 1] ** 2)
>>> round(float(laplacian(u).values[500]), 6)
8.0

pinneapple_core.optim.doc:
``PhysicsOptimizer(parameters, objective, constraints)``: one interface for several optimizer families.

>>> import torch
>>> from pinneapple_core.optim import PhysicsOptimizer, ineq
>>> opt = PhysicsOptimizer({"x": (-3, 3), "y": (-3, 3)},
...                        objective=lambda v: (v[0] - 2) ** 2 + (v[1] - 1) ** 2,
...                        constraints=[ineq(lambda v: v[0] + v[1] - 2)])       # x + y <= 2
>>> r = opt.minimize("slsqp")
>>> [round(float(t), 3) for t in r.x]
[1.5, 0.5]

The problem (parameters with bounds, an objective, inequality ``g(x) <= 0`` and equality ``h(x) = 0``
constraints) is written once. ``minimize(method)`` picks the family:

========================  =================================================================  ==========================
method                    what it is                                                          needs
========================  =================================================================  ==========================
``slsqp``                 sequential quadratic programming, autograd gradients               a torch objective
``adjoint``               the same SQP with a gradient you supply (adjoint, implicit solve)   ``grad=``
``penalty``               projected Adam on the objective plus a growing quadratic penalty    a torch objective
``augmented_lagrangian``  projected Adam with multiplier updates (exact constraints)           a torch objective
``differential_evolution`` population search, no …

Runtime pieces for app servers (apps/*, the MCP server, self-hosted services), standard library only.

==================  ======================================================================================

                    max concurrent jobs across server workers, resume after a restart
``APIKeyStore``     API keys: created once, stored hashed, revocable; sent as ``X-API-Key``
``UsageMeter``      usage per app, principal and unit with monthly free limits (``<PREFIX>_FREE_<UNIT>``)
``UploadStore``     uploads with a size limit, allowed suffixes, safe names and SHA-256
``data_dir``        where an app keeps this state (``<PREFIX>_DATA_DIR``, else ``PINNEAPPLE_APP_DATA/<app>``)
==================  ======================================================================================

The FastAPI routes on top of these are in ``apps/_shared/appkit.py`` (``install_runtime``).

pinneapple_core.service.apikeys.doc:
API keys for app servers: created once (the plain key is shown only then), stored as SHA-256, revocable.

    keys = APIKeyStore("/data/service.sqlite", app="campaign")
    created = keys.create("ci pipeline")                 # {"id": ..., "key": "pk_...", ...}; keep created["key"]
    keys.verify(created["key"])["id"] == created["id"]
    keys.revoke(created["id"])

Keys are 32 random bytes, so a plain SHA-256 is enough to store them (no password stretching needed); lookup is by
hash. Clients send the key in the ``X-API-Key`` header.
pinneapple_core.service.apikeys.doc1: API keys for app servers: created once (the plain key is shown only then), stored as SHA-256, revocable.

pinneapple_core.service.db.doc1: SQLite helpers shared by the service stores: one connection per thread, WAL, immediate transactions.

classes.doc1: One connection per thread to the same file (a connection must not be shared by concurrent transactions).

pinneapple_core.service.jobs.doc:
A persistent job queue for app servers: SQLite state, thread or process workers, progress, logs, cancel, retry.

    queue = JobQueue("/data/jobs.sqlite", app="campaign", max_concurrent=2)
    queue.register("plan", plan_campaign)               # fn(params: dict, ctx: JobContext) -> dict (JSON-able)
    job_id = queue.submit("plan", {"n": 40}, owner="key:ab12cd34")
    queue.wait(job_id)["status"]                        # "done"

``fn`` reports through ``ctx.progress(0.3, "sampling")`` and ``ctx.log("...")``; ``ctx.progress`` raises
:class:`JobCancelled` once a cancel was requested, so cancellation is cooperative in thread mode. In process mode
(``executor="process"``, ``fn`` must be importable at module level) the job runs in its own interpreter and cancel
or the time limit kills it.

The state lives in SQLite (WAL), so several server workers (``uvicorn --workers 2``) share one queue: a job is
claimed atomically, ``max_concurrent`` holds across all of them, and each running job has a heartbeat. A job whose
worker died (restart, crash) is found by its stale heartbeat and put back in the queue (``resume_interrupted``),
at most ``max_retries + 1`` extra times, then marked failed.
pinneapple_core.service.jobs.doc1: A persistent job queue for app servers: SQLite state, thread or process workers, progress, logs, cancel, retry.

pinneapple_core.service.metering.doc:
Usage metering per app, principal and unit, with free limits per calendar month (UTC).

    meter = UsageMeter("/data/service.sqlite", app="campaign",
                       limits={"cases_planned": 500, "campaigns": 20})
    meter.consume("ip:203.0.113.7", "cases_planned", 40)    # records it, or raises UsageLimitExceeded
    meter.usage("ip:203.0.113.7")                            # {"period": "2026-10", "units": {...}}

A principal is whoever the use is counted against: ``key:<id>`` (API key), ``user:<name>`` (login) or ``ip:<addr>``
(anonymous). Limits come from code defaults and the environment: ``<PREFIX>_FREE_<UNIT>`` (``CAMPAIGN_FREE_
CASES_PLANNED=1000``; ``unlimited`` or ``-1`` removes the limit). This is metering only; billing is not here.

Uploaded files with a size limit, safe names and a SHA-256, stored under one directory.

    store = UploadStore("/data/uploads", max_bytes=50 * 2**20, allowed_suffixes={".csv", ".parquet", ".json"})
    rec = store.save("cases.csv", fileobj, owner="ip:203.0.113.7")   # streams; UploadTooLarge past the limit

pinneapple_core.transforms.doc:
``pp.transforms``: composable, invertible transforms for tables, datasets and problems, with provenance.

A transform works on a *table* (``{name: array or tensor}``, columns for coordinates and fields), on a
:class:`~pinneapple_core.data.PhysicsDataset`, and, for the scaling transforms, on a ``PhysicalProblem``::

    nd = Nondimensionalize(problem)               # coordinates to [0, 1], fields to O(1), PDE parameters rescaled
    small = nd.apply(problem)                     # a new problem; small.metadata["transforms"] records what was done
    solve = nd.pull_back(solution.predict)        # predictions in the original coordinates and units

    t = Scale({"x": 2.0}) >> Coordinate("log", ("t",), ("logt",)) >> FourierFeatures(("x",), 8)
    out = t.forward(table); back = t.inverse(out)   # back == table

``a >> b`` composes (inverse runs in reverse order); a composition is invertible when every step is. Every ``apply`` appends a
record ``{name, params, invertible, input/output fingerprint}`` to the object's provenance (``problem.metadata["transforms"]``,
``dataset.provenance``).

Transforms: :class:`Scale`, :class:`Nondimensionalize`, :class:`Coordinate` (polar, cylindrical, spherical, log),
:class:`Symmetry` (reflection, rotation, with vector fields), :class:`Periodic` (cos/sin embedding of a periodic coordinate),
:class:`FourierFeatures` (random Fourier features). Problem-level support is for the scaling transforms only: the others act on
data or on model inputs, and …

On a ``PhysicalProblem`` it rescales the coordinates, the domain, the conditions and, for the PDEs in :func:`list_pde_rules`, the PDE parameters; PDEs without a rule raise rather than be left inconsistent. A source term is rescaled with …

Override with …

classes.doc1: Change of coordinates on table columns. ``kind``: ``polar`` ((x, y) -> (r, theta)), ``cylindrical`` ((x, y, z) -> (r, theta, z)), ``spherical`` ((x, y, z) -> (r, theta from +z, phi)) and ``log`` (x -> ln x, x > 0). Vector fields are not transformed (their components stay Cartesian); give ``center`` …

pinneapple_core.workflows.doc:
Simulation workflows: a DAG of steps, executors and adapters as plugins, traceable runs, datasets from runs.

It orchestrates tools that already exist (solvers, Docker, Slurm); it does not replace them.

==========================  ========================================================================================
``Workflow``, ``Step``      the DAG: dependencies, order, cycle check, JSON; ``workflow_from_cases`` per case table
``WorkflowRunner``          runs, resume, per-step state and log, retries, skip-done by content hash, cancel
``Executor`` + registry     where commands run: ``local``, ``docker``, ``slurm`` (sbatch scripts, dry run by
                            default); ``register_executor(name, cls)`` adds one
``Adapter`` + registry      what a step kind does: ``command``, ``python``, ``openfoam``, ``calculix``;
                            ``register_adapter(adapter)`` adds one (a GUI-driven step, another solver)
``dataset_from_run``        finished runs -> ``DatasetSpec`` + table (CSV / Parquet / HDF5) for training
``TEMPLATES``               whitelisted workflows for public servers (Python slab heating, CalculiX beam,
                            OpenFOAM cavity)
==========================  ========================================================================================

    from pinneapple_core.workflows import TEMPLATES, WorkflowRunner, dataset_from_run
    t = TEMPLATES["slab_heat"]
    cases = t.example_cases(6)
    runner = …
pinneapple_core.workflows.doc1: Simulation workflows: a DAG of steps, executors and adapters as plugins, traceable runs, datasets from runs.

pinneapple_core.workflows.adapters.doc:
Adapters: what a step of a given ``kind`` does. Each prepares its directory, runs commands through the step's
executor and returns its outputs (a JSON-able dict).

=============  ==================================================================================================
``command``    ``argv`` (list, ``{param}`` placeholders filled); outputs: ``outputs.json`` if the command wrote one
``python``     ``function: "module:fn"`` called in-process as ``fn(params, ctx)`` (local executor only), or
               ``script: path`` run with the executor as ``python script params.json``; outputs as for ``command``
``openfoam``   copies a case (``case`` directory, or ``case_from`` an upstream step), applies ``edits``
               (``openfoam.campaign.edit_file``), runs ``commands`` (default blockMesh + the solver) and reads the
               solver log health (``openfoam.campaign.parse_solver_log``)
``calculix``   copies ``inp`` (a file, or ``inp_from`` an upstream step's ``<job>.inp``), runs ``ccx -i <job>`` and
               reads the .frd (``calculix.frd.read_frd``): maximum displacement, node count
=============  ==================================================================================================

A new kind::

    class GuiStep(Adapter):
        kind = "gui"
        def run(self, ctx: StepContext) -> dict: ...
    register_adapter(GuiStep())

pinneapple_core.workflows.dag.doc:
Workflows as a DAG of steps: definition, validation (unknown dependencies, cycles), order, JSON.

    wf = Workflow("beam", [Step("mesh", "python", {"function": "pkg.mod:make_deck"}),
                           Step("solve", "calculix", {"inp_from": "mesh", "job": "job"}, needs=["mesh"])])
    wf.order()            # ["mesh", "solve"]
    wf.save("beam.workflow.json"); Workflow.load("beam.workflow.json")

``kind`` names an adapter (``command``, ``python``, ``openfoam``, ``calculix`` or one registered with
``register_adapter``); ``executor`` names an executor (``local``, ``docker``, ``slurm`` or one registered with
``register_executor``). ``workflow_from_cases`` expands a step template once per case of a table.

pinneapple_core.workflows.datasets.doc:
From a case table to a workflow, and from finished runs to a training dataset (``DatasetSpec`` + table).

    cases, skeleton = read_cases("campaign_cases.parquet")          # a Campaign Planner export (or any table)
    wf = workflow_from_cases("sweep", cases.to_dict("records"), template, id_column="case_id")
    summary = WorkflowRunner(root).run(wf)
    spec, path = dataset_from_run(runner, summary["id"], cases, output_step="solve", path="dataset.parquet",
                                  skeleton=skeleton)

Rows are the cases; columns are the case parameters, then the numeric outputs of ``output_step`` (nested dicts are
flattened as ``a.b``), then ``status`` and ``run_step``. Cases whose step did not finish keep empty outputs, and the
spec is marked ``partial``.

pinneapple_core.workflows.engine.doc:
Run workflows: traceable runs, per-step logs and states, retries, resume, skip-done by content hash.

    runner = WorkflowRunner("/data/runner")
    summary = runner.run(workflow)                    # a new run id
    runner.run(workflow, run_id=summary["run_id"])    # resume: done steps stay done, the rest runs again
    runner.steps(run_id), runner.log(run_id, "c01.solve")

Layout: ``<root>/runner.sqlite`` (runs, steps, the content-hash cache) and ``<root>/runs/<run id>/<step id>/``
(the step's files and ``log.txt``).

**Skip-done.** A step's hash covers its kind, its parameters, the content (SHA-256) of its ``inputs`` files and the
hashes of the steps it needs. A step whose hash already finished in any run, and whose directory still exists, is
not run again: it is marked ``skipped`` and its outputs and directory are reused.

**States.** pending, running, done, failed, skipped (done earlier, reused), cancelled (by request, or because a step
it needs failed). ``fail_fast`` stops starting new steps after a failure; otherwise independent branches go on.
A run interrupted by a crash or restart has steps left ``running``: running it again with the same id resumes it.

pinneapple_core.workflows.executors.doc:
Executors: where a step's command runs. A plugin interface, so other tools (a GUI agent, a cluster) add theirs.

=============  ==================================================================================================
``local``      a subprocess on this machine: timeout, environment, working directory, output to the step log
``docker``     ``docker run --rm`` with the step directory mounted at /work (no network, memory/CPU limits)
``slurm``      an sbatch script per step; ``dry_run=True`` (default) writes the script and does not submit it
=============  ==================================================================================================

Write your own::

    class MyExecutor(Executor):
        name = "mine"
        def run(self, argv, *, cwd, env=None, timeout=None, log=print, should_stop=lambda: False) -> ExecResult:
            ...
    register_executor("mine", MyExecutor)       # steps with executor="mine" now use it

An executor only runs commands (argv lists). It does not install solvers, schedule a queue or replace Slurm: it
hands the command to what is already there.

Active Learning for adaptive collocation in PINN training.

Strategies:
- ResidualBasedAL: sample where PDE residual is highest
- VarianceBasedAL: sample where model output variance is highest (needs UQ)

PINN-style training) and a dense structured-grid volume time series (for
grid-based neural operators like :class:`~pinneapple_neural.
architectures.neural_operators.fno.FNO3d`).

Promoted from the splash-pinneapple downstream project's own
``pipeline/splash_dataset.py`` / ``pipeline/splash_mesh.py`` (real,
already-used-in-production ingestion code, not a rewrite) so any project

parsing, a mesh cache to skip repeated (expensive) polyMesh
reconstruction, and (new here) reshaping into dense structured-grid
volumes for a structured single-block mesh -- none of …

pinneapple_data.audit.doc:
Physics audit of a training dataset: does the data solve its PDE? Split leakage, near duplicates, diversity and
units (#700). NumPy/SciPy only.

A model trained on wrong data inherits the error and model-level checks may never see it. Two open bugs of a widely
used library show how: generated Darcy data that did not solve the documented equation (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036) and
permeability samples with far less diversity than documented (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035). This audit checks the data
itself, before anyone trains on it.

Data layout: a split is a mapping ``{column: array}`` whose first axis is the sample (``(n,)`` for tabular columns,
``(n, ny, nx)`` for fields), as returned by ``pp.datasets.load`` or an ``.npz`` with ``<split>__<column>`` keys.

Checks (each returns pass / fail / not applicable with its evidence):

``finite``        every value finite.
``physics``       per-sample consistency with the stated PDE in the dataset's own discretisation
                  (:class:`DatasetPhysics`). Built in: ``"darcy"`` (``-div(a grad u) = f``, ``u = 0`` on the unit
                  square, cell-centred, the discretisation of ``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` and of the zoo set
                  ``darcy_2d_li2021``): the error of each stored ``u`` against the solution of the same discrete
                  problem, ``||u - A^-1 f|| / ||A^-1 f||`` (the residual measured in the ``A^-1`` norm), the boundary
                  values and the discrete flux balance. Distribution, …

pinneapple_data.cae.compare.doc:
Compare two results field by field: simulation vs simulation (different meshes or models), vs experiment
(sensor tables), vs AI predictions (point tables or meshes), vs analytical or benchmark data.

The candidate is interpolated onto the reference locations (cell centres for cell fields, nodes for point fields):
directly when both use the same locations, otherwise by linear (Delaunay) interpolation inside the candidate's
domain and nearest-neighbour outside it (counted and reported). Metrics per field and per component: MAE, RMSE,
maximum absolute error and where, bias, relative L2 error, NRMSE (RMSE / reference range), R². Cell fields are
volume-weighted when cell volumes are known.

pinneapple_data.collocation.doc:
Automated collocation point generation for PINN training.

Provides flexible, strategy-aware sampling from:
- Rectangular/hyperrectangular domains (from bounds or ProblemSpec)
- SDF-defined domains (from pinneapple_geom)
- Mesh-defined domains (from Mesh2D / MeshData)
- Pre-built PhysicsDomain2D objects

Sampling strategies:
- uniform   : independent uniform random
- lhs       : Latin Hypercube Sampling (better space-filling)
- sobol     : Sobol quasi-random sequence (very uniform)
- adaptive  : residual-based adaptive sampling (requires a trained model)

All outputs are numpy float32 arrays in a standard dict-batch format
compatible with the PINN training pipeline.

pinneapple_data.contracts.doc:
Open data contracts shared by the PINNeAPPle apps: ``ParameterSpace``, ``DatasetSpec``, ``ModelRef``,
``StudyResult``.

Every app imports and exports these, so a design of experiments from one app is the input of a run campaign in
another, whose finished runs become a dataset for a surrogate, whose model reference goes into an uncertainty study.
JSON (or YAML) on disk, JSON Schema for other languages (``schemas/`` in this package), tables as CSV / Parquet /
HDF5 with a ``.contract.json`` sidecar::

    from pinneapple_data.contracts import Parameter, ParameterSpace, DatasetSpec, write_table, read_table

    space = ParameterSpace(name="fin", parameters=[
        Parameter(name="height", low=0.01, high=0.05, unit="m", group="geometry"),
        Parameter(name="material", kind="categorical", values=["Al6061", "Cu"], group="material")],
        constraints=["height <= 0.04 or material == 'Al6061'"])
    cases = space.from_unit([[0.5, 0.2], [0.9, 0.8]])
    cases = cases[space.feasible(cases)]

pinneapple_data.contracts.models.doc:
The four data contracts shared by the PINNeAPPle apps and the library.

=================  ===========================================================================================
``ParameterSpace``  what may vary in a study: geometry, materials, boundary conditions, operating point, with
                    bounds, units, log scaling, categories and constraints between parameters
``DatasetSpec``     a table of cases or samples on disk: columns (inputs / outputs / ids) with units, the files
                    and their SHA-256, splits, the parameter space it samples and where it came from
``ModelRef``        a trained model somewhere (zoo, file, hub): its inputs and outputs, the dataset it was
                    trained on, held-out metrics and the range it is valid in
``StudyResult``     the outcome of a study (design of experiments, campaign, UQ, sensitivity, optimisation,
                    calibration, validation): a table, metrics, the checks that ran and their records, artifacts
=================  ===========================================================================================

Every contract is a pydantic model with ``kind`` and ``schema_version`` fields, so a file says what it is::

    space = ParameterSpace(name="fin", parameters=[Parameter(name="h", low=0.01, high=0.05, unit="m")])
    space.save("fin.space.json")
    assert load("fin.space.json") == space
    ParameterSpace.json_schema()          # JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for other languages …

Tables on disk with their contract: CSV, Parquet and HDF5, each with a JSON sidecar.

``write_table(df, "cases.parquet", contract)`` writes the table and ``cases.parquet.contract.json`` next to it.

pinneapple_data.data_health.doc:
Engineering data health: a physics-aware quality report for sensor / test / plant data.

``load_table(bytes, filename)`` reads CSV/TSV (delimiter and decimal comma detected), Excel,
Parquet, JSON and HDF5 (1-D datasets, with ``units`` attributes when present).
``analyze(df)`` returns a JSON-ready report:

* **Units and quantities** of every column, from the header (:mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`).
* **Completeness**: missing values and long missing runs.
* **Time axis**: timestamps that go backwards, duplicates, irregular sampling, gaps.
* **Validity**: physically impossible values (below absolute zero, relative humidity above 100 %,
  pressure below vacuum), sentinel / error codes (-999, 9999, 32767...), a unit that does not fit
  the values (a "°C" column that holds kelvin) and a unit that changes mid-recording.
* **Signal quality**: stuck sensors (flat lines), spikes (Hampel filter), clipping at a range limit,
  constant columns, coarse resolution.
* **Physics consistency** (only when the columns allow it): the thermal energy balance
  Q = rho * V * cp * dT between a supply/return temperature pair, the flow and the reported
  heat rate. A flow meter that under-reads produces plausible values one column at a time; only
  the balance shows it.
* **Score**: every issue has a severity and the share of the data it affects. Each category's score
  is 100 minus its issue penalties; the overall score is the weighted mean of the categories that
  apply. The formula is …

pinneapple_data.datasets.download.doc:
Download a URL once into a local cache, with retries (standard library only).

    >>> from pinneapple_data.datasets.download import fetch_cached
    >>> path = fetch_cached("https://example.org/catalog.csv", "data/.cache")
    >>> text = path.read_text()

The cache file is named after the MD5 hash of the URL (plus the URL's file extension), so the same URL is fetched
once and different URLs never collide. The body is written to a temporary file and renamed when complete: an
interrupted download never leaves a truncated file that a later call would mistake for a cached one.

pinneapple_data.doe.designs.doc:
Designs of experiments over a :class:`~pinneapple_data.contracts.ParameterSpace`.

Every design is built in the unit hypercube of the free parameters and mapped to values by the space (log scales,
integers, categories), then filtered by the space's bounds and constraints (and an optional ``feasible`` callable
for checks that are not expressions, such as a geometry validity test).

=======================  =====================================================================================
``lhs``                  Latin hypercube (scipy.stats.qmc), one point per stratum in every 1-D projection
``maximin``              the Latin hypercube with the largest minimum distance among ``n_restarts`` random ones
``sobol`` / ``halton``   scrambled low-discrepancy sequences (Sobol balance needs n = 2^m)
``random``               uniform random (reference only: clusters and gaps)
``full_factorial``       every combination of ``levels`` per parameter (all values of categories / integers)
``fractional_factorial`` two-level 2^(k-p) design with generated factors; reports the generators and resolution
``infill``               sequential: new points as far as possible from the existing cases (greedy maximin over a
                         Sobol candidate pool); with ``outputs`` the distance is weighted up where the existing
                         outputs vary most among neighbours (adaptive refinement)
=======================  …

pinneapple_data.expressions.doc:
Safe evaluation of constraint expressions such as ``"chord - 2 * thickness >= 0.01"``.

Only arithmetic, comparisons, ``and`` / ``or`` / ``not``, parameter names, numbers, strings and a few math functions
are allowed; anything else (attribute access, calls to other functions, subscripts, lambdas) is refused before the
expression runs. Every name is a column, so one call checks a whole table of cases at once.

The expression is interpreted node by node, never handed to ``eval``: this is the evaluator for any formula a user
sends to a server (constraints, boundary values, source terms). ``functions=`` replaces the callable table and
:func:`check` validates an expression for another consumer (e.g. before ``sympy.sympify``).
pinneapple_data.expressions.doc1: Safe evaluation of constraint expressions such as ``"chord - 2 * thickness >= 0.01"``.

pinneapple_data.formfill.doc:
Fill engineering forms from the documents that hold the data: read datasheets and specifications, find every item a
form asks for with its source, report conflicts between documents and missing data, and fill the fillable PDF.

The engine is generic; a ``FormSpec`` says what one form asks for. Built-in: ASME Form U-DR-1. Any other fillable
PDF works through ``FormSpec.from_pdf`` (or a JSON spec), and a local Ollama model can read what the rules miss.

>>> from pinneapple_data import formfill as ff
>>> spec = ff.get_spec("asme_u-dr-1")                       # or ff.FormSpec.from_pdf(blank) / ff.FormSpec.load(path)
>>> docs = [ff.read_document(p) for p in ("spec.pdf", "process.pdf", "mech.pdf")]      # priority order
>>> comp = ff.compile(docs, [c for d in docs for c in ff.extract_rules(d, spec)], spec)
>>> comp.gaps(), comp.conflicts(), comp.record()            # record(): the data for other forms and calculations
>>> pdf = ff.fill_pdf(open("blank.pdf", "rb").read(), comp)
pinneapple_data.formfill.doc1: Fill engineering forms from the documents that hold the data: read datasheets and specifications, find every item a form asks for with its source, report conflicts between documents and missing data, and fill the fillable PDF.

pinneapple_data.formfill.extract.doc:
Read datasheets and specifications, find each answer a form asks for, and keep where every value came from.

Pipeline: ``read_document`` (text per page plus the tables pdfplumber finds) -> ``extract_rules`` (the spec's label
patterns, applied to table cells and to text lines) -> optional ``llm.extract_with_llm`` (a local Ollama model) ->
``compile`` (one decision per item: value from the highest-priority document, conflicts and gaps reported).

Every candidate keeps the document, page and the exact text it was read from, so an engineer can check any value
in one click instead of trusting the tool.
pinneapple_data.formfill.extract.doc1: Read datasheets and specifications, find each answer a form asks for, and keep where every value came from.

pinneapple_data.formfill.llm.doc:
Optional extraction with a local LLM served by Ollama, for documents the label rules cannot read (free-form
specifications, odd layouts, forms whose items have no usual label).

Documents never leave the machine: the text of each document (with its tables and page numbers) is sent to an
Ollama server you run (``ollama serve``), by default ``http://localhost:11434``. The model answers in a JSON schema
built from the form spec (Ollama structured outputs) with, for each item it finds, the value, the page and the
**exact text it read it from**. An answer is kept only if

* that quote is found in the document's own text (whitespace and case ignored), and
* for text, numbers and quantities, the value itself is in the quote,

so a value the model made up is rejected and listed, never silently used. Accepted values go through the same parser
as the rule-based ones (units, yes/no, options).

Configuration: ``OllamaClient(url, model)`` or the environment variables ``OLLAMA_HOST`` (server URL) and
``PINNEAPPLE_OLLAMA_MODEL`` (any model you pulled with ``ollama pull`` that supports structured outputs). Only the
Python standard library is used.
pinneapple_data.formfill.llm.doc1: Optional extraction with a local LLM served by Ollama, for documents the label rules cannot read (free-form specifications, odd layouts, forms whose items have no usual label).

pinneapple_data.formfill.ocr.doc:
OCR for scanned pages (pages without a text layer), with Tesseract.

Datasheets are tables, and table grid lines are what OCR gets wrong: a border next to "1.27" is read as "427". So each
page is rendered at 300 dpi, deskewed, its grid lines are detected and erased before Tesseract reads it, and the
detected lines are then used to put every word back in its table cell. The result has the same shape as a page with a
text layer (text lines + table rows), so the same rules read it, and every word keeps Tesseract's confidence: values
read by OCR are marked as such, with their confidence, for the engineer to check against the scan.

Needs the ``tesseract`` program (``apt install tesseract-ocr``, or set ``TESSERACT_CMD``); page rendering uses
pypdfium2, which pdfplumber already depends on.

pinneapple_data.formfill.spec.doc:
What a form asks for, how documents phrase each item, and where each answer goes in the fillable PDF.

A ``FormSpec`` is data, not code: the same engine reads documents, compiles answers and fills the PDF for any spec.
Specs come from three places:

* built-in templates (``pinneapple_data.formfill.specs``, e.g. ASME Form U-DR-1),
* a JSON file (``FormSpec.load``): copy a template or a generated spec, add label patterns, mark required items,
* any fillable PDF (``FormSpec.from_pdf``): one item per AcroForm field, labelled from its tooltip or name. Rules find
  the items whose label is written in the documents; the local LLM finds the rest.

Field kinds: ``text``, ``quantity`` (number + unit, compared in SI), ``number``, ``bool`` (yes/no), ``choice`` (one of
``options``), ``multi`` (several of ``options``).
pinneapple_data.formfill.spec.doc1: What a form asks for, how documents phrase each item, and where each answer goes in the fillable PDF.

pinneapple_data.formfill.specs.asme_udr1.doc:
Built-in template: ASME BPVC Section VIII Division 1 Form U-DR-1, and where each answer goes in its fillable PDF.

Each ``Field`` is one answer on the form (User's Design Requirements for Single-Chamber Pressure Vessels, ASME BPVC
Section VIII, Division 1, Nonmandatory Appendix KK). ``pdf`` names the AcroForm field it is written to; for check
boxes and radio groups ``states`` maps an answer to the ``(field, export state)`` pair that represents it. The PDF
field names come from the 07/25 revision of the form; many are generic (``Group10``, ``Text7``), so the mapping was
made by overlaying each widget's rectangle on the rendered page (see ``tests/test_formfill.py``).

``patterns`` are the phrasings used in process datasheets, mechanical datasheets and client specifications for the
same item (case-insensitive regular expressions, matched at a label position). ``quantity`` names the physical
quantity for unit-aware comparison between documents. ``required`` marks the items without which a manufacturer
cannot start the design; missing ones are reported as data gaps.

The blank form itself is ASME's copyrighted document and is not shipped here: users upload their copy.

Data usually comes from the process datasheet or the relief load summary (relieving case, rate, fluid properties),
the PSV sizing calculation (orifice) and the piping/valve specifications (connections, materials).

pinneapple_data.grf_sampler.doc:
Gaussian Random Field (GRF) input-function sampler, the standard way to
draw random forcing/coefficient functions u(x) for operator-learning
benchmarks (e.g. Lu, Jin & Karniadakis 2019, "DeepONet", arXiv:1910.03193,
which draws every one of its input functions from a zero-mean GRF with an
RBF/squared-exponential covariance kernel, length scale 0.2 by default).
Useful any time a dataset needs many independent random functions sharing a
common smoothness/correlation structure — not just for DeepONet.

Design (1D, `sample_grf_batch`): one Cholesky factorization of the RBF
covariance on a fixed fine grid (n_grid points) per BATCH of draws, not one
per draw — draws are just L @ standard_normal, and each draw is wrapped in a
CubicSpline so downstream ODE/PDE solvers can query u(x) at whatever points
their own integrator lands on, not just the n_grid grid nodes (this is the
literature-standard implementation approach — DeepXDE's own GRF class does
the same thing: a spline over a fine grid, not GP-reconditioning at
arbitrary query time, which would be O(m^3) per query batch instead of
O(n_grid) once per draw).

Design (2D, `sample_grf_2d_batch`): a direct 2D generalization of the 1D
approach (Cholesky of the full covariance matrix) would need an (nx*ny) x
(nx*ny) covariance matrix — O((nx*ny)^3) Cholesky, e.g. a modest 64x64 grid
is already a 4096x4096 factorization per draw. Instead this uses the
standard spectral-synthesis / circulant-embedding-adjacent FFT method for
stationary …
