pinneapple_design.intent.doc:
Design from intent: a plain-language goal in, a buildable and verified design package out.

    import pinneapple as pp
    pkg = pp.design("I want a toy car that does a loop", out_dir="loop_design")
    print(pkg.summary())                      # design, verdict, probability, trust decision
    pp.design("a heat sink for a 40 W chip in still air")   # -> NeedsInput: asks for the temperature limit

Stages (each a typed object): :func:`formulate` (text -> :class:`RequirementSpec`, values with units and provenance),
:func:`plan` (-> :class:`PhysicsPlan` from a registered :class:`ProblemTemplate`), :func:`optimise` (closed-form
screening, optimisation on the reduced model with the design-study core), :func:`robustness` (Monte Carlo),
:func:`verify` (full solver), :func:`assess` (trust report and verdict), :class:`DesignPackage` (files and report).
Requests outside every template return an :class:`OutOfScope` that says what would be needed.

pinneapple_design.intent.parse.doc:
Intent -> RequirementSpec: pick a template, read the numbers with their units, fill the template's slots.

The deterministic parser needs no network: it finds every ``number unit`` pair (``2 kN``, ``40W``, ``85 °C``,
``30 cm``), checks the unit with :mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`, and gives each to the slot of the same
dimension whose keywords are closest in the sentence. Phrases map to values through the slots' cues ("still air" ->
0 m/s). Nothing is guessed: a value it cannot place is reported as unused, a critical slot it cannot fill becomes a
question.

An LLM can be plugged in behind :class:`IntentLLM` (anything with ``extract(text, schema) -> dict``). Its answer is
used only where it can be checked: the template must exist, every value must come with a quote that occurs in the
text and contains the number, and the unit must have the slot's dimension. The deterministic reading wins on
conflicts.

pinneapple_design.intent.physics.loop_tr.doc:
Loop-the-loop track for a small car: the track curve, a 1-D model of the car along it, the closed form, and the
Newton rigid-body scene of the same track.

The track lies in the x-z plane (z up), the car runs in +x and turns counter-clockwise through the loop. It is made
of five pieces: a launch run, an entry clothoid (curvature rising linearly from 0 to 1/R), a circular arc of radius R,
an exit clothoid (1/R back to 0) and a run-out. With clothoid length 0 the loop is a circle. In 3-D the loop is a
helix: the exit is shifted sideways by ``pitch`` (a smoothstep, no sideways kink) so that it clears the entry, the way
real toy tracks are built.

Three models of the same car on the same track, from cheap to expensive:

``closed_form``
    Energy balance with the loss terms evaluated at a mean speed, the top-of-loop condition
    ``v_top^2 >= g R`` (normal force >= 0) and the peak load at the end of the entry clothoid.
``along_track``
    The car as a point on its centre-of-mass path (the track offset by the CoM height ``h``), with the normal force
    ``N = m (v^2 kappa + g cos theta)``, rolling resistance ``C_rr N``, aerodynamic drag ``0.5 rho C_d A v^2`` and the
    rotating wheels as an added inertia. ``d(v^2)/ds`` is integrated with fourth-order Runge-Kutta, vectorised over
    many designs.
``newton_check``
    The car as a rigid sphere of the wheel radius in contact with the 3-D track mesh (strip and side rails, the
    helical exit), integrated by NVIDIA Newton (XPBD). …

pinneapple_design.intent.templates.brack.doc:
Angle (shelf) bracket that holds a load at the end of its arm: thickness, width, mounting-leg length, material.

Physics: linear elasticity. Models: cantilever beam theory (closed form), an in-house hexahedral finite-element model
of the L with the fillet as a staircase (:class:`SolidFEM`, C3D8I), and CalculiX on a gmsh tetrahedral mesh (C3D10)
of the exact geometry with the filleted corner and the bolt holes. Failure modes: yield at the root (peak von Mises,
the fillet's stress concentration measured by CalculiX), deflection at the load (when a limit is stated), and the
bolts in tension (moment about the toe of the mounting leg).
pinneapple_design.intent.templates.brack.doc1: Angle (shelf) bracket that holds a load at the end of its arm: thickness, width, mounting-leg length, material.

pinneapple_design.intent.templates.examp.doc:
Template-authoring example: a helical compression spring (the worked example of the guide
``docs/guides/design_from_intent.md``). It is not registered by default; ``register(CoilSpringTemplate())`` adds it.

Physics (Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., ch. 10): shear stress ``tau = K 8 F D / (pi d^3)`` with
``K = 1`` (closed form) or Wahl's curvature factor ``K_W = (4C - 1)/(4C - 4) + 0.615/C`` (reduced), spring rate
``k = G d^4 / (8 D^3 N_a)``; music wire ``S_ut = A / d^m`` with ``A = 2211 MPa mm^m``, ``m = 0.145`` (Table 10-4),
``G = 81.7 GPa`` (Table 10-5), static torsional yield ``S_sy = 0.45 S_ut`` (Table 10-6, set not removed).
pinneapple_design.intent.templates.examp.doc1: Template-authoring example: a helical compression spring (the worked example of the guide ``docs/guides/design_from_intent.md``). It is not registered by default; ``register(CoilSpringTemplate())`` adds it.

pinneapple_design.intent.templates.glide.doc:
Wing of a model glider: span, aspect ratio, taper and section for the lowest sink rate.

Physics: low-speed external aerodynamics. Lift from the wing's lift curve, induced drag from the span loading
(vortex lattice, :mod:`pinneapple_design.aero.vlm`), profile drag from a flat-plate skin friction times a thickness
form factor. Models: elliptic lifting line (closed form, e = 1), the vortex lattice on a coarse lattice (reduced),
and the vortex lattice on a fine lattice (full; a RANS model is the next step and is not run here).

Passive (or fan-cooled) plate-fin heat sink for a heat source: base, fins, material.

Reuses the heat-sink sizer physics: :mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.plate_fin_heatsink` (Elenbaas / Bar-Cohen
natural convection, Teertstra forced convection, fin efficiency, spreading resistance) and
:func:`pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.evaluate_design` (3-D finite-volume conduction in the base with the fins'
convection, energy balance and grid checks, and a +-15 % band on the heat-transfer coefficient).

pinneapple_design.intent.templates.loop_.doc:
Toy car through a loop-the-loop: track radius, clothoid entry, launch speed, car mass, track strip.

Physics: rigid-body dynamics of a small car on a curved track with contact (normal force >= 0), rolling resistance
and aerodynamic drag. Models: energy balance (closed form), the 1-D along-track ODE, and NVIDIA Newton (contact +
Coulomb friction of a rigid capsule on the track mesh) as the full check. Failure modes: the car leaves the track at
the top (normal force < 0) or stalls; the track strip yields under the peak contact load; the loop is taller than
the space available.

Unknown friction and drag are not guessed: the design must work over a stated *envelope* (rolling-resistance
coefficient up to ``crr_max``, drag coefficient over the bluff-to-streamlined range, launcher scatter), and the
build instructions say how to measure the real values.

pinneapple_design.qualitative.doc:
Qualitative physics preview of geometries and geometry changes, before the quantitative analysis.

Give it different geometries (or an ``Assembly`` whose parts you change) and a physical goal, and it tells you, from
cheap physical models, which way each geometry or change should push the result, how strongly, through which
mechanism, with what confidence, and where on the surface the physics acts; then ``quantify`` runs the accurate
computation only where it is worth it and checks the qualitative reading.

>>> from pinneapple_design.qualitative import preview, part_sensitivity, Assembly
>>> p = preview({"baseline": body, "rounded rear": body2}, "minimizar arrasto", {"U": 30})
>>> print(p.text()); p.figure("preview.png")
>>> part_sensitivity(Assembly({"base": plate, "fin_1": fin1, "fin_2": fin2}), "maximizar resfriamento").text()

pinneapple_design.qualitative.descriptor.doc:
Geometric descriptors of closed triangulated bodies and assemblies of named parts.

Everything the qualitative models need comes from the surface mesh: per-face areas, normals and centroids, the
volume and second moments (exact polyhedral integrals over signed tetrahedra), extents, projected (frontal) area,
sharp edges, and section properties along an axis from a voxelization. An ``Assembly`` keeps the parts separate, so
a change to one part (scaled, moved, removed, replaced) can be traced to its physical effect.

pinneapple_design.qualitative.models.doc:
Cheap physical models that turn a geometry into first estimates, the mechanisms behind them and a surface map.

They are meant for the qualitative step before any simulation: which way does each geometric change push the
result, how strongly, and why. Each model evaluates a closed triangulated body (or an ``Assembly`` of parts) face
by face, so a change in one part shows up in the mechanism and in the part it belongs to.

* ``ExternalFlow``: drag and lift of a body in a stream. Windward faces: modified Newtonian pressure
  ``Cp = Cp_stag sin^2(delta)``; leeward faces inclined less than the separation angle recover pressure, steeper ones
  are separated and see the base pressure; friction from the flat-plate skin-friction law on attached faces
  (Hoerner, *Fluid-Dynamic Drag*, 1965, ch. 3 and 6; Anderson, *Hypersonic and High-Temperature Gas Dynamics*, for
  the Newtonian law).
* ``ConvectiveCooling``: heat rejected by a body at uniform temperature: local flat-plate correlations from each
  part's leading edge (laminar 0.332 Re_x^0.5 Pr^(1/3), turbulent 0.0296 Re_x^0.8 Pr^(1/3)), reduced coefficient in
  separated regions, natural convection from the vertical-plate law, optional fin efficiency tanh(mL)/(mL)
  (Incropera & DeWitt, ch. 3, 7 and 9).
* ``Cantilever``: a body clamped at one end with a tip load: non-uniform Euler-Bernoulli beam with section
  properties from a voxelization, tip deflection, bending stress, mass and a Rayleigh estimate of the first
  frequency …

pinneapple_design.qualitative.preview.doc:
Qualitative preview: how each geometry, or each change to a part, should affect the result, before any
simulation; then the quantitative check.

>>> from pinneapple_design.qualitative import preview
>>> p = preview({"baseline": body, "longer tail": body2, "blunt rear": body3}, objective="minimizar arrasto",
...             conditions={"U": 30})
>>> print(p.text())                # direction, strength, mechanism and confidence for each variant
>>> p.figure("preview.png")        # surface maps (where the physics happens) and the expected changes
>>> check = p.quantify(lambda name, geom: run_cfd(geom))   # numbers only for the variants worth simulating

The preview is meant to be read first: it says *why* (the mechanisms that move the objective and by how much
relative to each other), flags side effects on the other quantities, and lowers its confidence where the cheap model
is known to be fragile (near a separation threshold, in the transition range, short beams, low fin efficiency...).
``quantify`` then compares those expectations with an accurate computation (CFD, FEM, ``pp.solve``, experiments) and
reports where the qualitative reading was right or wrong.

pinneapple_design.qualitative.quantitati.doc:
Quantitative counterparts of the qualitative models, for ``QualitativePreview.quantify``.

``voxel_fem_cantilever``: 3-D linear elasticity on the voxelized geometry (any shape: holes, flanges, tapers),
clamped at one end with a load spread over the other. Hexahedral elements with Wilson's incompatible modes
(Wilson, Taylor, Doherty & Ghaboussi 1973), whose three extra bubble modes per direction let a single element bend
without the shear locking of the plain trilinear brick; the bubbles are condensed out. It captures what beam theory
leaves out (shear deformation of short beams, stress concentration at section changes, flanges that do not work), so
it is the check for ``Cantilever`` previews.

pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.doc:
Surrogate-driven inverse design on closed-form physics, with the answer re-checked against the physics.

Five worked cases share one method (:mod:`.core`): sample the design space, label it with a closed-form model from
:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form`, train a small MLP, freeze it, run Adam on the design variables through it, and
grade the final design against the closed form (:class:`.core.VerificationCard`, also as a
:class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`). Each case adds one analysis of its own:

=====================  =========================================================  ===================================
module                 design                                                     extra analysis
=====================  =========================================================  ===================================
``heatsink_fins``      straight-fin heat sink (fin count, height, thickness)      2-D finite-volume fin-cell check
``brake_rotor``        vented brake rotor vanes (count, gap, thickness)           Monte Carlo of machining tolerances
``transdermal_patch``  membrane-controlled patch (area, membrane, concentration)  release over the wear time
``suspension_arm``     rectangular cantilever arm (width, thickness), min. mass   local sensitivities (elasticities)
``reflex_port``        bass-reflex port (radius, length) for a tuning frequency   volume-vs-accuracy trade-off sweep
=====================  …
pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.doc1: Surrogate-driven inverse design on closed-form physics, with the answer re-checked against the physics.

pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.brak.doc:
Vented brake rotor: the radial vanes between the two friction rings, as a fin array, under a sustained load.

Ground truth: the same 1-D fin-array formula as :mod:`.heatsink_fins` (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.
fin_array_conduction`) with cast iron (``k = 50 W/m K``) and rotor-scale geometry: the vanes are fins of length =
vent gap spread along the mean circumference, the friction ring is the base (extended-surface analysis of vented
rotor cooling: e.g. Limpert, *Brake Design and Safety*). Lumped and steady: a uniform convection coefficient per
driving profile and a sustained heat input (a long descent), not a single hard stop (that is a transient problem; see
the ``car_brake_thermal`` PDE preset). The temperature rise is linear in power, so the surrogate learns the thermal
resistance.

The analysis of its own: :func:`monte_carlo_uncertainty` propagates machining tolerances on vane thickness and gap
through the formula (:func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate`, uniform within the band) and grades
the 95th-percentile temperature against the safe limit.
pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.brak.doc1: Vented brake rotor: the radial vanes between the two friction rings, as a fin array, under a sustained load.

pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.core.doc:
The machinery shared by every case: a small MLP surrogate, gradient descent on the design through the frozen
surrogate, and a verification card that re-checks the answer against the ground truth.

The method (also called "backprop into the design"): sample the design space, label every sample with the ground
truth model, train an MLP on those labels, freeze its weights and treat the design variables as the only trainable
tensor. The surrogate is differentiable, so Adam can move the design along the gradient of the predicted objective
plus constraint penalties. The surrogate's answer is never reported on its own say-so: :class:`VerificationCard`
re-runs the ground truth on the final design and grades the gap.
pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.core.doc1: The machinery shared by every case: a small MLP surrogate, gradient descent on the design through the frozen surrogate, and a verification card that re-checks the answer against the ground truth.

pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.heat.doc:
Straight-fin CPU heat sink: fin count, height and thickness on a fixed 80 x 80 mm aluminium base.

Ground truth: the 1-D fin-array formula (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.fin_array_conduction`, Incropera &
DeWitt fin efficiency with an adiabatic-tip correction, convective plus 1-D base resistance) with a prescribed
convection coefficient per fan profile. ``k = 205 W/m K`` is the aluminium value of the ``cpu_heatsink_thermal``
preset. The formula's temperature rise is linear in power, ``T_j = T_amb + P * R(N, H, t, h)``, so the surrogate
learns the thermal resistance ``R`` (in log scale) and the power enters exactly.

Independent check of the formula itself: :func:`fin_cell_check` solves 2-D finite-volume conduction in one fin pitch
(:mod:`pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_cell`).

Scope: a fixed convection coefficient (no airflow solve, no fin-to-fin flow interaction), steady state, no
measurement. For plate-fin sizing with published forced / natural convection correlations, pressure drop and a 3-D
base-plate solve use :mod:`pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink` (the HeatSink Sizer app) instead.

Triangle meshes of the five designs, in millimetres, for a 3-D viewer or an STL download.

Each part is a set of individually closed bodies (``pinneapple_design.geometry.bodies``) concatenated, not a boolean
union: the fins of a heat sink or the vanes of a rotor touch their base without being fused into one manifold. That
is right for display and for a slicer that accepts several shells; a CNC or FEM pipeline that needs one watertight
body has to fuse them (for example with ``manifold3d``).

pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.refl.doc:
Bass-reflex port: radius and length that tune a cabinet to a target frequency, and the trade-off between a small
port and an accurate tuning.

Ground truth: the Helmholtz resonator (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.helmholtz_resonator`),
``f = c / (2 pi) sqrt(A / (V L_eff))`` with ``A = pi r^2`` and ``L_eff = L + 1.7 r`` (end correction of a port
flanged at both ends). Lumped: the air in the port moves as one mass, which holds while the port is short against the
wavelength; no cabinet modes, no port compression or air-speed limits, no driver model.

The analysis of its own: :func:`sweep_pareto_frontier` minimises
``lambda * volume_fraction + (1 - lambda) * rel_freq_error^2`` for a sweep of ``lambda``, where ``volume_fraction``
is the port volume over the largest port this case allows (6 % of the cabinet). Each weight starts gradient descent
from several points and keeps the candidate with the lowest loss evaluated with the closed form, not the surrogate.

pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.susp.doc:
Suspension arm as a rectangular cantilever: the lightest width x thickness that still reaches a fatigue life.

Ground truth (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.cantilever_fatigue`, e.g. Shigley, *Mechanical Engineering
Design*): root bending stress ``sigma = 6 F L / (w t^2)`` and Basquin's stress-life law ``sigma_a = sigma_f' (2N)^b``.
The life target is turned into an allowable stress (``sigma_allow = sigma_f' (2 N_target)^b``), which is how the
problem is posed in practice and is far better conditioned than cycles, which span orders of magnitude. The material
constants are typical table values for a spring steel (``sigma_f' = 1200 MPa``, ``b = -0.09``), not a measured
material. No endurance limit (the power law keeps extrapolating at low stress), no stress concentrations (holes,
fillets), a constant section, one load case.

The analysis of its own: :func:`compute_sensitivity`, local derivatives of life and mass by central differences on
the closed form (:func:`pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.local_derivatives`) and their elasticities
``(x / f) df/dx``. For this model the life is a pure power law, ``N ~ w^(-1/b) t^(-2/b)``, so the elasticities are
exactly ``-1/b`` and ``-2/b``: thickness always matters twice as much as width.

pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.tran.doc:
Membrane-controlled release patch: area, membrane thickness and reservoir concentration for a target release rate
and wear time, with the smallest area.

Ground truth: Fick's first law through a rate-limiting membrane (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.
membrane_diffusion`, the reservoir-type delivery model of Robinson & Lee, *Controlled Drug Delivery*):
``rate = D K C_res A / L``, reservoir mass ``M = C_res A L_res``, depletion time ``t_dep = L_res L / (D K)``. The
depletion time depends on the membrane thickness only (area and concentration cancel), so the wear-time constraint is
applied through the closed form and the surrogate learns the rate.

``D`` and ``K`` are generic order-of-magnitude values for a small solute in a polymer membrane, not the measured
coefficients of any drug, and the model is a steady 1-D membrane with sink conditions at the outer face (no skin
resistance, no saturation plateau). This is a mass-transfer design exercise, not a dosing or medical tool.

The analysis of its own: :func:`simulate_release_timeseries`, the release over the wear time (constant zero-order
phase, then a first-order tail once the reservoir is depleted).

pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling.doc:
The self-optimizing engineer: cool an overheating part on a board with a heat sink and the enclosure fans.

    from pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling import run_mission, DEFAULT_TEXT
    run = run_mission(DEFAULT_TEXT, out_dir="out")       # read -> baseline -> still air -> sample -> learn ->
                                                         # optimise + confirm -> verify -> deliver

Modules: ``mission`` (request, design space), ``simulate`` (coupled 3-D board + heat sink reference), ``learn``
(POD + Gaussian-process surrogate of the junction temperatures and the board map, hold-out), ``optimize`` (constrained
search, confirm-on-physics loop), ``verify`` (fine-grid solve, trust report), ``scene`` (3-D), ``report``
(figures, renders, report), ``agent`` (controlled tools and planners).

pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling..doc:
The self-optimizing engineer: a cooling request in plain language -> plan -> controlled tools -> evidence.

    run = run_mission(DEFAULT_TEXT, out_dir="out")           # deterministic planner, no API key needed
    run = run_mission(text, out_dir="out", planner="llm")    # a language model orders the same tools

The agent can only call the tools of :func:`toolbox` (library calls with declared arguments); every call is logged
with its arguments, a summary of its result and its wall time (:mod:`pinneapple_autolab.core`).

pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling..doc:
Fast approximation of the coupled reference: junction temperatures and the board-top temperature field.

Two parametric reduced-order models (:class:`pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.ParametricPOD`, POD + one
Gaussian process per coefficient) on ``log(T - T_air)``:

* the junction temperatures of every part, nominal and pessimistic (:func:`.simulate.response`);
* the board-top map (POD of the snapshots, ``MAP_SHAPE`` grid).

The Gaussian processes give a predictive standard deviation, carried back to °C (delta method) so the optimiser can
ask for the limit to hold at ``mean + k std`` and the trust report can check that the stated spread covers the
measured hold-out errors. :func:`holdout` measures it on designs the model never saw, against the nearest-snapshot
baseline every surrogate must beat.
pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling..doc1: Fast approximation of the coupled reference: junction temperatures and the board-top temperature field.

defaults of :func:`default_mission` and are listed as such.

Constrained search on the surrogate, verification on the reference, and the loop between them.

:func:`optimize`: lightest heat sink (mass from the closed form, exact) whose every part meets its junction limit
with pessimistic cooling at ``mean + k std`` of the surrogate, whose fan air power stays inside the budget and whose
fins keep the minimum gap; differential evolution with the fin count as an integer (``scipy.optimize``).

:func:`design_loop`: fit -> optimise -> run the reference on the optimum -> add it to the snapshots -> refit, until
the reference confirms the optimum (it meets every limit and lies inside the surrogate's +-2 std band) or the
rounds run out. Every round is kept (prediction, reference, error), so the evolution of the maximum temperature is a
measured history, not a story.

3-D scene of the cooled board: enclosure, fans, board temperature map, parts, heat sink and the warm air.

Everything coloured comes from a solve:

* board top: the board-top map of :func:`.simulate.simulate` (``MAP_SHAPE``), on jet;
* parts: their junction temperature;
* heat sink: base from the 3D finite-volume base solve (its top face), fins from the 1D fin equation from the local
  root temperature (``field3d`` of :func:`pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.evaluate_design`);
* air paths (forced convection only): straight paths along the flow from the fans, each coloured by the bulk
  temperature of its strip of air from an energy balance (heat from the board-top cells under the strip, and from the
  heat sink for strips through the fins, over ``rho cp V A`` of the strip). Paths do not mix sideways; they show where
  the heat goes, they are not a CFD solution.

:func:`timeline_scene` animates a sequence of states (bare board, still-air heat sink, the design rounds, the verified
design) on one geometry: the heat sink has room for the largest fin count of the sequence and unused fins collapse
to a point, so the vertex count stays fixed across frames.

pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling..doc:
Reference simulation of a cooled board: the 3D board model and the heat sink model, coupled.

* Board: :func:`pinneapple_physics.pcb.solve` (layered 3D finite volumes, JEDEC two-resistor packages, convection +
  radiation from both faces at the fan air speed).
* Heat sink on the hot part: :func:`pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.evaluate_design` (3D finite-volume base,
  fin correlations, pressure drop) gives the case-to-air resistance ``R = (T_source - T_air) / Q`` (interface
  material + spreading + fins) for the heat ``Q`` that actually goes up through the case.
* Coupling: ``Q`` depends on ``R`` (the rest goes into the board) and, in still air, ``R`` depends on ``Q``; the two
  are iterated to a fixed point (relative change of ``Q`` below ``tol``).

``simulate(..., pessimistic=True)`` repeats the coupled solve with the convection band of both models (board surface
coefficients x 0.8, heat-sink coefficient x 0.85: the H_BAND of each engine, typical correlation accuracy) so a design
can be required to meet its limits even with pessimistic cooling.

Board-top temperatures are returned on a fixed grid (``MAP_SHAPE``) whatever the solver grid, so solutions of
different fidelity can be compared point by point and used as snapshots of a field surrogate.

pinneapple_design.thermal.board_cooling..doc:
Independent verification of the chosen design and its trust report.

The design the loop confirmed is solved again with both models on finer grids (``FIDELITY["verify"]``: board cells
x2 in each direction, heat-sink base grid x2), so the decision does not rest on the grid the surrogate was trained
on. The trust report (:class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`) collects:

* limits: every junction at or below its limit with pessimistic cooling (critical), fan air power within budget
  (critical), heat sink inside the envelope (critical);
* physics: board energy balance, coupling fixed point converged, the heat-sink engine's own checks (energy balance,
  spreading by two methods, grid convergence, correlation range), grid convergence of the coupled solve
  (train vs verify grid);
* the surrogate: its prediction of the design within its +-2 std band of the fine solve plus the grid difference,
  hold-out error and coverage measured on unseen designs, applicability (inside the design space, no farther from
  a snapshot than the held-out designs whose error was measured).

pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_array_spee.doc:
How much faster is a trained surrogate than a numerical solve, and how far apart are they? A measured sweep over
seven plate-fin heat sinks.

The heat sink, its closed form and its surrogate are those of
:mod:`pinneapple_design.surrogate_inverse.heatsink_fins` (80 x 80 mm aluminium base, 3 mm thick, straight fins,
uniform film coefficient; MLP on the thermal resistance, trained on the fin-array formula of
:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.fin_array_conduction`). The numerical reference is the finite-volume fin pitch
of :func:`pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_cell.solve_fin_cell` (2-D cross-section, which is the same problem as the
3-D periodic cell because nothing depends on the fin depth), with its grid-halving check.

For each design the surrogate forward pass is timed (mean of ``timing_reps`` calls after one warm-up call) and the
reference solve is timed (wall clock, including its grid check), and the agreement is the difference of the
temperature rise above ambient, ``|dT_surrogate - dT_ref| / dT_ref``. The speed ratio depends on the machine and on
the reference solver: this reference is a sub-second 2-D solve, so the ratios are much smaller than against a meshed
3-D FEM run.

The seven designs stay at 55 W or more and inside the manufacturable box of ``heatsink_fins``.
pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_array_spee.doc1: How much faster is a trained surrogate than a numerical solve, and how far apart are they? A measured sweep over seven plate-fin heat sinks.

pinneapple_design.thermal.fin_cell.doc:
Finite-volume conduction in one fin pitch of a straight-fin heat sink: an independent check of the 1-D fin-array
formula (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.fin_array_conduction`).

The unit cell is one fin of thickness ``t`` and height ``H`` centred on a strip of base plate one pitch wide
(``pitch = spacing + t``) and ``t_base`` thick, the same cell a 3-D FEM check of a periodic fin array uses:

* bottom face: uniform heat flux, this fin's share of the power, ``q = P / (N * pitch * depth)``;
* exposed base top, fin sides and fin tip: convection ``-k dT/dn = h (T - T_amb)`` (Robin) with the same ``h`` as
  the formula;
* the two side planes ``x = 0`` and ``x = pitch``: symmetry with the neighbouring cells (zero flux);
* the two end planes along the depth: zero flux (the periodic simplification), with ``q`` and ``h`` uniform along
  the depth.

With nothing varying along the depth, the 3-D problem is exactly this 2-D cross-section problem (per unit depth),
which is what is solved here: cell-centred finite volumes on a grid that puts cell faces on the fin walls and the
fin root, two-point fluxes between cell centres (one material), half-cell resistances in series with ``1/h`` on convective
faces, and a direct sparse solve. Unlike the formula it resolves two-dimensional conduction in the fin (no 1-D fin
assumption, no corrected-length tip) and the spreading from the base into the fin root.

The result reports the energy balance (convected heat / applied heat) and, with …

Plate-fin heat-sink sizing (the engine of the HeatSink Sizer app).

    from pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink import DesignInput, OperatingInput, evaluate_design, SizingRequest, size
    r = evaluate_design(DesignInput(...), OperatingInput(...))        # closed-form network + 3D finite-volume base
    s = size(SizingRequest(...), load_surrogates())                   # screen thousands, verify the best with physics

Modules: ``engine`` (one design, verified), ``field`` (3D finite-volume base plate), ``sizer`` (requirements in,
designs out), ``surrogate`` (MLP screening model, training), ``trust`` (surrogate trust report).

pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.engin.doc:
Physics engine of the HeatSink Sizer: evaluates one design, fully verified.

Every number returned here comes from physics, not from the neural
surrogate: the closed-form network in
``pinneapple_physics.closed_form.plate_fin_heatsink`` (convection
correlations, fin efficiency, pressure drop) plus a 3D finite-volume solve
of the base (hotspot + temperature map). The two methods cross-check each
other, and each check is reported with a pass/warn/fail status.

pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.field.doc:
3D finite-volume conduction solve of the heat-sink base plate.

Independent of the closed-form spreading formula: it resolves the actual
rectangular source footprint (and an off-centre position) on the actual
rectangular base, so it both produces the temperature map shown to the
user and cross-checks :func:`spreading_resistance` (Lee et al.).

Model (same assumptions as the resistance network):
* bottom face: uniform heat flux Q/A_source over the footprint, adiabatic
  elsewhere; side faces adiabatic;
* top face: fins + exposed base lumped into a uniform effective
  coefficient ``h_eff = 1 / (R_fins * A_base)`` to ambient.

The linear system is assembled on cell centres (in-plane cell count held
roughly constant across aspect ratios) and solved directly (scipy.sparse); the energy balance (heat out through the top = Q) is
reported as a check.

pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.monot.doc:
Heat-sink surrogate trained with monotonicity constraints (zoo model ``heatsink_natural_mlp``).

The app's unconstrained natural-convection surrogate fits the physics engine to 0.7 % but gets the sign of the
conductivity effect wrong on 5 % of held-out designs: raising k by 5 % lowers the engine's resistance by only 0.13 %
(median over 400 designs), below the fit error, so a plain regression does not resolve it. :func:`train_monotone`
trains the same architecture (``bench_mlp`` 4 x 128 SiLU, same features, same split) with a hinge penalty
(:func:`pinneapple_neural.trainer.monotonic.monotonicity_penalty`) on d log R / d log k and d log R / d log(source
width), both required to be <= -``MARGIN``, evaluated on the training designs and on random in-range designs: the
library ``Trainer`` (Adam, best-val checkpoint; plain regression for ``WARMUP`` epochs, then the constrained
objective), then a full-batch L-BFGS polish of the same objective (``multi_round_lbfgs``).

Power is not constrained: the engine's own resistance rises with power on 0.5 % of designs (up to +0.7 % for a +5 %
step), so "more power, lower resistance" is not a law of the reference.

pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.sizer.doc:
Sizing: requirements in, verified heat-sink designs out.

1. Sample tens of thousands of manufacturable candidates inside the
   customer's envelope and process rules.
2. Screen them: with the PINNeAPPle surrogate (FVM-accurate, microseconds
   per design) when the request is inside its trained design space, else
   with the closed-form network (vectorised loop, still fast). The screen
   uses the surrogate's conformal 95% upper bound, so it errs on the safe
   side.
3. Round the best candidates to manufacturing precision and re-verify each
   one with the full physics engine (FVM base + pessimistic convection
   band). Only verified designs are recommended.

pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.surro.doc:
Neural surrogate of the physics engine, used only to *screen* designs.

The finite-volume-resolved physics takes ~40 ms per design; the sizer
needs to screen tens of thousands of candidates per request. A PINNeAPPle
MLP (``ModelRegistry`` + ``Trainer`` + L-BFGS finetune) learns the
base-to-ambient resistance (and pressure drop) over the design space, and
every design it proposes is then re-verified by the physics engine before
it is shown to the user.

One model per cooling mode (forced / natural): they depend on different
variables and a single model would have to learn a discontinuity at
``v = 0``.

Run ``python -m pinneapple_design.thermal.heatsink.surrogate`` (``--help`` for the
sizes) to regenerate the dataset, retrain and write ``surrogate_<mode>.pt`` + its
trust report into ``ARTIFACTS`` (``apps/heatsink_sizer/artifacts`` unless
``PINNEAPPLE_HEATSINK_ARTIFACTS`` is set).

pinneapple_design.topology.doc:
Density-based topology optimization: SIMP, density filter, Heaviside projection, OC and MMA.

Problems: structural compliance (MBB beam, cantilever), thermal compliance, Stokes flow with
Brinkman penalization (Borrvall-Petersson), and the iron of a machine rotor for torque
(:mod:`pinneapple_design.topology.magnetic`, built on ``pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics``).
See docs/guides/topology_optimization.md.
pinneapple_design.topology.doc1: Density-based topology optimization: SIMP, density filter, Heaviside projection, OC and MMA.

pinneapple_design.topology.driver.doc:
Optimization loop: design variables -> (symmetry) -> density filter -> Heaviside projection -> problem.

    from pinneapple_design.topology import Compliance2D, DensityFilter, optimize
    prob = Compliance2D.mbb(60, 20)
    res = optimize(prob, volfrac=0.5, filt=DensityFilter.grid(60, 20, r_min=2.4), optimizer="oc")
    res.x_phys  # physical densities, res.history["objective"]

The volume constraint ``sum(v x_phys) <= volfrac sum(v)`` acts on the physical (projected) densities.
Extra constraints ``g(x_phys) <= 0`` (with gradients) can be given to MMA as callables. With
projection, ``beta`` is doubled every ``beta_every`` iterations up to ``beta_max`` (continuation).

pinneapple_design.topology.filters.doc:
Density filter and Heaviside projection for density-based topology optimization.

Density filter (Bruns & Tortorelli 2001; Bourdin 2001): ``x_tilde = (H (v * x)) / (H v)`` with cone
weights ``H_ij = max(0, r_min - |c_i - c_j|)`` and element volumes ``v``. Works on any element
centroids (structured grids or the triangles of a rotor), built with a KD-tree.

Heaviside projection (Wang, Lazarov & Sigmund 2011)::

    x_bar = (tanh(beta eta) + tanh(beta (x_tilde - eta))) / (tanh(beta eta) + tanh(beta (1 - eta)))

``beta -> infinity`` gives a 0/1 design; ``beta`` is raised by continuation.

pinneapple_design.topology.magnetic.doc:
Topology optimization of rotor iron for torque, on the 2D A_z machine model.

Design domain: the rotor-core elements of a
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machine.SPMMachine` (with ``magnet_thickness=0`` it is a
reluctance rotor; with magnets, the iron under them). Material interpolation on the reluctivity,
``nu = nu0 + rho^p (nu_iron(|B|^2) - nu0)`` (linear or nonlinear iron). The torque at each rotor angle is
the Maxwell-stress (Arkkio) torque of the model and its sensitivity comes from one adjoint solve per
angle with the Newton tangent (:meth:`SPMMachine.torque_and_design_gradient`).

Objectives (``evaluate`` returns a value to minimise):

* ``"mean"``: ``-mean_k T(theta_k) / T_ref`` -- maximise the average torque over the given angles;
* ``"ripple"``: ``std_k T(theta_k) / T_ref`` -- use with :meth:`RotorTorqueProblem.mean_torque_constraint`.

Currents follow the rotor synchronously: ``i_k = I cos(p theta + gamma - 2 pi k / 3)`` (``gamma`` is the
electrical angle of the current vector relative to the rotor's reference axis at ``theta = 0``).

pinneapple_design.topology.optimizers.doc:
Design-update rules: optimality criteria (OC) and the method of moving asymptotes (MMA).

OC: the classical fixed-point update for one volume constraint and a non-increasing objective
(compliance-type problems), with a bisection on the Lagrange multiplier.

MMA: K. Svanberg, "The method of moving asymptotes -- a new method for structural optimization",
Int. J. Numer. Meth. Eng. 24 (1987) 359-373. Each iteration replaces the objective and the
constraints ``f_i(x) <= 0`` by convex separable approximations ``r_i + sum p_ij/(U_j - x_j) + q_ij/(x_j - L_j)``
and solves the subproblem through its dual, a smooth concave maximization over ``lambda >= 0``
(here with L-BFGS-B). Elastic variables ``y_i >= 0`` with cost ``c y + y^2/2`` keep the subproblem
feasible (the dual then stays bounded). The coefficient and asymptote-update formulas follow the
paper and Svanberg's later public note on MMA/GCMMA (2007): ``p = (U-x)^2 (1.001 g+ + 0.001 g- + eps)``,
``q = (x-L)^2 (0.001 g+ + 1.001 g- + eps)``, asymptote factors 0.7 / 1.2 on oscillation / monotone steps.
This implementation is written from those formulas, not from any existing MMA code.
pinneapple_design.topology.optimizers.doc1: Design-update rules: optimality criteria (OC) and the method of moving asymptotes (MMA).

classes.sig: (n, m, xmin=0.0, xmax=1.0, move=0.5, asyinit=0.5, asyincr=1.2, asydecr=0.7, c=1000.0, d=1.0)
classes.doc1: Method of moving asymptotes for ``min f0(x)  s.t.  f_i(x) <= 0,  xmin <= x <= xmax``.

pinneapple_design.topology.problems.doc:
Density-based topology-optimization problems on structured grids of square bilinear (Q4) elements.

Grid convention: ``nelx x nely`` elements of size ``h``, element ``e = i * nely + j`` (i along x,
j along y, y upwards), node ``n = i * (nely + 1) + j``. Element matrices are integrated with 2x2
Gauss quadrature (selective one-point integration for the incompressibility penalty).

Every problem exposes ``n`` (number of elements), ``volumes`` and ``evaluate(x) -> (f, df/dx)`` on
physical densities ``x`` in [0, 1].

* :class:`Compliance2D` -- plane-stress linear elasticity, SIMP ``E = Emin + x^p (E0 - Emin)``,
  compliance ``c = f^T u``, ``dc/dx_e = -p x_e^(p-1) (E0 - Emin) u_e^T k_e u_e``. Presets:
  :meth:`Compliance2D.mbb` (half MBB beam) and :meth:`Compliance2D.cantilever`.
* :class:`ThermalCompliance2D` -- steady conduction ``k = kmin + x^p (1 - kmin)``, uniform heat source,
  isothermal sink on a boundary segment, objective ``f^T T``.
* :class:`StokesDissipation2D` -- Stokes flow in a Brinkman medium (Borrvall & Petersson, Int. J.
  Numer. Meth. Fluids 41 (2003) 77-107): inverse permeability
  ``alpha(x) = a_min + (a_max - a_min) q (1 - x) / (q + x)`` (x = 1 fluid), velocity-driven, objective the
  potential power ``0.5 u^T K u`` (viscous + Brinkman + incompressibility penalty) whose sensitivity is
  ``0.5 u_e^T (d alpha/dx_e) m_e u_e`` (the minimum of a quadratic energy over a fixed affine space).
  Incompressibility is imposed by a penalty with one-point (reduced) …

pinneapple_flow.doc:
PINNeAPPle Flow: engineering flows as typed node graphs, planned from a description, run headless or in Flow Studio.

    import pinneapple_flow as pf

    plan = pf.plan("heat in a 2D plate with fixed edges, compare a PINN with finite differences")
    flow = plan.proposals[0].flow          # a Flow (JSON schema pinneapple-flow/1)
    result = pf.run(flow, workdir="work")   # on the pinneapple_core.workflows engine (cache, logs, retries)
    result.report("validate")["metrics"]

    python -m pinneapple_flow run flow.json        # the same, from the shell
    python -m pinneapple_flow studio               # the GUI on http://127.0.0.1:8765

=====================  ==============================================================================================
:mod:`.schema`         the flow document (``Flow``, ``Node``, ``Edge``), ``validate_flow``, ``flow_json_schema``
:mod:`.types`          port types and which output may feed which input
:mod:`.registry`       node types (``NodeSpec``, ``Port``, ``Param``, ``REGISTRY``, ``@node``)
:mod:`.nodes`          the built-in catalog: each node wraps a library call
:mod:`.runtime`        ``run``: flows on the workflow engine, per-node status, artifacts
:mod:`.planner`        description -> proposals (heuristic offline planner, LLM planner with validation/repair)
:mod:`.store`          flows, versions, runs and node outputs in SQLite or any SQLAlchemy database
:mod:`.learn`          surrogate architectures, preview, training, …
pinneapple_flow.doc1: PINNeAPPle Flow: engineering flows as typed node graphs, planned from a description, run headless or in Flow Studio.

Command line: ``python -m pinneapple_flow <command>``.

run flow.json [--workdir DIR] [--from NODE] [--only NODE ...] [--json OUT] [--no-cache]

pinneapple_flow.autocalls.doc:
Library-call nodes generated from the public API (``auto.<module>.<function>``).

:func:`generate` imports every library module that no curated node reaches, takes its public functions (``__all__``
or the public names defined in it) and keeps those a form can call safely:

* every required argument has a simple type (number, text, choice, flag, list, mapping) read from its annotation or
  default, so the parameter form is generated like the curated ``lib.*`` nodes;
* no argument names a path, URL, host, command, expression or credential, and the function body does not evaluate
  text, start processes, open sockets or write files (``eval``, ``sympify``, ``subprocess``, ``open(``, ``.save``...):
  a flow document can only choose values, never code or files;
* the name is not a server, CLI, upload / download or install entry point.

The result is committed as ``autocalls.json`` (callables with their parameter forms, plus a reason for each module that
has none) so the catalog and the coverage table load without importing those modules; a module is imported when one
of its nodes runs. ``python -m pinneapple_flow autocalls`` regenerates it, ``tests/test_flow_library_nodes.py`` fails
when a public module is neither covered by a node nor given a reason.
pinneapple_flow.autocalls.doc1: Library-call nodes generated from the public API (``auto.<module>.<function>``).

functions.doc1: Node entries for one module, or the reason it has none.

functions.name: generate
functions.doc1: Scan ``modules`` (default: every module the curated nodes and reasons leave open) and return the data.

functions.name: smoke
functions.doc1: Call each generated node's function with its form defaults, in a fresh interpreter in an empty folder, and record the outcome in ``entry["check"]`` (shown with the node): ``runs with its defaults`` or ``needs input`` with the error the defaults gave.

functions.name: prune
functions.doc1: Drop entries whose check shows they return a function or a class (building blocks for Python code, not a result a node can show); a module left with none gets that as its reason.

pinneapple_flow.config.doc:
Settings from the environment (and an optional ``.env`` file): LLM provider, database URL, folders, server.

==================================  ==========================================================================
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_HOME``            folder for the SQLite store and run folders (default ``~/.pinneapple_flow``)
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_DB_URL``          SQLAlchemy URL (``postgresql+psycopg://...``); default SQLite in HOME
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_DATA``            the only folder data-ingest nodes may read files from (default HOME/data)
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_HOST`` / ``_PORT``  server bind address (default ``127.0.0.1:8765``)
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_LLM_PROVIDER``    ``none`` | ``ollama`` | ``openai`` | ``openai_compatible`` | ``anthropic``
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_LLM_MODEL``       model name (e.g. ``llama3.1``, ``gpt-4o-mini``)
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_LLM_BASE_URL``    OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM, LM Studio, llama.cpp, a hosted model)
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_LLM_API_KEY``     key for that endpoint (``OPENAI_API_KEY`` / ``ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`` also read)
``OLLAMA_HOST``                     Ollama URL (default ``http://127.0.0.1:11434``)
==================================  ==========================================================================

When the server listens on anything but localhost, the security of :mod:`appkit` applies with prefix ``FLOW``
(``FLOW_USER`` / ``FLOW_PASSWORD_HASH``, rate limits, CSRF, headers); see the app README.

pinneapple_flow.coverage.doc:
Which PINNeAPPle capabilities are flow nodes, and why the others are not.

:func:`coverage` walks every ``pinneapple*`` package and its first-level modules, maps the registered node types onto
them (by the library calls each node declares) and attaches a curated reason (:data:`REASONS`) to whatever has no
node. ``python -m pinneapple_flow coverage -o docs/flow_studio/COVERAGE.md`` writes the table (git-ignored: the docs
build generates it, ``tools/gen_flow_docs.py``) and exits 1 when a module has neither a node nor a reason.

pinneapple_flow.decisions.doc:
Decision records: what a flow decided, who decided it, why, on which references and evidence, how confident.

Every automatic choice (identified equations, dimension, conditions and coefficients, method, architecture,
hyperparameters and HPO ranges, twin design, validation thresholds, the planner's alternative routes) and every
user edit becomes a :class:`Decision`. A decision with neither a reference nor library evidence is marked
``no reference``, gets a lower confidence and says how to raise it.

    d = rule_decision("method.fd", node="fd", what="solve with finite differences", value={"method": "fd"})
    d.confidence, d.label, [r["key"] for r in d.references]     # 0.85, 'high', ['leveque2007fd', 'hairer1996odes2']
    u = user_decision("eq", "coefficients", "alpha = 2e-5", value={"alpha": 2e-5}, notes="handbook value")

Records travel as JSON in ``flow.meta["decisions"]`` (planner / user) and in each node's report
(``report["decisions"]``, decisions taken while running); the store keeps them per flow version and run.
pinneapple_flow.decisions.doc1: Decision records: what a flow decided, who decided it, why, on which references and evidence, how confident.

pinneapple_flow.examples.doc:
Every ``examples/*`` study as a flow: the inventory, the quick configurations, the measured comparisons.

* the flows are ``pinneapple_flow/flows/examples/<domain>/<name>.json``; ``meta.example`` names the example folder,
  ``meta.quick`` the parameter overrides of its quick configuration (``{node id: {param: value}}``);
* :data:`INVENTORY` (``flows/examples/inventory.json``) gives, per example folder, its status when a flow does not
  reproduce all of it (``needs`` a tool, ``not_convertible`` with the reason) and notes;
* :data:`MEASURED` (``flows/examples/measured.json``) is written by :func:`run_example`: the outcome of each flow run
  (full or quick), its seconds and the ``examples.compare`` rows, flow number against the example's committed one;
* :func:`scan` lists the library calls of an example's scripts and whether a node's declared calls cover them;
* :func:`markdown` renders ``docs/flow_studio/EXAMPLES_AS_FLOWS.md`` from these three (git-ignored: the docs build
  generates it, ``tools/gen_flow_docs.py``); :func:`problems` is the CI gate (an example folder with neither a flow
  nor a stated reason).

    python -m pinneapple_flow example-flows list
    python -m pinneapple_flow example-flows run flight_dynamics/03_takeoff [--quick]
    python -m pinneapple_flow example-flows doc -o docs/flow_studio/EXAMPLES_AS_FLOWS.md
    python -m pinneapple_flow example-flows check

pinneapple_flow.identify.doc:
Identify the governing equations of a problem from its description and, when given, from data.

:func:`identify` returns ranked candidates, each a complete equation system (PDEs, conservation law, constitutive
relation, dimension, conditions, coefficients) with a confidence, the reasoning and decision records with their
references. The heuristic path is offline (keywords, units, explicit values; :func:`pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.
capabilities.identify_pde` as a second opinion); an LLM, when configured, adds a candidate that is parsed and checked
like any other. :func:`discover_pde` fits the PDE to gridded space-time data by sparse regression over candidate
derivative terms (STRidge, :class:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.missing_term.SINDyIdentifier`) and says whether
the data confirm a candidate.

    res = identify("a steel rod cools down, its ends held at 20 C, diffusivity 1.2e-5 m^2/s")
    best = res["candidates"][0]           # family, pdes, conditions, coefficients, confidence, reasoning, decisions
    found = discover_pde(axes, u, ["x", "t"])   # {"equation": "u_t = 0.0998*u_xx", "r2": ..., "family": "heat"}
pinneapple_flow.identify.doc1: Identify the governing equations of a problem from its description and, when given, from data.

functions.sig: (text, *, dimension=None, units=None, n=3, llm=None, call=None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc1: Ranked candidate equation systems for a description (see the module text). ``dimension`` overrides the detected one; ``units`` (quantity -> unit) are recorded; ``llm`` = ``{"provider", "model", "base_url", "api_key"}`` adds an LLM candidate (validated; dropped with a warning when it does not parse).

functions.sig: (axes, values, coords, *, field='u', threshold=0.05, trim=3) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc1: Sparse regression of ``u_t`` (and ``u_tt``) on candidate terms (u, u^2, u^3, first and second spatial derivatives, u u_x) of gridded data ``values`` (shape: axis lengths in ``coords`` order). Returns the equation with the best fit, its coefficients, R^2 and the family it classifies as.

functions.name: confirm
functions.doc1: Does the discovered equation agree with a candidate (same family; coefficients where they can be read)?

pinneapple_flow.lab_status.doc:
The Lab seal of a flow's validated item and what would raise it, read through ``pinneapple_lab``.

Flow Studio never grades anything itself: the letter comes from the Lab curation (``pinneapple_lab.curation``) and
the seal API (``pinneapple_lab.seal``). Both are feature-detected, so the same code shows the A-F seal scale and
``curation.next_steps`` once the Lab provides them, and today's curation tier (A-D) or "not curated" before that.

* :func:`seal_status` - letter, its name, the reason; for the lowest letters the failing check and how to raise it.
* :func:`next_steps` - the gaps to the next letter with the Lab's suggested action and, when that action is a
  registered node type (or a library call a registered node wraps), the nodes to insert.
* :func:`insert_nodes` - add those nodes to a flow, wired by port type from an anchor node.
pinneapple_flow.lab_status.doc1: The Lab seal of a flow's validated item and what would raise it, read through ``pinneapple_lab``.

functions.doc1: The seal letter of a Lab item with its reason, as the Lab states it. ``letter`` is None when the item was never curated.

Curated nodes come before …

functions.doc1: What the item misses for the next seal letter, with the Lab's action and the nodes that carry it out.

pinneapple_flow.learn.doc:
Surrogates for flow nodes: build (MLP blocks, DeepONet, FNO, POD + MLP), preview as a layer graph, train, tune.

The architectures are the library's (:class:`~pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators.deeponet.DeepONet`,
:class:`~pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators.fno.FourierNeuralOperator`,
:class:`~pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.pod.POD`); this module wires them to one dataset format, normalises
inputs and outputs, and measures held-out errors.

Operator dataset (``.npz``): ``A`` (samples, m) inputs (parameters or an input function at m sensors), ``Y``
(samples, points * fields) outputs on a fixed grid, ``grid`` (points, d) the query coordinates.

    cfg = {"kind": "pod_mlp", "rank": 8, "blocks": [{"type": "dense", "width": 64, "activation": "tanh"}] * 2}
    preview = architecture(cfg, in_dim=2, out_dim=1600)           # layer graph + parameter count, no training
    model, info = fit(cfg, data, epochs=800)                       # info["metrics"]["test_rel_l2"]

pinneapple_flow.libcalls.doc:
Library calls as nodes: a curated allowlist of public PINNeAPPle callables, their parameter forms generated by
introspection, and user-defined node types built on them.

Each entry of :data:`CALLS` names a callable (``module:attr``, or ``module:Class.method`` with constructor arguments)
plus curated metadata: title, category, references, which inputs come from ports (a series, a dataset, a surrogate,
a solution) and which parameters to leave out. The parameter schema is read from the signature (numbers, strings,
booleans, ``Literal`` choices, lists, dicts), so adding a capability is one entry, not a hand-written node.

Only entries of :data:`CALLS` run. A user-defined node (:func:`custom_spec`) picks an entry, fixes or hides some of
its parameters and gets a title; it is stored as data and can never name a callable that is not in the allowlist.

    for spec in library_specs(): REGISTRY.register(spec)        # done on import of pinneapple_flow.nodes
    custom_spec({"type": "custom.my_sobol", "base": "uq.sobol", "title": "Sobol (n=4096)",
                 "params": {"n": {"default": 4096, "hidden": True}}})

pinneapple_flow.nodes_ext.examples.doc:
The node that checks a flow against the committed results of the example it reproduces (``examples/<name>``), and
the helpers the example-domain nodes share (object artifacts, the checkout's ``examples`` folder).

``examples.compare`` takes the metrics of the nodes upstream of it and, for each comparison it is given, looks up the
reference number in the example's own files: a key path into a committed results file
(``results/takeoff.json:nominal.light_ga.distance_35ft_m``, list items selected by field values with
``runs[aircraft=a320,seed=0].dnz_cg_rms``), a metric of its manifest (``manifest:distance_35ft_a320``) or a metric of
another upstream node that reads a committed file the example keeps in a solver format (``node:committed.tip_uz_m``),
or a cell of a markdown table in the guide the example's numbers are published in when the example commits no
results file (``doc:docs/core_concepts/free_surface.md|+2°|Peak k``). A comparison
passes when ``|flow - reference| <= atol + rtol |reference|``; the tolerance is part of the flow document, next to a
note saying where it comes from, or is a number of the example itself (``atol_ref``, e.g. the spread over the seeds
of a stochastic study). The checks are recorded on the output port, so the run's experiment manifest
carries them.

pinneapple_flow.palette.doc:
The node palette: sections along an engineering workflow, human titles, one-line summaries, search ranking.

Flow Studio shows the palette this module describes; any other front end can use it the same way::

    from pinneapple_flow import palette
    palette.sections()                       # [{"id": "problem", "title": "Problem & geometry", ...}, ...] in order
    palette.entry(REGISTRY.get("train.pinn"))  # section, title, summary, tags, package, curated, install hint
    palette.search("pinn")                   # ranked hits: curated nodes above generated ``auto.*`` library calls

Every curated node type is placed in a section here (``SECTION_OF``); a node type registered by another package
can say where it goes with ``tags=["section:<id>"]`` on its spec, or falls back on its category. Generated
library calls (``auto.*``) always go to the last section, "Library calls (advanced)", grouped by package.

    from pinneapple_flow.planner import plan
    res = plan("transient heat in a 2D plate with fixed edges")             # heuristic, offline
    res = plan(text, backend="llm", provider="ollama", model="llama3.1")   # LLM, validated, falls back on failure

pinneapple_flow.planner.extensions.doc:
The planner's public extension hook: another package (the example-domain nodes of
:mod:`pinneapple_flow.nodes_ext`, PINNeAPPle-CFD, a user's own nodes) declares *capabilities* and the heuristic
planner proposes them for a matching description, with a decision record per choice.

A :class:`Capability` names what it does (``title``, ``domain``), how to recognise it in a description
(``keywords``: phrase -> weight, matched at word starts like the planner's own keywords; ``min_score``), what it needs
(``inputs``: the things a user must supply, shown in the proposal), which node types it uses (``nodes``) and which
usually follow (``downstream``), the references that back it (``references``: keys of
:mod:`pinneapple_flow.references`, or ``uncited`` saying why there is none; the decision is then recorded as
"no reference", with a lower confidence) and how to build its flow: ``template`` (an example flow,
``<domain dir>/<stem>`` under ``pinneapple_flow/flows/examples``, optionally in its quick configuration) and / or
``build(text, detected) -> FlowBuilder`` for flows that depend on the text. ``adapt(doc, text, detected)`` may edit
the template's document (for instance keep only the aircraft the text names)::

    from pinneapple_flow.planner.extensions import Capability, register_capability
    register_capability(Capability(
        id="cfd.external_aero", title="External aerodynamics with OpenFOAM", domain="CFD",
        keywords={"drag": 2, "external flow": 3, "ahmed": 3}, …

The offline planner: keywords (English and Portuguese), quantities with units and explicit coefficient values
detect the physics (PDE family, dimension, steady or transient, boundary conditions) and what is asked (solve,
compare, identify a coefficient, a fast surrogate, a twin, a forecast, a take-off); each proposal is a flow built

pinneapple_flow.planner.llm.doc:
The LLM planner: the node catalog and the flow schema go in the prompt, the model answers JSON, and every
proposal is validated against the catalog. Invalid output is repaired (unknown types and parameters dropped, bad
edges removed, missing required inputs wired from a compatible upstream output, equations re-checked by the safe
parser); what cannot be repaired falls back to the heuristic planner, and the result says which planner produced
each proposal.

Providers go through :func:`pinneapple_llm.call_llm`: a local Ollama, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint
(``base_url``: vLLM, LM Studio, llama.cpp, a user-hosted model), OpenAI or Anthropic with a key.

Invalid output is repaired (unknown types and parameters dropped, bad edges removed, missing required inputs wired from a compatible upstream output, …

The guided wizard of "New flow": problem -> physics / equations -> geometry / data -> methods -> validation ->
outputs. Each step is a choice from :data:`STEPS` (or free text); :func:`plan_from_answers` turns the answers into
a description the heuristic planner reads, and when the problem step picked a registered capability
(:mod:`pinneapple_flow.planner.extensions`) its flow is the first proposal. The result is the planner's own
(proposals with decision records), so a wizard flow is as editable as any other.

    plan_from_answers({"problem": "heat in a plate", "physics": "heat", "geometry": "2d", "methods": ["pinn", "fd"],

pinneapple_flow.references.doc:
The curated reference registry (``references.yaml``) and the check every cited reference goes through.

A reference is *registry* when its key is in the curated file, *verified* when a DOI / URL given by someone else (an
LLM, a user) resolved over the network, and *unverified* otherwise. Nothing here invents a citation: an unknown key
stays an unknown key, shown as such.

    ref("raissi2019pinn")["doi"]                     # '10.1016/j.jcp.2018.10.045'
    check({"key": "lu2021deeponet"})["status"]       # 'registry'
    check({"title": "Some paper", "doi": "10.1/x"})  # 'unverified' (offline) or 'verified' / 'not found' (online)
pinneapple_flow.references.doc1: The curated reference registry (``references.yaml``) and the check every cited reference goes through.

pinneapple_flow.registry.doc:
Node types: typed ports, parameter schemas (rendered as forms by any GUI), and the library call each one makes.

A node type is a :class:`NodeSpec` registered in :data:`REGISTRY`. Only registered types run; a flow document names
types and gives parameter values, never code::

    @node("solver.fd", "Finite differences", category="Solvers",
          inputs=[Port("problem", "problem")], outputs=[Port("solution", "solution"), Port("metrics", "metrics")],
          params=[Param("n", "int", 64, minimum=8, maximum=512, help="nodes per axis")],
          calls="pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.symbolic_fd.solve_fd")
    def fd(ctx, inputs, params):
        ...
        return {"solution": ctx.save_npz("solution", ...), "metrics": {...}}

``params_schema()`` is a JSON Schema per node (the GUI generates its form from it); ``check_params`` validates values.
pinneapple_flow.registry.doc1: Node types: typed ports, parameter schemas (rendered as forms by any GUI), and the library call each one makes.

pinneapple_flow.rules.doc:
The heuristic rules behind every automatic decision of a flow, with the references they rest on.

A rule cites keys of the curated registry (:mod:`pinneapple_flow.references`), or says plainly why it has none
(``uncited``): reading the user's own words, a project convention, a rule of thumb. ``evidence`` points at what in
this repository backs the rule (a test, an example result, a library constant). ``tests/test_flow_decisions.py``
checks that every rule cites a registry key or is flagged uncited, and that every evidence path exists.
pinneapple_flow.rules.doc1: The heuristic rules behind every automatic decision of a flow, with the references they rest on.

functions.doc1: Add a heuristic rule (another package's decisions). It must cite registered references (:func:`pinneapple_flow.references.register_references` first) or say why it has none; an existing id is refused unless the rule is the same.

pinneapple_flow.runtime.doc:
Run a flow on the workflow engine of :mod:`pinneapple_core.workflows`.

Each node becomes a :class:`~pinneapple_core.workflows.Step` of kind ``pinneapple_flow.node``; the engine gives the
order, per-node logs and states, retries, cancel and **skip-done**: a node whose type, parameters and upstream are
unchanged reuses its earlier outputs (state ``cached``). ``from_node`` re-runs one node and everything downstream of it
(upstream nodes are reused from the cache when they ran before).

    from pinneapple_flow import run
    result = run("flow.json", workdir="work")
    result.status, result.nodes["pinn"]["status"], result.nodes["pinn"]["report"]["metrics"]
    u = result.load("fd", "solution")            # arrays of an artifact output

Values on edges are JSON; arrays, weights and figures are files in the node's folder, referenced as
``{"$artifact": "<absolute path>", "kind": "npz" | "json" | "png" | "pt"}``.

pinneapple_flow.schema.doc:
The flow document (``pinneapple-flow/1``): nodes, edges, metadata; load, save, validate, JSON Schema.

A flow is plain JSON, so any app (Flow Studio, the PINNeAPPle-CFD app, a script) can write and read it::

    {
      "schema": "pinneapple-flow/1",
      "id": "heat-rod", "name": "Heat in a rod", "description": "...",
      "nodes": [{"id": "geo", "type": "geometry.domain", "params": {"shape": "interval"},
                 "position": {"x": 0, "y": 0}, "label": "Rod"}],
      "edges": [{"id": "e1", "source": "geo", "source_port": "geometry",
                 "target": "eq", "target_port": "geometry"}],
      "meta": {"planner": "heuristic", "prompt": "heat in a rod ..."}
    }

Only node types registered in the catalog run (:mod:`pinneapple_flow.nodes`); the document never carries code.
:func:`validate_flow` checks the structure, the parameters against each node's schema, the port types of every edge
(:func:`pinneapple_flow.types.compatible`), required inputs and cycles, and returns a list of :class:`Issue`.
pinneapple_flow.schema.doc1: The flow document (``pinneapple-flow/1``): nodes, edges, metadata; load, save, validate, JSON Schema.

The operations Flow Studio (or any other front end, e.g. the PINNeAPPle-CFD app) exposes, as plain methods.

The app's HTTP routes are one-liners over :class:`FlowService`: planning, validation, the node catalog, flow
storage with versions, background runs with live per-node status, node results, architecture and equation previews,
and safe access to run artifacts (figures, 3-D scenes) inside the run folder only.

pinneapple_flow.store.doc:
Where flows, their versions, runs and per-node outputs live: SQLite by default, any SQLAlchemy URL otherwise.

    store = FlowStore()                                            # ~/.pinneapple_flow/flow.sqlite
    store = FlowStore("postgresql+psycopg://user:pw@host/db")      # Postgres (pip install psycopg)
    v = store.save_flow(flow, note="first draft")                  # -> version 1, 2, ...
    store.get_flow(flow.id)                                        # latest version (a flow document)
    store.get_run(run_id)["nodes"]["pinn"]["report"]["metrics"]

The URL comes from the argument, else ``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_DB_URL``, else the SQLite file under
``PINNEAPPLE_FLOW_HOME`` (default ``~/.pinneapple_flow``). Artifacts (arrays, figures, weights) stay on disk in the run
folder; the store keeps their paths.

pinneapple_flow.templates.doc:
Equation templates per PDE family and dimension: the PDEs, conditions, coefficients and (when one is known) the
exact solution a planner proposes and a user then edits.

Everything is text in the grammar of :mod:`pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.text`, so a template is exactly what the
equations node shows. ``exact`` is an expression in the coordinates, or the name of a library reference
(``"cole_hopf"`` for viscous Burgers, :func:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.pinn.cole_hopf`).

    t = template("heat", dimension=2)
    t["pdes"]          # ['u_t = alpha*lap(u)']
    t["exact"]         # 'exp(-2*alpha*pi**2*t)*sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)'

functions.doc1: The equations of a template family moved to another dimension (the 2-D <-> 3-D switch). PDEs written with ``lap()`` keep their text; conditions on ``boundary`` stay; a known template is rebuilt for the new dimension.

pinneapple_flow.twin.doc:
A digital twin built automatically from an identified equation system.

:class:`PDETwinModel` turns the system into a twin model for :class:`pinneapple_systems.operations.twin.TwinRuntime`
(the library's ensemble Kalman filter): the state is the field on a coarse grid (the identified PDE as a fast,
reduced-resolution model) plus the coefficients to calibrate, carried as random-walk states, plus one state per
sensor: the field linearly interpolated at the sensor's position (so a sensor between grid nodes is observed where it
is, not at the nearest node). The runtime then gives state estimation, calibration of the coefficients, alerts when a coefficient leaves its
expected range (an anomaly: the asset no longer behaves like the model) and consistency tests of the innovations.

    model = PDETwinModel(system, bounds, n=21, dt=0.01, estimate={"alpha": 0.1})
    plant = PDETwinModel(system, bounds, n=81, dt=0.01)                 # a finer simulator as the "real" asset
    readings = simulate_sensors(plant, sensors=[0.25, 0.5, 0.75], t_end=2.0, every=5, noise=0.002,
                                coefficients={"alpha": 0.1}, fault={"t": 1.0, "alpha": 0.15})
    twin, result = run_twin(model, readings, limits={"alpha": (0.07, 0.13)})
pinneapple_flow.twin.doc1: A digital twin built automatically from an identified equation system.

functions.sig: (plant, *, sensors, t_end, every=1, noise=0.0, coefficients=None, fault=None, seed=0) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc1: Readings of a simulated asset (``plant``, usually a finer grid than the twin): sensor values every ``every`` steps with Gaussian noise; ``fault`` = ``{"t": t_fault, coefficient: new value}`` changes the asset at ``t``. Returns columns ``t`` and ``s0, s1, ...`` plus ``truth_<coefficient>``.

functions.doc1: Assimilate ``readings`` (columns ``t``, ``s0``...) into ``model`` with :class:`TwinRuntime`. Returns the runtime and a summary (history of estimates, alerts, final calibrated coefficients).

Port types of the flow graph and the rule that says which output may feed which input.

Every node port has one of the types below. An edge ``source.port -> target.port`` is valid when the types are equal,
when the target accepts ``any``, or when the pair is in :data:`CONVERSIONS` (a value of the source type carries what
the target needs, e.g. a ``problem`` holds its ``geometry``).

The values that travel along edges are JSON: small values inline, arrays and weights as artifact files written by the
node (``{"$artifact": "solution.npz"}``, resolved against the node's run folder).

pinneapple_hub.doc:
Model hub client: ``push_to_hub``/``from_pretrained`` + ``ModelCard``.

See ``hub.py`` and ``model_card.py`` module docstrings for the design
rationale (piggybacking on the Hugging Face Hub's real infrastructure
rather than building new hosting, and why a ``ModelCard``'s
``validation_metrics`` are mandatory).

pinneapple_hub.hub.doc:
``push_to_hub`` / ``from_pretrained`` for PINNeAPPle models, built on the
Hugging Face Hub's own storage/auth/versioning infrastructure rather than
a new hosting service this repository would have to build, operate, and
secure itself. This is a deliberate, common pattern (many domain-specific
libraries piggyback on HF Hub this way) -- the value PINNeAPPle adds is
the ``pinneapple_config.json`` sidecar convention that lets a checkpoint
be reconstructed into a live model without the downloader having to
already know its exact architecture kwargs, plus the ``ModelCard`` (see
``model_card.py``) reproducibility contract every push carries.

Requires the ``hub`` extra (``pip install "pinneapple[hub]"``, i.e.
``huggingface_hub``) and a Hugging Face account/token for anything beyond
downloading public repos.

pinneapple_hub.library.doc:
The PINNeAPPle Hub index: every ready-made thing in the repository -- tools (public functions, Flow Studio nodes,
recipes, MCP tools), trained models, geometries, datasets, flows and examples -- as one generated list, each item
with a runnable snippet whose recorded run is checked by a test.

    from pinneapple_hub import library as hub
    index = hub.load_index()                              # data/web/hub/index.json (generated, not committed)
    hits = hub.search(index, "airfoil", kind="model")     # ranked items

    python -m pinneapple_hub.library build              # regenerate index.json from the sources
    python -m pinneapple_hub.library run [--stale]      # run every snippet, record its output (snippet_runs/)

``examples`` …

pinneapple_hub.library.compose.doc:
"Create your own": a custom tool composed from existing blocks (Flow Studio node types, optionally a bundled flow
to start from and a library geometry), returned as a flow document and the Python that runs it.

    from pinneapple_hub.library.compose import compose
    out = compose({"name": "Heat rod", "blocks": [
        {"type": "geometry.domain", "params": {"dimension": 1}},
        {"type": "geometry.mesh", "params": {"n": 41}}]})
    out["flow"]          # pinneapple-flow/1 document (open it in Flow Studio, or pf.run it)
    out["code"]          # Python: build the flow, validate, run, print each node's metrics
    out["issues"]        # validation issues (pinneapple_flow.validate_flow) and inputs that could not be wired

A whole flow can be the start too (``"flow": <pinneapple-flow/1 document>``, what Flow Studio's "Publish to Hub"
sends), and ``"expose": [{"node": id, "param": name}]`` turns those parameters into variables at the top of the
generated Python, so the published tool reads as a function of them.

Blocks are appended in order; each new block's required inputs are wired from the block before it, then from that
block's ancestors, then from any earlier block with a compatible output
(:func:`pinneapple_flow.lab_status.insert_nodes`). Only registered node types are accepted, and parameters are
checked against each node's schema, so a composed tool never contains code a visitor typed.
pinneapple_hub.library.compose.doc1: "Create your own": a custom tool composed from existing blocks (Flow Studio node types, optionally a bundled flow to start from and a library geometry), returned as a flow document and the Python that runs it.

functions.doc1: See the module doc. ``spec``: ``name``, ``description``, ``blocks`` ([{type, params}]), optional ``start`` (a bundled flow name to append the blocks to) and ``geometry`` (a geometry library entry the code loads).

pinneapple_hub.library.flowlink.doc:
The Hub and Flow Studio on one registry: a ready flow around any node type, and links between the two apps.

    from pinneapple_hub.library.flowlink import flow_for_node, flow_link, add_link
    out = flow_for_node("geometry.mesh", {"n": 41})     # {"flow", "issues", "ok", "source", "node"}
    flow_link(out["flow"], base="http://127.0.0.1:8765")   # Flow Studio opens it (?flow=<base64url JSON>)
    add_link("geometry.mesh", {"n": 41}, base=...)          # Flow Studio adds the node to a flow the user picks (?add=)

``flow_for_node`` builds *inputs -> the tool -> a report*:

1. when a bundled flow (``pinneapple_flow/flows``) uses the node type, its upstream nodes with their wiring and
   parameters, as committed and validated there;
2. otherwise a producer for each required input, chosen among node types without required inputs of their own (or,
   up to three levels, with inputs that can be produced the same way) whose output feeds that input type;
3. then ``export.report`` on the node's outputs (``items: any``), unless the node already ends in a report.

Every node is a registered type and every parameter is checked against its schema (``NodeSpec.check_params``); the
wiring is ``pinneapple_flow.lab_status.insert_nodes``, the one the Flow Studio GUI uses.

pinneapple_hub.library.flowruns.doc:
Recorded runs of the bundled flows (``pinneapple_flow/flows``), shown in the Hub on each flow's page and on the
page of every node type the flow uses.

    python -m pinneapple_hub.library flowruns [names ...]    # run them headless, write data/web/hub/flow_runs.json
    from pinneapple_hub.library.flowruns import read_flow_runs, runs_for_node
    runs_for_node(read_flow_runs(), "geometry.mesh")          # [{flow, node, status, metrics, summary}, ...]

Each flow runs in the sandbox (:func:`pinneapple_hub.library.sandbox.run_snippet`, its own interpreter and time limit)
with ``pinneapple_flow.run``; what is kept per node is its status and the metrics and summary its report holds. A run
is current while the flow file has the SHA-256 it was recorded with; a flow that fails or times out is recorded as
such, with the error, and its nodes show nothing.

from pinneapple_hub.library.myhub import MyHub
mine = MyHub("~/.pinneapple/hub")                   # the Hub app keeps one folder per caller
item = mine.save(compose_result, name="Heat rod", run=validation)   # -> {"id": "mine:heat_rod", ...}

pinneapple_hub.library.sandbox.doc:
Run a code snippet in a short-lived, separate interpreter and keep what it printed and drew.

    from pinneapple_hub.library.sandbox import run_snippet
    r = run_snippet('import pinneapple as pp\nprint(pp.geometries.list()[:3])', timeout=60)
    r["ok"], r["stdout"], r["seconds"], r["figures"]       # figures: PNG bytes of the matplotlib figures left open

The snippet runs in a fresh temporary directory (its working directory, deleted afterwards) with matplotlib on
Agg, no GPU, a wall-clock time limit and, on POSIX, address-space / CPU-time / file-size limits (``setrlimit``) so a
runaway snippet is killed with every process it started. Network access is not blocked here: deploy the app that
calls this on a network without egress (apps/deploy) when the snippets come from visitors.
