pinneapple_hub.model_card.doc:
``ModelCard``: the reproducibility contract every hub-pushed model
carries.

Why this exists: a physical claim ("matches DNS to 2%") is only as good
as its provenance. Without architecture + exact training config + data
lineage + a computed (not just asserted) validation-metrics block bound to
the weights, a downloaded checkpoint's claims cannot be re-checked by
anyone but the person who trained it -- exactly the kind of unverifiable
claim ``pinneapple_llm``'s ``PhysicsGuardrail`` (see that module) exists to
catch. ``ModelCard`` is the structured version of what this very project's
own ``problem_config.json`` recorded by hand (physics/domain/BC/IC/
forcing/data/training/reference sections) for a single case; this is the
general, hub-wide schema.
pinneapple_hub.model_card.doc1: ``ModelCard``: the reproducibility contract every hub-pushed model carries.

pinneapple_hub.verified_card.doc:
Model cards whose ``validation_metrics`` come only from a guardrail run against the model, refused otherwise.

:func:`certify_model` builds (or loads) a model for a registered preset, trains it when no weights are given,
runs :class:`pinneapple_llm.PhysicsGuardrail` on it and builds a :class:`~pinneapple_hub.model_card.ModelCard`
with :func:`card_from_guardrail`: every numeric check value goes into ``validation_metrics`` under the check's
name, every pass/fail-only check as ``<name>_passed`` (1.0 / 0.0), and ``reference_source`` says what was run on
how many fresh points. A card that fails ``ModelCard.validate()`` (for example because nothing computable ran)
raises :class:`CardRefused` instead of being returned, the same rule ``push_to_hub`` applies.

Re-auditing an existing card can only re-run the schema check: the weights and the exact preset kwargs behind a
card's numbers do not travel in the card JSON, so its physics claims cannot be re-executed from it alone.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``physics_verified_model_cards`` product (GovernedCard); the HTTP service is
``apps/governed_card``.

pinneapple_hub.zoo.doc:
``pp.zoo``: pre-trained, verified PINNeAPPle models in one line -- load, predict, evaluate against the stored
reference, validate (physics checks + validity range), benchmark and fine-tune with a held-out guard.

    import pinneapple as pp
    pp.zoo.list()                                       # ['airfoil_cst_rans_mlp', 'heatsink_forced_mlp', ...]
    card = pp.zoo.info("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp")          # ModelCard: task, inputs/outputs + units, validity range,
                                                        # metrics vs reference, training data, licence, citation
    m = pp.zoo.load("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp")
    m.predict(T0=0.17, T1=0.15, T2=0.13, M0=0.02, M1=0.05, M2=0.03, alpha_deg=4.0)
    pp.zoo.evaluate("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp")             # recomputes the card's metrics on the stored reference
    pp.zoo.validate("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp").decisao     # TrustReport: APPROVED | REVIEW | REJECT
    print(pp.zoo.catalogue())                           # every model and dataset: metrics, size, Hub link
    res = pp.zoo.finetune("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", (X_new, Y_new), save_to="my_airfoil")  # refused if worse

Only models that passed the zoo's gate ship (see ``_catalog.py`` and ``docs/dev/model_dataset_inventory.md``).
Weights and datasets are listed in ``manifest.json`` with SHA-256 and versions; small files are bundled, the rest is
downloaded lazily from the Hugging Face Hub (``PINNeAPPle-Labs``). ``pp.datasets`` is :mod:`pinneapple_hub.zoo.datasets`.
pinneapple_hub.zoo.doc1: ``pp.zoo``: pre-trained, verified PINNeAPPle models in one line -- load, predict, evaluate against the stored reference, validate (physics checks + validity range), benchmark and fine-tune with a held-out guard.

pinneapple_hub.zoo._artifacts.doc:
Artifact store of the zoo: manifest, SHA-256 checks, local cache and lazy download from the Hugging Face Hub.

Every file a model or dataset needs is listed in ``manifest.json`` with its size, SHA-256 and the Hub repo/revision
that hosts it. A file is resolved in this order:

1. bundled with the package (``pinneapple_hub/zoo/assets/...``; only small files, < ~2 MB),
2. the local cache (``$PINNEAPPLE_ZOO_CACHE`` or ``~/.cache/pinneapple/zoo``),
3. downloaded from the Hub (``huggingface_hub`` if installed, else plain HTTPS), checked, then cached.

A checksum that does not match raises :class:`ChecksumMismatchError` (a corrupt cache entry is deleted and fetched
again when the network is allowed). Offline (``PINNEAPPLE_OFFLINE=1``, ``HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`` or ``offline=True``)
nothing is downloaded. A file the Hub does not have yet raises :class:`ArtifactNotPublishedError`, which says how to
publish it.

pinneapple_hub.zoo.checks.doc:
Per-query trust checks of the zoo models, and the verdict they add up to.

``pp.zoo.validate`` judges a model as a whole (its metrics, its physics checks). This module judges one *query*:
is this input inside the validity range, are the outputs physical, does the ensemble agree as well as it did on
held-out data, do the model's physics checks hold *here*? Each check has the rule ID of ``pinneapple check``
(PC601 out-of-range query, PC602 sparse region, PC402/PC403 unphysical or non-finite output, PC302 model residual).

A check is a value computed from the query and a comparison with a limit (``check_spec``). The values come from a
``torch`` module (:func:`checks_module`), the same one :func:`pinneapple_hub.zoo.export.export_onnx` puts in the
ONNX graph, so a browser evaluating the graph and Python evaluating :func:`query_checks` agree to float precision.
:func:`verdict` turns the statuses into one decision: any failing check -> ``fail`` ("outside the validity range,
an extrapolation"), any warning -> ``warn`` ("use with caution"), else ``pass``. Design constraints (``kind ==
"design"``) are reported but never enter the verdict: they say whether a design is acceptable, not whether the model
can be trusted.

    import pinneapple as pp
    r = pp.zoo.query_checks("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", {"T0": .17, "T1": .15, "T2": .13, "M0": .02, "M1": .07,
                                                     "M2": .06, "alpha_deg": 16})[0]
    r["verdict"]["status"]       # 'fail': alpha 16 …

pinneapple_hub.zoo.datasets.doc:
``pp.datasets``: ready-made, verified datasets in one line.

    import pinneapple as pp
    pp.datasets.list()                                   # names
    pp.datasets.info("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6")           # schema, splits, provenance, verification, licence
    test = pp.datasets.load("airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6", split="test")
    test["Cl"], test.columns, test.xy(["T0", "alpha_deg"], ["Cl"])

Each dataset is stored as npz files (no pickles) whose arrays are named ``<split>__<column>``: either one ``data.npz``
holding every split, or one ``<split>.npz`` per split (large datasets; a split may be sharded into ``<split>-NN.npz``,
concatenated along the rows on load, and only the requested split is downloaded). Small files are bundled with the
package; the others are downloaded once from the Hugging Face Hub (``PINNeAPPle-Labs/<name>``), checked against the
SHA-256 in the manifest and cached (see ``pinneapple_hub.zoo._artifacts``).

What the zoo's demo Space shows, computed by the library: each model's prediction along a sweep of each input,
with its ensemble spread or conformal bound and where its query checks warn or fail, and the files of the static
Space that shows them.

The Space (``huggingface.co/spaces/PINNeAPPle-Labs/zoo-demo``, a static Space: no server) is the page in
``apps/zoo_space/`` over the files :func:`export_space` writes:

* ``models/<name>.sweeps.json`` (:func:`precompute`): for every input, a sweep from 15 % below to 15 % above its
  range, the other inputs at a held-out test case; the predictions, their band, and the verdict of the query checks
  at every point (pass / warn / fail); the checks at the test case and the model's trust decision;

``export_onnx(name, path)`` writes one ONNX graph from the model card's physical inputs to its physical outputs:

pinneapple_hub.zoo.parquet.doc:
Parquet copies of the zoo datasets, for the Hugging Face dataset viewer and ``datasets.load_dataset``.

The npz files stay the source of truth: their SHA-256 are in the manifest and ``pp.datasets.load`` reads them. The
Parquet files are derived from them, deterministically (same npz and same pyarrow version -> same bytes):

* each split becomes ``data/<config>/<split>-NNNNN.parquet``. Splits with the same columns share a config; the
  config holding ``train`` (else ``test``, else the first split) is ``default``, any other one is named after its
  first split (a grid, a convergence study, an independent reference with other columns);
* scalar columns stay plain columns; an array column becomes a fixed-size list column of the same shape (``List(
  List(float32, length=64), length=64)`` in ``datasets``; ``with_format("numpy")`` gives the arrays back);
* a sample larger than :data:`EXPLODE_ROW_BYTES` whose array columns share a leading axis (a time series of fields)
  is stored as one row per step of that axis, with ``sample`` (row of the npz split) and ``step`` columns; the
  per-sample columns are repeated on every step. This keeps every row small enough for the viewer;
* a shard holds at most :data:`MAX_SHARD_BYTES` of uncompressed data and a row group at most :data:`ROW_GROUP_BYTES`,
  so the viewer can page any split;
* each field's metadata keeps its numpy dtype and per-row shape, so :func:`read_parquet` returns the npz arrays bit
  for bit.

pinneapple_hub.zoo.relations.doc:
Metamorphic relations the physics of each zoo model implies (#698), checked without any reference solution by
:func:`check_zoo_relations` (``pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorphic``).

Each model has groups of relations; each group samples its own box of inputs (a nominal design with some inputs
varied), so the relation is tested inside the model's validity range.

* ``airfoil_cst_rans_mlp``: mirroring the camber line and the angle of attack (``M -> -M``, ``alpha -> -alpha``) flips
  the sign of lift and moment and keeps the drag (geometric symmetry of the incompressible flow); lift grows with the
  angle of attack in the attached range (up to 8 degrees, below the stall of the training set).
* ``heatsink_forced_mlp``: more air speed gives no higher thermal resistance and no lower pressure drop; a better
  conductor gives no higher resistance; above 2 m/s the resistance does not depend on the dissipated power (to 2 %).
  Below 2 m/s it does, in the physics engine too (+6.5 % when the power doubles at 0.6 m/s), so it is not tested there.
pinneapple_hub.zoo.relations.doc1: Metamorphic relations the physics of each zoo model implies (#698), checked without any reference solution by :func:`check_zoo_relations` (``pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorphic``).

pinneapple_lab.doc:
PINNeAPPle Lab: run many experiments reproducibly and grow a database of results and datasets.

An experiment is a class with parameters and a ``run(ctx)`` method. The runner gives every run an id from the
experiment, its version and its parameters, records its inputs, outputs, metrics, validation checks,
figures and datasets in one folder, keeps its status (running, completed, failed, failed_validation) and indexes
everything in SQLite, so runs can be queried, compared, exported as training sets and summarised in a catalogue.

    from pinneapple_lab import Experiment, register, run, sweep, LabStore

    @register
    class Oscillator(Experiment):
        name = "oscillator"
        params = {"zeta": 0.1, "omega": 2.0, "dt": 0.01}

        def run(self, ctx):
            t, x = simulate(**ctx.params)
            ctx.output("trajectory", x)
            ctx.metric("l2_error", err)
            ctx.check("accurate", err < 1e-3)
            ds = ctx.dataset("trajectories")
            ds.add(t=t, x=x, label=ctx.params["zeta"])

    run("oscillator", {"zeta": 0.3})                          # cached: same params -> same run
    sweep("oscillator", grid={"zeta": [0.05, 0.1, 0.5]}, n_jobs=3)
    LabStore().catalog()                                       # CATALOG.md with tables and thumbnails

Command line: ``python -m pinneapple_lab list | run NAME -p k=v | sweep NAME -g k=v1,v2 | status | report | export``.

Any script becomes an experiment with a manifest, a Lab item and a grade: …
pinneapple_lab.doc1: PINNeAPPle Lab: run many experiments reproducibly and grow a database of results and datasets.

pinneapple_lab.__main__.doc:
``python -m pinneapple_lab ...`` -- run experiments and inspect the lab database.

    python -m pinneapple_lab list
    python -m pinneapple_lab run oscillator -p zeta=0.3 -p method=rk4
    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep cylinder_lbm -g Re=40,80,120,160 -j 4
    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep oscillator -n 50                     # Latin hypercube over the experiment's space
    python -m pinneapple_lab status
    python -m pinneapple_lab report --html                              # lab/CATALOG.md, DATASETS.md, index.html
    python -m pinneapple_lab export cylinder_lbm vorticity out/cylinder_vorticity.npz
    python -m pinneapple_lab serve --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8093                # the catalogue as a web app
    python -m pinneapple_lab examples --run --match use_cases                # examples and use cases into the lab
    python -m pinneapple_lab curate                                          # A flagship .. F not usable, per run
    python -m pinneapple_lab brief --tier A,B --use paper -o paper_candidates.pdf     # reports, one or many items
    python -m pinneapple_lab review kepler_law --novelty 4 --story "..." --approve paper,marketing
    python -m pinneapple_lab seal repo_results/ahmed_body -o seal.svg                # the item's quality seal
    python -m pinneapple_lab stamp repo_results/ahmed_body render.jpg -o out.jpg     # seal a figure / GIF / MP4
    python -m pinneapple_lab stamp --all --out export/sealed                         # every figure of every …

pinneapple_lab.capture.doc:
``pinneapple_lab.experiment(...)``: wrap a script or an example so it leaves a manifest, a Lab item and a grade.

    from pinneapple_lab import experiment

    with experiment("plate_hole", title="Plate with a hole, Kt", domain="structural mechanics",
                    methods=["FEM (CalculiX)"], params={"mesh": 0.5}) as ex:
        kt = solve(...)
        ex.log_metric("Kt", kt, unit="", how="max von Mises / nominal stress at the hole edge")
        ex.check("kt_vs_peterson", value=kt, reference=3.03, rtol=0.03, kind="reference", label="Kt vs Peterson")
        fig.savefig("results/stress.png")          # recorded automatically (and stamped files too)
        ex.add_file("results/wake.mp4")             # movies and viewers

    @experiment("oscillator_demo", title="Damped oscillator", domain="system dynamics")
    def main(ex): ...

On exit it records the git commit, the environment and the wall time, writes ``experiment.json`` (default: the
script's folder), imports it into the Lab as an item (the ``manifest`` experiment, so its checks are graded A-F
with next steps), and re-curates. ``register=False`` writes the manifest only; ``curate=False`` skips the
re-curation. A failure inside the block is recorded (the Lab run fails, so the item is graded F) and re-raised.
pinneapple_lab.capture.doc1: ``pinneapple_lab.experiment(...)``: wrap a script or an example so it leaves a manifest, a Lab item and a grade.

pinneapple_lab.curation.doc:
Experiment curation: which runs are good enough to become a product, a paper, marketing or training data.

Every run is assessed on ten dimensions computed from what the lab already stored (checks, metrics, files, code
snapshot, datasets, the experiment's description and docs) plus an optional human review. The vocabulary and the
rules are those of ``pinneapple_veriphysics.applicability``: a dimension with no evidence is NOT_RUN (never a neutral
pass), evidence is VERIFIED (a check measured it in this run), INFERRED (indirect: metrics, names, files) or
UNSUPPORTED (nothing), and no number is invented here -- the assessment only classifies what exists.

Dimensions (score 0-1, or None when not run)
    quantitative: validation, reference, baseline, physics, generalization, uncertainty, reproducibility, data
    qualitative:  assets (figures, movies, renders, 3-D viewer), documentation (description, docs, papers),
                  review (human: novelty, clarity, visual appeal, a one-line story, approvals)

Tiers A-F (gates, not a weighted sum: a strong figure never hides a failed check; the first rule that holds wins)
    F  not usable    the run crashed, a divergence check failed (non-finite, not converged), a physics check failed
                     (conservation, symmetry, equilibrium), or every reference check failed with no other
                     independent check passing (it contradicts the reference)
    E  known issues  any other failing check: a reference check …
pinneapple_lab.curation.doc1: Experiment curation: which runs are good enough to become a product, a paper, marketing or training data.

pinneapple_lab.dataset.doc:
Datasets produced by experiment runs: samples written in shards, with a card describing them.

A sample is a dict: arrays (any shape) and scalars / strings (labels, parameters). Samples are buffered and
written as ``shard_XXXXX.npz`` (arrays stacked when shapes agree, else stored per sample) with a
``samples.jsonl`` index of the scalar fields, and ``card.json`` (schema with shapes, dtypes, units and value
ranges, sample count, provenance, licence, checksum). ``LabStore.export_dataset`` concatenates the datasets of
many runs into one training set.

Wraps ``examples/black_hole_weather`` (train_forecaster.py and evaluate.py), so it runs from a source checkout of

pinneapple_lab.experiments.bricks.doc:
Self-modifying interlocking-brick builds (``pinneapple_design.bricks``): a build is checked by a static equilibrium
analysis with stud clutch, mutated, and checked again, until it meets a goal.

* ``cantilever`` -- the longest stable reach past a table edge with at most 8 parts.
* ``bridge``     -- the fewest parts that span a 96 mm gap and carry 1 N at mid-span.
* ``tower``      -- the tallest tower on a 6 x 6 stud footprint that survives a 10 mN push at the top.

Every run first checks the physics against closed forms (harmonic stacking, tipping, stud cantilever, tower push,
beam reactions; Newton replays when installed), then runs NSGA-II evolution and a GP-surrogate-guided search with
the same budget and seeds, and stores the best build (LDraw, glTF), the evolution GIF and the comparison chart.

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep bricks -g case=cantilever,bridge,tower
pinneapple_lab.experiments.bricks.doc1: Self-modifying interlocking-brick builds (``pinneapple_design.bricks``): a build is checked by a static equilibrium analysis with stud clutch, mutated, and checked again, until it meets a goal.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.calculix_case.doc:
CalculiX through ``pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.study``: CAD-like parts meshed by gmsh (C3D10),
structured beams (C3D8I), and the analyses an engineer runs first, each against a closed-form reference.

* ``plate_hole``       -- a plate with a central hole in tension: stress concentration against Heywood, mesh
                          convergence, equilibrium.
* ``l_bracket``        -- an L bracket with a fillet and a bolt hole, base clamped, side load on the upright: bending
                          stress in the upright against M c / I, mesh convergence of the peak stress, equilibrium.
* ``modal_cantilever`` -- eigenfrequencies and mode shapes of a cantilever against Euler-Bernoulli.
* ``buckling_column``  -- the buckling load of a column fixed at the base and free at the top against Euler.
* ``fin_heat``         -- steady conduction in an aluminium fin with convection, against the 1-D fin solution.

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep calculix_case -g case=plate_hole,l_bracket,modal_cantilever,buckling_column,fin_heat
pinneapple_lab.experiments.calculix_case.doc1: CalculiX through ``pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.study``: CAD-like parts meshed by gmsh (C3D10), structured beams (C3D8I), and the analyses an engineer runs first, each against a closed-form reference.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.car.doc:
Road-vehicle aerodynamics with a parametric car body and a Physics AI surrogate.

* ``car_lbm``       -- one design of a 2-D car side profile (``pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.car2d``, Ahmed-type,
                       no wheels) in a virtual wind tunnel: lattice-Boltzmann D2Q9 with Smagorinsky LES, moving
                       ground at the free-stream speed, slip ceiling. Drag and lift by momentum exchange, mean
                       fields, a vorticity movie. Dataset: geometry (mask, SDF), mean velocity and pressure,
                       coefficients; plus vorticity snapshots.
* ``car_surrogate`` -- trains on every ``car_lbm`` run in the database: an FNO (``pinneapple_neural``) maps the
                       geometry to the mean flow, with and without a physics loss (mass conservation, no-slip on
                       the body), and an MLP ensemble maps the six design parameters to drag and lift. Both are
                       scored on designs they never saw, against simple baselines. The surrogate then searches
                       the design space for the lowest drag and the winner is verified by a new LBM run.

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep car_lbm -n 48 -j 2
    python -m pinneapple_lab run car_surrogate
pinneapple_lab.experiments.car.doc1: Road-vehicle aerodynamics with a parametric car body and a Physics AI surrogate.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.discovery.doc:
Discovering physical laws from data with PINNeAPPle.

* ``kepler_law``     -- real orbital data (planets, and the moons of Jupiter and Saturn): the period-radius law and
                         its dependence on the central mass, by sparse regression over power laws.
* ``pendulum_video`` -- law -> video -> law -> video: a pendulum is filmed (rendered), its angle is measured from
                         the frames, the equation of motion is discovered (SINDy) and re-simulated, and the new video
                         is compared with the observed one, also beyond the observed window.
* ``lorenz_discovery`` -- AI-Lorenz style (De Florio, Kevrekidis & Karniadakis 2024): noisy, sparse samples of a
                         chaotic system, smoothed by an extreme-learning-machine fit (the free function of X-TFC) with
                         analytic derivatives, then SINDy recovers the equations.
* ``oscillator_discovery`` -- reuses the ``oscillator`` runs already in the lab database: recovers zeta and omega
                         of every trajectory from the data alone.
pinneapple_lab.experiments.discovery.doc1: Discovering physical laws from data with PINNeAPPle.

functions.doc1: ELM fits on overlapping windows (long chaotic records); returns y, y' at t (window centres stitched).

functions.sig: (t, u, du_hat, library, width, n_test, p=4)
functions.doc1: Weak (integral) form of u'' = f(u, u') (Messenger & Bortz's weak SINDy): with compactly supported test functions phi_k, integrate by parts so no derivative of the data is needed for the left side or the u' term: int phi u'' = int phi'' u, int phi u' = -int phi' u. ``library(u, du)`` returns …

functions.name: sindy
functions.doc1: Sparse law selection: least squares on every subset of up to ``max_terms`` library terms, keep the one with the lowest BIC. Exhaustive search is affordable for the small libraries used here and, unlike thresholded regression, does not keep collinear look-alikes (θ and θ³ next to sin θ).

pinneapple_lab.experiments.em_pinn.doc:
Physics-informed networks on the electromagnetics presets with closed-form solutions (``em_*``): electrostatics
across a dielectric interface, magnetostatics of a round wire, a TM cavity mode and the skin effect.

The examples ``examples/electrodynamics/01..06`` train their own loops and commit only figures; this experiment
solves the same physics through the library (``pp.solve(problem, "pinn")``) and scores it against the exact field
(``pp.compare(..., reference="analytic")``) on 4096 points, so the error is measured, not read from a plot.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.examples.doc:
Every example and use case of the repository as a lab experiment.

``example_script`` runs one script of ``examples/`` (``script`` parameter, a path relative to the repository) the way
a user would (``python examples/...`` from the repository root, one thread per library), then collects what it
produced: every file it created or changed anywhere in the checkout. Figures become run figures, JSON files become
outputs and their numbers metrics, arrays (.npy / .npz / .csv) become the ``artifacts`` dataset, the console output
is kept, and the script plus the Python files next to it are snapshotted as the code that ran.

Scripts run in a git worktree of HEAD under ``<lab>/_worktree`` (``isolated``, the default), so they never write
into the working checkout and the run records the exact commit. Without git (or with ``isolated=False``) they run in
the checkout itself: tracked data files they overwrite are restored, untracked files they leave are moved into the
run, and sources and docs are never touched.

    python -m pinneapple_lab examples                     # list every runnable example with its group
    python -m pinneapple_lab examples --run --match use_cases --timeout 1800
    python -m pinneapple_lab run example_script -p script=examples/getting_started/01_harmonic_oscillator.py

Validation: the script exits with status 0 within ``timeout`` seconds. Scripts that need a GPU, a download or an
optional dependency that is missing fail and are recorded as such, which also …

The cases on the PINNeAPPle Labs landing page that live in public companion repositories, as lab runs.

``benchmark_case`` imports one finished experiment of PINNeAPPle-Benchmark (or PINNeAPPle-Climate): it re-checks the
headline claim against the numbers in the experiment's own ``results.json`` (the model against its baseline, the
reproduction against the improvement), records the headline metrics, the figures, the arrays the paper's figures read
(``results/*.npz`` as the ``arrays`` dataset), the paper link, and the experiment's source as the code that ran.
The experiments themselves take hours to days (100 crash simulations, ten years of hourly weather), so the lab
stores their published results instead of repeating them.

The companion repository is found at ``$PINNEAPPLE_BENCHMARK`` / ``$PINNEAPPLE_CLIMATE``, next to this checkout
(``../pinneapple-benchmark``), or is cloned (shallow, public) into ``<lab>/_external``.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.pipes.doc:
Internal flow in pipes and static mixers (OpenFOAM, ``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.internal_flow``).

``pipe_flow`` runs one case of the structured O-grid pipe solver:

* ``laminar_pipe`` -- Hagen-Poiseuille flow at Re 500: friction factor against 64/Re, centreline speed against 2 U.
* ``bend_90``      -- turbulent flow (Re 5e4, k-omega SST) through a 90 degree bend of radius 2 D: the friction factor
                     downstream against Colebrook, the bend loss coefficient against Ito's correlation, the Dean
                     vortices (secondary flow) after the bend.
* ``kenics_mixer`` -- laminar flow (Re 50) through Kenics static-mixer elements cut into the pipe by snappyHexMesh,
                     with a passive scalar entering on half of the inlet; an empty pipe of the same mesh is the
                     baseline. Mixing (coefficient of variation along the pipe), the pressure-drop ratio Z and the
                     scalar balance.

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep pipe_flow -g case=laminar_pipe,bend_90,kenics_mixer

pinneapple_lab.experiments.repo_results.doc:
Results already produced in this repository, imported into the lab as validated runs and datasets.

Each source reads the artefacts a repository script wrote (benchmarks/_out, examples/*/results, ...), re-checks
them against their reference (exact solution, published value, solver baseline), and records metrics, figures and
datasets, so the lab database also holds the long runs that are too expensive to repeat on every sweep. The
scripts that produced the artefacts are snapshotted with each run (``code_files``).

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep repo_results -g source=burgers_pinn,fin_inverse_2d,fin_inverse_3d,...

More sources (electric machines, electromagnetics, aero, rover, forecasting, design apps) live in
``repo_sources``, which also states what each check kind means for the curation.
pinneapple_lab.experiments.repo_results.doc1: Results already produced in this repository, imported into the lab as validated runs and datasets.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.repo_sources.doc:
More committed results for ``repo_results``: electric machines and electromagnetics, the airfoil hand-off package,
the airliner CFD, the lunar rover, the near-random forecasting study, the design-from-intent demos, topology
optimisation, the free-surface trough, the benchmark arena, the SPM motor and the weather model.

Each source re-reads the files a repository script committed and turns their numbers into lab checks. A check's
``kind`` says what it is evidence of (``RunContext.check``):

* ``reference`` only for an independent result: a published experiment or simulation by another group, an exact
  solution of the same problem, or another code that does not share the model's inputs (XFOIL against OpenFOAM);
* ``verification`` for a second code or method that shares the model's geometry, materials or loads (GetDP on the
  same Prius polygons, a reduced model against the full solver of the same pipeline), and for solver checks on
  canonical problems: they answer "is the solver right", never "is the result right", so they never lift a tier;
* ``physics`` for a law the result was not fitted to (energy, mass, force balance, symmetry, a physical bound).

Tolerances that the producing script did not state are declared here, in the check's detail, before reading the
result into a tier; nothing is widened to get a pass. Where a result has no independent reference, the source says
so in ``LIMITATIONS`` and the curation keeps it below tier A.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.rom.doc:
Reduced-order models on the lab's own solvers (``pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom``).

``rom_study`` runs one case:

* ``cylinder_wake``   -- vortex shedding behind a cylinder at Re 100 (lattice Boltzmann). POD of the velocity
                         fluctuations (the travelling-wave mode pair), DMD (the shedding frequency from the spectrum
                         of the linear operator) and Operator Inference (quadratic latent dynamics) forecasting the
                         wake beyond the training window, against persistence.
* ``beam_parametric`` -- a parametric ROM of the 3-D solid FEM: a cantilever whose height, width and load direction
                         vary; POD of the displacement and von Mises fields with the coefficients regressed by RBF
                         and Gaussian processes, with and without the amplitude / shape split, against the nearest
                         training design; error on unseen designs and the speed-up over the solver.

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep rom_study -g case=cylinder_wake,beam_parametric

pinneapple_lab.experiments.structures.doc:
3-D structural mechanics with the solid finite-element solver (``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.solid_fem``,
8-node hexahedra with incompatible modes), checked against closed-form beam and torsion theory and against CalculiX
on the same mesh, drawn the way a post-processor draws it (deformed mesh, von Mises in discrete bands, legend).

* ``cantilever``       -- a steel beam clamped at the root with a load on its tip face: tip deflection against
                          Timoshenko beam theory, bending stress against M c / I.
* ``simply_supported`` -- a wide beam on two line supports under pressure on its top face: mid-span deflection and
                          bending stress against beam theory.
* ``torsion``          -- a square bar clamped at one end, twisted at the other: rate of twist and the largest shear
                          stress against Saint-Venant torsion of a square section.

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep solid_fem -g case=cantilever,simply_supported,torsion

pinneapple_lab.experiments.vehicles3d.doc:
3-D vehicles in OpenFOAM with photoreal renders: a road car and a launch vehicle.

``vehicle_cfd`` builds the vehicle (``pinneapple_design.geometry.vehicles3d``), runs steady RANS around it with the
generic ``ExternalFlow`` (snappyHexMesh, simpleFoam k-omega SST, wall functions; half model), and keeps the
coefficients, the skin pressure and friction, streamlines and wake planes. It renders the vehicle with Blender Cycles
(a beauty shot under a physical sky, the skin Cp, the streamlines coloured by speed, the wake vorticity) and writes
the three.js viewer, so the run can be browsed in 3-D from the lab server.

* ``car``    -- a coupé at 30 m/s over a road moving with the flow, wheels on the road. Checked: drag coefficient
               in the range of passenger cars with exposed, non-rotating wheels; pressure drag dominant.
* ``rocket`` -- a two-stage launcher with four tail fins at 4 degrees angle of attack (low-speed flight right after
               lift-off, incompressible). Checked against Barrowman's equations: normal-force slope and the centre
               of pressure from the CFD skin forces; the static margin.

    python -m pinneapple_lab run vehicle_cfd -p vehicle=car
    python -m pinneapple_lab run vehicle_cfd -p vehicle=rocket
pinneapple_lab.experiments.vehicles3d.doc1: 3-D vehicles in OpenFOAM with photoreal renders: a road car and a launch vehicle.

pinneapple_lab.experiments.wear.doc:
Sliding wear of bars of different materials (``pinneapple_physics.tribology``).

* ``bar_wear``         -- one material: a crowned bar end pressed on a flat counterface and slid until it has run in;
                         Archard wear with the contact pressure redistributed on an elastic layer. Checks the exact
                         facts (worn volume = K F s, the closed-form initial contact, the flat-punch steady rate, the
                         running-in distance); renders the worn end in 3-D coloured by wear depth and a movie of the
                         profile and the pressure.
* ``bar_wear_ranking`` -- every ``bar_wear`` run in the database side by side: wear rate, life to 1 mm of wear and
                         the ranking of the materials.

    python -m pinneapple_lab sweep bar_wear -g material="mild steel","60/40 brass",PTFE,stellite,...
    python -m pinneapple_lab run bar_wear_ranking

pinneapple_lab.explorer.doc:
The experiments page: every PINNeAPPle experiment with its A-F seal, trust card, measured metrics, next steps,
figures, movies, viewers and links, served by the Lab server (``/experiments``) or exported as static HTML.

What it lists, from two sources and nothing else:

* every item of the Lab curation (``<lab>/curation.json``): tier and seal reason, the six-stage trust card, the
  best run's measured metrics, its figures (stamped with the seal), movies and 3-D viewer, the failing check for E
  and F, and the path to the next letter (``pinneapple_lab.curation.next_steps``);
* every experiment manifest under ``examples/`` (``pinneapple_lab.manifest``). A folder whose scripts the Lab has
  curated shows those items and the best letter among them; any other shows "not curated" with the command that
  curates it (``python -m pinneapple_lab register <folder>``).

Counts per letter are counted from the list itself. Nothing is invented: an entry without metrics shows none.

    from pinneapple_lab.explorer import collect, coverage, write_static
    data = collect(LabStore("lab"))                       # what the page and /api/experiments show
    write_static(LabStore("lab"), "site/experiments")      # index.html + media/ (stamped figures, seals, movies)
    python -m pinneapple_lab site --out site               # the catalogue and site/experiments/
    python -m pinneapple_lab coverage -o docs/lab/coverage.md

pinneapple_lab.manifest.doc:
Experiment manifests: one file per experiment that the site, the curation and the Flow Studio all read.

An experiment is described by ``experiment.json`` next to its scripts or results (format ``pinneapple.experiment/1``,
below). A Lab run folder (``run.json``) is read as a manifest too, without a file, so every Lab run is an experiment
with no extra step. New experiments get their manifest written for them:

* scripts and examples: ``with pinneapple_lab.experiment("name", title=..., domain=...) as ex:`` (``capture.py``)
  records parameters, the git commit, environment and timing, ``ex.log_metric``, ``ex.check``, and every figure saved
  through ``Figure.savefig`` / ``sealed_savefig``, plus movies and viewers added with ``ex.add_file``; on exit it writes
  the manifest, registers it in the Lab and re-curates (A-F and next steps);
* Lab runs (``pinneapple_lab.run`` / ``sweep``) write ``experiment.json`` into the run folder;
* ``pinneapple_core.workflows`` runs write one into the run folder;
* ``pp.solve(...).to_experiment(path)`` and ``pp.compare(...).to_experiment(path)``;
* Flow Studio runs: :func:`from_flow_run`.

    from pinneapple_lab import manifest
    m = manifest.load("examples/flight_dynamics")              # a folder, an experiment.json, or a Lab run folder
    errors = manifest.validate(m, "examples/flight_dynamics")  # [] when valid
    for path, m in manifest.scan():                            # examples/*, the Lab runs, results folders
        ...
    python …

pinneapple_lab.next_steps.doc:
What an item lacks for the next letter, and the PINNeAPPle action that would close each gap.

The curation (``pinneapple_lab.curation``) computes, for every run, the exact gaps between its letter and the next one
up from the same evidence that gave the letter: the failing checks (with the measured value against its tolerance or
bound) for E and F, the trust-card stage nobody answered for D, the missing independent check or the reproducibility
score for C, the flagship gates for B, and for A what would strengthen it further (a second independent reference, a
quantified uncertainty, a benchmark comparison, a human review). Each gap carries the library actions that address it,
from a curated registry (:data:`ACTIONS`), with the item's own experiment and parameters filled in. A gap with no
registered action says so (``no PINNeAPPle action yet``); nothing outside the library is ever suggested, and a test
resolves every action's import path or command.

    from pinneapple_lab.curation import next_steps
    for gap in next_steps("repo_results/benchmark_arena"):        # from lab/curation.json
        print(gap.to, gap.why, [a.command for a in gap.actions])

    python -m pinneapple_lab seal --explain repo_results/benchmark_arena [--lang pt]
    python -m pinneapple_lab improve repo_results/benchmark_arena [--run]

Stable API (the Flow Studio reads it): :class:`Gap` (``type``, ``to``, ``stage``, ``check``, ``why`` / ``why_pt``,
``short`` / ``short_pt``, ``measured``, ``actions``) …

pinneapple_lab.reports.doc:
Reports from the lab: one experiment (or case), or many selected by a filter, as HTML, Markdown or PDF.

A report carries, for each item: what it is, the one-line story, the key figures, the headline metrics, every
validation check (with what it is evidence of), the evidence dimensions and tier, the readiness for product /
publication / marketing / training data, the limitations, the path forward (actions, effort, what they unlock) and
how to reproduce it (run id, commit, code, command). Everything comes from the lab record and the curation
(``pinneapple_lab.curation``); nothing is written by hand here.

    python -m pinneapple_lab brief --item kepler_law -o kepler.html
    python -m pinneapple_lab brief --tier A,B --use paper -o papers.pdf          # everything closest to a paper
    python -m pinneapple_lab brief --ready marketing --format md -o marketing.md
    python -m pinneapple_lab brief --experiment benchmark_case -o landing.html   # every case of one experiment
pinneapple_lab.reports.doc1: Reports from the lab: one experiment (or case), or many selected by a filter, as HTML, Markdown or PDF.

pinneapple_lab.results_rules.doc:
Rules that turn the results an example commits into manifest metrics and checks (``manifest.from_results``).

Only values in the results files are used. A check is one of:

* ``Flag``: a verdict the study recorded itself (a boolean in its results, e.g. ``stall_margin_ok``);
* ``CheckList``: check records the study wrote (each with its own ``passed``, value, reference, tolerance or limit);
* ``Bound``: a measured value against the acceptance threshold the study's own test applies to it, cited as
  ``file:line``; the literal must appear on that line (a test checks every citation), so no threshold is invented.

Paths are dotted, ``*`` matching every key of a dict or index of a list; a name template is formatted with the
matched keys (``{0}``, ``{1}``) and the object the last ``*`` matched (``{o[aircraft]}``).

Folders curated through a Lab ``repo_results`` source (its scripts live there) need no rule: the page links them
to that item. Folders with no measured results stay "not curated".

pinneapple_lab.seal.doc:
The PINNeAPPle quality seal: a small badge with the tier the Lab curation gave an item, stamped on its figures,
renders and movies.

The tier always comes from the curation record (``<lab>/curation.json``, written by ``pinneapple_lab.curation``);
there is no argument to set it by hand, and stamping again after a re-curation picks up the new tier. The one-line
reason under the wordmark is the item's ``headline`` from the same record: the passing check it was compared with
(``check_line``), or for E and F the failing check, never free text.

Every tier is sealed, A to F, so a figure always says where its result stands:

    A  green        independent reference            D  orange      exploratory, not validated
    B  light green  reference pending                E  red         known problems
    C  yellow       partly checked                   F  dark red    not usable

E and F seals always carry the main problem (the failing check, the crash or the divergence) and the next step to
the tier above it (``headline["hint"]``), whatever ``reason`` says, and have no compact form. ``tiers=("A", "B")``
on :func:`seal_for` or :func:`stamp_all` (``--tiers A,B`` on the command line) keeps a selection to the validated
items: anything else raises :class:`SealError` or is skipped.

    from pinneapple_lab.seal import seal_for, render_seal, stamp_figure, stamp_file
    s = seal_for("repo_results/ahmed_body")             # tier and reason from lab/curation.json
    …

pinneapple_lab.server.doc:
Serve the lab catalogue over HTTP: the browsable page, every run's files, a JSON API and dataset downloads.

    python -m pinneapple_lab serve --root lab --port 8093          # http://localhost:8093

Standard library only (no web framework). The page is rebuilt when the database changes (new runs from a sweep
running next to the server, or a ``reindex`` every ``--refresh`` seconds), thumbnails are made on demand and kept in
memory, and dataset exports are cached on disk under ``<root>/_exports``.

Routes::

    GET /                                    the catalogue page
    GET /health                              liveness
    GET /api/catalog                         everything the page shows (experiments, runs, metrics, checks, datasets)
    GET /api/status                          run counts per experiment and status
    GET /api/runs?experiment=NAME&status=S   run index rows
    GET /api/runs/RUN_ID                     one run: record, metrics, validation, file list
    GET /api/datasets                        dataset cards
    GET /api/curation                        quality tier, dimensions and readiness of every run and experiment
    GET /report.html|.md|.pdf?items=&experiment=&tier=&use=&ready=&tag=   a report for one item or a filtered set
    GET /files/EXPERIMENT/RUN_ID/PATH        a run's file (figures, inputs, outputs, code, logs, cards)
    GET /thumb/EXPERIMENT/RUN_ID/PATH        a JPEG thumbnail of a run's figure
    GET /download/EXPERIMENT/DATASET.npz     …

pinneapple_lab.showcase.doc:
Animated showcase panel of the Lab's best results, generated from the curation.

``panel()`` lays out a 1080 x 1350 (4:5) panel on ``#090C14``: the PINNeAPPle header, one hero tile with a slow
Ken Burns zoom, a 3 x 3 grid of Tier A tiles, a row of two Tier B tiles and the footer, and writes an MP4 (H.264,
yuv420p, faststart), a GIF (720 wide, 12 fps, palettegen) and a still PNG.

What goes in it, and every word of evidence on it, comes from ``<lab>/curation.json``:

* tiles are picked from the curation, Tier A first (hero and grid), then the strongest Tier B (the B row); an item
  curated at C to F is never shown, whatever the override list says (the seals of C to F exist, for stamping the
  item's own figures, but the panel shows validated results only);
* an override list (``picks``) chooses items and which of their figures to show, in order; an item lands in the
  grid only if the curation gave it A, in the B row if it gave B, so a re-curation moves it;
* each tile's green "✓" (A) or amber "◐" (B) line is the item's curation headline, the passing check it was
  compared with (``pinneapple_lab.curation.headline``); a tile without one is not shown;
* each tile carries the item's seal (``pinneapple_lab.seal``), so the tier on the tile is the curation's tier.

Animated figures (GIF, MP4) play in their tiles, resampled to run once over the loop (8 s at 15 fps); static ones
stay still. Tiles are cropped only at empty rows and columns of the figure, so a colour bar or an axis …
pinneapple_lab.showcase.doc1: Animated showcase panel of the Lab's best results, generated from the curation.

pinneapple_lab.uq.doc:
Uncertainty evidence for lab runs: the checks that answer the trust card's "where may the result not be
reliable?" with numbers instead of declared limitations.

* ``coverage_check``   -- a learned model's predictive interval (mean +- z sigma) must hold its nominal fraction of
                          unseen data: 90 % intervals that contain 60 % of the truth are not uncertainty, they are
                          optimism. Kind "uncertainty".
* ``gci``              -- grid convergence index (Roache 1994; Celik et al., J. Fluids Eng. 130, 2008) of a solver
                          result from two or three meshes: the discretisation error band of the fine-mesh value.
* ``gci_check``        -- records the GCI band as a metric and checks it is below a tolerance. Kind "uncertainty".
* ``ensemble_spread``  -- relative spread of a quantity over repeated runs (seeds, members).

    from pinneapple_lab.uq import coverage_check, gci_check
    coverage_check(ctx, "displacement", y_true, mean, std, level=0.9)
    gci_check(ctx, "Kt", [kt_coarse, kt_fine], [h_coarse, h_fine], order=2, max_band=0.05)
pinneapple_lab.uq.doc1: Uncertainty evidence for lab runs: the checks that answer the trust card's "where may the result not be reliable?" with numbers instead of declared limitations.

functions.doc1: Record the empirical coverage of the ``level`` interval on unseen data and check |coverage - level| <= tol (calibrated: neither over- nor under-confident).

functions.doc1: Grid convergence index of the finest value. ``values`` and ``h`` (representative cell sizes) from coarse to fine. With three meshes the observed order is computed (Celik et al. 2008); with two, ``order`` is the formal order of the scheme and the safety factor is 3 (1.25 with three meshes).

pinneapple_llm.doc:
LLM-assisted physics-AI pipeline drafting, gated by a physics-grounded
verification layer.

See ``draft.py``, ``geometry_draft.py``, ``twin_draft.py``,
``research.py`` and ``guardrail.py`` module docstrings for the design
rationale: the LLM only ever *selects and parametrises* one of
PINNeAPPle's own already-implemented presets/generators/config schemas
(never invents new physics/CAD/twin machinery), and ``PhysicsGuardrail``
is the mechanical, re-computed check every result should pass before
being reported as trustworthy -- whether or not an LLM was involved in
producing it.

``local_llm.py`` and ``conversation_store.py`` add a fully local path
(Ollama + a SQLite conversation log, no hosted API, no data leaving your
machine); ``finetune.py`` fine-tunes a local model on that logged data.

pinneapple_llm._dispatch.doc:
Provider-agnostic LLM call dispatch, shared by ``draft.py``,
``geometry_draft.py``, ``research.py`` and ``twin_draft.py`` -- one place
that knows how to reach Anthropic, OpenAI, or a local Ollama server, and
one place that logs every call to a :class:`ConversationStore` when one is
configured (see that module's docstring for why: auditability of what was
actually asked/answered, and the dataset :mod:`finetune` trains on).

Logging is opt-in per call (pass ``conversation_store=``) rather than a
hidden global default, so "every LLM call in this process gets written to
disk" is something a caller chooses, not something that happens to them.

pinneapple_llm.agent_loop.doc:
A genuine multi-step LLM agent loop: the LLM itself decides, turn by
turn, which real tool to call next, observes the result, and decides the
next step -- grounded in :func:`pinneapple_llm._dispatch.call_llm` (a
real, single-call LLM dispatch across anthropic/openai/ollama) plus a
real tool registry (:class:`pinneapple_worldmodel.physics_tools.PhysicsToolRegistry`
by default, or any object exposing the same ``get``/``available_tools``
query interface).

This is deliberately NOT the same thing as
:func:`pinneapple_problemdesign.knowledge.mapping.available_orchestrator_tools`
(a read-only, single-shot bridge used only to *list* tools for plan
generation) nor :class:`pinneapple_worldmodel.orchestrator.PhysicsOrchestrator`
(a hand-written, goal-directed tool *chain* -- its own planning logic
decides what runs next, not an LLM). Here, each step's tool choice is a
live LLM decision: the loop builds a prompt naming the goal, the history
of what has happened so far, and the tools currently available (queried
live from the registry, never hardcoded), asks the LLM to respond with
either a tool call or a final answer, actually invokes the chosen tool
via the registry, and feeds the real result back into the next turn's
prompt.

JSON-response parsing mirrors the house pattern used by
``pinneapple_problemdesign/extractor.py`` (``_strip_code_fences`` /
``_extract_first_json_object``) rather than importing it -- this module
depends only on ``pinneapple_llm`` and (optionally, …

pinneapple_llm.cad_draft.doc:
LLM-assisted CAD/geometry generation -- the same constrained pattern
as ``draft.py``'s ``draft_problem`` and ``geometry_draft.py``'s
``draft_geometry``, extended to genuinely NEW (not just named-catalog)
geometry: instead of picking one fixed preset name, the LLM composes a
recipe out of PINNeAPPle's own already-implemented, already-tested
building blocks -- primitive mesh builders
(``pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.primitives.build_mesh``, e.g. box,
sphere, cylinder) combined via real boolean CSG operations (union/cut/
intersect), optionally nested to arbitrary depth -- or, for a genuine
parametric CAD (STEP-exportable) part, one of
``pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.cadquery_gen``'s registered CadQuery
templates (e.g. a finned plate, a channeled cold-plate).

This is still never "the LLM writes CAD code": every recipe node is a
plain JSON dict of ``{"name": <real builder name>, <params...>,
"boolean": {"op": ..., "other": {<recursive node>}}}`` -- checked,
recursively, against the real registry before a single line of geometry
code runs. An LLM that names a builder or CSG op that doesn't exist gets
rejected exactly like ``draft_problem`` rejects a hallucinated preset
name, at any depth of nesting, not just the top level.

Two "kinds" of result, because they answer different questions:

- ``"mesh_recipe"``: a (possibly CSG-composed) triangle mesh, always
  available (no optional CAD-kernel dependency beyond ``trimesh``,
  already required by ``pinneapple_design.geometry``). …

pinneapple_llm.catalog_match.doc:
pinneapple_llm.catalog_match — ``resolve_problem()``: a two-stage,
never-raises front end to ``draft_problem()``.

``draft_problem()`` already sends the *entire* preset catalog (name +
accepted kwargs) to the LLM in one shot and mechanically rejects any
hallucinated name/kwarg — safe, but it (a) sends the whole catalog on
every call even when most of it is obviously irrelevant, and (b) raises
on any failure (missing API key, network error, malformed response),
with no fallback. ``resolve_problem()`` adds:

1. A cheap keyword-overlap pre-filter narrowing the full catalog down to
   a shortlist before ever calling an LLM (cheaper prompts, and a second,
   independent signal the caller can inspect even when the LLM step
   succeeds).
2. A deterministic, LLM-free fallback — the top keyword match — used
   automatically if the LLM step fails for any reason at all.

Never raises: if you need ``draft_problem()``'s strict "raise on
hallucination" behavior instead, call that directly.
pinneapple_llm.catalog_match.doc1: pinneapple_llm.catalog_match — ``resolve_problem()``: a two-stage, never-raises front end to ``draft_problem()``.

functions.sig: (description, *, provider='anthropic', model=None, api_key=None, conversation_store=None, top_k=12) -> ResolveResult
functions.doc1: Resolve ``description`` to a registered PDE preset — the shortlist step always runs; the LLM step is attempted next and its result used if it succeeds, else the top keyword match is returned instead. Never raises.

pinneapple_llm.conversation_store.doc:
SQLite-backed conversation log for every ``pinneapple_llm`` LLM call.

Zero extra dependency (``sqlite3`` is Python stdlib). Every call through
``draft.py``'s ``_call_anthropic``/``_call_openai``/``local_llm``'s
``_call_ollama`` is logged here when a store is configured -- this is
useful for two independent reasons: (1) auditability (every physics-
relevant LLM interaction this library made is inspectable and replayable,
not just trusted after the fact -- the same transparency principle
``PhysicsGuardrail`` applies to *results*, applied here to *inputs*), and
(2) it is the dataset :mod:`finetune` fine-tunes a local model on.

pinneapple_llm.draft.doc:
LLM-assisted ``ProblemSpec`` drafting -- deliberately constrained to
selecting and parametrising one of PINNeAPPle's own already-implemented,
already-testable presets, never to inventing new PDE machinery from
scratch.

This constraint is the actual point, not a limitation to work around: an
LLM asked to "write CFD code" freely can silently fabricate boundary
conditions or produce code that runs while violating conservation, with no
mechanism to catch it. Restricted to *choosing among a known preset
catalog* (``pinneapple_physics.list_presets()``) and filling in the
numeric parameters a human would otherwise pass to ``get_preset(name,
**kwargs)`` by hand, the LLM's only possible failure modes are (a) picking
a preset that doesn't match the user's actual problem, or (b) picking
physically-wrong parameter values -- both of which
``pinneapple_llm.guardrail.PhysicsGuardrail`` (a fixed, re-computed
residual + parameter-sanity check, not a language model's confidence) can
catch mechanically, downstream of this module and independent of it. This
module never asks the LLM to write or approve physics; it asks it to name
one.

Provider-agnostic: ``"anthropic"``/``"openai"`` (optional deps, bring your
own API key) or ``"ollama"`` (a local model, no API key, no data leaves
your machine -- see ``local_llm.py``). ``pip install "pinneapple[llm]"``
for the hosted providers' SDKs; ``ollama`` needs only ``requests`` (a
common transitive dependency already) plus a local Ollama install.
pinneapple_llm.draft.doc1: LLM-assisted ``ProblemSpec`` drafting -- deliberately constrained to selecting and parametrising one of PINNeAPPle's own already-implemented, already-testable presets, never to inventing new PDE machinery from scratch.

pinneapple_llm.finetune.doc:
LoRA fine-tuning of a local causal LM on data logged via
``conversation_store.ConversationStore``.

Scope, stated plainly: this fine-tunes a local Hugging-Face-format causal
LM's weights (via ``transformers``+``peft``, optional deps -- ``pip
install "pinneapple[finetune]"``). It does **not** fine-tune an Ollama
model directly -- Ollama itself does not do full/LoRA weight fine-tuning
(its ``Modelfile`` mechanism customises a system prompt/imports an
already-trained adapter, it doesn't train one). The realistic local
pipeline is: (1) fine-tune a HF-format base model here, on your logged
conversations; (2) if you want to *serve* the result via Ollama
afterwards, convert it to GGUF with ``llama.cpp``'s own conversion tooling
and ``ollama create`` from it -- both are separate, well-documented steps
outside this module's scope (GGUF conversion is its own significant tool,
not something to silently wrap).

pinneapple_llm.guardrail.doc:
``PhysicsGuardrail``: the actual anti-hallucination mechanism.

State this precisely, because overclaiming it is exactly the failure mode
it exists to prevent: **this does not guarantee a result is correct, and
nothing can.** What it does is compute a small set of independent,
numeric, re-checkable signals -- a re-evaluated PDE residual on fresh
points, dimensional/units sanity of the declared parameters, a
conservation-law balance (for the pde_kind families where one has a known
closed form), and (when a reference is supplied) an error metric against
real data -- and refuse to label a result "trustworthy" unless every
signal it can compute passes. A raw LLM asked to solve a physics problem,
by contrast, produces an answer with no residual behind it at all; there
is nothing to check. The differentiation this module gives PINNeAPPle
over "just ask a language model" is not that its answers are smarter,
it's that every claim is required to pass through this gate, or be
reported as *not* having passed it -- explicitly, with the failing check
named, not silently.

Independent of ``pinneapple_llm``'s drafting module (``draft.py``): this
is useful on *any* ``solve_pde``/``pipeline`` result, whether or not an
LLM was involved in producing the ``ProblemSpec`` at all.

Coverage is explicit, not implied
----------------------------------

and the conservation check -- are only *real, structural* verification
for a …

paid API/external network call at all: run a model entirely on your own

pinneapple_llm.qa.doc:
Scientific and industrial quality assurance for ``pinneapple_llm`` artifacts.

This package is the pipeline described in the module docstrings of its
parts, in execution order::

    spec.py        stage A  typed, serializable physical specification
    static.py      stage C  AST + real API-introspection validation
    sandbox.py     stage D  controlled execution (and its honest limits)
    validators/    stage E  units, numeric, physics, geometry, temporal, sensors
    references.py  stage F  comparison against independent reference data
    repair.py      stage G  diagnosis + bounded automatic repair
    levels.py       Q0-Q4  what the run's evidence actually earns
    report.py              machine-readable, self-contained run record
    pipeline.py            wires A-G; never generates the artifact itself

The one rule that holds everywhere here: no step contributes a ``PASS`` it
did not observe. ``NOT_RUN``, ``BLOCKED`` and ``NOT_APPLICABLE`` stay
distinct all the way into the JSON report and into the quality level.
pinneapple_llm.qa.doc1: Scientific and industrial quality assurance for ``pinneapple_llm`` artifacts.

pinneapple_llm.qa.examples.doc:
Runnable reference examples for the quality pipeline.

``pipe_wear_twin`` is the end-to-end benchmark (stages A-G over a 3D
pipeline-wear twin). It is imported lazily by ``__main__`` so that simply
importing this package does not build a scene.
pinneapple_llm.qa.examples.doc1: Runnable reference examples for the quality pipeline.

pinneapple_llm.qa.examples.pipe_wear_twi.doc:
End-to-end reference example: a 3D digital twin of a pipe under wall wear.

What this builds, using only APIs that already exist in this repository:

* a **hollow** pipe mesh (outer wall, inner wall, two annular end faces)
  from :func:`pinneapple_twin3d.primitives.revolve`;
* a wear zone (``pinneapple_twin3d.wear``) whose per-cell wear depth
  evolves over time, with per-cell meshes from
  :func:`pinneapple_twin3d.wear.geometry.cell_mesh`;
* a ``pinneapple_twin3d.Scene`` built by ``scene_from_wear`` and exported
  to real files (``scene.json``, ``geometry.glb``, ``fields.bin``);
* four ultrasonic thickness readings as sensors, one of them reserved as
  holdout, positioned at real cell centres.

Two operating conditions are provided, both synthetic:
``anomaly=False`` (uniform 1.2 mm/year wear, staying under the limit) and
``anomaly=True`` (a localised hotspot that breaches the 2 mm minimum wall).

Honesty note, repeated in the report: this is a **verification** example.
The reference it compares against is the closed-form uniform-wear solution,
so agreement demonstrates that the pipeline, the mesh and the field
plumbing are consistent -- it says nothing about a real pipe. The dataset
is marked ``synthetic`` and the quality level is capped at Q3 by
construction (Q4 needs operational evidence).

pinneapple_llm.qa.generation.doc:
Stage B informed: the LLM's structured claims, and why they are not evidence.

The specification requires that a generated artifact arrive with more than
code: the assumptions it was built on, its dependencies, the units it uses,
the equations it believes it implemented, and its known limitations. This
module captures exactly that, and then does the part that matters -- it
confronts those declarations with the specification and with reality:

* declared units must parse, and must agree with the specification's units
  for the same quantity;
* declared dependencies must be in the static import allowlist, so the
  artifact will not claim a dependency the validator will reject;
* an assumption the specification does not contain is recorded as an
  **unverified extra assumption**, not silently merged into the spec;
* missing declarations are reported as missing.

The language model's own description is never treated as evidence that the
code is correct. It is an input to stage C/E, and every claim in it that can
be checked mechanically is checked. This is the difference between "the
model says it used SI units" and "the units in the artifact are SI".
pinneapple_llm.qa.generation.doc1: Stage B informed: the LLM's structured claims, and why they are not evidence.

pinneapple_llm.qa.levels.doc:
Quality levels Q0-Q4, awarded from what actually ran -- never from an LLM.

The levels are cumulative and each one names the *evidence* that grants
it. Two rules keep this from decaying into a badge:

* A level is granted only when every step it requires is present and
  ``PASS``. ``NOT_RUN``, ``BLOCKED`` and (for a validation the spec itself
  required) ``NOT_APPLICABLE`` all fail to grant it.
* ``Q4`` cannot be reached from inside this repository at all. It requires
  operational evidence supplied by a human, and :func:`evaluate_level`
  only accepts it when the evidence names a reviewer, an environment, a
  date and monitoring data. Test-suite output is not operational
  evidence, no matter how many tests pass.

What each level means in this pipeline:

===  ==========================================================================
Q0   artifact generated; nothing verified
Q1   syntax, schema, imports, real-API use and security checks passed
Q2   the scientific/numeric validators the spec required passed
Q3   comparison against independent reference data passed the declared metrics
Q4   operational evidence supplied by a human reviewer (cannot be automated)
===  ==========================================================================

pinneapple_llm.qa.pipeline.doc:
The quality pipeline: stages A-G wired into one reproducible run.

Stage map (the letters are the specification's, kept so a report can be
read against it):

===  ========================================================  ============================
A    :class:`~pinneapple_llm.qa.spec.PhysicalSpecification`      supplied by the caller
B    artifact generation                                       supplied (LLM or otherwise)
C    static/structural validation                              :mod:`pinneapple_llm.qa.static`
D    controlled execution                                      :mod:`pinneapple_llm.qa.sandbox`
E    scientific/numeric validation                             :mod:`pinneapple_llm.qa.validators`
F    independent reference comparison                          :mod:`pinneapple_llm.qa.references`
G    diagnosis and bounded repair                              :mod:`pinneapple_llm.qa.repair`
===  ========================================================  ============================

The pipeline never generates the artifact itself. Generation -- from an
LLM or from code -- is stage B and stays outside, so "the model wrote it"
can never be confused with "the pipeline checked it". What the pipeline
does is run the checks, record exactly what passed, what failed and what
was never run, and compute the quality level from that record.
pinneapple_llm.qa.pipeline.doc1: The quality pipeline: stages A-G wired into one reproducible run.

pinneapple_llm.qa.references.doc:
Stage F: comparison against independent reference data.

Without reference data a pipeline can only show *internal consistency*:
the artifact respects its own constraints. That is genuinely useful and it
is not evidence of fidelity to the physical system. This module makes the
difference explicit rather than rhetorical:

* it refuses to invent or default a reference (:class:`ReferenceData`
  requires an origin, a version and its known limitations);
* it refuses to compute an "acceptable" threshold -- the criteria come
  from the caller/specification;
* when predictions are compared on data that was also used for
  calibration, that is reported, because the resulting metric is an
  in-sample fit, not a validation;
* every metric is recorded with the subset it was computed on.

pinneapple_llm.qa.report.doc:
Reproducible quality report -- the machine-readable output of every run.

Two design commitments, both from the same failure mode (a pipeline that
says PASS because nothing ran):

1. There is no boolean "ok" anywhere. Every step carries one of
   :class:`Status`, and ``NOT_RUN``/``NOT_APPLICABLE`` are never folded
   into ``PASS``. A consumer that only wants a yes/no has to state which
   steps it requires.
2. The report is self-contained: it carries the spec it was given, the
   hashes of the artifacts it saw, the versions of the software, and the
   exact command that reproduces the run. Reading it does not require the
   conversation that produced it.
pinneapple_llm.qa.report.doc1: Reproducible quality report -- the machine-readable output of every run.

pinneapple_llm.qa.sandbox.doc:
Stage D: controlled execution of generated artifacts.

Read this before relying on it
------------------------------
The isolation implemented here is **subprocess isolation with in-process
policy enforcement**, not an operating-system sandbox. Concretely, an
artifact runs as a separate process (:mod:`subprocess`) in its own
temporary directory, with:

* a scrubbed environment (no inherited secrets, ``HOME`` pointing at the
  temporary directory);
* POSIX resource limits (CPU time, address space, file size, open files,
  no core dumps) applied with :mod:`resource` before the interpreter
  starts;
* a wall-clock timeout after which the process is killed;
* a Python audit hook installed *inside* the child process that refuses
  network connections, process spawning, and file access outside the
  artifact directory and the interpreter's own library paths;
* every produced file recorded with its SHA-256.

What this does **not** do: it does not stop C extensions or ``ctypes``
from issuing syscalls directly, it does not create a container, a user
namespace, a seccomp filter or a chroot, and it does not stop a process
that escapes the audit hook. A determined artifact can read memory it
should not. The audit hook is a *policy* layer that catches the ordinary
failure modes (a generated script phoning home, writing to ``~/.ssh``,
shelling out) and reports them; it is not a security boundary between
hostile code and the host.

Because of that, :class:`SandboxExecutor` refuses to run …

pinneapple_llm.qa.spec.doc:
Typed, serializable physical specification -- stage A of the quality pipeline.

The point of this module is to make "what was asked for" inspectable
*before* any code or twin is generated, and to keep the four kinds of
statement a physics answer quietly mixes together visibly separate:

``USER``        stated by the requester;
``SOURCE``      read from a cited reference (with ``source`` filled in);
``ASSUMPTION``  adopted by the system and marked as such;
``ESTIMATED``   inferred, never verified.

Nothing in this module invents a value to fill a gap. A field that is
absent stays absent, and :meth:`PhysicalSpecification.missing_information`
is what the pipeline reports as ``BLOCKED``/limitation instead of
silently defaulting it.

Invariants are *declarative* on purpose (``kind`` + ``params``), never
Python source to ``eval``: the specification may come from an LLM, and a
spec that can execute code is a security hole, not a feature. The
supported kinds are listed in :data:`INVARIANT_KINDS` and evaluated by
``pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.physics``.
pinneapple_llm.qa.spec.doc1: Typed, serializable physical specification -- stage A of the quality pipeline.

classes.doc1: Raised when a specification is structurally invalid.

classes.doc1: A number with a unit, a provenance tag, and (optionally) an uncertainty.

classes.doc1: A physical constraint the artifact must satisfy. Declarative, not code.

pinneapple_llm.qa.static.doc:
Stage C: static and structural validation of generated artifacts.

What this module actually is: an AST walk plus real introspection of the
PINNeAPPle modules. What it is not: a sandbox, a type checker, or proof
that the code does what it claims. The docstring says so because
"validated statically" is exactly the kind of phrase that gets read as
"safe and correct" when it means "we parsed it and looked things up".

Three checks are worth naming precisely, because they are the ones that
catch the failure modes ordinary syntax checks miss:

``static_api_contracts``
    Every ``pinneapple_*`` attribute the artifact touches is resolved
    against the *installed* module with :func:`getattr`. A call to
    ``pinneapple_twin3d.primitives.torus(...)`` -- a function that does
    not exist -- fails here, before execution, with the closest real
    names suggested.

``static_signatures``
    Where a called function could be resolved, its :func:`inspect.signature`
    is compared with the call node: too many positional arguments, or a
    keyword the function does not accept, is reported. This is still
    static -- ``*args``/``**kwargs`` and dynamically built calls are out
    of reach, and a passing signature says nothing about argument
    *semantics*.

``static_security``
    Imports and calls that escape the artifact's intended scope are
    refused: process spawning, raw sockets, ``eval``/``exec``,
    ``ctypes``/``marshal``/``pickle`` loads, filesystem deletion, and
    writes …
pinneapple_llm.qa.static.doc1: Stage C: static and structural validation of generated artifacts.

pinneapple_llm.qa.units.doc:
Dimensional analysis for the quality pipeline -- dependency-free, deliberately small.

Why not ``pint``: this repo keeps ``pinneapple_llm`` importable with no
heavy dependency (see ``pyproject.toml``'s optional extras), and adds
``pint`` -- a large package with a plugin system -- for the handful of
quantities a physics artifact actually declares would be a bad trade. The
cost is real and is stated rather than hidden: this parser understands a
FIXED grammar over a FIXED unit table. An unknown unit raises
:class:`UnitError`; it is never silently treated as dimensionless, which
would turn "I don't recognise this unit" into "everything is compatible".

Grammar accepted::

    unit      := factor (('*' | '/' | '.') factor)*
    factor    := name ('^' | '**')? integer?
    name      := a key of ``_UNITS``, optionally SI-prefixed

Examples: ``"m"``, ``"mm"``, ``"m/s"``, ``"m^2"``, ``"kg/m^3"``,
``"mm/year"``, ``"W/(m*K)"``, ``"1/s"``.

Base dimensions are the SI seven, in this order: length, time, mass,
temperature, electric current, amount, luminous intensity.
pinneapple_llm.qa.units.doc1: Dimensional analysis for the quality pipeline -- dependency-free, deliberately small.

classes.name: UnitError
classes.doc1: Raised for an unparsable unit string or an incompatible conversion.

classes.name: Unit
classes.doc1: An SI-scaled unit: ``si_value = value * scale + offset``.
