functions.doc1: Parse a unit string into a :class:`Unit`. Raises :class:`UnitError`.

functions.name: are_compatible
functions.doc1: True if two unit strings have the same physical dimension.

functions.name: convert
functions.doc1: Convert ``value`` between two compatible units. Raises on incompatibility.

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.doc:
Scientific validators and their registry (stage E).

``available()`` lists what is registered; ``run(name, ctx)`` executes one.
The built-ins are registered as a side effect of importing
:mod:`pinneapple_llm.qa.validators`, so a caller that has imported the
package can enumerate them without knowing the module layout.
pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.doc1: Scientific validators and their registry (stage E).

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.base.doc:
Validator protocol, shared context and registry.

A validator answers one question about one artifact and returns evidence
for its answer. Two conventions are load-bearing:

* A validator that does not apply returns ``NOT_APPLICABLE`` **with a
  reason**, never ``PASS``. A pipeline that counted inapplicable checks as
  passes would award Q2 to an empty artifact.
* A validator that would apply but was not given the data it needs returns
  ``BLOCKED`` (or ``NOT_RUN`` if the caller disabled it) -- also never
  ``PASS``. The distinction the spec asks for between "not applicable",
  "not run" and "passed" survives all the way into the report.
pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.base.doc1: Validator protocol, shared context and registry.

classes.name: SensorReading
classes.sig: (id, position, unit, quantity, series, holdout, position_unit)
classes.doc1: One sensor: where, what unit, and the series over the artifact's time axis.

classes.name: ValidationContext
classes.sig: (spec, meshes, fields, field_units, times, time_unit, sensors, payload, model, extra)
classes.doc1: Everything a validator may look at. Absent data means "not supplied".

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.geometry.doc:
Geometry validation, including the hollow-body check the spec calls out.

The specific failure this module exists to catch: a request for a *hollow*
pipe answered with a solid cylinder. Both are valid meshes; only one is the
object that was asked for. The check is numerical, not visual -- the mesh's
enclosed volume is computed from its triangles and compared with the
volume the specification's own dimensions imply:

* a hollow pipe of outer radius ``R``, wall thickness ``t`` and length ``L``
  encloses ``pi*(R^2 - (R-t)^2)*L``;
* a solid cylinder of the same outer radius encloses ``pi*R^2*L``.

If the measured volume is closer to the solid value than to the hollow one,
the artifact is reported as not being a hollow body. If the mesh is not
closed, its volume is undefined and the check returns ``BLOCKED`` rather
than guessing.
pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.geometry.doc1: Geometry validation, including the hollow-body check the spec calls out.

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.guardrail.doc:
Bridge to the existing :class:`pinneapple_llm.guardrail.PhysicsGuardrail`.

This exists so the pipeline reuses the repo's real anti-hallucination
machinery instead of re-implementing a weaker copy. It applies only when
the caller supplies a trained model *and* the ``ProblemSpec`` it was
trained on; otherwise it is ``NOT_APPLICABLE``. Every guardrail check
becomes one finding, so a pipeline report shows exactly which physical
signals were recomputed and which were absent from the guardrail's own
coverage.

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.numeric.doc:
Numeric integrity: finite values, shapes, degenerate fields.

The shape check is the one the specification calls out explicitly: a field
whose time axis does not match the number of timestamps, or whose value
count does not match the mesh it is attached to, is wrong even when the
code that produced it compiles and runs.
pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.numeric.doc1: Numeric integrity: finite values, shapes, degenerate fields.

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.physics.doc:
Physical invariants declared by the specification (stage E, part 3).

Every invariant in the specification is evaluated here against the
artifact's own arrays. The invariants are declarative (``kind`` +
``params``) -- this module never evaluates generated Python, which is the
whole reason :mod:`pinneapple_llm.qa.spec` refuses expression strings.

An invariant whose target the artifact does not provide is ``BLOCKED``,
not skipped: "the constraint we said mattered was never checked" is
exactly the state that must not look like success.
pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.physics.doc1: Physical invariants declared by the specification (stage E, part 3).

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.sensors.doc:
Sensor / observation consistency.

Checks that a reading is attached to a place that exists, a time that
exists and a quantity the artifact actually models -- and that readings
used to calibrate are separated from readings reserved for validation.
That last one is a warning, not a pass: a twin with no holdout data can be
internally consistent and still have no evidential value.

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.temporal.doc:
Temporal consistency: ordering, sample counts, validity window.

A transient artifact that reports 12 timestamps and 10 time steps of
field data is wrong in a way no syntax check notices, and that a viewer
will happily render as if nothing were missing.
pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.temporal.doc1: Temporal consistency: ordering, sample counts, validity window.

pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.units.doc:
Dimensional consistency across geometry, parameters, fields and sensors.

What this checks: that every declared quantity *has* a parseable unit, that
lengths agree with lengths, that a field's declared unit matches the unit
the specification declared for the same quantity, and that sensor units
agree with the fields they observe. What it does **not** check: that the
equation a field appears in is dimensionally sound. Dimensional analysis
can prove an expression inconsistent; it can never prove one correct.
pinneapple_llm.qa.validators.units.doc1: Dimensional consistency across geometry, parameters, fields and sensors.

pinneapple_llm.research.doc:
Literature/repository search integrated with an LLM -- built entirely
on PINNeAPPle's own already-existing, real API-backed search
(``pinneapple_tools.hpo_experiments.sources.ArxivSource``/
``GithubSource``, which call the real arXiv and GitHub search APIs), never
an LLM asked to "recall" papers or repositories from training data (which
is exactly the class of hallucination -- plausible-looking but
non-existent or wrong citations -- this module exists to avoid).

The LLM's role here is strictly downstream of the real results: it may be
asked to *summarise or rank the papers/repos actually returned by the real
API calls*, never to add to or invent items in that list. Every citation
in :class:`ResearchReport` traces back to a real ``ArxivPaper``/
``GithubRepo`` object with a real, dereferenceable URL from the API
response itself, not from the LLM.
pinneapple_llm.research.doc1: Literature/repository search integrated with an LLM -- built entirely on PINNeAPPle's own already-existing, real API-backed search (``pinneapple_tools.hpo_experiments.sources.ArxivSource``/ ``GithubSource``, which call the real arXiv and GitHub search APIs), never an LLM asked to "recall" papers or …

pinneapple_llm.twin_draft.doc:
LLM-assisted digital twin drafting -- same constrained pattern as
``draft.py``/``geometry_draft.py``: the LLM proposes values for
``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.DigitalTwinConfig``'s own real,
introspected fields (update interval, assimilation method, anomaly
threshold, ...), never a free-form twin implementation. The actual twin is
always built by the real ``build_digital_twin`` factory, never by code the
LLM wrote.

"3D digital twin" here means composing three already-real, already-tested
pieces -- a trained PINN surrogate (from ``solve_pde``/``pipeline``), the
real ``DigitalTwin`` live-inference/assimilation loop, and
``pinneapple_blender``'s export bridge -- into one function that, on each
twin update tick, also drops a ``.ply`` frame for Blender to pick up (see
``export_live_frame``). This is not a new 3D-twin subsystem; it is glue
between three subsystems that already independently work.

pinneapple_llm.workbench.doc:
PINNeAPPle Agent Workbench: a team of coding and engineering agents running on a local model.

A lead agent talks to you, plans, and hands parts of the work to specialists (explorer, researcher, coder, tester,
reviewer, physics engineer, reporter). They read and change your project, run commands, search the internet, follow
background jobs, call GitHub, start parallel sessions and show you files, with approvals for anything risky. Every
conversation and every model call is stored (SQLite or PostgreSQL) so you can rate turns and fine-tune the model on
your own work.

Start it with ``python -m pinneapple_llm.workbench serve --workspace <project>``; ``doctor`` checks the setup. See
``docs/guides/agent_workbench.md``.
pinneapple_llm.workbench.doc1: PINNeAPPle Agent Workbench: a team of coding and engineering agents running on a local model.

pinneapple_llm.workbench.__main__.doc:
``python -m pinneapple_llm.workbench <command>`` (also ``pinneapple-workbench``).

serve      start the web app (default command): the agents work in --workspace
doctor     check the machine, the model server and the model, and print what to fix
pull       download the recommended model (or --model) with Ollama
run        one task in the terminal, no browser: run "fix the failing test"
eval       measure a model on the built-in tasks
finetune   export the dataset from the database, train a LoRA adapter, serve it
vscode     install the VS Code extension (opens the workbench beside your editor)

pinneapple_llm.workbench.agents.doc:
The agent definitions: one Markdown file per agent, with a small front matter (name, title, description, tools)
and the system prompt as the body. ``prompts/_common.md`` is appended to every agent.

The built-in agents live in ``pinneapple_llm/workbench/prompts/``. Your own versions override them by name: put
``<name>.md`` in ``~/.pinneapple/workbench/agents/`` (all projects) or ``<workspace>/.pinneapple/agents/`` (one
project). A new name adds a new agent; the lead can delegate to it.
pinneapple_llm.workbench.agents.doc1: The agent definitions: one Markdown file per agent, with a small front matter (name, title, description, tools) and the system prompt as the body. ``prompts/_common.md`` is appended to every agent.

pinneapple_llm.workbench.backend.doc:
Chat-with-tools backends: Ollama, any OpenAI-compatible server (LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, MLX), and a scripted
backend for tests.

Every backend takes OpenAI-style messages plus JSON-schema tool specs and returns one :class:`Reply`: the text and the
tool calls the model asked for. Models without native tool calling still work: the tools are described in the system
prompt and a JSON object in the reply is read as the call (``tool_mode="json"``).
pinneapple_llm.workbench.backend.doc1: Chat-with-tools backends: Ollama, any OpenAI-compatible server (LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, MLX), and a scripted backend for tests.

pinneapple_llm.workbench.evaluate.doc:
A small, checkable benchmark of the workbench on your machine and model.

Each task builds a tiny project in a temporary folder, gives the lead a request, and checks the outcome mechanically
(the project's tests pass, a file has the expected content, the answer names the right place). It reports pass/fail,
wall time, model calls and tokens per task: numbers measured on your hardware, for comparing local models with each
other. It is not a substitute for the public agentic-coding benchmarks.
pinneapple_llm.workbench.evaluate.doc1: A small, checkable benchmark of the workbench on your machine and model.

pinneapple_llm.workbench.finetune.doc:
Fine-tune the local model on your own workbench sessions.

1. ``export_dataset(store, "data/")`` writes ``train.jsonl`` and ``valid.jsonl`` in the chat format with tools that
   ``mlx_lm`` and TRL read (``{"messages": [...], "tools": [...]}``). By default one example is one agent run: the
   full trajectory of model calls, tool calls and tool results up to the agent's final answer. Turns you rated -1 are
   left out, and with ``min_rating=1`` only turns you rated +1 are kept. Tokens and keys that look like secrets are
   masked.
2. ``train_mlx(...)`` (Apple Silicon, ``pip install mlx-lm``) or ``train_peft(...)`` (NVIDIA, ``pip install
   "pinneapple[finetune]" trl``) trains a LoRA adapter on that data.
3. ``serve_mlx_command(...)`` serves the base model with the adapter on an OpenAI-compatible port; start the workbench
   with ``--backend openai --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1`` to use it, and ``evaluate`` to compare it with the
   base model on the same tasks.

The base model must be the same family as the one that produced the data (its chat template decides how tool calls
are written). Use the Hugging Face / MLX version of the model you run in Ollama.
pinneapple_llm.workbench.finetune.doc1: Fine-tune the local model on your own workbench sessions.

pinneapple_llm.workbench.models.doc:
Which local model to run, from the machine's memory.

No local model matches the large hosted models on long, multi-file agent work. The recommendations below are the
strongest open-weight models with tool calling that fit each memory size, served by Ollama (Metal on Apple Silicon,
CUDA on NVIDIA). ``python -m pinneapple_llm.workbench eval`` measures the model you pick on the workbench's own tasks,
so you can compare models on your machine rather than trust a table.
pinneapple_llm.workbench.models.doc1: Which local model to run, from the machine's memory.

functions.doc1: The default model for a machine with ``memory_gb`` of memory (detected when omitted).

pinneapple_llm.workbench.runtime.doc:
The agent loop: the lead talks to you, calls tools, keeps a plan and delegates parts of the work to the specialist
agents, each running its own loop with its own prompt and tools.

Every step is an event (``user``, ``message``, ``tool_call``, ``tool_result``, ``plan``, ``file``,
``approval_request``, ``question``, ``delegate_start`` / ``delegate_end``, ``error``, ``done``) passed to ``on_event``
and stored, so the UI shows the work live and can replay it. Approvals and questions block the loop until
:meth:`Session.answer` is called. Every model call goes to ``on_model_call`` with its exact input and reply: the
fine-tuning data.

Besides the workspace tools, the runtime provides ``todo`` (the plan), ``delegate`` (a specialist agent),
``ask_user`` (a question, optionally with choices) and, when the server wires them through ``hooks``,
``schedule`` (a message back into this session later), ``start_session`` / ``send_to_session`` /
``list_sessions`` / ``session_status`` (other sessions working in parallel).
pinneapple_llm.workbench.runtime.doc1: The agent loop: the lead talks to you, calls tools, keeps a plan and delegates parts of the work to the specialist agents, each running its own loop with its own prompt and tools.

pinneapple_llm.workbench.server.doc:
The workbench web app: FastAPI routes over :class:`~.runtime.Session` and the :class:`~.store.Store`, plus the
static single-page frontend in ``static/`` (no build step).

The database is a local SQLite file or a PostgreSQL server (``db="postgresql://..."``); every conversation and
model call is kept there for fine-tuning. It binds to 127.0.0.1 by default: the agents run commands on your machine, so do not expose it to a network. Set
``token`` to require ``Authorization: Bearer <token>`` (or ``?token=``) on every API call.
pinneapple_llm.workbench.server.doc1: The workbench web app: FastAPI routes over :class:`~.runtime.Session` and the :class:`~.store.Store`, plus the static single-page frontend in ``static/`` (no build step).

pinneapple_llm.workbench.tools.doc:
The tools the agents use, confined to one workspace folder.

Files: ``list_dir``, ``read_file``, ``write_file``, ``edit_file`` (exact string replacement), ``search`` (regex over
files), ``glob``. Commands: ``run`` (a shell command with a timeout, run in the workspace: git, tests, scripts).
Background jobs: ``run(background=true)``, ``job_output``, ``job_stop``. Internet: ``web_search`` and ``fetch_url``
(see :mod:`.web`); off with ``Workspace(web=False)``. GitHub: ``github`` (REST calls with ``GITHUB_TOKEN``). Showing
work: ``show_file`` puts an image, HTML page, PDF or text file in the chat. Engineering reasoning: ``reason_chain``,
``reason_library``, ``reason_check`` (:mod:`pinneapple_reason`: every physical claim comes from a computed check). A path that resolves outside
the workspace is refused, symlinks included. Whether a command needs your approval is the
:class:`ApprovalPolicy`'s call: ``"ask"`` asks for every command and every write, ``"auto"`` lets read-only and test
commands through and asks for the rest, ``"yolo"`` asks for nothing.

pinneapple_mcp.config.doc:
Limits and locations of the MCP server. Every value has a safe default and an environment variable.

| setting | default | environment variable |
|---|---|---|
| working directory (results, jobs) | ``./pinneapple_mcp_work`` | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_WORKDIR`` |
| wall time per job [s] | 600 | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_SECONDS`` |
| memory per job [MB] (address space of the job process) | 8192 | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_MEMORY_MB`` |
| concurrent jobs | 2 | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_JOBS`` |
| training epochs per run | 20000 | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_EPOCHS`` |
| grid points of a checked field | 250000 | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_POINTS`` |
| size of a file read by ``trust_card`` [MB] | 200 | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_MAX_FILE_MB`` |
| network inside jobs | off | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_ALLOW_NETWORK=1`` |
| roots files may be read from | working directory and current directory | ``PINNEAPPLE_MCP_ROOTS`` (``os.pathsep`` separated) |

pinneapple_mcp.expressions.doc:
Safe arithmetic expressions of the coordinates, e.g. ``"sin(pi*x)*sinh(pi*y)/sinh(pi)"``.

Agents describe boundary values, sources and closed-form references as text. The text is parsed with ``ast`` and
only numbers, the coordinate names, ``pi`` / ``e``, ``+ - * / ** %`` and a fixed list of NumPy functions are
accepted: no attribute access, no subscripts, no other names, nothing is passed to ``eval``.

pinneapple_mcp.jobs.doc:
Long work as jobs: a separate process per job, with a wall-time limit, a memory limit and no network.

Each job has a directory ``<workdir>/jobs/<job_id>/`` holding ``request.json``, ``status.json``, ``log.txt`` and
whatever the job writes (``result.json`` and its files). The status lives on disk, so ``job_status`` still answers
after the server restarts (a job whose process is gone is reported as ``lost``).

pinneapple_mcp.problems.doc:
A physics problem from JSON: a preset, or a box problem described field by field.

Preset::

    {"preset": "burgers_1d", "preset_kwargs": {"nu": 0.003}}

Box problem (any PDE kind the physics compiler knows; values and sources are expressions of the coordinates)::

    {"name": "plate", "domain": {"x": [0, 1], "y": [0, 1]}, "fields": ["T"], "pde": "laplace",
     "params": {}, "source": "0",
     "bcs": [{"kind": "dirichlet", "field": "T", "on": "y_max", "value": "sin(pi*x)"},
             {"kind": "dirichlet", "field": "T", "on": "y_min", "value": 0},
             {"kind": "dirichlet", "field": "T", "on": "x_boundary", "value": 0}],
     "exact": "sin(pi*x)*sinh(pi*y)/sinh(pi)"}

``on`` is ``"<coord>_min"``, ``"<coord>_max"``, ``"<coord>_boundary"`` (both ends) or ``"boundary"`` (every face).

pinneapple_neural.doc:
pinneapple_neural — Neural network architectures, training, and inference.

Sub-modules
-----------
architectures  (was pinneapple_models)
    Neural network architectures and registry: SIREN, ModifiedMLP, HashGridMLP,
    AFNO, MeshGraphNet, ModelRegistry, ModelCatalog.

trainer        (was pinneapple_train)
    Full training infrastructure: Trainer, TwoPhaseTrainer, TimeMarchingTrainer,
    DDPPINNTrainer, CausalPINNTrainer, loss combiners, weight schedulers,
    normalizers, data splitters, HPC utilities (FSDP, SLURM, profiler).

predictor      (was pinneapple_inference)
    Post-training inference: batched_inference, grid evaluation (1-D / 2-D),
    FlowVisualizer, isosurface, streamlines, design-opt plots.

Integration helpers
-------------------
``build_model(name, **kwargs)``      — ModelRegistry.build shortcut
``train_model(model, losses, ...)``  — Trainer shortcut
``predict(model, x, ...)``           — batched_inference shortcut
``train_and_predict(...)``           — full pipeline in one call

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_neural import build_model, train_model, predict
>>> model = build_model("siren", in_dim=2, out_dim=1, hidden_dim=64, n_layers=4)
>>> # loss_fn(model, y_hat, batch) -> Tensor | dict[str, Tensor] (with "total")
>>> # train_loader yields dict batches (or (x, y) tuples) per Trainer.fit
>>> result = train_model(model, loss_fn, train_loader, epochs=5000)
>>> pred = predict(model, x_test)

License guards for optional third-party integrations.

Some integrations wrap code or pretrained weights whose licenses do not allow
production or commercial use. Those integrations stay available for research,
but they must never train, serve or deliver models or services to clients.

- Commercial mode (environment variable ``PINNEAPPLE_COMMERCIAL_MODE=1``, set by
  client-facing products such as PINNeAPPle-CFD): instantiation raises

pinneapple_neural.architectures.base.doc:
BaseModel and ModelOutput for Pinneapple model family.

This module defines a minimal *contract* that enables the Arena and Trainer to
run heterogeneous model families in a consistent way.

Key idea
--------
Every model can be executed in two ways:
  1) ``forward(x)``: classic PyTorch signature.
  2) ``forward_batch(batch)``: takes a dict batch (PINN / operator / graph / TS).

The default ``forward_batch`` implementation simply picks ``batch['x']`` (or
``batch['x_col']``) and calls ``forward(x)``.

Models that need different inputs (coords+params, graph objects, sequences,
fields, etc.) should override ``forward_batch``.

MeshGraphNet — Encoder-Process-Decoder GNN for mesh-based simulation.

Reference: Pfaff et al., ICLR 2021
  "Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks"
  https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.03409

Scope
-----
This implements the single-edge-type variant of MeshGraphNet, appropriate
for domains without external contact (e.g. CFD / continuum meshes where a
single fixed mesh connectivity fully determines interactions). The full
paper additionally defines a *world-space* edge set — dynamically rebuilt
each step from spatial proximity, with its own edge encoder/embedding — to
let the network learn contact effects (e.g. cloth self-collision) that are
not captured by mesh-space (rest-pose) connectivity alone. That second edge
type is not implemented here; ``edge_index``/``edge_attr`` are treated as a
single, fixed mesh-space edge set for the whole rollout.

Architecture
------------
1. Node encoder  : MLP(node_in_dim [+ pos_dim]) → hidden_dim, LayerNorm
2. Edge encoder  : MLP(edge_in_dim [+ pos_dim+1]) → hidden_dim, LayerNorm
                   (omitted when no edge features and use_pos=False)
3. Processor     : K rounds of _ProcessorBlock (edge-then-node update, residual)
4. Node decoder  : Linear(hidden_dim → out_dim)  — no activation, no LayerNorm

Batch convention
----------------
All tensors carry an explicit batch dimension:
  node features : (B, N, node_in_dim)
  edge features : (B, E, edge_in_dim)   — optional
  positions     : (B, N, pos_dim)        — optional, used when …

pinneapple_neural.architectures.graphnn..doc:
Transient mesh dynamics on top of :class:`MeshGraphNet`.

Reproduces the training/inference recipe of Pfaff et al. (ICLR 2021) and of
the PhysicsNeMo ``vortex_shedding_mgn`` example:

* node inputs  = [velocity_t, one-hot node type]   (normalised)
* edge inputs  = [rel. position, |rel. position|]  (normalised, static)
* node outputs = [Δvelocity, pressure_{t+1}]       (normalised)
* training-time noise on the velocity of NORMAL nodes, with the Δv target
  corrected so the net learns to undo the noise
* free-running rollout where non-NORMAL nodes (walls, inlet, obstacle) are
  clamped to their prescribed values.

Meshes may differ per sample; each call processes one graph (B = 1), which is
what the reference examples do as well.

pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_o.doc:
ONNX export of Fourier neural operators.

The FNO's spectral convolution uses ``rfft2`` / ``irfft2`` and complex weights; neither the TorchScript nor the
dynamo ONNX exporter of PyTorch 2.x handles complex tensors. For a fixed grid, the truncated transforms are small
dense matrices, so the same layer can be written in real arithmetic:

* forward transform on the retained modes: ``X = E_h^T x E_w`` with ``E = cos - i sin`` restricted to the rows
  ``k1 in [0, m1) U [H - m1, H)`` and the columns ``k2 in [0, m2)``;
* the complex product with the weights split into real and imaginary parts;
* inverse ``irfft2`` of a spectrum that is zero outside those modes:
  ``y = Re(G O V^T c) / (H W)`` with ``G = e^{+i alpha}``, ``V = e^{+i beta}`` and ``c = 1`` for the zero (and the
  Nyquist) column, 2 otherwise -- exactly what ``irfft2`` computes (it discards the imaginary part of those columns).

:func:`to_exportable` returns a copy of a model with every ``_SpectralConv2d`` replaced by :class:`RealSpectralConv2d`
(identical outputs to float32 round-off, checked by :func:`export_onnx`), which then exports with the standard
exporter and runs in onnxruntime.

pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_o.doc:
Noether (Emmi AI) architecture bridge for PINNeAPPle.

**RESEARCH ONLY.** The Noether framework's license prohibits production use and the
AB-UPT weights are CC BY-NC 4.0. Instantiating anything here emits a
``ResearchOnlyWarning`` and is refused with ``PINNEAPPLE_COMMERCIAL_MODE=1``
(see ``pinneapple_neural._licencas``).

Wraps the transformer-based neural surrogate architectures from
``emmiai-noether`` (UPT, AB-UPT, Transolver, Transformer, and their
aerodynamics variants) as ``NeuralOperatorBase`` subclasses so that they
are usable through PINNeAPPle's ``NeuralOperatorCatalog`` and can be
trained with the standard ``Trainer`` or the dedicated
``NoetherSurrogateTrainer``.

Install the optional dependency first:
    pip install emmiai-noether

Model overview
--------------
NoetherUPT          — Universal Physics Transformer (arXiv:2402.12365)
NoetherABUPT        — Anchored-Branched UPT (arXiv:2502.09692)
NoetherTransformer  — vanilla transformer backbone (Noether wrapper)
NoetherTransolver   — Physics-Attention Transolver (arXiv:2402.02366)
NoetherAeroUPT      — UPT with CFD surface/volume domain routing
NoetherAeroABUPT    — AB-UPT with CFD domain routing
NoetherAeroTransformer — Transformer for CFD aerodynamics
NoetherAeroTransolver  — Transolver for CFD aerodynamics

Parametric reduced-order models: design parameters -> full field, without running the solver.

A POD basis of the snapshot fields (one snapshot per parameter point) and a regression of the POD coefficients on
the parameters: radial basis functions (POD-RBF), a Gaussian process with predictive uncertainty (POD-GPR), or the
nearest training snapshot (the baseline every surrogate must beat). Works with any solver whose fields share one
mesh (same node or cell numbering across the parameter points).

    rom = ParametricPOD(energy=0.9999, regressor="gpr").fit(P_train, X_train)   # P: (n, p), X: (n, D)
    X_hat, X_std = rom.predict(P_test, return_std=True)

pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.stud.doc:
Reduced-order model study: which ROM, at which rank, for which error and speed, measured on held-out snapshots.

``rom_study(snaps)`` takes a :class:`pinneapple_data.snapshots.SnapshotSet` (time series or parametric results on one
mesh), holds out test snapshots (later times, interleaved times or unseen parameter points), fits every method at
several ranks on the training snapshots only and reports, per method and rank:

* the relative L2 error on the test snapshots (mean, max, per snapshot) and the POD projection error at that rank
  (the floor no method using that basis can beat);
* the fit time and the inference time per snapshot (``pinneapple_analysis.cost.time_per_query``) and, when the
  full-order model's time per snapshot is known, the speed-up;
* the singular values and cumulative energy of the training snapshots.

Methods (all from ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom``):

``pod_rbf``   POD + radial-basis interpolation of the coefficients in the parameters (or in time)
``pod_gpr``   POD + one Gaussian process per coefficient (parametric data)
``nearest``   the nearest training snapshot (baseline every surrogate must beat; parametric data)
``persistence`` the latest training snapshot at or before the time (the baseline of a forecast)
``dmd``       dynamic mode decomposition: a linear map between consecutive snapshots (uniform time step); exact
              (uncentred) DMD, so the mean field is one of its ``rank`` modes
``opinf``     operator inference: a quadratic …

pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.trus.doc:
Latent surrogate that says when not to trust it: error bounds, envelope check and physics residual per query.

A parametric reduced-order model (:class:`~.parametric.ParametricPOD`: encode the fields in a POD latent space,
regress the latent coordinates on the design parameters, decode) answers in microseconds, and answers just as fast
where it is wrong. :class:`TrustedLatentSurrogate` wraps it with three independent checks per query, and turns them
into the library's :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`:

1. **Error bound** — the latent regressor's predictive spread (a Gaussian process's own standard deviation, or a
   bootstrap ensemble of RBF latent regressors) gives a spread ``s(p)`` of the decoded field;
   normalised split-conformal prediction (Lei et al. 2018; Angelopoulos & Bates 2022) on a held-out calibration set
   scales it to a bound ``q * s(p)`` that covers the true relative error with probability ``1 - alpha`` for queries
   drawn like the calibration set.
2. **Envelope** — the mean distance to the ``k`` nearest training designs (scaled parameters) converted to a
   conformal p-value against the calibration designs. Catches holes inside the parameter box and extrapolation,
   where the coverage of 1. no longer holds (exchangeability is lost) and the spread may be overconfident.
3. **Physics residual** — optional ``residual(p, x) -> float``: the discrete governing equations evaluated on the
   decoded field (a sparse mat-vec, no solve). Independent …

pinneapple_neural.callbacks.doc:
Physics checks during training in PyTorch Lightning, PhysicsNeMo and Hugging Face (#704).

Most models are trained outside PINNeAPPle and validated once, at the end. These callbacks run the checks of
``pp.validate`` on a fixed validation batch every N steps, log them to the framework's logger, warn (or stop) when a
physics metric worsens for K consecutive checks while the training loss improves, and write the validation report and
trust card at the end of training.

The core, :class:`PhysicsMonitor`, is framework-free; the adapters are thin:

* ``PhysicsValidationCallback(monitor)`` -- a ``lightning.pytorch.Callback`` (or ``pytorch_lightning``): logs to
  every logger of the Trainer (TensorBoard, W&B, MLflow, CSV) at each check, puts the metrics in
  ``trainer.callback_metrics`` (for checkpointing or early stopping on them) and sets ``trainer.should_stop``.
* ``PhysicsTrainerCallback(monitor)`` -- a ``transformers.TrainerCallback``: logs through ``trainer.log`` (its
  ``report_to`` integrations) when attached with ``.attach(trainer)``, else into ``state.log_history``; sets
  ``control.should_training_stop``.
* :class:`PhysicsNeMoHook` -- for a PhysicsNeMo training loop (PhysicsNeMo has no trainer class): call
  ``hook(model, step, loss, log=launch_logger)``; metrics go to a ``physicsnemo.utils.logging.LaunchLogger`` (which
  forwards to W&B / MLflow when initialised) or any callable.

None of the frameworks is a dependency: the Lightning and Hugging Face classes are built on …

pinneapple_neural.lpm.doc:
Large Physics Model (LPM) building blocks: one model for a whole design space.

Definition used (Luminary, "Vocabulary of Physics AI", 2026): an LPM is "a single trained model
that covers a design space wide enough to stand in for many individual simulations". In practice
(Luminary SHIFT models; "Demystifying Physics AI: the five stages to scale"; "How Large Physics
Models gain spatial context") that means:

1. **spatial context** for every query point:
   - multi-scale neighbourhoods (fine radius -> local curvature, coarse radius -> where on the
     body the point is), as GeoTransolver's multi-scale ball queries do;
   - Fourier positional encoding of coordinates against the spectral bias toward smooth
     functions (Tancik et al., "Fourier features let networks learn high frequency functions",
     NeurIPS 2020, arXiv:2006.10739);
2. **a geometry code** shared by all points of a design (permutation-invariant pooling, DeepSets:
   Zaheer et al., NeurIPS 2017, arXiv:1703.06114) and conditioning on operating parameters;
3. **query independence**: the prediction at a point does not depend on batching or order;
4. **uncertainty and out-of-distribution flags on every prediction** (deep-ensemble heads,
   Lakshminarayanan et al. 2017, arXiv:1612.01474; distance of the geometry code to the
   training designs);
5. **fine-tuning** on a few new simulations instead of retraining.

This module provides those pieces around a compact network; a production LPM swaps the head for
a …

pinneapple_neural.physicsnemo_bridge.doc:
pinneapple_neural.physicsnemo_bridge -- PhysicsNeMo <-> PINNeAPPle integration glue.

Promotes example-level PhysicsNeMo integration code from
``examples/pinneapple_and_physicsnemo/`` and ``examples/vs_physicsnemo/``
into a maintained core package. Those two directories contain real, working
scripts demonstrating three integration patterns
(``examples/vs_physicsnemo/README.md``, "Padroes de integracao"): (1)
PhysicsNeMo trains a model, PINNeAPPle operates/UQs/twins it; (2) PINNeAPPle
active-learning selects points, PhysicsNeMo retrains; (3) PhysicsNeMo
MeshGraphNet output validated by PINNeAPPle -- but the glue was never
promoted beyond the example scripts, so every user wanting it had to
copy-paste from ``example.py`` rather than ``import`` a real module. This
package fixes that for patterns 1 and 2 (pattern 3 -- physics validation and
ONNX/TorchScript export of a PhysicsNeMo MeshGraphNet, demonstrated in
``examples/vs_physicsnemo/06_combined_meshgraphnet_valid/example.py`` -- is
out of scope here; it belongs with PINNeAPPle's own validation/export
modules, not this bridge). The example scripts themselves are left
untouched.

This follows the same relocation convention as
``pinneapple_analysis.verification`` (a similar promotion of
previously-siloed logic done in a prior session): the real, working
integration logic is extracted into tested, reusable functions/classes
here, without reinventing anything the examples or PINNeAPPle's own …

pinneapple_neural.physicsnemo_bridge.act.doc:
PINNeAPPle active learning -> PhysicsNeMo retrain bridge.

Promotes "Padrao 2" from ``examples/vs_physicsnemo/README.md``::

    PINNeAPPle ResidualBasedAL -> pontos hard de collocation
    PhysicsNeMo retreina FNO nesses pontos (GPU rapido)
    -> loop: AL seleciona -> PhysicsNeMo retreina -> AL seleciona...

That README documents the pattern with a diagram but, unlike patterns 1 and
3, neither ``examples/pinneapple_and_physicsnemo/`` nor
``examples/vs_physicsnemo/`` contains a runnable script that actually wires
it up. This module builds the real loop directly on top of
:mod:`pinneapple_data.active_learning`'s real, already-tested
``ResidualBasedAL`` / ``ActiveLearningConfig`` strategy classes -- the same
ones ``AdaptiveCollocationTrainer`` uses -- so point *selection* is fully
delegated rather than reimplemented; only the *retrain* half (a plain
Adam-optimizer training loop, mirroring the style of ``train_fno`` in
``examples/vs_physicsnemo/04_physicsnemo_fno_operator/example.py`` and
``train_surrogate`` in
``examples/vs_physicsnemo/05_combined_fno_digital_twin/example.py``) is new
glue.

``physicsnemo`` is a genuinely optional dependency here: the retrain loop
operates on any ``torch.nn.Module`` -- a plain PINNeAPPle model or a trained
physicsnemo one, since physicsnemo models are themselves ``nn.Module``
instances -- so nothing in this module requires physicsnemo to be
importable.

pinneapple_neural.trainer.adaptive_sweep.doc:
Automatic (adaptive) hyperparameter search.

``pinneapple_neural.trainer.parallel.run_parallel_sweep``/``SweepConfig``
already exist and work, but they are a **grid** sweep: the caller supplies
every combination to try up front, evaluates all of them in parallel, and
there is no mechanism that uses early trial results to decide what to try
next, or to stop a clearly-bad trial early. That is not "automatic" in the
sense normally meant by hyperparameter tuning -- it is parallel brute
force over a manually-specified grid.

``AdaptiveSweep`` is the actual adaptive search: a TPE (TreeParzenEstimator)
Bayesian sampler over a continuous/categorical parameter *space*
(``suggest_float``/``suggest_int``/``suggest_categorical`` ranges, not a
fixed grid) with a median pruner that can stop an unpromising trial after
only a few of its intermediate reports -- both via Optuna (optional
dependency, ``pip install "pinneapple[tuning]"``). A dependency-free
fallback (random search, no pruning) is used automatically if Optuna is
not installed, so the feature isn't entirely gated behind an extra.

functions.doc1: Run an adaptive (Bayesian/TPE via Optuna, or random-search fallback) hyperparameter search.

pinneapple_neural.trainer.collocation.doc:
Adaptive collocation point sampling for PINN training.

Standard PINN training uses a fixed set of collocation points drawn uniformly
from the domain.  In practice, the PDE residual is not uniform — it is high in
regions where the solution changes rapidly or where the network is still learning.

Residual-based Adaptive Refinement (RAR) periodically resamples the active
collocation set with a density biased toward high-residual regions:

    p_i = α · r_i² / Σ r_j²  +  (1-α) / N_pool

where r_i is the PDE residual magnitude at pool point i, α is ``residual_frac``,
and 1-α is the uniform component (prevents collapse onto a single point).

This technique can halve the number of epochs needed to reach a target accuracy
for problems with sharp gradients or complex boundaries.

References
----------
Lu et al. (2021). "DeepXDE: A deep learning library for solving differential
equations." SIAM Review 63(1). (adaptive resampling appendix)

Wu et al. (2023). "A comprehensive study of non-adaptive and residual-based
adaptive sampling for physics-informed neural networks." Comput. Methods Appl.
Mech. Engrg. 403.

Usage
-----
::

    from pinneapple_neural.trainer.collocation import (
        AdaptiveCollocationSampler, AdaptiveCollocationConfig,
    )

    # Build pool — any torch.Tensor of shape (N_pool, D)
    pool = sample_domain_points(n=40_000)

    cfg     = AdaptiveCollocationConfig(n_active=8000, resample_every=200)
    sampler = AdaptiveCollocationSampler(pool, cfg)

    for …

pinneapple_neural.trainer.graybox.doc:
Gray-box PINN training (AI-Aristotle style): a main network learns the
state variables while one or more small auxiliary networks learn an unknown
functional term in an otherwise-known governing equation.

Convention: the caller supplies a `known_residual_fn(main_model, coords,
learnable, known, graybox_nets) -> Tensor` that assembles whatever residual
their governing equation needs, calling into `graybox_nets[name](coords)`
wherever an unknown term belongs — the same "supply the physics, we handle
the training loop" pattern used elsewhere in this package (e.g. the
`reaction_kinetics_network` PDE kind's `rate_fn` convention). No equation is
hardcoded here, so this works for any PDE/ODE with one or more unknown terms,
not a fixed catalog of problem types.

Typical workflow
-----------------
>>> from pinneapple_neural.trainer.graybox import GrayBoxNet, train_graybox
>>> def known_residual_fn(model, coords, learnable, known, graybox_nets):
...     # e.g. heat equation with an unknown source: dT/dt - alpha*d2T/dx2 = h(x,t)
...     ...
...     h = graybox_nets["source"](coords.detach())
...     return known_part - h
>>> graybox_nets = {"source": GrayBoxNet(n_in=2, n_out=1)}
>>> main_model, graybox_nets, learned_params, history = train_graybox(
...     main_model, graybox_nets, known_residual_fn,
...     obs_coords, obs_values, learnable_params={"alpha": 0.1},
... )

pinneapple_neural.trainer.heteroscedasti.doc:
Heteroscedastic (input-dependent variance) uncertainty quantification.

Complementary to a fixed-noise-scalar Bayesian PINN: instead of one global
noise level, the model predicts a per-point variance alongside its mean
prediction, learned jointly via a Gaussian negative-log-likelihood loss.
Combined with MC-dropout, this decomposes total predictive uncertainty into
aleatoric (irreducible, data-noise) and epistemic (reducible, model/data-
scarcity) components via the law of total variance.

Architecture-agnostic by design: wrap ANY base network whose output layer
has been sized to `2 * n_out_physical` columns (first half = mean, second
half = log-variance) — works with an MLP, a Fourier feature network, a graph
network, a neural operator, or anything else, rather than a fixed set of
hardcoded per-architecture subclasses.

Typical workflow
-----------------
>>> from pinneapple_neural.trainer.heteroscedastic import (
...     HeteroscedasticWrapper, init_logvar_bias, heteroscedastic_nll_loss,
...     compute_aleatoric_epistemic_uq,
... )
>>> base = MyNetwork(n_in=2, n_out=2 * n_physical_outputs, dropout=0.1)
>>> init_logvar_bias(base.output_layer, n_physical_outputs)  # optional but recommended
>>> model = HeteroscedasticWrapper(base, n_out_physical=n_physical_outputs)
>>> mean, logvar = model.forward_uq(x)
>>> loss = heteroscedastic_nll_loss(mean, logvar, target)
>>> # ... after training, with dropout > 0 in `base`:
>>> uq = compute_aleatoric_epistemic_uq(model, query_coords, …

Advanced HPC utilities for large-scale PINN training.

Extends pinneapple_train.parallel with production-grade features:

Memory-efficient parallelism:
  wrap_fsdp()               Fully Sharded Data Parallel (PyTorch FSDP)
  wrap_zero_optimizer()     ZeRO-1 optimizer state sharding

Accelerated compute:
  CUDAGraphModule           Captures CUDA graphs for static shapes
  CUDAGraphContext          Context manager for manual graph capture

Communication efficiency:
  PowerSGDCompressor        Low-rank gradient compression for DDP
  TopKGradCompressor        Top-K sparsification hook for DDP

Cluster / multi-node:

pinneapple_neural.trainer.inverse_pinn.doc:
Inverse PINN: jointly optimize network weights and unknown scalar
physical parameters from sparse sensor observations plus a PDE/ODE residual.

Convention: the caller supplies `residual_fn(model, x_col, param_values) ->
Tensor | Sequence[Tensor]` that assembles whatever residual their governing
equation needs, using `param_values[name]` (a dict of the current
`InverseParam` values, differentiable) wherever an unknown parameter
belongs -- the same "supply the physics, we handle the training loop"
pattern used elsewhere in this package (e.g. `pinneapple_neural.trainer.
graybox`'s `known_residual_fn`, or the `reaction_kinetics_network` PDE
kind's `rate_fn`). No equation is hardcoded here, so this works for any
inverse problem with one or more unknown scalar parameters, not a fixed
catalog of problem types.

Robustness features (built in, not opt-in extras):
- Gradient clipping applied to both network weights and inverse parameters
- Early stopping on a plateau of the unweighted loss ``L_pde + L_data`` (see
  ``InversePINN``'s ``patience``)
- PDE-vs-data loss weighting: fixed equal weights by default
  (``weighting="equal"``); ``weighting="adaptive"`` sets the PDE weight from an
  EMA of each loss's own magnitude (``graybox``'s balancing rule). On the
  inverse Burgers benchmark the adaptive rule raised the PDE weight as the PDE
  loss fell, traded data fit for a smaller residual and left nu 12x off
  (``benchmarks/vs_frameworks/REPORT.md``, track C)
- Pluggable collocation …

pinneapple_neural.trainer.lbfgs_finetune.doc:
Multi-round L-BFGS fine-tuning: resample-per-round quasi-Newton polish.

A single L-BFGS run on one fixed batch keeps improving right up to its
iteration budget -- promising, but risky: quasi-Newton steps on a single
fixed sample can overfit to that sample's particular noise instead of the
true objective (observed in practice on a PINN training run: a single
600-iteration/large-batch L-BFGS phase thrashed memory for days with zero
usable progress, traced to ``history_size=50``'s curvature-pair buffer
never resetting across one very long phase at a large batch). Splitting
the same total iteration budget into several rounds, each on a freshly
resampled (and optionally larger) batch, keeps the fast local convergence
L-BFGS is good at while forcing every few dozen steps to re-check
themselves against new points -- closer in spirit to stochastic
optimization, without giving up the second-order convergence rate within
each round -- and bounds ``history_size``'s memory growth to one round's
worth of curvature pairs instead of the whole budget's.

pinneapple_neural.trainer.loss_balancer.doc:
Advanced automatic loss weight optimisation for PINNs.

New methods added on top of the existing weight_scheduler.py:

ReLoBRaLo  — Relative Loss Balancing via Residuals and Losses (Bischof & Kraus, 2021).
             Very cheap (no extra backward pass), works excellently in practice.
             Uses per-step loss change ratios with EMA smoothing.

SoftAdapt  — Adaptive loss weighting based on rates-of-change of individual losses
             (Heydari et al., 2019).  Focuses effort on the term that is improving
             most slowly.

AugmentedLagrangian — Treats BC/IC losses as inequality constraints solved via
             dual ascent (λ_i += ρ · L_i).  Gradually tightens constraints.
             Strong theoretical basis for constrained PDE problems.

PCGrad     — Gradient Surgery: projects conflicting task gradients onto each
             other's normal plane.  Eliminates gradient cancellation between PDE
             and BC terms.  Requires per-loss backward passes (more expensive).

InverseDirichlet — Sets weights proportional to the inverse of per-layer
             gradient statistics, balancing training "stiffness" across terms.
             (Van der Meer et al., 2022). Very cheap, one backward pass.

LRAnnealing — Rescales each term's weight so the reference term's max
             gradient matches the term's mean gradient, over the *full*
             network (not a single layer). (Wang, Teng & Perdikaris, 2021,
             Algorithm 1). Very cheap, one …

pinneapple_neural.trainer.monotonic.doc:
Monotonicity constraints for regression surrogates: a hinge penalty on input-output derivatives.

Many physical responses are monotone in some inputs (a more conductive fin never raises a thermal resistance, more
airflow never lowers a pressure drop). When the effect is small compared with the fit error, a plain regression
gets its sign wrong on part of the input space even though the training data are monotone. Adding

    penalty = mean( relu( sign_j * d f / d x_j * scale_j + margin )^2 )

to the loss, evaluated on the training inputs and on random in-range inputs, enforces
``sign_j * d f / d x_j <= -margin`` wherever it is sampled. ``scale_j`` converts the derivative from the network's
(standardised) coordinates to the physical ones, so ``margin`` is in physical units.

    from pinneapple_neural.trainer.monotonic import monotonicity_penalty
    loss = mse + lam * monotonicity_penalty(model, z, cols=[7, 8], signs=[-1, -1], scale=s, margin=3e-4)

pinneapple_neural.trainer.multiadam.doc:
MultiAdam: Adam with separate moment statistics per loss term.

Implements Algorithm 1 of

    Yao, Su, Hao, Liu, Su & Zhu, "MultiAdam: Parameter-wise Scale-invariant Optimizer for
    Multiscale Training of Physics-informed Neural Networks", ICML 2023, arXiv:2306.02816.

Each loss term ``L_i`` (PDE residual, boundary terms, data, ...) gets its own first and
second moments, so a term that is orders of magnitude larger than the others cannot
dominate the step::

    g_i = grad L_i
    m_i = beta1 m_i + (1 - beta1) g_i,       v_i = beta2 v_i + (1 - beta2) g_i**2
    theta -= lr * mean_i( m_i_hat / (sqrt(v_i_hat) + eps) )

Rescaling one term leaves its update unchanged (up to ``eps``). PINNacle
(``src/optimizer/multiadam.py``, MIT) ships the same algorithm. This module is an
independent PyTorch implementation of the paper; no code was copied.

pinneapple_neural.trainer.multistart.doc:
Multi-restart PINN training with NaN watchdog and best-model selection.

Many PINNs are sensitive to initialisation: a bad random seed leads to divergence
or a poor local minimum.  ``MultiRestartTrainer`` runs the training function N
times with different seeds, keeps a NaN watchdog, and returns the best result
according to a user-supplied (or default) score function.

The pattern is taken directly from industrial PINN workflows (e.g. Rate-PINN for
blast-furnace wear modelling) and is model-agnostic: you supply a factory and a
training function; the trainer handles seeds, watchdog, and selection.

Usage
-----
::

    from pinneapple_neural.trainer.multistart import MultiRestartTrainer, MultiRestartConfig

    def make_model(seed):
        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        return MyPINN(...)

    def train_fn(model, seed):
        # Returns (history_dict, final_loss) or (history_dict,)
        ...
        return history, final_loss

    mrt = MultiRestartTrainer(make_model, train_fn,
                              config=MultiRestartConfig(n_restarts=10))
    best = mrt.fit()
    best_model = best.model

pinneapple_neural.trainer.self_scaled_qn.doc:
Self-scaled quasi-Newton optimizers: BFGS, SSBFGS and SSBroyden (dense inverse Hessian).

Implements the self-scaled Broyden family exactly as written in

    Urban, Stefanou & Pons, "Unveiling the optimization process of physics informed
    neural networks: How accurate and competitive can PINNs be?", J. Comput. Phys. 523
    (2025) 113656, arXiv:2405.04230 -- Section 3.2, eqs. (7)-(23), and Appendix B.

with the parameter choices the paper takes from Al-Baali & Khalfan (SSBroyden, its
ref. [68]) and Al-Baali (SSBFGS, its ref. [69]). The same optimizers are distributed for
JAX/Optimistix by CrunchOptimizer/PINNs (MIT), whose benchmarks (Euler/HLLC, Helmholtz,
inviscid Burgers, Stokes, stiff PK-PD) come from Jnini, Kiyani, Shukla et al.,
"Curvature-Aware Optimization for High-Accuracy PINNs", arXiv:2604.05230. This module is
an independent PyTorch implementation of the published formulas; no code was copied.

Update (eq. 10), with s = Theta_{k+1} - Theta_k and y = grad_{k+1} - grad_k::

    H_{k+1} = (1/tau) * (H - (H y)(H y)^T / (y.H y) + phi * v v^T) + s s^T / (y.s)
    v = sqrt(y.H y) * (s / (y.s) - H y / (y.H y))

- BFGS: tau = 1, phi = 1.
- SSBFGS (eqs. 11-12): tau = min(1, y.s / (s.H^{-1} s)), phi = 1.
- SSBroyden (eqs. 13-23): tau and phi from the auxiliary quantities b, h, a, c, rho, theta, sigma.

``s.H^{-1}s`` is never formed by inverting H: since s = -alpha H g, it equals
``-alpha s.g`` (Appendix B, eq. B.1). The step length comes from a strong-Wolfe line
search. …

pinneapple_neural.trainer.weight_schedul.doc:
Automatic loss weight scheduling for PINN training.

PINNs balance multiple competing loss terms (PDE residual, boundary conditions,
initial conditions, data). The relative magnitudes of these terms change during
training, making fixed weights suboptimal. This module provides several
automatic strategies to adjust weights on the fly.

Methods
-------
SelfAdaptiveWeights (SA-PINN)
    Learnable log-weights updated by *gradient ascent* (opposite direction to
    model weights). Weights increase where the model struggles, focusing
    training effort on the hardest terms.
    Ref: McClenny & Braga-Neto (2020). arXiv:2009.04544

GradNormBalancer
    Adjusts weights so gradient norms of all tasks at a shared layer remain
    proportional to a target ratio. Prevents any single term from dominating.
    Ref: Chen et al. (2018). ICML. arXiv:1711.02257

LossRatioBalancer
    Heuristic: keeps the ratio L_term / L_pde near a target value using
    exponential moving averages. Simple and effective for most cases.

NTKWeightBalancer
    Uses the trace of the Neural Tangent Kernel to set weights proportional

pinneapple_neural.workflows.dense_volume.doc:
A reusable train/predict workflow for a grid-based neural operator
(:class:`~pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators.fno.FNO3d`)
trained on a DENSE-in-time real volume time series -- e.g. the output of
:func:`pinneapple_data.adapters.load_dense_volumes` from a ``.splash``
OpenFOAM archive, but this module itself takes plain numpy arrays and
never imports anything splash-specific, so it works for any
``(T, C, D, H, W)`` real time series.

Promoted from the splash-pinneapple downstream project's own
``pipeline/train_fno3d.py`` (single-step training + a text-only
autoregressive rollout sanity check) with one real fix added here:
:func:`train_dense_volume_operator`'s default config now also trains
with the **pushforward trick** (Brandstetter, Worrall & Welling 2022,
"Message Passing Neural PDE Solvers" -- the same idea independently
used to stabilize FNO/neural-operator rollouts elsewhere in the
literature): occasionally roll the model forward K>1 steps using its
OWN prediction as the next input (no gradient through steps 1..K-1),
and backprop only through the LAST step's loss against the real frame
K steps ahead. This exposes the model to the input DISTRIBUTION it will
actually see at autoregressive inference time (its own prior
predictions, which carry error, not always the clean ground truth) --
without this, a model trained purely on ground-truth-in/ground-truth-out
single steps can achieve a low single-step loss while still diverging
catastrophically once fed its …

pinneapple_neural.workflows.hybrid_surro.doc:
Hybrid model: a data-driven surrogate for intermediate quantities + an explicit physics post-model.

When the quantity of interest is *derived* from the flow by an established physics model (erosion from
particle impacts, fatigue from loads, heat-transfer correlations from wall quantities, ...), learning the
derived quantity end to end hides the physics model inside the regressor. The alternative implemented
here keeps it explicit:

    params --(surrogate, learned)--> intermediate quantities --(post-model, physics)--> derived quantity

* the surrogate learns only the intermediate quantities (e.g. impact-velocity/angle statistics at a
  wall), from simulation data;
* the physics post-model is a plain function of those intermediates and the parameters, with a name and a
  scientific source. It is never trained, so it stays auditable and can be swapped (another erosion
  correlation, other material constants) **without retraining** (:meth:`HybridSurrogatePhysics.with_post_model`);
* when the surrogate gives a predictive distribution (mean/std, or samples), the uncertainty is pushed
  through the post-model by Monte Carlo. The post-model is usually nonlinear, so the derived quantity
  evaluated at the surrogate mean is *not* the mean of the derived quantity; both are reported.

This module is numpy-only. :class:`GaussianProcessSurrogate` uses scikit-learn's
``GaussianProcessRegressor`` when it is installed (the same choice …

pinneapple_neural.workflows.parametric_d.doc:
A joint, multi-case extension of :mod:`dense_volume_operator`: one
:class:`~pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators.fno.FNO3d`
trained across SEVERAL real dense-in-time volume time series that share
the same physical problem but differ in a scalar (or low-dim) physical
parameter ``theta`` -- e.g. several real OpenFOAM channel-flow runs at
different friction Reynolds numbers ``Re_tau``.

Why a new module instead of extending :func:`dense_volume_operator
.train_dense_volume_operator` in place: that function's signature and
checkpoint schema are a real, shipped contract (``PINNeAPPle-SplashCFD``'s
``channel_wale_fno3d`` model was trained and is served through it) --
changing its meaning out from under existing callers would be a breaking
change, not an addition. This module is purely additive: it reuses
``FNO3d`` completely unmodified (no new architecture code), it just adds
``theta`` as extra constant input channels, broadcast over the spatial
grid -- the exact mechanism ``FNO3d``'s own ``use_grid=True`` already uses
for coordinate channels, generalised from "channels the network can't
predict, only condition on" (grid coordinates) to "a channel that also
happens to be a channel the network can't predict, only condition on"
(the physical parameter). See ``PINNeAPPle-SplashCFD/ROADMAP.md`` item 1
("The parametric/multi-case PINN track") for the product motivation.

pinneapple_orchestration.doc:
pinneapple_orchestration — an optional Prefect-based pipeline layer
wiring together capabilities that already exist elsewhere in PINNeAPPle:
``pinneapple_registry`` (artifact storage), ``pinneapple_systems
.component_library`` (trainable components), and ``pinneapple_systems
.digital_twin``. No orchestration layer (Prefect, Airflow, or otherwise)
previously existed anywhere in this repo — confirmed via repo-wide grep.

Kept deliberately lean — five flows, not a large numbered pipeline suite,
since this is a generic library, not a single product with a fixed
vertical pipeline:

1. ``flow_data_generation``  — sample scenarios via a caller-supplied
   solver thunk, persist into ``DatasetStore``.
2. ``flow_training``         — build + train a registered component,
   log the run into ``ExperimentStore``.
3. ``flow_benchmark``        — rank every architecture registered for a
   ``component_type``.
4. ``flow_registry_publish`` — the terminal, human-confirmed stage
   promotion (``development`` -> ``staging``/``production``).
5. ``flow_digital_twin_prep``— build a live ``DigitalTwin`` from a
   registry-stored, stage-gated model.

Real Prefect (retries, scheduling, a UI, deployments) is available once
you ``pip install "pinneapple[orchestration]"``; without it, every flow
and task here is still a plain, directly callable Python function (see
``_prefect_compat.py``) — nothing in this package requires Prefect to be
usable or testable.

    from pinneapple_orchestration.flows import …

``pinneapple_llm.guardrail.PhysicsGuardrail._load_reference_from_upd_zarr``'s
own docstring both flagged as missing: until this module, ``pinneapple_pdb``
had exactly one name->dict lookup (``templates.schema_templates()``, which
returns physical-*schema* metadata -- governing equations, units policy --

docstring for the pattern this mirrors).

entries, not a comprehensive benchmark suite. Two are the astrophysically

star / white-dwarf core; n=3: Eddington …

pinneapple_perception.doc:
pinneapple_perception — extract physics observations from images,
video, and audio, for use as `DataConstraint` targets or boundary
geometry anywhere else in PINNeAPPle.

This is the inverse direction of `pinneapple_worldmodel` (which renders
physics simulations INTO photorealistic synthetic images/video for
training data generation) -- here, real-world images/video/audio go IN
and physics observations (velocity fields, boundary geometry, modal
frequencies) come OUT.

Sub-modules
-----------
video_piv
    Cross-correlation Particle Image Velocimetry: extract a velocity
    field from a video of a seeded/textured flow -- the standard
    experimental-fluid-dynamics technique, not a generic optical-flow
    method repurposed for this.
image_geometry
    Extract a boundary point cloud (and, for round parts, a fitted
    circle) from an image -- e.g. a photo or scan of a part's
    cross-section -- for use as domain geometry.
audio_modal
    Extract dominant vibration/acoustic frequencies from a recording
    (e.g. an impulse-response test) via FFT peak-picking with sub-bin
    frequency refinement -- for calibrating/validating structural-
    dynamics presets against a real measured part.

All three depend only on numpy/scipy (already core PINNeAPPle
dependencies) -- no new third-party dependency required. Every technique
here was validated against a synthetic, known-ground-truth case before
being shipped (see `tests/test_perception.py`): PIV against a known
sub-pixel image …

pinneapple_perception.image_geometry.doc:
Extract boundary/geometry point clouds from an image -- e.g. a photo
or scan of a physical part's cross-section -- for use as a domain
boundary in `pinneapple_design.geometry` or as boundary-condition
selector data. Depends only on numpy/scipy (already core PINNeAPPle
dependencies).

Method: binarize the image (threshold), then extract the boundary as the
set of foreground pixels adjacent to a background pixel (a standard
morphological boundary: `foreground AND NOT erode(foreground)`), and
order them into a single closed contour by nearest-neighbor walking
(sufficient for simple, single-blob shapes; a genuinely disconnected or
highly concave/branching shape may need per-component ordering -- see
`extract_boundary_points`'s `ordered` parameter).

pinneapple_perception.piv_tools.doc:
Around :mod:`.video_piv`: reading frames from a video or image files, the vector-grid size a setting gives, a
summary of a PIV result, and window / search-margin advice from the expected displacement.

* :func:`decode_video` -- a video file to a (T, H, W) float grayscale array through ``ffprobe`` / ``ffmpeg``
  subprocesses (``FFmpegMissing`` when they are not on PATH).
* :func:`decode_image_frames` -- image files (PNG, JPEG, ...; Pillow) to (T, H, W), in file-name order.
* :func:`piv_grid_count` -- vectors per frame pair, with the same loop bounds as ``piv_velocity_field``: a window
  is used only when its whole search region fits in the image (half window + search margin from every border).
* :func:`summarize_piv` -- vector count, the windows withheld for border safety (against a grid that only needs
  room for the window), mean / max speed. ``piv_velocity_field`` has no correlation-quality (signal-to-noise)
  rejection; the only vectors it drops are those border windows.
* :func:`piv_parameter_guide` -- the one-quarter rule (Raffel, Willert, Wereley & Kompenhans, *Particle Image
  Velocimetry: A Practical Guide*, 3rd ed., Springer 2018): keep the particle displacement below about a quarter
  of the interrogation window, a search margin of 1.5 x the displacement, 50 % overlap.

pinneapple_perception.video_piv.doc:
Extract a velocity field from a video (image pair/sequence) using
cross-correlation Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) -- the actual
standard technique experimental fluid dynamicists use to turn a video of
a seeded/textured flow into a velocity field, not a generic computer-
vision optical-flow method repurposed for this. Depends only on
numpy/scipy (both already core PINNeAPPle dependencies) -- no new
third-party dependency needed.

Algorithm (per pair of consecutive frames):
  1. Divide the first frame into square interrogation windows on a grid
     (with optional overlap).
  2. For each window, cross-correlate it (FFT-based, normalized) against
     the corresponding region of the second frame.
  3. The correlation peak location gives the most likely pixel
     displacement for that window; a 3-point parabolic fit around the
     peak in each axis gives sub-pixel accuracy (the standard PIV
     sub-pixel refinement, e.g. Raffel et al., "Particle Image
     Velocimetry: A Practical Guide").
  4. Displacement -> velocity via the frame interval `dt` and an optional
     physical calibration (`units_per_pixel`).

The extracted (x, y, u, v) field is a plain numpy array bundle -- pass it
directly as `x_data`/`y_data` to `solve_pde`/`compile_problem` (e.g. as a
`DataConstraint` on a `navier_stokes_incompressible`-family preset) to
train a PINN surrogate constrained by real video-derived velocity
observations, the same way any other sparse tracking/data-constraint
this library …

pinneapple_physics.doc:
pinneapple_physics — Physics problem definition and PINN solving.

Sub-modules
-----------
pde_environment  (was pinneapple_environment)
    PDE problem specification: ProblemSpec, boundary/initial conditions,
    presets (NS, heat, wave, Burgers, elasticity …), RANS turbulence models,
    and PDE-family knowledge base.

pinn_solver      (was pinneapple_pinn)
    PINN compiler: translates a ProblemSpec into callable loss functions.
    Includes DoMINO domain-decomposition PINN.

symbolic_pde     (was pinneapple_symbolic)
    SymPy-to-autograd compiler: define PDE residuals as SymPy expressions,
    get a PyTorch-differentiable residual function. HardBC / SoftBC support.

closed_form
    Real, closed-form (non-PDE) engineering physics: fin-array
    conduction, cantilever bending/fatigue, membrane diffusion,
    Helmholtz resonance. Fast, dependency-free ground truth / training
    data for problems that don't need a full PDE solve.

Integration helpers
------------------
``define_problem(pde_type, ...)``   — quick ProblemSpec builder
``compile_physics(spec)``           — wraps pinn_solver.compile_problem
``solve_pde(spec, model, ...)``     — one-shot: compile → train
``identify(description)``           — wraps pde_environment.identify_pde

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_physics import ProblemSpec, DirichletBC, compile_physics, identify
>>> spec = ProblemSpec(...)
>>> losses = compile_physics(spec)
>>> info = identify("Navier-Stokes incompressible 2D")

pinneapple_physics.advection_diffusion_1.doc:
Periodic 1-D advection-diffusion u_t + c u_x = nu u_xx on [0, 2 pi): exact solution, classical finite-difference
schemes and the PDE residual of any predicted space-time field.

A small, exactly solvable test bed for comparing and ensembling physics models: each Fourier mode decays and travels
exactly, u_k(t) = u_k(0) exp((-i c k - nu k^2) t), so any surrogate, numerical method or PINN can be scored without a
reference solver. The schemes have known, regime-dependent errors: first-order upwind adds numerical diffusion
(LeVeque 2002, §8.6), Lax-Wendroff is second order but dispersive, and a coarse grid loses accuracy when nu is small.

Apparent places of the Sun, Moon and planets (and catalogue stars) for an observer on Earth.

The reduction follows the classical chain (Explanatory Supplement 3rd ed. ch. 7; IERS Conventions 2010):
light-time iteration on the barycentric ephemeris, gravitational deflection by the Sun, relativistic annual +
diurnal aberration, frame bias / precession / nutation to the true equator and equinox of date, then the local
horizon with the apparent sidereal time, and optionally atmospheric refraction.

pinneapple_physics.astro.conditions.doc:
Observing conditions for tonight from open numerical weather prediction (Open-Meteo, CC BY 4.0).

The ensemble API returns every member of an ensemble forecast (e.g. ICON-EPS / GFS-ENS). Per hour this module turns
the members into: the probability of a clear sky (total cloud < 30 %), the median and 10-90 % range of the cloud
cover, a transparency index from humidity and cloud, and a seeing proxy from the upper-level (250 hPa) wind, the jet
stream being the main source of high-altitude turbulence.

What it is and is not: the probabilities are the ensemble's own spread, not yet recalibrated against observations
at the site (that needs a history of forecasts and observations, see ``calibrate``); the seeing proxy is a ranking
(good / average / poor), not arc-seconds.

pinneapple_physics.astro.conjunction.doc:
Conjunction screening: closest approach in Clohessy-Wiltshire relative motion, collision probability, J2 orbits.

* :func:`cw_closest_approach` -- time and distance of closest approach of a deputy to its chief, from the exact
  Clohessy-Wiltshire solution (``presets.astrophysics._cw_exact_state`` / :func:`cw_exact_velocity`): a dense
  scan brackets the minimum of |rho(t)|^2, a bounded scalar minimiser refines it, and the residual
  ``|rho . v| / (|rho| |v|)`` (zero at a true closest approach) is reported.
* :func:`collision_probability_2d` -- the 2-D Gaussian collision probability in the encounter plane (Foster &
  Estes 1992; Alfano 2005): the mass of N((xm, zm), diag(sx^2, sz^2)) inside the hard-body disk of radius r_c
  centred at the origin, by adaptive quadrature. :func:`collision_probability_centered` is the closed form for a
  centred isotropic Gaussian, 1 - exp(-r_c^2 / (2 sigma^2)) (Chan 2008), used to check the quadrature.
* :func:`screen_cw_conjunction` -- the two together, with the assumptions written into the result.
* :func:`two_body_j2_rhs` / :func:`propagate_two_body_j2` -- two-body + J2 acceleration
  a = (3/2) J2 mu Re^2 / r^5 [x(5 z^2/r^2 - 1), y(5 z^2/r^2 - 1), z(5 z^2/r^2 - 3)] (Vallado 2013, ch. 9), the
  same model as the ``satellite_j2_perturbation`` preset, integrated with DOP853.

Scope, as for the source app (PINNeAPPle-apps ``satellite_conjunction_screening``): CW is linear relative motion
about a circular reference orbit, valid for short windows …

pinneapple_physics.astro.decay.doc:
Orbit decay of low-Earth-orbit satellites by atmospheric drag, with a physics-informed model and its checks.

Physics (near-circular orbit, orbit-averaged): da/dt = -B rho(h) sqrt(mu a), B = C_D A / m (m^2/kg), h = a - R_E.
The thermospheric density comes from NRLMSIS 2.0 (``pymsis``, MIT; Emmert et al. 2021) driven by the solar flux
F10.7 and the geomagnetic index Ap, averaged around the orbit (latitude band of the inclination, all local times).
Without ``pymsis`` a piecewise-exponential standard atmosphere is used (Vallado, *Fundamentals of Astrodynamics*,
table 8-4, mean solar activity).

* :func:`reference_decay`  classical integration (adaptive RK) of the ODE, with a Monte-Carlo envelope over the
  uncertain inputs (solar activity, ballistic coefficient)
* :func:`train_decay_pinn` a PINN a(t) = a0 + tau s g_theta(tau) (initial condition exact) trained on the residual
  of the ODE; judged against the reference integration and its envelope
* :func:`sgp4_decay`       the altitude trend that SGP4 itself predicts from a TLE (its own power-law density and
  the fitted B*), an independent drag model
pinneapple_physics.astro.decay.doc1: Orbit decay of low-Earth-orbit satellites by atmospheric drag, with a physics-informed model and its checks.

classes.doc1: log-density on an altitude grid, interpolated (NumPy and PyTorch) so models can be evaluated fast.

functions.name: orbit_mean_density
functions.doc1: Orbit-averaged NRLMSIS 2.0 total mass density (kg/m^3) at altitudes ``h_km``: mean over latitudes sampled along the orbit (|lat| <= inclination, weighted by the time spent there) and over all local times.

SGP4's B* is a fitted drag term for its own power-law atmosphere, not a physical ballistic coefficient (converted with B* = B rho0 / 2 it is typically an order of magnitude …

Solar-system ephemeris on top of a JPL DE kernel (public domain), read by :mod:`.spk`.

pinneapple_physics.astro.facts.doc:
Facts and curiosities about the objects in the sky, for a general audience, in English and Portuguese.

A versioned dataset (``data/facts/``): the Sun, planets, Moon, dwarf planets and major moons (NASA fact sheets), the
brightest stars (Yale BSC + Hipparcos 2007 parallaxes), the 88 constellations (IAU; areas computed from the
boundaries), the 110 Messier objects (positions from d3-celestial; distances from the literature where cited) and
the satellites the observatory tracks. Every number carries a ``source`` (a key of ``data/facts/sources.json``); the
text is written for this project in both languages (none copied).

    from pinneapple_physics.astro import facts
    c = facts.card("saturn", "pt")              # name, summary, numbers with sources and comparisons, curiosities, quiz
    facts.search("cruzeiro")                    # ids, in either language
    facts.did_you_know("en", seed=3)

Comparisons ("9.4 times the Earth's diameter", "light takes 8.3 min") are computed from the card's own numbers and
carry the source ``computed``.

pinneapple_physics.astro.frames.doc:
Reference-frame rotations: frame bias, precession (IAU 2006), nutation (IAU 1980, terms above 5 mas),
geodetic observer positions (WGS84), horizon (alt-az) and ecliptic coordinates.

Truncating the nutation series to its 18 largest terms leaves < 0.02" (validated against IAU 2000A in
``tests/test_astro_accuracy.py``), well inside the arcsecond budget of the observatory.

pinneapple_physics.astro.journey.doc:
A journey from your place on Earth to a planet, a moon, the Sun or a star: the geometry of the trip.

Positions are heliocentric, in km, on ICRS (J2000 equatorial) axes: Solar System bodies from the JPL ephemeris at
the date of the trip, the observer from the Earth's position plus the geocentric position of the site (WGS84, Earth
rotation), stars from their J2000 direction and parallax. The module gives the distances, the light time, how long the
trip would take at real speeds, and how the target grows and brightens as you approach (apparent magnitude
m = M + 5 log10(d / 10 pc) for stars, the inverse-square law at a fixed phase for planets; angular diameter
2 asin(R / d)). Galactic coordinates use the IAU 1958 definition on J2000 axes (Hipparcos introduction, vol. 1, §1.5.3).

    from pinneapple_physics.astro import journey, Observer, Time
    j = journey.plan(Observer(-23.55, -46.63, 760), "mars", Time.from_iso("2026-10-14T00:00:00Z"))
    j["distance_km"], j["light_time_s"], j["travel_times"]

pinneapple_physics.astro.nbody.doc:
Classical N-body integrators for the Sun-planets(-Moon) problem, with conservation diagnostics.

* ``leapfrog``   kick-drift-kick, 2nd order, symplectic
* ``yoshida4``   Yoshida (1990) 4th-order symplectic composition of leapfrog
* ``rk4``        classical Runge-Kutta 4 (not symplectic: energy drifts secularly; shown for contrast)
* ``dop853``     SciPy's adaptive 8th-order Dormand-Prince, rtol 1e-12 (reference)

Units: km, s, km^3/s^2. Initial conditions come from the JPL ephemeris (:func:`initial_state`); the result can be
compared back against the ephemeris to show what Newtonian point masses miss (relativity, asteroids, figure effects).
pinneapple_physics.astro.nbody.doc1: Classical N-body integrators for the Sun-planets(-Moon) problem, with conservation diagnostics.

functions.name: energy
functions.doc1: Total energy per unit G (km^2/s^2 * km^3/s^2 / ... consistent units: sum mu_i v_i^2/2 - sum mu_i mu_j/r_ij).

functions.name: integrate
functions.sig: (r0, v0, mu, t_end_s, dt_s, method='yoshida4', n_out=200)
functions.doc1: Integrate from t=0 to ``t_end_s``; returns dict with times (s), r (n_out, N, 3), v, and the relative energy error and angular-momentum drift histories.

pinneapple_physics.astro.neural_propagat.doc:
A learned propagator for near-Earth asteroids: one network for many bodies.

The network maps (osculating elements at the epoch, time) -> the deviation of the true heliocentric position from
the Kepler orbit of those elements, over one year. It is trained once on a synthetic NEO-like population integrated
with the full propagator of :mod:`.smallbodies` (Sun + planets + Moon from DE421, solar relativity), and evaluated on
held-out bodies and on real objects (Apophis, Phaethon, Ceres). Its error is reported next to the Kepler-only
error, with the speed-up and a physics check: the Tisserand parameter with respect to Jupiter, nearly conserved by the
true motion, must stay as conserved along the learned trajectories.

    model = NeuralPropagator.load()              # shipped weights (scripts/astro/train_neural_propagator.py)
    r = model.predict(body, jd)                  # heliocentric ICRF km
pinneapple_physics.astro.neural_propagat.doc1: A learned propagator for near-Earth asteroids: one network for many bodies.

functions.doc1: NEO-like osculating elements: a 0.7-2.6 AU, e 0.02-0.65 (perihelion > 0.2 AU), i 0-35 deg, random angles.

functions.doc1: Inputs: a, e, sin/cos i, angles as sin/cos, tau = t / span, and the Kepler mean anomaly at t (sin/cos).

functions.doc1: Radial / transverse (along-track) / normal unit vectors of the Kepler orbit, (n, 3, 3) rows R, T, N.

functions.doc1: Features and targets: the deviation from the Kepler orbit in its R/T/N frame (milli-AU).

functions.doc1: Tisserand parameter w.r.t. Jupiter from heliocentric states (ICRF axes; inclination to the ecliptic).

functions.doc1: Errors of the learned propagator and of Kepler alone against the full integrator, per body, plus timing.

functions.doc1: Verdict of the shipped network from its held-out evaluation: to be useful it must beat Kepler by 5x on the median of the per-body maximum error over unseen bodies (and not be worse than Kepler at the 90th percentile).

pinneapple_physics.astro.observing.doc:
An observing session, with honest physics: plan a night, set up a telescope, slew to a target and track it.

* Visibility: altitude / azimuth / airmass curves, rise, transit and set (Solar System bodies through
  :func:`.phenomena.rise_transit_set`; stars and deep-sky objects from their apparent places, the same root finder and
  the standard 34' refraction at the horizon), astronomical twilight, the Moon's altitude, phase and separation, and the
  best window of the night.
* The atmosphere: air mass (Kasten & Young 1989, :func:`.astrometry.airmass`), extinction per band, and the sky
  brightness from the Moon (Krisciunas & Schaefer 1991) and twilight.
* Telescope optics: magnification, true field, exit pupil, resolving power (Dawes, Rayleigh), limiting magnitude,
  image scale and camera field.
* The mount: slew time with a trapezoidal velocity profile per axis, horizon and meridian limits (meridian flip of a
  German equatorial mount), and the field rotation of an alt-azimuth mount.

    from pinneapple_physics.astro import observing, Observer, Time
    v = observing.visibility("saturn", Observer(-23.55, -46.63, 760), Time.from_iso("2026-10-13T21:00:00Z"))
    o = observing.optics(observing.TELESCOPES["newton200"], eyepiece=observing.EYEPIECES["plossl25"])

pinneapple_physics.astro.phenomena.doc:
Almanac phenomena: rise / transit / set, twilight, Moon phase, planet magnitudes and elongations,
oppositions and conjunctions, equinoxes and solstices, lunar and solar eclipses, transits of Mercury and Venus.

Every event is found the same way: sample a smooth function of time on a grid finer than the phenomenon,
bracket the sign changes (or the minima), then refine by bisection / golden-section to < 1 s.
