pinneapple_physics.physical_problem.doc:
``PhysicalProblem``: one description of a physics problem for every part of the library.

Before this module there were three overlapping classes, each covering part of a problem:

* ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.spec.ProblemSpec`` -- the executable PDE definition (coordinates,
  fields, PDE term, boundary/initial/data conditions, domain bounds). The PINN compiler consumes it.
* ``pinneapple_problemdesign.schema.ProblemSpec`` -- the elicited, mostly free-text description of a problem
  (goal, task type, data, validation and deployment needs) produced by the problem-design assistant.
* ``pinneapple_data.physics_case.PhysicsCase`` -- a bundle that references geometry, a PDE ``ProblemSpec``,
  a solver choice, results and a reference benchmark.

``PhysicalProblem`` holds all of that in one place and adds what none of them had: **parameters with units
and a role** (fixed, design, uncertain, unknown), so the same object can drive a forward solve, a design
optimization, an uncertainty study or a parameter-discovery run, plus **quantities of interest** and a
stable **fingerprint** for provenance.

The three existing classes keep working unchanged. They are adapters:

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> prob = pp.PhysicalProblem.from_preset("burgers_1d", nu=0.01)
>>> spec = prob.to_pde_spec()                 # what the PINN compiler consumes, same object shape as before
>>> pp.PhysicalProblem.from_pde_spec(spec).to_pde_spec() == spec
True

Units are optional but checked when …

pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.doc:
Physics audit: which model to use, when to trust it and when its physical formulation itself must be revisited.

"It is in the fundamental knowledge that we must look for the cause of a model's imperfections." The modules here
add, on top of the predictive models (PINN, FNO, GNN, DeepONet, CNN, solvers), the layers that judge them by their
physics:

========================  =====================================================================================
layer                     module
========================  =====================================================================================
physical evaluation       :mod:`.monitor` (residuals, conservation, bounds, boundary, invariants, extrapolation:
                          no ground truth needed), :mod:`.assumptions` (each model's assumptions and the
                          conditions they hold in), :mod:`.regime` (dimensionless numbers)
adaptive decision         :mod:`.routing` (compatibility of the current case with each model's physics, as a prior
                          on the weights of :class:`~pinneapple_physics.ensemble.PhysicsEnsemble`; sleeping
                          experts; escalation to the solver)
diagnosis and evolution   :mod:`.attribution` (probable cause of a failure, with evidence and confidence),
                          :mod:`.improvement` (next experiment or change of highest value), :mod:`.knowledge`
                          (graph of phenomena, equations, assumptions, …

pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.assumpt.doc:
Physics assumptions of a model, the conditions under which each holds, and an auditor that checks them case by
case.

Every surrogate, PINN or solver rests on simplifications: incompressible flow, laminar regime, constant properties,
small strains. Each holds inside a range of dimensionless numbers. A model used outside that range can still return
a smooth, plausible field, and its PDE residual can even stay low (it satisfies *its* equations, which no longer
describe the case). So the first place to look for the cause of an error is the model's own physical foundations.

* :class:`Condition`: ``lo <= feature <= hi``, with a soft band around the edges (in decades for numbers that span
  orders of magnitude) so the auditor says *marginal* near a transition instead of flipping from valid to violated;
* :class:`Assumption`: a named simplification, its conditions, the phenomenon that appears when it breaks and the
  physical mechanism the model then lacks. :data:`ASSUMPTIONS` holds the common ones; the factory functions
  (:func:`laminar`, :func:`incompressible`...) build them with other thresholds;
* :class:`Envelope`: where the model was trained (box of feature ranges, optionally the training samples for a
  nearest-neighbour distance), for extrapolation;
* :class:`ModelProfile`: the model card the audit reads: equations, assumptions, mechanisms represented, envelope;
* :func:`audit_assumptions` / :class:`AssumptionAudit`: one case against one profile, with a status per …

pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.attribu.doc:
Physics failure attribution: not only *that* a prediction is wrong (or suspect), but its probable cause, with the
evidence and a confidence.

The causes, and the evidence each one rests on:

=========================  ==============================================================================
``pde_violation``          the governing-equation residual fails its tolerance or jumps above its baseline
``conservation``           a conserved total (mass, energy, momentum) is off
``boundary_condition``     the prediction does not meet the boundary condition
``regime_change``          the case violates an assumption of the model (the physics changed under it)
``extrapolation``          the assumptions hold but the case is outside the training envelope
``numerical_resolution``   grid or time-step dependence (GCI, change under refinement), non-finite or out-of-
                           bounds values from an unresolved solution
``measurement``            the reference itself is suspect (sensor check), so the "error" may not be the model's
``missing_physics``        the model satisfies its own equations, inside its assumptions and envelope, and still
                           disagrees with the reference: its equations miss a mechanism (model-form error)
=========================  ==============================================================================

Each cause gets a score in [0, 1] from its evidence; the scores, plus an "unexplained" share when nothing points
anywhere, …

pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.improve.doc:
Physics-guided model improvement: when no model is good enough, which experiment or change is worth most?

:func:`recommend` turns the diagnosis of one case (an :class:`~.attribution.Attribution`, optionally the
assumption audit and the knowledge graph) into ranked actions; :func:`improvement_plan` aggregates many cases (a
validation campaign, a week of operation) so the actions that fix the most frequent and most confident causes come
first. Each action says what to do, why (the evidence), the expected gain and the cost:

=========================  ===================================================================================
cause                      actions
=========================  ===================================================================================
``regime_change``          high-fidelity runs in the new regime; train or adapt a model for it; switch to a
                           model or equation that represents the missing mechanism (from the knowledge graph)
``extrapolation``          high-fidelity runs at and around the case (design points given); active learning
``pde_violation``          more collocation points or residual weight where it fails; hard constraints
``conservation``           conservation projection (``pinneapple_physics.conservation``) or a penalty in the loss
``boundary_condition``     check the boundary data; enforce the condition exactly (ansatz or projection)
``numerical_resolution``   refine the mesh or the time step; run …

Physics knowledge graph: phenomena, equations, assumptions, parameters, mechanisms and model families, and the
relations between them.

Nodes have a kind (``phenomenon``, ``equation``, ``assumption``, ``parameter``, ``mechanism``, ``model``); edges a
relation:

=====================  ===================================================================
``assumes``            equation or model -> assumption it rests on
``valid_when``         assumption -> parameter (with the condition, in the edge data)
``breaks_into``        assumption -> phenomenon that appears when it fails
``triggered_by``       phenomenon -> parameter (with the trigger condition)
``requires``           phenomenon -> mechanism a model needs to capture it
``uses``               model -> equation
``represents``         model or equation -> mechanism
=====================  ===================================================================

:func:`default_graph` builds the common fluid, heat and solid relations from the assumption catalogue. The queries the
router, the attribution and the improvement advisor use: :meth:`~PhysicsKnowledgeGraph.phenomena_triggered` (which
phenomena a case is in or near), :meth:`~PhysicsKnowledgeGraph.unrepresented` (triggered phenomena whose mechanism a
model lacks: "Re went up, is turbulence represented?"), :meth:`~PhysicsKnowledgeGraph.models_for` (models that
represent a mechanism) and :meth:`~PhysicsKnowledgeGraph.explain`. :meth:`~PhysicsKnowledgeGraph.to_mermaid` draws …

pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.routing.doc:
Physics-aware model routing: weight each model by how well the *current* case fits its physical foundations, not
only by the errors it made on earlier cases.

For one case the router reads its features (dimensionless numbers, from ``features_fn(query)``) and, for each
model, the audit of its assumptions and training envelope (:func:`~.assumptions.audit_assumptions`). The
compatibility ``c_i`` in [0, 1] becomes a prior on the model's weight:

    w_i  proportional to  w_learned_i * max(c_i, floor) ** strength * exp(-cost_weight * cost_i / max cost)

A model whose assumptions the case violates is *asleep* (``c_i < abstain_below``): it is not used for this case
and, inside a :class:`~pinneapple_physics.ensemble.PhysicsEnsemble`, its weight is not changed by the case either
(the sleeping-experts rule: its loss is set to the mixture's). So a laminar correlation is not punished for the
turbulent cases it was never meant for, and is ready again when the flow returns to its regime, without waiting for
its weight to recover. When no model is compatible (best ``c_i < escalate_below``) the router escalates to the
reference solver named by ``escalate_to``.

Use standalone (:meth:`PhysicsAwareRouter.route`) or inside the ensemble: ``PhysicsEnsemble(experts,
router=PhysicsAwareRouter(profiles, features_fn))``. The learned weights and the residual look-ahead of the ensemble
still apply on top, so history and the current residual correct a compatibility that is wrong.

pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler..doc:
Electromagnetic PDE kinds of the problem compiler: Maxwell's equations in differential and integral form.

Every kind returns a list of residual tensors ``(N, 1)`` at the collocation points (the compiler squares and
averages them). Units are the caller's: ``eps``, ``mu``, ``sigma`` default to 1 (a non-dimensional problem); for
SI pass the SI values or, better, scale the problem (``x / L``, ``t c / L``, fields by a reference amplitude) so the
network sees O(1) numbers. Space- or field-dependent material maps come from ``ctx`` callables
``eps_fn(X, ctx)``, ``mu_fn``, ``nu_fn``, ``sigma_fn`` evaluated at the points (piecewise-constant maps are the
usual case; a preset may put them in the PDE ``params``, under the caller's ``ctx``; in the differential kinds
their jumps are not differentiated, so interface conditions are only
imposed by the integral kinds, which evaluate the maps on the edges of each control square).

Differential kinds (``fields`` in brackets):

``electrostatics`` [phi]               div(eps grad phi) + rho = 0, rho from ``ctx["rho_fn"]`` (or ``source_fn``)
``magnetostatics_az`` [Az]             div(nu grad Az) + Jz = 0, ``nu = 1/mu``, Jz from ``ctx["J_fn"]``
``eddy_current_az`` [Ar, Ai]           nu lap(A) - j omega sigma A + Js = 0 (phasor ``exp(+j omega t)``, A = Ar + j Ai)
``maxwell_tm`` [Ez, Hx, Hy] + t        eps dEz/dt - (dHy/dx - dHx/dy) + sigma Ez + Jz = 0, mu dHx/dt + dEz/dy = 0,
                                       mu dHy/dt - dEz/dx = 0 (2-D TMz; …

An equation like ``Derivative(T(t), t) - a*S(t) + b*(T(t) - Tamb(t))`` uses ``S`` and ``Tamb``
as *known* functions of time (weather data), not as network outputs. The factory needs their
values at whatever points it evaluates the residual (collocation, conditions, data). A provider
is either a tensor with one row per point of that batch, or a callable ``f(*inputs) -> Tensor``
that can be evaluated anywhere -- ``TabulatedSignal`` is the usual choice for sampled data.

pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.factory.s.doc:
SymPy-based compiler for symbolic equations to torch-callable lambdas.

Design note — two SymPy→PyTorch compilation paths exist in this codebase:

* **This module** (``SympyTorchCompiler``): uses ``sympy.lambdify`` to emit a
  fast Python lambda.  Gradients do *not* flow through the symbolic evaluation
  itself; the lambdified call is opaque to autograd.  Suitable when PDE losses
  are evaluated at fixed collocation points and runtime speed is the priority.

* ``pinneapple_symbolic.SymbolicPDE``: walks the expression tree with
  ``torch.autograd.grad``, so gradients *do* flow through the evaluation.
  Use that path when you need the symbolic expression to participate in the
  autograd graph (e.g. differentiating the residual w.r.t. model weights for
  meta-learning, or computing higher-order cross derivatives).

pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.stochasti.doc:
Latent-conditioned (stochastic) PINN training utilities.

A deterministic PINN, ``f(x) -> y``, is the wrong tool for a chaotic
system with only a handful of real observed snapshots to fit against: with
too few, decorrelated snapshots to learn genuine dynamics from, a
pointwise-MSE-trained deterministic network is pushed towards either an
over-smoothed, near-constant predictor (nothing left to distinguish
different points) or an overfit one that memorises the specific noisy
values of whatever snapshots it saw, at the cost of any coherent spatial
structure (observed in practice on a wall-bounded turbulent-channel LES
surrogate: a deterministic model trained on two real, 36-time-units-apart
instantaneous snapshots produced non-physical, spatially disconnected
low-velocity blobs scattered through the flow's core, rather than the
wall-hugging streaky structure the real LES has).

This module instead makes the model take an additional latent code ``xi``
(typically ``xi ~ N(0, I)``), turning ``f(x) -> y`` into a family
``f(x, xi) -> y`` -- a *distribution* of physically-plausible outputs at
each ``x``, trained so that:

- every ``(x, xi)`` still satisfies the governing PDE residual and any
  boundary conditions (physics must hold for *every* plausible
  realisation, not just an average one) -- pass ``xi`` straight through to
  whatever residual function you already use, since the residual only
  needs `torch.autograd.grad` w.r.t. the coordinates ``x``, never ``xi``;
- one or more …

pinneapple_physics.solid.axisymmetric.doc:
Axisymmetric linear elasticity in cylindrical coordinates ``(r, z)``, by autograd.

A displacement field ``u(x)`` with ``x = [r, z]`` (``(N, 2)``, ``requires_grad``) and ``u = [u_r, u_z]`` or
``[u_r, u_z, u_theta]`` (``(N, 2)`` or ``(N, 3)``, computed from ``x``) is independent of ``theta``. With the
optional torsional component ``u_theta`` (torsion of a solid of revolution) the small strains are

    e_rr = du_r/dr,   e_tt = u_r / r,   e_zz = du_z/dz,   e_rz = (du_r/dz + du_z/dr) / 2,
    e_rt = (du_t/dr - u_t / r) / 2,     e_tz = (du_t/dz) / 2          (tensor shear strains),

Hooke's law ``sigma = lambda tr(e) I + 2 mu e`` with ``lambda = E nu / ((1 + nu)(1 - 2 nu))``,
``mu = E / (2 (1 + nu))``, and the equilibrium equations without body force are

    R_r = d s_rr/dr + d s_rz/dz + (s_rr - s_tt) / r
    R_z = d s_rz/dr + d s_zz/dz + s_rz / r
    R_t = d s_rt/dr + d s_tz/dz + 2 s_rt / r.

The meridional (``u_r, u_z``) and torsional (``u_theta``) problems decouple. Reference: S. P. Timoshenko and
J. N. Goodier, *Theory of Elasticity*, 3rd ed., McGraw-Hill (1970): equilibrium and strain-displacement relations in
cylindrical coordinates, the solid of revolution under axisymmetric load and torsion of shafts of variable diameter;
the thick-walled cylinder (Lame) solution ``u_r = A r + B / r`` is the test case of ``tests/test_axisymmetric.py``.

Units are whatever ``x``, ``u`` and ``E`` use (``E`` in Pa with ``u`` and ``x`` in the same length unit gives Pa).
pinneapple_physics.solid.axisymmetric.doc1: Axisymmetric linear elasticity in cylindrical coordinates ``(r, z)``, by autograd.

pinneapple_physics.solving.doc:
``pp.solve`` and ``pp.compare``: one entry point to solve a problem by any method and compare methods.

>>> import pinneapple as pp
>>> sol = pp.solve("burgers_1d", method="pinn", epochs=2000)          # a PINN
>>> exact = pp.solve("burgers_1d", method="analytic")                 # Cole-Hopf closed form
>>> print(pp.compare("burgers_1d", methods=["pinn"], reference="analytic", options={"pinn": {"epochs": 2000}}))

``problem`` may be a ``PhysicalProblem``, a PDE ``ProblemSpec`` or a preset name. Built-in methods:

* ``"reference"`` -- the classical solver named in the problem's ``reference_solver`` (a preset's ``solver_spec``).
  Its grid output is interpolated linearly in between grid points. If that solver does not produce a field on a
  grid over **every** coordinate of the problem, ``solve`` raises ``MethodNotAvailable`` instead of returning a
  partial answer (for example a transient solver that keeps only the last time step).
* ``"pinn"`` -- a physics-informed network from the model registry trained with ``solve_pde``.
* ``"analytic"`` -- a closed-form solution the library knows for this problem (``list_analytic()``), for example the
  Cole-Hopf solution of the ``burgers_1d`` preset. Raises ``MethodNotAvailable`` when none is registered.
* ``"exact"`` -- a closed-form or manufactured solution passed as ``fn=lambda X: ...``.

* ``"fem"`` -- a classical P1 finite-element solve of steady ``poisson`` / ``laplace`` problems on a box with
  Dirichlet conditions (1D, 2D or …

pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.doc:
pinneapple_symbolic — Symbolic PDE compiler for PINNeAPPle.

Converts SymPy PDE residual expressions into callable PyTorch autograd functions
and provides hard / soft boundary condition implementations.

Quick start::

    import sympy as sp
    from pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde import SymbolicPDE, HardBC

    x, y = sp.symbols("x y")
    u = sp.Function("u")

    # Poisson: u_xx + u_yy + 2*pi^2 * sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y) = 0
    expr = (
        u(x, y).diff(x, 2)
        + u(x, y).diff(y, 2)
        + 2 * sp.pi**2 * sp.sin(sp.pi * x) * sp.sin(sp.pi * y)
    )
    pde = SymbolicPDE(expr, coord_syms=[x, y], field_syms=[u])

    # Hard BC: u = 0 on unit-square boundary via distance-function ansatz
    phi = lambda pts: pts[:,0:1]*(1-pts[:,0:1])*pts[:,1:2]*(1-pts[:,1:2])
    import torch
    hard_bc = HardBC(phi, lambda pts: torch.zeros(pts.shape[0], 1, device=pts.device))
    wrapped_model = hard_bc.wrap_model(base_model)

    residual_fn = pde.to_residual_fn(wrapped_model)
    res = residual_fn(x_col)   # (N, 1) PDE residual tensor

pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.bc.doc:
Boundary condition enforcement for PINNeAPPle symbolic PDE module.

Provides hard (by-construction) and soft (penalty) BC implementations:

- HardBC    : distance-function ansatz — BCs are satisfied exactly at every step.
- PeriodicBC: coordinate-embedding trick to enforce periodicity exactly.
- DirichletBC: soft Dirichlet penalty loss.
- NeumannBC : soft Neumann penalty loss via autograd normal derivative.

pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.compiler.doc:
Symbolic PDE compiler for PINNeAPPle.

Converts SymPy PDE residual expressions into callable PyTorch autograd functions.

Design note — two SymPy→PyTorch compilation paths exist in this codebase:

* **This module** (``SymbolicPDE``): walks the expression tree recursively using
  ``torch.autograd.grad``.  Gradients flow *through* the evaluation, so you can
  differentiate the residual loss with respect to model weights.  Use this when
  you need higher-order autograd or want the symbolic expression to participate
  directly in the training graph.

* ``pinneapple_pinn.factory.sympy_backend.SympyTorchCompiler``: uses
  ``sympy.lambdify`` to emit a Python lambda; faster to evaluate but the
  lambdified call is opaque to autograd (no gradient tape through the symbolic
  tree).  Use that path when the PDE loss is evaluated at fixed collocation
  points and speed matters more than differentiability through the expression.

``SymbolicPDE`` also supports a pluggable ``grad_method`` (default
``"autograd"``, unchanged from the original behavior above): pass
``grad_method="finite_difference"`` or ``"spectral"`` plus a ``grid``
(``GridAxisSpec``) to evaluate the SAME symbolic residual over grid-shaped
field tensors (e.g. an FNO's output) instead of a continuous model's output
at scattered points — see ``gradient_backends.py`` and
``to_grid_residual_fn``. Note: this module's ``compile_problem``-based
sibling, ``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.compile`` (the actual
engine behind …

pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.gradient.doc:
Pluggable derivative backends for :class:`SymbolicPDE`.

Design note -- this mirrors a pattern found in PhysicsNeMo's
``PhysicsInformer(grad_method=...)`` (see ``physicsnemo/sym/eq/phy_informer.py``
upstream, Apache-2.0; this module reimplements the *architecture pattern*,
not their code): separate "what is the PDE" (the SymPy expression, unchanged)
from "how do we compute a derivative given the shape of the data". The same
symbolic residual can then be evaluated either

* over scattered collocation points from a continuous model (PINN-style),
  differentiated via ``torch.autograd.grad`` -- the ``"autograd"`` backend,
  which is exactly ``SymbolicPDE``'s original (and still default) behavior, or
* over a structured grid (e.g. an FNO's output), differentiated via
  finite-difference or spectral (FFT) stencils -- the ``"finite_difference"``
  / ``"spectral"`` backends below.

The finite-difference and spectral math here is **not reimplemented**: it
calls straight through to ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.neural_operators
.pino``'s ``fd_derivative`` / ``spectral_derivative``, the same functions
already used (and exercised) by the PINO wrapper. This module only adds the
bookkeeping to (a) map SymPy coordinate names to grid tensor axes/extents and
(b) compose repeated/mixed partial derivatives (e.g. ``u_xx``, or a mixed
``u_xy``) out of those single-axis primitives.

pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.pinn.doc:
A parsed equation system (:mod:`.text`) as a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.validation.pinn.PINNProblem`.

The residual is evaluated by autograd from the same SymPy expressions the finite-difference solver uses, so a PINN
and a classical solution of one edited system are comparable point for point. Dirichlet and initial conditions
become the problem's ``boundary`` / ``initial`` samplers (checked by ``validate_pinn``); conditions with derivatives
(Neumann, Robin, ``u_t = ...`` at ``t = 0``) become ``constraints``. Coefficients listed in ``unknowns`` are trainable
scalars (an inverse PINN, with ``train_pinn(..., data=(X, Y))``).

    P, model = pinn_problem(system, {"x": (0, 1), "t": (0, 1)})
    net, info = train_pinn(P, model, adam_steps=2000, lbfgs_steps=200)
    report = validate_pinn(net, P)

pinneapple_physics.symbolic_pde.text.doc:
Equations as text, parsed safely into SymPy: ``"u_t = alpha*lap(u) + sin(pi*x)"``.

The text is read with :mod:`ast` and translated node by node into SymPy objects; nothing is handed to ``eval`` or
``sympify``. Allowed: numbers, ``+ - * / ** ^``, parentheses, coordinates, fields, coefficient names and the
functions in :data:`FUNCTIONS`, plus three operators:

==================  ===========================================================================================
``u_t``, ``u_xx``   derivative shorthand: a field, an underscore, then one coordinate letter per derivative
``d(f, x, ...)``    derivative of any expression (chain rule applied), e.g. ``d(u**2, x)`` or ``d(u, x, x)``
``lap(f)``          Laplacian over the *spatial* coordinates (so the same text works in 1-D, 2-D and 3-D)
==================  ===========================================================================================

Any other name is a coefficient: it needs a value (``coefficients={"alpha": 0.1}``) before the system is solved, or
it is declared unknown (an inverse problem). Attribute access, subscripts, keywords, strings, lambdas, comprehensions
and calls of anything not listed are refused with :class:`EquationSyntaxError`.

    sys_ = parse_system(["u_t = alpha*lap(u)"], [{"kind": "dirichlet", "on": "x_min", "equation": "u = 0"}],
                        coords=["x", "t"], fields=["u"], coefficients={"alpha": 0.1})
    sys_.classify()["family"]       # "heat"

pinneapple_physics.tribology.doc: Tribology: sliding wear of a bar against a counterface (Archard's law with contact-pressure redistribution).
pinneapple_physics.tribology.doc1: Tribology: sliding wear of a bar against a counterface (Archard's law with contact-pressure redistribution).

pinneapple_physics.tribology.archard.doc:
Sliding wear of a bar end pressed against a rigid, flat counterface.

Archard's law, local form: the wear depth grows as dh/ds = K p, with K = k / H the specific wear rate
(mm³ / (N·m)), p the contact pressure (MPa = N/mm²) and s the sliding distance (m). The bar end is crowned (a
cylinder of radius R across the sliding direction), so at first only its middle touches; the pressure comes from an
elastic (Winkler) layer, p = E' / t · max(0, δ - g(x) - h(x)), with the approach δ set by the load at every step. Wear
removes the crown, the contact spreads and the pressure tends to the flat-punch value F / A: running-in, then
steady wear at dh/ds = K F / A.

Exact facts the solver must keep (checked in the lab experiment ``bar_wear``):

* worn volume = K F s at every moment (global Archard, any pressure distribution);
* the initial contact is the closed-form Winkler solution for a parabolic gap (``winkler_parabolic_contact``);
* after running-in the wear rate is K F / A.

The materials are the classic pin-on-ring data of Archard and Hirst (1956), as tabulated in Hutchings and Shipway,
*Tribology* (2nd ed., 2017), table 5.2 (k dimensionless, H Vickers hardness): order-of-magnitude values for dry
sliding at low load, not design data for a specific pair.
pinneapple_physics.tribology.archard.doc1: Sliding wear of a bar end pressed against a rigid, flat counterface.

pinneapple_physics.weather.data.doc:
ERA5 from WeatherBench2 (public Google Cloud bucket, no account) as a local, normalised array for training and
evaluating global forecast models, plus the climatology needed for anomaly scores.

The default grid is 64 x 32 (5.625 degrees), the coarsest WeatherBench2 grid: a model trains on a laptop CPU, and the
published forecasts of IFS HRES, GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, Keisler and NeuralGCM exist on the same grid for 2020, so
the skill of a new model can be put next to theirs case by case.

``download(dest, years)`` writes ``dest/state.npy`` (time, channel, lat, lon) in float16 after normalising every
channel by its mean and standard deviation (kept in ``dest/meta.json``), ``dest/constants.npy`` (land-sea mask and
surface geopotential) and ``dest/times.npy``. :class:`Era5Store` reads it back lazily (memory map).

pinneapple_physics.weather.evaluate.doc:
Skill of global forecasts by lead time, and how far ahead each forecast can be trusted.

Scores (area-weighted, as in WeatherBench2): RMSE and anomaly correlation (ACC, anomalies from the 1990-2019
climatology). Reference forecasts on the same cases: persistence, climatology, and the published forecasts of
IFS HRES, Pangu-Weather, Keisler's GNN and NeuralGCM (WeatherBench2, 64 x 32 grid).

Horizons:

* ``useful``: first lead at which the ACC falls below 0.6, the usual limit of a useful synoptic forecast;
* ``no_skill``: first lead at which the RMSE reaches that of climatology (the forecast no longer adds anything);
* ``per forecast``: an ensemble (perturbed initial states) gives the spread at every lead; the spread at which,
  on average, the ACC crosses 0.6 is measured on validation forecasts, and each new forecast reports the lead at
  which its own spread reaches it: a flow-dependent horizon, known before the truth arrives.

pinneapple_physics.weather.model.doc:
Global forecast network on an equiangular latitude-longitude grid.

A U-Net whose convolutions see the sphere: longitude is periodic (circular padding), and the rows padded beyond a
pole are the rows on the other side of that pole, shifted by half the circle (what a stencil crossing the pole
actually touches). The network maps the state at t and t - 6 h, the fixed fields (land-sea mask, orography) and the
forcing (top-of-atmosphere sunlight at t and t + 6 h, latitude, longitude) to the 6-hour change of the state.
Longer forecasts are made by feeding predictions back (autoregressive rollout); training continues on rollouts of
several steps so that errors made by the network itself are part of what it learns to correct.

Training of the global forecast network: one 6-hour step first, then rollouts of growing length.

Loss: mean squared error of the normalised state, weighted by the area of each grid cell (cosine of latitude) and
by channel (geopotential and temperature at 500/850 hPa and the surface fields count more: they are what forecasts
are judged on). Mixed precision bf16 on CPUs with AMX/AVX-512 bf16, fp32 elsewhere. Checkpoints keep the best model
on the validation years (2-day rollout error).

pinneapple_presets.doc:
Industrial presets: engineering problems already set up, solved and validated with PINNeAPPle.

    import pinneapple as pp
    pp.presets.names()                                   # catalogue
    p = pp.presets.load("water_hammer_valve_closure")
    p.card()                                             # data sheet: inputs (SI, defaults with sources), outputs
    r = p.run(t_close=4.0)                               # solver; fidelity="surrogate" for the trained surrogate
    print(r)                                             # outputs, decision, trust report

pinneapple_problemdesign.autonomy.doc:
Autonomy safety-boundary gate for the autonomous physics research loop.

This module is the **non-negotiable safety floor** for the autonomous
research loop being built on top of :class:`~.unified_agent.UnifiedPhysicsAgent`
and ``run_agent_loop`` elsewhere in this repo. The research loop is meant to
run many iterations *without* a human approving every step -- that is the
whole point of "autonomous". But some actions cross outside pure sandboxed
simulation/computation/validation: they cost real money, invoke a licensed
external tool per-run, or would affect something outside this repo's
sandbox (an external service, an account, a filesystem/network resource
that isn't just "read a local input, write a local output"). Those actions
-- which this module calls *consequential* -- always require an explicit
human approval gate, **regardless of how autonomous the loop is otherwise
configured to be.**

This is by design, not a bug or a temporary limitation. ``FULL_AUTONOMOUS``
means "don't bother a human about ordinary simulation/compute steps" -- it
does not, and must never, mean "don't bother a human before spending money
or invoking a licensed external solver." See
:class:`ConsequentialActionClassifier` and :class:`ApprovalGate` below --
:meth:`ApprovalGate.check` enforces this floor unconditionally at every
autonomy level, and it *fails closed*: if no human approver is wired up
and human approval is required, the action is **not** approved.

Recommend a numerical method + turbulence closure from a computed flow regime.

Three real pieces already exist in this repo but nothing connects them:

  * :func:`pinneapple_analysis.verification.dimensional_analysis.classify_flow_regime`
    computes Reynolds number from physical parameters and classifies the flow
    as laminar/transitional/turbulent (geometry-aware: internal pipe flow vs.
    external bluff-body flow have different transition thresholds).
  * :class:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.registry.SolverRegistry`
    holds the real, buildable numerical PDE solvers (``lbm``, ``fem``,
    ``fvm``, ``fdm``, ``spectral``, ``sph``, ...).
  * :func:`pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.turbulence_selector.get_turbulence_closure`
    builds/validates a real turbulence closure once a
    :class:`~pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.turbulence_selector.TurbulenceModel`
    has already been chosen.

This module is the missing "given these problem characteristics, here's the
recommended numerical approach" step: it calls the real ``classify_flow_regime``
to get a regime, applies a small explicit decision table to pick a real,
registered solver name, and (where turbulence closure is relevant) calls the
real ``get_turbulence_closure`` to validate the recommended
``TurbulenceModel`` is actually constructible for that solver family.

LLM-assisted preset *drafting*, gated by a real, automatically-generated
self-consistency check -- not a preset *authoring pipeline* in the sense of
producing something trusted for production use.

Why this module exists
-----------------------
Every physics domain PINNeAPPle can currently solve needs a human to
hand-author a preset in ``pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets``
ahead of time. Full automatic physics discovery (an LLM correctly inventing
a governing equation for a genuinely new phenomenon, unaided) is a real,
open research problem and is explicitly *out of scope* here. What this
module does instead is the safe half of that idea:

1. Ask an LLM to *propose* a governing PDE (plus BCs/ICs) for a plain-
   English phenomenon description, grounded in real, citable equations
   already in this repo's knowledge base
   (``pinneapple_problemdesign.knowledge.physics_knowledge``) wherever a
   relevant entry exists.

   parse), compile it with the real symbolic-PDE machinery

   manufactured-solutions (MMS) check against it -- the exact technique
   ``tests/test_manufactured_solutions.py`` uses for this repo's real,
   human-authored presets: plug a known closed-form exact solution into
   the compiled residual (using real autograd derivatives) and confirm

pinneapple_problemdesign.research_loop.doc:
``AutonomousResearchAgent``: the autonomous research cycle on top of
``UnifiedPhysicsAgent``.

This closes the loop the rest of this package's pieces were built for,
composing them exactly as designed -- none of their internals are touched:

* :class:`~.unified_agent.UnifiedPhysicsAgent` -- plain-English problem
  description -> real elicitation -> real ``PhysicsOrchestrator`` execution.
* :class:`~.autonomy.ApprovalGate` -- the non-negotiable safety floor.
  Every iteration's dispatch is gated through it before the loop is allowed
  to actually run the orchestrator, AND (via ``PhysicsOrchestrator``'s real,
  additive ``tool_gate`` hook -- see below) every *individual* tool the
  orchestrator selects and runs internally is gated through the same
  ``ApprovalGate`` too, not just the loop's own per-iteration dispatch.
* :class:`pinneapple_registry.experiment_memory.ExperimentMemory` --
  persistent cross-run memory: each attempt is logged, and prior similar
  attempts (successes AND failures) are consulted before a new one starts.
* :func:`pinneapple_analysis.verification.physics_confidence_score.compute_physics_confidence`
  and :class:`pinneapple_llm.guardrail.PhysicsGuardrail` -- real,
  already-executed-check-based validation of what the loop just produced,
  used to decide "good enough, stop" vs. "keep going."

The cycle, per iteration
-------------------------
::

    query memory for similar past attempts (iteration 0 only)
        -> gate this iteration's dispatch …

pinneapple_problemdesign.unified_agent.doc:
Compose ``DesignAgent`` and ``PhysicsOrchestrator`` into one working loop.

This repo has two independent, real, separately-tested agent/orchestration
systems:

* :class:`pinneapple_problemdesign.agent.DesignAgent` — natural-language
  problem *elicitation*. It is staged via :class:`~.state.DesignState`
  and produces a :class:`~.schema.DesignReport` (spec + gaps + plan) once
  enough information has been gathered.
* :class:`pinneapple_worldmodel.orchestrator.PhysicsOrchestrator` — given a
  :class:`~pinneapple_worldmodel.orchestrator.ProblemStatement`, selects and
  *executes* real tools from
  :class:`~pinneapple_worldmodel.physics_tools.PhysicsToolRegistry` to
  actually accomplish a physics goal.

Design decision: composition, not a class-hierarchy merge
-----------------------------------------------------------
Both systems are live and used elsewhere in this repo (``DesignAgent`` by
the problem-design CLI/examples, ``PhysicsOrchestrator`` directly by
downstream physics workflows). Rewriting their internals into one merged
class hierarchy would risk breaking either system for its existing callers,
for a purely cosmetic gain. ``pinneapple_problemdesign.knowledge.mapping``
already established the pattern this module follows: reach into the other
system read-only/compositionally, never edit it, never assume it must be
present.

existing *read-only* bridge (which only lists tool *names* inside a …

pinneapple_quantum.doc:
pinneapple_quantum — PINNeAPPle Quantum Module (PQM).

Official extension for hybrid classical–quantum physics-informed machine
learning. Combines variational quantum circuits (VQCs) with PDE-constrained
loss functions to solve quantum mechanical problems on both simulators and
real quantum hardware.

Supported workflows
-------------------
VQ-PINN (Variational Quantum PINN)
    Variational quantum circuit as wavefunction ansatz ψ(x).
    Physics loss = Rayleigh quotient ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩ / ⟨ψ|ψ⟩ (VQE objective).
    Solves: Schrödinger equation (1D / 2D), ground state + excited states.

Hybrid PINN
    Classical neural network pre-encodes features → quantum circuit.
    Useful for multi-scale / high-dimensional problems.

Hamiltonian Learning
    Discover the Hamiltonian operator from energy measurement data.

Quantum Kernel PINN
    Quantum-enhanced feature map K(xᵢ, xⱼ) = |⟨φ(xᵢ)|φ(xⱼ)⟩|² for
    kernel-based surrogate modelling.

Backend support
---------------
PennyLane   — CPU/GPU simulators, parameter-shift gradients, real QPUs.
Qiskit/Aer  — Aer statevector / QASM simulators.
Classical   — Built-in PyTorch state-vector simulation (no quantum deps).

The module falls back automatically to the classical engine if PennyLane or
Qiskit are not installed, so the full API is always available.

Quick start
-----------
>>> import pinneapple_quantum as pqm

>>> # Circuit and model
>>> cfg = pqm.QuantumCircuitConfig(n_qubits=4, depth=3)
>>> model = pqm.QuantumModel(cfg)

>>> # Physics …

pinneapple_query.doc:
Physics Query Engine: ask a physical quantity at a stable physical reference, under conditions, to an accuracy;
get the value with its unit, uncertainty, validity domain, provenance and the method that produced it, and whether it
was *read* from a solved state or *predicted* for an unsolved one.

    from pinneapple_condense.query import package_engine
    engine, model = package_engine(pkg)
    a = engine.query("T", "die@0.3,0.7", conditions={"power": P}, accuracy=0.1)
    a.value, a.unit, a.uncertainty, a.kind, a.method

Generic parts here (:mod:`.core`: query, offers, planner, answers; :mod:`.refs`: physical references); the methods of
a given physics live with it (chip package: :mod:`pinneapple_condense.query`).
pinneapple_query.doc1: Physics Query Engine: ask a physical quantity at a stable physical reference, under conditions, to an accuracy; get the value with its unit, uncertainty, validity domain, provenance and the method that produced it, and whether it was *read* from a solved state or *predicted* for an unsolved one.

pinneapple_query.core.doc:
The physics query engine: ask for one quantity, at one physical place, under given conditions, to a stated
accuracy, and get the value with its uncertainty, validity, provenance and the method that produced it.

    engine.query("T", "die@0.31,0.72", conditions={"power": P}, accuracy=0.05)

Two kinds of answer are kept apart (:attr:`Answer.kind`):

* ``"read"``: the conditions were already solved; the value is read from that state (interpolation error only).
* ``"predicted"``: nothing was solved for these conditions; the value is computed from other states or a model
  (superposition of solved states, a bound, a condensed or learned model) or by a new solve (``"solved"``).

A :class:`Planner` asks every registered :class:`Method` for an *offer* (can it answer, at what expected cost, with
what error bound, inside its validity domain) and takes the cheapest offer whose bound meets the accuracy target; if
none does, the last-resort method (a full solve) answers. Every answer records the offers it chose from.
pinneapple_query.core.doc1: The physics query engine: ask for one quantity, at one physical place, under given conditions, to a stated accuracy, and get the value with its uncertainty, validity, provenance and the method that produced it.

pinneapple_reason.doc:
pinneapple_reason: the chain of whys of an engineering design, computed.

Why does a roof slope? Because flat tiles let the rain through the laps: capillarity, wind and the ponded storm push
water higher than a flat lap rises. Why a ceiling? Because on a clear night the tile radiates to the sky and its
underside drops below the dew point of the room air. This package makes that reasoning explicit and quantitative for
any project:

    requirement -> naive concept -> physical check (numbers) -> failure mode found (mechanism + the number that
    proves it) -> countermeasure (new element, with cost and expected effect) -> check again -> ... -> all pass

    from pinneapple_reason import reason, cases, write_report
    chain = reason(*cases.roof())
    print(chain.explain())                          # version 0 -> version N, and why
    write_report(chain, "roof_report")              # chain.json, report.md / .html, timeline and margin figures

Parts: :mod:`.chain` (data model), :mod:`.library` and :mod:`.modes` (failure modes and countermeasures by physical
domain), :mod:`.engine` (the loop), :mod:`.trust` (trust report and six-stage card), :mod:`.report`, :mod:`.cases`,
:mod:`.llm` (an LLM may propose candidates; it never supplies a number).

pinneapple_reason.cases.doc:
Worked cases at different scales and in different fields, each starting from the naive concept.

* :func:`roof`: flat tiles -> pitch (rain through the laps) -> ceiling with a ventilated attic (condensation on a clear
  night) -> what the warm ceiling still needs (radiant heat on a sunny day).
* :func:`footbridge`: girders sized for strength only -> deeper girders (deflection) -> lateral bracing
  (lateral-torsional buckling) -> tuned mass damper or stiffer girders (resonance with footfall).
* :func:`power_board`: a MOSFET on a bare board -> heat sink (Joule heating, natural convection) -> forced air.
* :func:`pumped_main`: pump above the sump and a fast-closing valve on the main -> lower pump (cavitation) -> slow
  closure (water hammer, column separation).

Every value of a case is a premise (written in ``Concept.sources``) or a cited standard value; the results are what
the failure modes compute. No client data.

The chain of whys: requirement -> naive concept -> physical check -> failure found -> countermeasure -> check ...

Every object here is plain data (``to_dict`` / ``from_dict`` round-trip through JSON) so a chain can be saved, sent to
an agent, drawn in the Flow Studio and re-read later. Nothing in this module computes physics: the numbers in a
:class:`Verification` come from a failure mode of :mod:`pinneapple_reason.library`, and the engine
(:mod:`pinneapple_reason.engine`) is the only thing that builds a :class:`Chain`.

Text meant for people is stored in both languages as ``{"pt": ..., "en": ...}`` (see :func:`tr`).

pinneapple_reason.engine.doc:
The reasoning engine: check every requirement, find the first failure, try the countermeasures, keep the best,
check again, until every requirement passes.

    from pinneapple_reason import reason, cases
    chain = reason(*cases.roof())            # requirements, naive concept, title
    print(chain.explain())                   # version 0 -> version N, and why

At each step the engine

1. runs every failure mode of every requirement on the current concept (in the order the requirements and their
   modes are given) and takes the **first** one that fails;
2. applies each countermeasure the library has for that mode (plus any an advisor proposes) to a copy of the concept,
   and re-runs **every** check on the copy: which requirement each option fixes or breaks, the target margin before and
   after, and what it costs;
3. keeps the cheapest option that fixes the failure without breaking anything that passed (among options within 1 %
   of the lowest cost: the one leaving most checks passing, then the largest margin); if none fixes it alone, the one that improves the target margin most (then the cheapest),
   and goes on; an option that brings back an earlier version is refused (no cycles).

An advisor (an LLM through :class:`pinneapple_reason.llm.LLMAdvisor`) may add candidate countermeasures from the
library; it never supplies a number: every margin, cost and mechanism comes from the checks.

pinneapple_reason.library.doc:
The library of failure modes and countermeasures, by physical domain.

A :class:`FailureMode` is a quantitative check: given the parameters of a concept it computes the demand and the
capacity that decide whether the mode occurs, every intermediate number, the mechanism in words built from those
numbers, the applicability range of the models it used and its own internal checks. A :class:`Countermeasure` is a
change to the concept (a new element, a resized parameter) that acts on the mechanism of one or more modes; it
declares its expected physical effect and computes its cost from the change it made.

New domains plug in with :func:`register_mode` / :func:`register_countermeasure` (or the ``@mode`` /
``@countermeasure`` decorators); the built-in ones live in :mod:`pinneapple_reason.modes`.

Costs are ``quantity x unit cost``: the quantity (extra area, steel mass, fan power, ...) is computed from the change;
the unit cost is a relative index declared by the countermeasure as a premise (adjustable per case through the
concept parameter ``cost.<countermeasure>``). The engine only compares costs of options for the same finding.

pinneapple_reason.llm.doc:
An LLM as an advisor of the reasoning: it may propose candidate countermeasures and a first concept, never a number
that decides anything.

``LLMAdvisor`` wraps any object with ``extract(text, schema) -> dict`` (the
:class:`pinneapple_design.intent.IntentLLM` protocol; :class:`pinneapple_design.intent.CallLLM` reaches Anthropic,
OpenAI or a local Ollama model through :func:`pinneapple_llm.call_llm`). What it returns is filtered:

* countermeasures: only names that exist in the library are kept; the engine applies them and computes their effect,
  cost and side effects like any other option (the option records ``proposed_by="llm"``);
* concept parameters: only parameters some failure mode of the requirements declares (``Need``) are kept, each
  marked ``"llm proposal (premise)"`` in ``Concept.sources`` so the report shows where it came from.

Without an LLM nothing changes: the library's own countermeasures are always tried.

pinneapple_reason.modes.corrosion.doc:
Corrosion: galvanic coupling of two metals in an aerated electrolyte.

When a less noble metal (anode) is connected to a more noble one (cathode) in water, the cathode reaction in aerated
near-neutral water is oxygen reduction, usually limited by oxygen diffusion: ``i_lim = n F D C / delta`` with n = 4
(Jones, *Principles and Prevention of Corrosion*, 2nd ed., 1996, ch. 3 and 6). The anode supplies that whole current
over its own area, so its dissolution current density is ``i_a = i_lim A_c / A_a`` and its wall loss rate follows
Faraday's law ``CR = i_a M / (z F rho)``. A small anode next to a large cathode corrodes fast; the classic remedies
are to break the electrical path (insulating kit) or to coat the cathode (never only the anode).
pinneapple_reason.modes.corrosion.doc1: Corrosion: galvanic coupling of two metals in an aerated electrolyte.

functions.name: faraday_rate
functions.doc1: Uniform wall-loss rate (m/s) of ``metal`` dissolving at current density ``i`` (A/m^2).

pinneapple_reason.modes.fluids.doc:
Liquids in pipes: pump cavitation (NPSH), water hammer on valve closure, column separation.

* ``pump_cavitation``: net positive suction head available, ``NPSH_a = (p_atm - p_v)/(rho g) - z_s - h_f``, with the
  suction friction from the Colebrook friction factor (:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.pipe_flow`) plus minor
  losses, against the pump's required NPSH plus a margin (Karassik et al., *Pump Handbook*, 4th ed., ch. 2).
* ``water_hammer`` and ``column_separation``: transient after the valve at the end of a main closes, by the method of
  characteristics (:func:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.water_hammer_moc.valve_closure_moc`), wave speed
  from Korteweg's formula; Joukowsky and Michaud as the closed-form references.
pinneapple_reason.modes.fluids.doc1: Liquids in pipes: pump cavitation (NPSH), water hammer on valve closure, column separation.

pinneapple_reason.modes.structural.doc:
Structures: bending strength, deflection, lateral-torsional buckling and pedestrian-induced resonance of steel
girders; flexural buckling of a column; fatigue (Basquin); wind uplift of a roof covering.

Girders are doubly symmetric I-sections (``h``, ``b``, ``t_f``, ``t_w``), simply supported over ``span``, sharing the
deck load equally (``n_girders``). Section properties are computed from the plates (thin-walled formulas for ``J`` and
``I_w``). Steel constants from EN 1993-1-1, 3.2.6; partial factors EN 1990 Table A1.2(B) (1.35 / 1.5) and
EN 1993-1-1 6.1 (gamma_M0 = gamma_M1 = 1.0); footbridge live load from EN 1991-2, 5.3.2.1.
pinneapple_reason.modes.structural.doc1: Structures: bending strength, deflection, lateral-torsional buckling and pedestrian-induced resonance of steel girders; flexural buckling of a column; fatigue (Basquin); wind uplift of a roof covering.

pinneapple_reason.modes.thermal.doc:
Heat: condensation under a roof on a clear night, radiant heat from a sun-baked roof, Joule heating of a power
device.

Roof (``roof_network``): a steady one-dimensional network per m^2 of roof. Outer tile surface: absorbed sun, long-wave
exchange with the clear sky (Swinbank sky temperature), wind convection (Watmuff et al.). Tile: conduction. Without a
ceiling the tile underside faces the room; with a ceiling and a ventilated attic: tile underside <-> ceiling top by
radiation (parallel grey plates), both to the attic air by convection, attic air to outside by ventilation, ceiling
by conduction, ceiling underside to the room. Surface coefficients by heat-flow direction from ISO 6946 Annex C
(``h = h_c + eps 4 sigma T_m^3``). The nonlinear system is solved with ``scipy.optimize.fsolve``; the global energy
balance closes to round-off and is reported as a self-check.

Joule heating (``joule_heating``): conduction loss of a MOSFET, ``P = I^2 R_on(T_j)`` with
``R_on = R_25 (1 + a (T_j - 25))``, coupled to the thermal path until ``T_j`` is consistent (electrothermal fixed
point; the loop gain ``a I^2 R_25 R_th`` >= 1 means thermal runaway). Thermal paths: the board (3-D finite-volume
board model :mod:`pinneapple_physics.pcb`), or a plate-fin heat sink in natural or forced convection
(:mod:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.plate_fin_heatsink`).
pinneapple_reason.modes.thermal.doc1: Heat: condensation under a roof on a clear night, radiant heat from a sun-baked roof, Joule heating of a power device.

pinneapple_reason.modes.water.doc:
Water: rain getting through the laps of a roof covering (capillarity, wind pressure, ponding / falling film).

Lapped coverings (tiles, corrugated sheets) are not watertight joints: they are hydraulic barriers. Water reaches the
joint and three heads push it up the lap (Garden 1963 lists the forces that move rain through a joint: gravity,
kinetic energy, surface tension, air pressure difference):

* capillary rise in the gap ``w`` between the overlapping pieces, ``h_c = 2 sigma cos(theta) / (rho g w)`` (two
  parallel plates; de Gennes, Brochard-Wyart & Quere, *Capillarity and Wetting Phenomena*, 2004, ch. 1);
* the wind pressure across the covering during the storm, ``h_w = Cp 1/2 rho_air V^2 / (rho g)``;
* the water depth over the joint: on a slope the rain runs off as a laminar falling film,
  ``delta = (3 nu q / (g sin(alpha)))^(1/3)`` with ``q = i L`` per unit width (Nusselt film; Bird, Stewart &
  Lightfoot, *Transport Phenomena*, sec. 2.2); on a flat roof nothing drives the water off and the design storm
  ponds: ``h = i t``.

The lap resists with the height it rises: ``L_lap sin(alpha)``. The covering leaks when the heads exceed it.
pinneapple_reason.modes.water.doc1: Water: rain getting through the laps of a roof covering (capillarity, wind pressure, ponding / falling film).

pinneapple_registry.doc:
pinneapple_registry — a local, self-hosted artifact registry: versioned
model storage, dataset storage, experiment tracking, and problem-spec
history, plus Triton Inference Server export.

Why this exists alongside ``pinneapple_hub``: ``pinneapple_hub`` publishes
a *finished* model to the Hugging Face Hub (external storage, network +
auth required, one artifact type). Day-to-day work needs something that
runs entirely offline, versions every intermediate checkpoint (not just
the one you choose to publish), tracks datasets and experiment runs next
to those models, and can hand a model straight to a local Triton
Inference Server — none of which ``pinneapple_hub`` does or is meant to
do. The two are complementary: a model developed and versioned here can
still be pushed to the Hub via ``pinneapple_hub.push_to_hub`` once it's
ready to share.

    from pinneapple_registry import ArtifactRegistry

    registry = ArtifactRegistry("./my_registry")
    registry.models.save("pipe_flow", trained_pipe_model, metadata={"metrics": {"rmse": 0.02}})
    registry.models.promote("pipe_flow", registry.models.latest("pipe_flow"), "production")
    run_id = registry.experiments.start_run("pipe_flow")
    registry.experiments.log_metrics(run_id, {"val_loss": 0.01}, step=10)
pinneapple_registry.doc1: pinneapple_registry — a local, self-hosted artifact registry: versioned model storage, dataset storage, experiment tracking, and problem-spec history, plus Triton Inference Server export.

pinneapple_registry.dataset_store.doc:
pinneapple_registry.dataset_store — ``DatasetStore``: local, per-
problem/scenario storage for simulation datasets (coords + field arrays),
with auto-computed summary statistics.

Not a replacement for ``pinneapple_data``'s Zarr-sharded UPD pipeline
(that is the right tool for large, shardable, streaming datasets) — this
is the lightweight complement for "one simulation run's worth of arrays,
versioned by problem+scenario", the shape ``pinneapple_registry``'s other
stores (model/experiment) already assume.
pinneapple_registry.dataset_store.doc1: pinneapple_registry.dataset_store — ``DatasetStore``: local, per- problem/scenario storage for simulation datasets (coords + field arrays), with auto-computed summary statistics.

pinneapple_registry.experiment_memory.doc:
pinneapple_registry.experiment_memory -- ``ExperimentMemory``: persistent
cross-run memory for an (separately built, not part of this repo) autonomous
research loop.

Why this exists: a research loop that starts every new run from zero re-tries
approaches that already failed, and re-discovers lessons that a previous run
already learned. This module gives such a loop a place to ask, before it
commits compute to a new attempt, "has something like this been tried
before, and what happened?" -- by logging every attempt as a durable
``ExperimentRecord`` and letting later runs query for similar past attempts
and their outcomes/lessons.

This module does not implement its own storage. ``ExperimentMemory`` is a
thin layer on top of the real ``pinneapple_registry.experiment_store
.ExperimentStore`` (a SQLite-backed run tracker): every ``ExperimentRecord``
is logged via ``ExperimentStore.start_run``/``log_metrics``/``finish_run``
and read back via ``ExperimentStore.list_runs``, exactly the same durable
on-disk store the rest of ``pinneapple_registry`` already uses. The only
extra thing this module does beyond calling that real API is (a) pack the
free-text/record fields that ``ExperimentStore`` has no dedicated columns
for into the ``final_metrics`` JSON blob it already stores per-run, and (b)
a small read-only ``SELECT DISTINCT problem_id FROM experiments`` against
the store's own schema, needed because ``ExperimentStore`` has no
"list every problem_id it has ever seen" method -- …
pinneapple_registry.experiment_memory.doc1: pinneapple_registry.experiment_memory -- ``ExperimentMemory``: persistent cross-run memory for an (separately built, not part of this repo) autonomous research loop.

Deliberately minimal — a run tracker, not a full experiment-management

pinneapple_registry.gateway.doc:
``ModelGateway``: publish physical models as versioned endpoints, run them, and record every run.

Built on ``ModelStore`` (versions ``vYYYYMMDD_HHMMSS``, ``latest``, stages, the REJECT-blocks-publication rule).
A published version is a directory with ``metadata.json`` (ModelStore's) and the model files; three kinds of
model are served through one ``predict``:

``pinneapple.surrogate``  a ``pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.SurrogateModel`` (Surrogate Studio, the arena), with its
                          OOD gate (training range + nearest-neighbour distance);
``pinneapple.zoo``        a pre-trained zoo model (``pp.zoo``), with the validity box of its model card;
``onnx``                  an ONNX graph (``inputs (n, d) -> outputs (n, p)``) with declared input / output names and
                          validity bounds, run with onnxruntime;
``remote``                a model served by another app with this API (``https://host/v1/models/<name>``, e.g. the
                          Surrogate Studio): this gateway enforces its validity bounds and OOD policy, logs and meters
                          the call, and forwards the rows it accepts (``GatewayClient``).

``publish_ref`` publishes from a ``ModelRef`` (``pinneapple_data.contracts``): ``zoo:<name>`` or an http(s) gateway
URI; its input ranges become the validity bounds. Publishing a remote model makes this server call that URL: let only
trusted callers publish.

Each version has an ``ood_policy``: ``"warn"`` (predict and …

pinneapple_registry.gateway_api.doc:
The gateway's REST shape (FastAPI), shared by every app that serves models: ``/v1/models/...``.

==========================================================  ==========================================================
``GET  /v1/models``                                          published models: latest version, kind, method, trust
``GET  /v1/models/{name}``                                   the latest version's metadata, ModelRef fields, versions
``GET  /v1/models/{name}/versions/{version}``                one version (``latest``, a stage name or ``v...``)
``POST /v1/models/{name}/predict``                           ``{"inputs": ..., "version"?, "ood_policy"?}``
``POST /v1/models/{name}/versions/{version}/predict``        the same, for one version
``GET  /v1/models/{name}/runs?limit=``                       the run log of the model, newest first
``GET  /v1/metrics?model=``                                  calls, rows, errors, OOD rows, latency p50 / p95
``GET  /v1/models/{name}/versions/{version}/export/{fmt}``   ``torchscript`` or ``onnx`` (PyTorch surrogates, ONNX)
==========================================================  ==========================================================

``inputs`` is ``{input: value or list}``, a list of row objects, or a list of rows in the model's input order.
``on_rows(request, n)`` runs before a prediction (metering: raise to refuse); ``caller(request)`` names the caller
in the run log. (No ``from __future__ import annotations`` here: …

pinneapple_registry.gateway_client.doc:
``GatewayClient``: call any server that exposes the gateway API (``/v1/models/...``) from Python.

Standard library only (``urllib``), so it runs wherever PINNeAPPle does::

    from pinneapple_registry.gateway_client import GatewayClient

    gw = GatewayClient("https://models.pinneapple.org", api_key="...")
    print(gw.models())
    r = gw.predict("zoo-airfoil-cst-rans", {"T0": 0.15, ..., "alpha_deg": [2, 4]})
    print(r["outputs"]["Cl"], r["ood"])

Errors from the server raise ``GatewayError`` with the HTTP status and the server's message.

pinneapple_registry.problem_store.doc:
pinneapple_registry.problem_store — ``ProblemStore``: versioned problem
definitions with history.

Two save paths, because a ``ProblemSpec`` cannot always be losslessly
round-tripped through JSON:

- :meth:`save_from_preset` — the RELIABLY reconstructable path. Presets
  are deterministic (``get_preset(preset_id, **kwargs)``), so this just
  records ``(preset_id, kwargs)`` and :meth:`load` calls ``get_preset``
  again rather than trying to serialize/deserialize ``ProblemSpec``'s
  nested dataclasses.
- :meth:`save_snapshot` — records ``dataclasses.asdict(spec)`` (or any
  plain dict) for history/inspection. This is explicitly NOT guaranteed
  round-trippable back into a live ``ProblemSpec``; :meth:`load_snapshot`
  returns the plain dict, not a reconstructed object.

``examples/vs_physicsnemo`` comparison notes — this closes that gap for

pinneapple_science.doc:
PINNeAPPle science (``pp.science``): experiments by area of science, at academic and research level, theory
and practice (a virtual bench), in 0-D (lumped), 1-D, 2-D, 3-D and 3-D + time; and the atlas of every area.

    import pinneapple as pp
    pp.science.atlas()                                  # every area: available / partial / planned, with pointers
    pp.science.experiments(area="electromagnetism", dim="3D+t")
    r = pp.science.run("em.faraday_induction")          # a magnet falling through a loop, 3-D in time
    print(r)                                            # computed vs reference, physics checks, trust decision
    r.save("out/faraday")                               # result.json, figures, the animation

Every experiment declares its area, level (``academic`` / ``research``), kind (``theory`` / ``practice``) and
dimensions, and every result carries comparisons with cited references, physics checks and a trust report
(:class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`). Committed results, Lab manifests and seals:
``python -m pinneapple_science report all`` (:mod:`.report`). The atlas is data
(``pinneapple_science/data/atlas.json``) and points to the code that already covers each area elsewhere in the
library; electromagnetism is built on ``pp.em`` and ``pp.maxwell``. See docs/guides/science.md.
pinneapple_science.doc1: PINNeAPPle science (``pp.science``): experiments by area of science, at academic and research level, theory and practice (a virtual bench), in 0-D (lumped), 1-D, 2-D, 3-D and 3-D + time; and the atlas of every area.

pinneapple_science.atlas.doc:
The atlas of science areas: what :mod:`pinneapple_science` covers, what the rest of the library already covers,
and what is planned.

The atlas is data (``pinneapple_science/data/atlas.json``, schema ``pinneapple.science.atlas/1``, versioned with
the package): areas, subareas, a status per subarea (``available``, ``partial``, ``planned``) and pointers to the
code that covers them -- a ``pp.science`` experiment, a library module, a problem preset
(``pp.list_presets()``) or a Lab experiment (``pinneapple_lab.available()``). The atlas points to existing code and
never copies it. :func:`validate` checks every pointer against the repository (without importing the modules) and
every registered experiment against the atlas, so the page cannot drift from the code.

    import pinneapple as pp
    a = pp.science.atlas()
    print(a)                       # one line per area with its status and counts
    a.rows()                       # one dict per subarea (area, subarea, status, pointers)
    a.to_markdown()                # the table of docs/guides/science.md
    a.to_html("atlas.html")        # a single-file page with search and filters

pinneapple_science.core.doc:
The common shape of a science experiment: what it declares, what every run returns.

An experiment declares

* ``area``: an area id of the atlas (``"physics.electromagnetism"``), and the ``topic`` inside it;
* ``level``: ``"academic"`` (didactic, checked against a textbook value) or ``"research"`` (configurable, with a
  convergence check and an uncertainty);
* ``kind``: ``"theory"`` (a numerical or symbolic derivation checked against a closed form, a published value or a
  scaling law) or ``"practice"`` (a virtual bench: instruments with noise, a fit with its uncertainty);
* ``dims``: the dimensions it runs in, from ``"0D"`` (lumped elements: circuits, no spatial coordinate), ``"1D"``,
  ``"2D"``, ``"3D"`` and ``"3D+t"`` (three space dimensions and time, the fourth dimension).

``Experiment.run(dim=..., **params)`` returns a :class:`Result`: the measured values (each with its unit and how it
was measured), the comparisons with their references (computed, reference, relative error, tolerance, source),
the physics checks, the trust report (:class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`), the figures and the data
behind them. ``Result.save(folder)`` writes ``result.json`` and the figures; :func:`pinneapple_science.report.write`
adds the Lab manifest ``experiment.json`` and the seal.

Nothing in a result is typed in: every value is computed by the run, every reference carries its source.

pinneapple_science.em.bench.doc:
Bench experiments (practice): a virtual laboratory with instruments that add noise, calibration error and
resolution, a fit with its uncertainty, and the comparison with the value the bench was built with.

* :class:`Mu0Solenoid` -- measure mu0 from B(I) at the centre of a solenoid with a Hall probe and an ammeter
  (3-D field of the real helix, Earth's field as an offset), the dimensions read with a caliper.
* :class:`RCDischarge` -- measure a capacitance from the discharge of an RC circuit on an oscilloscope.

Each ends with a GUM uncertainty budget (type A from the fit, type B from the instrument specifications) and a
Monte Carlo of the whole bench (fresh instruments each time) that measures how often the stated expanded
uncertainty covers the true value: the uncertainty claim is itself checked.

                                               "eps_r": 4.0}]})
    out = run_fdtd(cfg, snapshots=24)
    out.power, out.pattern(theta), out.frames, out.checks

pinneapple_science.em.induction.doc:
Induction and circuits, academic level: Faraday's law with a magnet falling through a loop (3-D + time) and
the RC, RL and series RLC circuits (lumped, 0-D in space).

The falling magnet is a uniformly magnetised cylinder, i.e. a sheet of bound current ``K = M`` on its side
(Griffiths sec. 6.2), discretised into polygonal rings. At every time step the flux through the loop is the
circulation of their vector potential around the loop (Stokes: ``Phi = oint A . dl``, exact A of straight
filaments, ``pp.em.statics.vector_potential``), and the EMF is ``-dPhi/dt`` by central differences: a 3-D field,
in time; the animation shows B (``pp.em.statics.biot_savart``). The
reference is Maxwell's mutual-inductance formula of coaxial circles (``pp.em.statics.mutual_inductance_coaxial_loops``)
summed over the rings, and the kinematics of free fall.

pinneapple_science.instruments.doc:
Virtual laboratory instruments and the fits a bench experiment ends with.

An instrument reads a true value through what a real one adds: a gain error and an offset fixed for the
instrument (drawn once from its calibration uncertainty), random noise on every reading, and the resolution of its
display or converter. The bench knows only the specification (``noise``, ``gain_u``, ``offset_u``,
``resolution``), as on a data sheet, never the drawn errors, so the uncertainty it reports is the one a student or
a metrologist would compute (GUM type A from the scatter of the fit, type B from the specification).

    probe = FieldProbe(noise=2e-6, gain_u=0.005, offset_u=1e-6, resolution=1e-7, seed=1)
    ammeter = Ammeter(noise=1e-4, gain_u=0.002, resolution=1e-3, seed=2)
    B = probe.read(B_true)                     # one reading
    fit = linear_fit(I, B, sigma_y=probe.sigma(B))
    fit.slope, fit.slope_u                     # with the type-A standard uncertainty

References: JCGM 100:2008 (GUM), sec. 4.2-4.3 (type A and type B) and 5.1 (combined uncertainty); a uniform
distribution of half-width ``a`` (the resolution) has standard uncertainty ``a / sqrt(3)`` (GUM 4.3.7).

pinneapple_science.numerics.doc:
Small numerical building blocks shared by the experiments: graded tensor grids, a finite-volume solver for
``div(eps grad phi) = -rho`` in 1-D, 2-D and 3-D with fixed-potential nodes and mirror (symmetry) faces, the
discrete field energy, and a scalar Helmholtz eigen-solver for waveguide cross-sections.

The finite-volume scheme is the standard two-point flux on a tensor grid of nodes: the flux through the face
between nodes ``i`` and ``i+1`` is ``eps_face (phi_{i+1} - phi_i) / (x_{i+1} - x_i)`` times the face area (the
product of the dual widths along the other axes); ``eps_face`` is the harmonic mean of the two node values. It is
second-order accurate on smooth graded grids and conservative (Patankar, *Numerical Heat Transfer and Fluid
Flow*, 1980, ch. 4). The discrete energy ``1/2 sum eps_face (dphi)^2 A / dx`` equals ``1/2 Q V`` of the
discrete system, so capacitance from the energy converges like the solution. ``mean="arithmetic"`` with
``eps = r`` on an ``(r, z)`` grid gives the axisymmetric operator ``(1/r) d/dr (r dphi/dr) + d2phi/dz2`` (each
radial face weighted by its radius).

pinneapple_security.doc:
pinneapple_security — data and process security for scientific and industrial Physics AI.

What it covers, and where:

=====================  ==============================================================================================
``integrity``          SHA-256 of files, arrays and records; Merkle manifests of datasets and model folders
``signing``            Ed25519 / HMAC signatures, DSSE envelopes, detached file signatures
``attestation``        in-toto + SLSA provenance of runs and experiments; CycloneDX SBOM of the environment
``audit``              hash-chained, tamper-evident audit trail (ALCOA+ attributes)
``encryption``         AES-256-GCM at rest for bytes, files and arrays (scrypt key derivation)
``privacy``            PII detection (incl. CPF/CNPJ), redaction, keyed pseudonymisation, k-anonymity, log sanitising
``dp``                 differential privacy: Laplace/Gaussian mechanisms, DP statistics, RDP accountant, DP-SGD
``model_security``     pickle/checkpoint scanning, safe loading, adversarial sensitivity of surrogates
``anomaly``            physics-residual CUSUM and replay detection of manipulated sensor data (OT security)
``cps``                grey-box physics residuals (mass balances, flow laws) + CUSUM: false-data-injection detection
``cps_bench``          three-tank water-network benchmark: attacks, data-driven baselines, ROC/delay/false alarms
``secrets_scan``       credentials in code, notebooks, configs and solver cases
``classification``     …
pinneapple_security.doc1: pinneapple_security — data and process security for scientific and industrial Physics AI.

pinneapple_security.__main__.doc:
``python -m pinneapple_security <command>``: manifests, signatures, scans and log sanitising from the shell.

manifest DIR [-o manifest.json]          write the Merkle manifest of a folder
verify-manifest DIR manifest.json        compare a folder with its manifest (exit 1 if anything changed)
keygen KEYFILE [--hmac]                  new Ed25519 (or HMAC) key; prints the public key JSON

pinneapple_security.anomaly.doc:
Physics-based detection of manipulated sensor data (false data injection, spoofing, replay) in industrial streams.

An attacker who changes a sensor reading keeps it plausible on its own; what breaks is consistency with the physics
linking several measurements (mass and energy balances, a pump curve, a heat-exchanger model, a digital-twin
surrogate). The detector watches the *physics residual* r_t = measured − predicted (or a balance that should be zero):

1. :meth:`ResidualCUSUM.fit` learns the residual's normal mean and spread from trusted data;
2. two-sided CUSUM (Page 1954) accumulates standardised deviations beyond a slack ``k`` and raises an alarm when the
   sum crosses ``h`` — small persistent biases (a slow ramp attack) are caught, not only big jumps;
3. :func:`replay_score` flags a window that repeats an earlier window too exactly (a replayed recording has the
   same noise; a live sensor does not).

The defaults (k = 0.5, h = 5 in units of σ) give an in-control average run length of roughly 465 samples for a
standard normal residual (Montgomery, Introduction to Statistical Quality Control, Table 9.3; it varies with the
edition); tune ``h`` to the false-alarm rate the plant accepts.
pinneapple_security.anomaly.doc1: Physics-based detection of manipulated sensor data (false data injection, spoofing, replay) in industrial streams.

Provenance attestations (in-toto Statement v1 with a SLSA Provenance v1 predicate) and a CycloneDX SBOM.

An attestation answers "what produced this model / dataset / result, from what inputs, where": the *subjects* are the
artifacts with their digests, ``resolvedDependencies`` are the inputs (datasets, base checkpoints, the code commit),
``externalParameters`` is the run configuration and ``runDetails`` the builder (machine, library versions, times).
Signed with :func:`pinneapple_security.signing.sign_json`, it becomes evidence a third party can check without trusting
the person who trained the model.

The SBOM lists the installed Python distributions (name, version, purl, licence) in CycloneDX 1.5 JSON, the format
supply-chain scanners (Dependency-Track, Grype, Trivy) read.

pinneapple_security.audit.doc:
Tamper-evident audit trail: an append-only JSON-lines log where every record carries the hash of the previous one.

Editing, deleting or reordering any past record breaks the chain from that point, and :meth:`AuditLog.verify` reports
the first bad line. With a ``key`` the chain is an HMAC chain, so someone who can write the file but does not hold the
key can not rebuild a valid chain after tampering (without a key the log detects accidents and naive edits, not a
forger who recomputes every hash).

Each record holds the ALCOA+ attributes regulated research and industry ask of electronic records (attributable,
legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate): who (``actor``), what (``action`` + ``data``), when (UTC time), why
(``reason``), and on which object (``target``). This is a building block for 21 CFR Part 11 §11.10(e) style audit
trails, not a certified system by itself.
pinneapple_security.audit.doc1: Tamper-evident audit trail: an append-only JSON-lines log where every record carries the hash of the previous one.

pinneapple_security.classification.doc:
Data classification and handling policy for datasets, models and results.

Every artifact gets a :class:`DataLabel`: confidentiality level, owner, whether it holds personal data, export-control
status (e.g. an ECCN under the US EAR, or dual-use under EU Regulation 2021/821 — the label records what the owner
declared; it does not decide classification), licence and retention. :class:`HandlingPolicy` answers "may I do X with
this artifact?" for the actions that matter in research and industry (publish, share externally, train a model on it,
send to a cloud service, export to another country) and says why not. A model trained on several inputs inherits the
strictest label (:func:`combine`).

pinneapple_security.compliance.doc:
Which pinneapple_security capability produces evidence for which control of the frameworks industry and research
are audited against — and a self-assessment report from the evidence a project actually has.

This maps; it does not certify. A framework control is met by an organisation's processes; the library only provides
technical means and machine-checkable evidence (manifests, signatures, attestations, audit-log verification, scans).

Frameworks (identifiers as published): NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (functions GV, ID, PR, DE, RS, RC);
IEC 62443-3-3 foundational requirements FR1–FR7 (industrial automation and control systems); ISO/IEC 27001:2022
Annex A (selected controls); 21 CFR Part 11 (US FDA electronic records and signatures); LGPD (Lei 13.709/2018) and
GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679); NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF) and SLSA v1.0 for the software and model supply chain.

pinneapple_security.cps.doc:
Physics-residual detection of false data injection in cyber-physical systems (water, process, HVAC, grids).

An attacker who rewrites a sensor stream keeps every value plausible on its own and close to its own history, which
is what a purely data-driven detector learns. What the attacker cannot keep without a model of the plant is the
physics that ties several sensors together: tank levels must integrate the measured in- and outflows, a valve or
orifice passes ``q = sqrt(a + b * dh)`` for the head difference across it, a heat exchanger obeys its energy balance.
This module turns those laws into residual channels, identifies their constants from trusted data (grey-box twin, no
hand-tuned coefficients) and runs a two-sided CUSUM (Page 1954) per channel:

1. components (:class:`MassBalance`, :class:`FlowLaw`, or any object with ``fit(D)`` and ``residual(D)``) map a
   dict of sensor columns to one residual series each;
2. :class:`PhysicsResidualDetector` standardises each channel with robust statistics of trusted data, accumulates
   the deviations with a CUSUM and calibrates the alarm threshold to a target false-alarm rate on attack-free data;
3. :meth:`PhysicsResidualDetector.detect` reports alarms and the channel that raised them (which balance broke →
   where the manipulated sensor sits).

What it cannot see: an attacker who knows the plant model and injects physically consistent data (a coordinated
replay of every sensor, a stealthy attack in the sense of Liu, Ning & …
pinneapple_security.cps.doc1: Physics-residual detection of false data injection in cyber-physical systems (water, process, HVAC, grids).
