pinneapple_security.cps_bench.doc:
Open, reproducible benchmark for false-data-injection detection: a three-tank gravity water network.

Public ICS security datasets either need a signed request (SWaT, WADI) or are not reachable from every network, so
this module simulates a small plant whose physics is textbook and whose attacks are the ones reported in the
literature. Every number it produces can be regenerated from a seed.

Plant (SI units, one sample per minute)::

    reservoir --pump Fp--> T1 --valve F12--> T2 --valve F23--> T3 --demand Fd--> consumers

* tanks with floor elevations 3.0 / 1.5 / 0.0 m and areas 2.0 / 1.5 / 1.8 m^2;
* gravity valves ``q = c sqrt(head difference)``; the pump runs under on/off level control of T1 (1.0 to 2.5 m);
* demand: diurnal pattern x random daily factor x AR(1) fluctuation; it is throttled when T3 runs nearly empty;
* sensors: three levels (noise 3 mm) and four flow meters (noise 1.5 % of nominal), flows averaged over the minute.

Attacks (:func:`inject`) rewrite the *reported* readings in ``[start, start + length)``:

=====================  ===========================================================================================
``bias``               constant offset on the F12 flow meter (4 % of its mean, about 3 noise sigmas)
``ramp``               slow drift of the T2 level sensor, 0 → 8 cm over the episode
``stuck``              T3 level sensor frozen at its value at the onset
``delayed``            F23 replaced by its own reading 24 h earlier (plausible value, …

pinneapple_security.dp.doc:
Differential privacy: noise mechanisms, private statistics, a privacy accountant and DP-SGD for PyTorch models.

Use case in Physics AI: a surrogate or a digital twin trained on a client's proprietary operating data (or on several
clients' data) must not let anyone recover individual records from the published model. Differential privacy bounds
how much one record can change any output: (ε, δ)-DP.

* :func:`laplace_mechanism` (pure ε-DP) and :func:`gaussian_mechanism` ((ε, δ)-DP, classic calibration valid for ε ≤ 1).
* :func:`dp_mean` and :func:`dp_histogram` with clipping to known bounds (the bounds must not be computed from the data).
* :class:`RDPAccountant`: Rényi-DP accounting of the sampled Gaussian mechanism at integer orders (Mironov, Talwar &
  Zhang 2019, "Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism", arXiv:1908.10530), converted to (ε, δ).
* :class:`DPSGD`: per-sample gradient clipping and Gaussian noise (Abadi et al. 2016, "Deep Learning with Differential
  Privacy", arXiv:1607.00133) for any ``torch.nn.Module`` and per-sample loss, using ``torch.func``.

References for the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms: Dwork & Roth, "The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential
Privacy", 2014, §3.3 and Appendix A.

pinneapple_security.encryption.doc:
Encryption at rest: AES-256-GCM for bytes, files and arrays, with keys from a passphrase (scrypt) or random.

File format (``PPSEC1``): magic (6 bytes) | salt (16) | nonce (12) | ciphertext+tag. The header is authenticated as
associated data, so changing the salt, nonce or any byte of the ciphertext makes decryption fail instead of returning
corrupted data. GCM authenticates: a wrong key or tampered file raises, it never silently decrypts to garbage.

Needs the ``cryptography`` package (``pip install pinneapple[security]``); key derivation uses the standard library
(``hashlib.scrypt`` with n=2**15, r=8, p=1).

Integrity: content digests of files, arrays and records, and Merkle manifests of datasets and model folders.

A manifest lists every file of a folder with its SHA-256 and size, and a Merkle root over the sorted entries, so one

removed or changed. Arrays are hashed with their dtype and shape (two arrays with the same bytes but a different shape
are different data). Records (dicts) are hashed in canonical JSON (sorted keys, no whitespace).

pinneapple_security.model_security.doc:
Model security: scan checkpoints for code execution before loading, load safely, and measure adversarial
sensitivity of surrogates.

PyTorch ``.pt``/``.pth`` files (and plain pickles) can run arbitrary code when loaded: the pickle stream names Python
callables that are called during unpickling. :func:`scan_checkpoint` reads the pickle opcodes *without executing them*
and lists every global the file would import; anything outside the allow-list (tensor rebuilding, OrderedDict, NumPy
array reconstruction) is reported, and known-dangerous ones (``os``, ``subprocess``, ``builtins.eval``...) make the file
unsafe. :func:`safe_load` refuses unsafe files and loads the rest with ``torch.load(weights_only=True)``.

:func:`adversarial_sensitivity` runs a projected-gradient (PGD, Madry et al. 2018, arXiv:1706.06083) search for the
input perturbation of size ``eps`` (relative to each input's range) that moves a surrogate's output the most: a large
change from a small, physically plausible perturbation means a noisy or manipulated sensor can steer the model.

installed, and verification of bcrypt hashes (``$2b$...``, as written by ``caddy hash-password`` or ``htpasswd -B``)
when ``bcrypt`` is installed.

A stored hash is self-describing, so the scheme can change without a migration:

==================================  ======================================================================
``$scrypt$n=16384,r=8,p=1$<salt>$<key>``  :func:`hashlib.scrypt`, salt and key in URL-safe base64 (no padding)
``$argon2id$v=19$m=...``            argon2-cffi ``PasswordHasher`` format
``$2a$`` / ``$2b$`` / ``$2y$``      bcrypt (verify only)
==================================  ======================================================================

``python -m pinneapple_security hash-password`` prints a hash for an environment variable such as
``HSS_PASSWORD_HASH`` (see ``apps/_shared/README.md``).

pinneapple_security.privacy.doc:
Personal and sensitive data in text and tables: detection, redaction, pseudonymisation, k-anonymity, log sanitising.

* :func:`find_pii` finds e-mails, phone numbers, IP addresses, payment card numbers (Luhn-checked), IBANs (mod-97
  checked) and the Brazilian CPF and CNPJ (check digits verified, so random 11/14-digit numbers are not flagged).
* :func:`redact` replaces each finding with a label; :func:`pseudonymize` replaces a value with a keyed token (HMAC):
  the same input always gives the same token, so joins still work, and without the key the token can not be reversed
  or recomputed by a dictionary attack.
* :func:`k_anonymity` measures the smallest group sharing the same quasi-identifiers (a table is k-anonymous when every
  row is indistinguishable from at least k-1 others on them) and lists the groups below ``k``.
* :func:`sanitize_log` removes from solver/training logs what identifies people and machines (user names in home
  paths, host names, e-mails, IPs) before a log is shared with a vendor, a client or a public issue.

Regex detection has false negatives (free-text names, addresses): it is a safety net, not a guarantee of anonymity.

Find credentials committed to code, notebooks, configs and solver cases before they are shared or published.

Detectors: known token formats (cloud, Git hosting, chat, payment and AI-API keys), private key blocks, connection
strings with an embedded password, ``password = "..."``-style assignments, and long high-entropy strings (Shannon

is never printed or returned in full.

pinneapple_security.signing.doc:
Signatures for artifacts and records: Ed25519 (public-key, needs ``cryptography``) or HMAC-SHA256 (shared key, stdlib).

Signed JSON uses the DSSE envelope (Dead Simple Signing Envelope, used by in-toto and Sigstore): the payload is signed
together with its type through the pre-authentication encoding ``PAE``, so a signature over one kind of document can
not be replayed as another. Every signature carries a ``keyid`` (SHA-256 of the public key, or of the HMAC key), so a
verifier knows which key to use and a wrong key fails instead of passing by accident.

>>> key = generate_key()                         # Ed25519 private key (keep it secret; give out key.public())
>>> env = sign_json({"model": "burgers_pinn", "sha256": "..."}, key)
>>> verify_json(env, key.public())               # the payload, or VerificationError

pinneapple_simulation.doc:
pinneapple_simulation — Physics simulation back-ends and data generation.

Sub-modules
-----------
numerical_solvers  (was pinneapple_solvers)
    PDE solvers (FDM, FEM, CFD): HeatConduction3D, NavierStokes3D,
    LidDrivenCavitySolver3D, ChannelFlowSolver3D, ElasticWave3D.
    Optional bridges to OpenFOAM and FEniCS. SolverRegistry, generate_pinn_dataset.
    CAD-to-CFD pipeline (CADToCFDPipeline).

particle_dynamics  (was pinneapple_dynamics)
    Differentiable particle / continuum dynamics: rigid-body (RigidBody,
    RigidBodySystem), MPM (MPMSimulator), SPH (SPHParticles). All in pure
    PyTorch for autograd compatibility.

external_solvers   (was pinneapple_integrations)
    External tool bridges: OpenFOAM case staging & field extraction, MATLAB
    engine wrapper, Modelica / FMU simulation (via fmpy / OMPython), FEniCS
    workflow. All optional — graceful degradation when tool not installed.

Integration helpers
-------------------
``simulate(scenario, ...)``
    Dispatch function: routes to the appropriate solver/simulator based on
    scenario string (``"heat_3d"``, ``"ns_3d"``, ``"mpm"``, ``"sph"``, …).
``generate_data(scenario, n_samples, ...)``
    Generates a dataset of trajectories using the matching solver.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_simulation import simulate, generate_data, HeatConduction3D
>>> output = simulate("heat_3d", t_end=1.0, nx=32, ny=32, nz=32)
>>> dataset = generate_data("ns_3d", n_samples=50)
pinneapple_simulation.doc1: pinneapple_simulation — Physics simulation back-ends and data generation.

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.doc:
Faster implicit pressure solves for OpenFOAM, verified against plain OpenFOAM.

OpenFOAM's pressure-based solvers (PISO, PIMPLE, SIMPLE) spend most of a time step in the pressure equation.
This package changes only the *initial guess* of that linear solve and leaves the solver and its stopping test
to OpenFOAM, so the converged fields satisfy the same tolerance as a plain run:

- ``plugin/pinneWarmStart.C`` -- an OpenFOAM linear-solver wrapper (``solver pinneWarmStart;``) that projects
  each new pressure system on the span of the last solutions (Galerkin projection), or asks Python for a guess
  through named pipes, then calls the ordinary inner solver (PCG, GAMG, ...). It can also write every system
  to disk. :func:`build.build_plugin` compiles it against the installed OpenFOAM.
- :mod:`ldu` -- read those systems (lduMatrix arrays) and convert them to SciPy / PyTorch sparse matrices.
- :mod:`solvers` -- CG with Jacobi, DIC and AMG (pyamg) preconditioners and a PyTorch CG (float64 or mixed
  precision), all with OpenFOAM's normalised-residual stopping test.
- :mod:`warm_start` -- projection on past solutions and POD of earlier runs; :mod:`learned` -- a small graph
  network that corrects the guess (PyTorch).
- :mod:`guess_server` -- serve Python guesses to a running OpenFOAM solver.
- :mod:`case` -- write the benchmark cases, run them, parse logs and compare fields; :mod:`benchmark` -- the
  comparisons reported in ``docs/core_concepts/openfoam_acceleration.md``.
pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.doc1: Faster implicit pressure solves for OpenFOAM, verified against plain OpenFOAM.

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.b.doc:
The comparisons behind ``docs/core_concepts/openfoam_acceleration.md``.

- :func:`openfoam_comparison` -- the same case run by plain OpenFOAM and with ``pinneWarmStart``, same inner
  solver and tolerances; iterations and times from the logs, field differences against the plain run and
  against a reference solved to a much tighter tolerance.
- :func:`offline_benchmark` -- the pressure systems of one run, re-solved in Python with each combination of
  initial guess and solver, at OpenFOAM's stopping test.
- :func:`markdown_table` -- format rows for the documentation.

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.b.doc:
Compile the ``pinneWarmStart`` linear-solver library against an installed OpenFOAM.

The C++ source (``plugin/pinneWarmStart.C``) is part of this package. Building it needs the OpenFOAM
headers of the installed version and a C++ compiler:

- a full OpenFOAM installation (``$FOAM_SRC/OpenFOAM/lnInclude`` exists): those headers and ``$FOAM_LIBBIN``;
- a binary-only installation (e.g. the Debian/Ubuntu ``openfoam`` package, which ships no headers): the
  source tree of the *same* version, e.g. ``apt-get source openfoam`` (needs a ``deb-src`` entry), passed
  as ``openfoam_src`` or ``$PINNEAPPLE_OPENFOAM_SRC``. Its headers are only read at build time; nothing is
  copied into this repository.

The library is cached under ``~/.cache/pinneapple/accelerated_foam`` keyed on the source and the flags, and
loaded by a case with ``libs ("<path>");`` in ``controlDict``.

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.g.doc:
Serve initial guesses from Python to a running OpenFOAM solver (``pinneWarmStart`` with ``guess external``).

Two named pipes in ``pipe_dir`` carry the exchange. Before each solve the wrapper writes to ``request``
a message ``[1, count, nCells, nFaces, len(name)] (int64) + name + lowerAddr, upperAddr (int32) + diag,
upper, source, psi (float64)``, then reads from ``reply`` ``[status] (int64) + guess (float64)``
(status 1 = use the guess). After the solve it writes ``[2, count, nCells, 0, len(name)] + name + psi``
(no reply), which is how the guesser sees converged solutions. Any object with ``guess(system, x_prev)`` and
``update(x)`` can serve (:class:`ProjectionWarmStart`, :class:`PODWarmStart`, :class:`LearnedWarmStart`).

    with GuessServer(pipe_dir, {"p": PODWarmStart().fit(snapshots)}) as srv:
        run_case(case_dir, "icoFoam")          # fvSolution: guess external; pipeDir "<pipe_dir>";
    srv.stats                                   # per-field number of guesses served, Python time spent

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.l.doc:
OpenFOAM lduMatrix systems in Python: read the systems written by ``pinneWarmStart`` and convert them.

OpenFOAM stores a matrix over a mesh as three coefficient arrays and an addressing (``lduMatrix``):
``diag`` (one per cell), ``upper`` and ``lower`` (one per internal face), and for each internal face the owner
cell ``lowerAddr`` and the neighbour cell ``upperAddr``. The product ``A x`` is

    (A x)[c]  = diag[c] x[c]
    (A x)[l] += upper[f] x[u]      for every face f with l = lowerAddr[f], u = upperAddr[f]
    (A x)[u] += lower[f] x[l]

so ``A[l, u] = upper[f]`` and ``A[u, l] = lower[f]`` (equal for the symmetric pressure matrix). Boundary
conditions that are not coupled are already folded into ``diag`` and the source when the solver is called;
coupled interfaces (processor, cyclic) are not part of the arrays, which is why a dump records how many there
are (:attr:`LduSystem.n_coupled`) and :meth:`LduSystem.to_csr` refuses a system with coupled interfaces.

The stopping test of OpenFOAM's iterative solvers is a normalised L1 residual (``lduMatrix::solver::normFactor``),
reproduced by :func:`normalised_residual` so that Python solvers stop at the same point an OpenFOAM solver would.

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.l.doc:
A learned correction of the initial guess: a small graph network on the matrix graph (PyTorch).

The network sees, per cell, the right-hand side, the projection guess (:class:`ProjectionWarmStart`) and its
residual, all scaled by the matrix diagonal; it passes messages along the matrix's off-diagonal couplings
(the mesh faces) and outputs a correction ``x = x_proj + s * net(features)``, ``s`` the size of a Jacobi step
on the projection's residual. It is trained to minimise the
residual ``||b - A x|| / ||b - A x_proj||`` on systems written by an earlier run. At use, the guess is kept
only when its residual is below the projection's (a safeguard), so a bad prediction costs one product.

A purely local network can remove high-frequency residual (it learns something close to a smoother); the
low-frequency error that sets the Krylov iteration count is global. Expect a modest effect; the benchmark
reports whatever it measures.

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.s.doc:
Krylov solvers for extracted pressure systems, with OpenFOAM's stopping test.

Every solver stops when the normalised residual (:func:`ldu.normalised_residual`, normalisation computed at the
initial guess, as OpenFOAM does) is below ``tolerance`` or below ``rel_tol`` times its initial value, so an
iteration count here can be compared with an OpenFOAM log line at the same settings.

- :func:`pcg` -- preconditioned conjugate gradients in NumPy/SciPy, with
  :func:`jacobi`, :func:`dic` (OpenFOAM's diagonal incomplete Cholesky) or :func:`amg` (pyamg, optional) preconditioners.
- :func:`torch_pcg` -- the same Jacobi-preconditioned CG in PyTorch (GPU when one is available), in float64 or
  float32 with float64 residual replacement (mixed precision).

The pressure matrix of an incompressible solver is negative definite; CG is applied to it unchanged (the
preconditioners carry the sign).

pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.w.doc:
Initial guesses for a sequence of pressure systems.

A transient pressure-velocity solver solves a new pressure system every corrector, with a matrix and a
right-hand side that change slowly. OpenFOAM starts each solve from the current pressure field. The guesses
here are never worse than that in the energy norm of the current matrix, because that field is in the space
they project on:

- :class:`ProjectionWarmStart` -- Galerkin projection on the last ``k`` solutions (Fischer 1998). This is the
  algorithm of the ``pinneWarmStart`` OpenFOAM wrapper (``guess projection``); the Python version is used
  for the offline benchmarks and to check the C++ one.
- :class:`PODWarmStart` -- Galerkin projection on a POD basis of solutions from earlier runs (a design of
  experiments, a previous simulation), plus the current field.

Both use only ``A x`` products, so they apply to any matrix the solver hands over.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.doc:
Electromagnetics and electrodynamics in SI: references, materials, solvers and machines.

Statics and machines (2-D, P1 triangles):

* :mod:`.mesh` -- polar ring mesher with a moving band for rotation, structured rectangles; gmsh importer.
* :mod:`.materials` -- linear media, permanent magnets, nonlinear B-H curves.
* :mod:`.hysteresis` -- Froehlich-Kennelly saturation curve, Jiles-Atherton hysteresis.
* :mod:`.fem` -- A_z magnetostatics: assembly and Newton solver with Dirichlet and (anti-)periodic constraints.
* :mod:`.electrostatics` -- -div(eps grad phi) = rho with electrodes; capacitance from the field energy.
* :mod:`.eddy` -- time-harmonic eddy currents in solid conductors with imposed net currents.
* :mod:`.postprocess` -- Maxwell-stress and co-energy torque, flux linkage, back-EMF, iron and magnet losses.
* :mod:`.machine` -- surface-PM / reluctance machine model (cogging, torque vs current angle, losses,
  rotor design sensitivities).

Fields, waves and references:

* :mod:`.constants` -- CODATA 2022 constants; :mod:`.units` -- SI dimensions and a dimensional check of
  Maxwell's equations.

* :mod:`.statics` -- capacitors, Biot-Savart, loops, solenoids, inductances in closed form.
* :mod:`.waves` -- Fresnel, multilayers, skin depth, waveguides, cavities, dipoles, cylinder scattering,
  surface plasmons.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.a.doc:
Closed-form references for verifying the 2D A_z solvers.

* :func:`wire_field` -- round conductor with uniform current (Ampere's law).
* :func:`coax_field` -- coaxial cable, inner conductor ``+I``, outer ``-I``.
* :func:`magnetized_cylinder` -- uniformly magnetized cylinder (``mu_r = 1``) inside a circular
  boundary with ``A = 0``: ``A = f(r) sin(phi - alpha)``; inside the field is uniform,
  ``B = (Br/2)(1 - a^2/R^2)`` along the magnetization (``Br/2`` as ``R -> infinity``).
* :func:`skin_effect_wire` -- current density and per-unit-length impedance of a round wire carrying
  a sinusoidal current (Bessel functions of complex argument).
* :class:`RadialLayers` -- one spatial harmonic ``cos(p phi), sin(p phi)`` of a field in concentric
  layers of linear media with radially magnetized magnets and current densities: each layer obeys
  ``f'' + f'/r - p^2 f/r^2 = rhs(r)`` and the interfaces carry continuity of ``A`` and of
  ``H_phi = -nu dA/dr``. This is the subdomain (exact 2D) solution of a slotless machine, used to check
  the air-gap field and the torque of the FEM model.

All quantities SI. Torque per metre of stack in air between radii ``r`` of a field
``A = a(r) cos(p phi) + b(r) sin(p phi)`` from the Maxwell stress tensor is
``T = (p pi r / mu0) (a b' - a' b)`` (derived in :meth:`RadialLayers.torque`).

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.a.doc:
An open parametric antipodal Vivaldi antenna (AVA) for the EMerge FEM solver, written from scratch.

Geometry (millimetres; the board lies in the x-y plane, the antenna radiates end-fire along +y, z is normal to the
board; the substrate spans ``0 <= y <= Lb``, ``|x| <= W/2``, ``0 <= z <= h``):

* top layer (z = h): a 50-ohm microstrip of width ``wf`` (Pozar, *Microwave Engineering*, 4th ed., eq. 3.197) from
  the board edge y = 0 to ``y = xs``, then the top flare towards +x: inner edge
  ``x(y) = c1 exp(R (y - xs)) + c2`` from ``-wf/2`` at ``y = xs`` to ``Wa/2`` at the mouth ``y = Lb``, outer edge a
  quarter ellipse from ``+wf/2`` to the board side ``W/2`` (semi-axis ``(Lb - xs)/2`` along y), then straight;
* bottom layer (z = 0): the ground of width ``Wg`` from y = 0 to ``y = Lo`` (the microstrip ground), a linear taper
  to ``wf`` at ``y = xs`` (the microstrip-to-parallel-strip transition, the balun), then the mirror image
  (x -> -x) of the top flare;
* optional ``nslot`` rectangular corrugations of depth ``Ls``, width ``ws`` and pitch ``ps`` cut into the outer
  straight edge of both arms, counted from the mouth;
* optional elliptical director (semi-axes ``dir_a`` along y and ``dir_b`` along x) on the top layer, centred at
  ``(0, dir_x)`` in the flare opening;
* substrate ``er`` 3.55, ``tand`` 0.003, ``h`` 1.524 mm (a hydrocarbon-ceramic laminate class, e.g. 60-mil
  RO4003C-type values; change them freely), PEC conductors of zero thickness;
* air box with a margin of …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.a.doc:
Physical limits on the directivity of a travelling-wave (end-fire) or aperture (broadside) antenna.

An end-fire antenna of length ``L`` (a Vivaldi, a Yagi, a helix, a dielectric rod) behaves like a continuous
end-fire line source of the same length. Its maximum directivity (C. A. Balanis, *Antenna Theory*, 4th ed., ch. 6,
directivity of uniform end-fire arrays with ``N d = L``) is

* ordinary end-fire (phase velocity = c): ``D ~= 4 L / lambda``;
* Hansen-Woodyard end-fire (the increased-directivity condition, slow wave): ``D ~= 1.805 * 4 L / lambda``
  (7.22 L / lambda; this module uses the rounded design value 7.28 L / lambda, 0.04 dB higher), the practical upper
  bound of a single travelling-wave antenna.

A broadside aperture of physical area ``A`` and aperture efficiency ``eta`` has ``G = eta 4 pi A / lambda^2``
(Balanis ch. 12). This is the wrong limit for an end-fire antenna, whose aperture faces along the board: a printed
Vivaldi of 100 mm x 200 mm has a large "broadside" area but its end-fire mouth is only ``W x h``. Use
:func:`endfire_directivity` for it.

:func:`min_length` inverts the end-fire limit (the shortest antenna that can reach a target gain at a frequency)
and :func:`feasibility_frequency` gives the lowest frequency at which a board of length ``L`` can reach it. Example:
10 dBi at 2 GHz needs ``L >= 10 / 7.28 * 149.9 mm = 206 mm`` in the Hansen-Woodyard limit.

Consistency checks of one antenna result, as :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.Check` / ``TrustReport``.

Each check is a relation the numbers must satisfy whatever solver produced them (IEEE Std 145 definitions):

=============================  ===========================================================  ========
check                          relation                                                     critical
=============================  ===========================================================  ========
``realized_gain``              ``G_realized = G_IEEE + 10 log10(1 - |S11|^2)``                no
``efficiency_is_G_over_D``     ``e_rad = G / D`` (``10 log10 e = G_dBi - D_dBi``)             no
``efficiency_le_1``            ``e_rad <= 1`` (a passive antenna cannot radiate more than    yes
                               it accepts)
``peak_ge_boresight``          the pattern peak is not below the boresight value             no
``directivity_le_hw``          ``D <= 7.28 L / lambda`` (+ 0.5 dB), :mod:`.bounds`           no
``s11_resolved``               an S11 interpolated by a rational (vector) fit is only        no
                               trusted with enough solved frequencies in the band
``power_closure``              radiated power from the far-field pattern = Poynting flux     no
                               through the radiation surface (within 10 %): the mesh
                               resolves the fields the far field is computed …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.a.doc:
Design loop of a printed end-fire antenna: DOE, multi-objective optimisation, active learning with solver
verification, multi-fidelity bias correction and a trust card per prediction.

* :func:`doe` -- Latin hypercube or Sobol samples of :data:`AVA_RANGES` (configurable), mapped by
  :func:`ava_transform` (director and slots switched on/off, the director placed as a fraction of the length) and
  filtered by :func:`.ava.layout` (unbuildable designs are skipped and counted);
* :func:`optimize` -- NSGA-II (:mod:`pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.methods`) on surrogates: maximise the
  minimum realized gain over the band, minimise the board area, subject to ``max S11 <= -10 dB`` over the band;
* :func:`active_learning` -- rounds of: fit the GP, pick candidates by predictive variance
  (:class:`pinneapple_data.active_learning.VarianceBasedAL`), simulate them, record the error of the prediction made
  *before* the simulation (prospective error, never in-sample), add them;
* :func:`multi_fidelity` -- coarse simulations (``res`` 0.25 wavelength) for many designs, fine ones (``res`` 0.2)
  for a few: the coarse-to-fine bias per frequency is learnt on the fine designs and validated leaving one fine
  design out;
* :func:`prediction_card` -- a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport` for one surrogate prediction: inside
  the training domain, geometry buildable, uncertainty below a threshold, below the physical limit, surrogate
  out-of-sample error known.

Read an external study package from a local folder and re-run one of its designs.

A package is a folder with a results table (one row per (design, frequency), the columns of :mod:`.runner`) and,
optionally, the parametric command-line script that produced it. Nothing from it is copied into the repository:
it is read where it is. An optional ``package.json`` says which files to use and how to call the script::

    {"table": "results.csv",
     "script": "ava_cli.py",
     "argv": ["{python}", "{script}"],           # the command before the design / frequency flags
     "flags": {"params": "--params", "freq": "--freq", "out": "--out", "tag": "--tag"},
     "length_col": "Lb"}

Without it the first ``*.csv`` / ``*.tsv`` / ``*.txt`` table and the first ``*.py`` script are used with the flags of
:mod:`.ava` (``--params JSON --freq GHz --out DIR --tag TAG``, ``result.json`` in the output folder).

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.a.doc:
Drive an external parametric simulator script, one process per sample (and per frequency), and read its tables.

:class:`CLISimulator` runs any command-line script that takes a design and frequencies and writes its result
(``result.json`` with ``{"status": "ok" | "invalid", "rows": [...]}`` by default, or anything a ``parse`` callable
reads). Each call is a separate process with a timeout, so a crash, a memory blow-up or a hung solve costs one sample,
not the study. Lessons measured while running EMerge on a 4-core, 15 GB machine, built in as defaults:

* EMerge's PARDISO backend can die with SIGBUS when MKL is not usable: on SIGBUS the sample is retried once with
  ``fallback_args`` (for :mod:`.ava` the default is already SuperLU; ``--pardiso`` opts in);
* three frequencies in one process with SuperLU went past 15 GB and were SIGKILLed: ``per_frequency=True`` runs one
  frequency per process (each frequency also gets its own mesh sized to its wavelength);
* ``grid.model_S`` (the rational S-parameter model) fails with a single frequency: :mod:`.ava` reads ``grid.S``.

Every run records its exit status, wall time and peak memory (``ru_maxrss`` of that child, from ``os.wait4``).

The table format, one row per (design, frequency): ``tag``, the design parameters, ``f_GHz``, ``S11_dB``,
``D_bore_dBi``, ``G_bore_dBi``, ``Greal_bore_dBi``, ``D_peak_dBi``, ``Greal_peak_dBi``, ``rad_eff`` (extra columns
are kept). :func:`read_table` reads it from CSV, TSV or whitespace-separated …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.a.doc:
Surrogates of an antenna quantity over (design, frequency), and honest validation of them.

Models (all ``fit(table, target)`` / ``predict(params_list, f_ghz) -> (mean, std)``):

* :class:`FrequencyMean` -- the mean of the target over the training designs at each frequency (interpolated in
  frequency): the baseline any model must beat;
* :class:`HWOffset` -- the Hansen-Woodyard limit ``10 log10(7.28 L / lambda)`` plus one fitted offset (one
  parameter: physics carries the length and frequency dependence);
* :class:`LinearPhysics` -- ridge regression on physical features (:func:`physical_features`: ``log(L/lambda)``,
  ``W/lambda``, ``Wa/lambda``, slots on/off, director on/off);
* :class:`GPModel` -- Gaussian process (squared-exponential, one length scale per feature, hyper-parameters by
  maximum marginal likelihood) on the same features plus the HW limit as its mean; returns a predictive std.

Validation: :func:`lodo` (leave one *design* out: every frequency of the held-out design leaves together, so the
model never sees the design it predicts) and :func:`holdout` (a fixed set of test designs). Leaving one row out
would leak the design through its other frequencies and flatter the model.

Physical constants of electromagnetics, SI, CODATA 2022 (NIST, https://physics.nist.gov/cuu/Constants/).

Since the 2019 SI redefinition ``c``, ``e``, ``h`` and ``k_B`` are exact and ``mu0`` is measured
(``mu0 = 4 pi alpha hbar / (e^2 c)``); ``eps0 = 1 / (mu0 c^2)`` follows from it. ``mu0`` differs from the
pre-2019 value ``4 pi 1e-7`` by about 5e-10 relative, far below any discretisation error in this package.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.e.doc:
Time-harmonic 2D eddy currents in A_z with solid conductors (linear media).

Phasors with ``exp(+j omega t)``. In a solid conductor ``c`` the current density is
``J = sigma (-j omega A + u_c)`` where ``u_c`` is the (uniform) voltage per metre along z, an extra
unknown fixed by the net current ``int_c J dS = I_c`` (``I_c = 0`` for an insulated piece such as a
magnet segment). The system::

    int nu grad A . grad v + j omega int sigma A v - sum_c u_c int_c sigma v = int J_s v
    -j omega int_c sigma A + u_c int_c sigma                                 = I_c

is assembled with P1 elements (consistent mass matrix) and solved with a sparse direct solver.
Losses are ``int |J|^2 / (2 sigma)`` (time average, peak phasors).

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.e.doc:
2-D electrostatics on P1 triangles: ``-div(eps grad phi) = rho`` with electrodes at fixed potentials.

It is the operator of :func:`.fem.solve_magnetostatic` with ``nu -> eps`` and ``J -> rho`` (the two problems are
the same Poisson equation with a piecewise-constant coefficient), so it inherits that solver's assembly and
constraints. Per unit length along z: the energy is ``W = (1/2) int eps |grad phi|^2 dA`` and the capacitance
between an electrode at ``V`` and grounded ones is ``C = 2 W / V^2`` (F/m), which converges at twice the order of
the potential's H1 error (second order on P1 for smooth fields).

Planar (``x, y``) geometry only; axisymmetric electrostatics would need the ``r`` weight.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.f.doc:
Finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) solution of Maxwell's curl equations on the Yee grid, in 1-D, 2-D and 3-D.

One code path for all dimensions: the grid has ``(nx, ny, nz)`` nodes and an axis with one node is a direction of
invariance (``d/dz = 0`` in 2-D, where the six components hold the TMz set ``Ez, Hx, Hy`` and the TEz set
``Hz, Ex, Ey`` at once). Component positions follow Yee (1966): ``Ex`` at ``(i+1/2, j, k)``, ``Ey`` at
``(i, j+1/2, k)``, ``Ez`` at ``(i, j, k+1/2)``, ``Hx`` at ``(i, j+1/2, k+1/2)`` and so on; E at integer time steps,
H at half steps (leapfrog). References: A. Taflove and S. C. Hagness, *Computational Electrodynamics: The
Finite-Difference Time-Domain Method*, 3rd ed., Artech House, 2005 (TH below), ch. 3-4 (scheme, Courant limit,
numerical dispersion), ch. 5 (total-field / scattered-field), ch. 7 (CPML), ch. 9 (dispersive media).

* **Stability.** ``dt <= 1 / (c sqrt(sum 1/dx_i^2))`` (TH eq. 4.65); :class:`YeeGrid` refuses a larger step
  unless ``allow_unstable=True`` (used by the test that shows the blow-up).
* **Boundaries** per side: ``"pec"`` (tangential E = 0 on the outer node plane), ``"pmc"`` (tangential H = 0 half a
  cell outside it, by an odd image), ``"periodic"``, ``"bloch"`` (Floquet phase ``exp(-j k_b L)`` across the
  period; complex fields) and ``"cpml"``: the convolutional PML of Roden and Gedney (Microw. Opt. Technol. Lett. 27,
  2000; TH sec. 7.9) on the outer ``npml`` cells with polynomial grading of ``sigma`` and ``kappa`` …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.f.doc:
2D magnetostatics in the z-component of the magnetic vector potential, P1 triangles.

Strong form, with ``B = curl(A_z e_z) = (dA/dy, -dA/dx)`` and the constitutive law ``H = nu(|B|^2) (B - Br)``::

    -div( nu grad A ) = J_z + (curl of nu Br)_z

Weak form solved here, for every test function ``v``::

    int nu grad A . grad v  =  int J v  +  int nu (Br_x dv/dy - Br_y dv/dx)

It is the stationarity condition of the energy functional (per metre of stack)::

    Pi(A) = sum_e area_e [ w_e(|B_e|^2) - nu_e Br_e . B_e ] - int J A

with ``w = nu |B|^2 / 2`` for linear media and ``w = int_0^|B| H db`` for nonlinear iron. ``Pi`` is convex
for monotone B-H curves, so Newton's method with a backtracking line search on ``Pi`` converges from
any start. ``-Pi`` at the solution equals the magnetic co-energy up to a term that does not depend on
the rotor angle; this is what :func:`pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.postprocess.torque_coenergy`
differentiates.

Boundary conditions: Dirichlet values on any node set, and periodic / anti-periodic node pairs
``A[slave] = sign * A[master]`` (eliminated through a sparse map ``A = P a + A_D``). Nodes with neither
are natural (zero tangential H, i.e. flux crosses the boundary at right angles).

Magnets are linear (``mu_r``, ``Br``); iron may be nonlinear. Materials are passed per element.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.h.doc:
Nonlinear magnetisation: the Froehlich-Kennelly saturation curve and the Jiles-Atherton hysteresis model.

:class:`FrohlichKennelly` is single-valued: ``B = mu0 H + H / (alpha + beta |H|)`` (Froehlich 1881, Kennelly
1891; the polarisation saturates at ``1/beta``, the initial relative permeability is
``1 + 1 / (mu0 alpha)``). It exposes the interface of :class:`.materials.BHCurve` (``h``, ``nu``, ``dnu``,
``energy`` as functions of ``s = |B|^2``) with every quantity in closed form, so it plugs straight into the
Newton solver of :mod:`.fem`.

:class:`JilesAtherton` is the hysteresis model of D. C. Jiles and D. L. Atherton, *Theory of ferromagnetic
hysteresis*, J. Magn. Magn. Mater. 61 (1986) 48-60. With the effective field ``He = H + alpha M``, the
anhysteretic ``Man = Ms L(He / a)`` (``L(x) = coth x - 1/x``), the split ``M = Mrev + Mirr``,
``Mrev = c (Man - Mirr)`` and the pinning law ``dMirr/dHe = delta_M (Man - Mirr) / (delta k)``
(``delta = sign(dH/dt)``; ``delta_M = 1`` when ``delta (Man - M) > 0``, else 0, which keeps the irreversible
susceptibility non-negative), the chain rule gives, with ``u = delta_M (Man - M) / (delta k)`` and
``g = dMan/dHe``::

    dM/dH = (u + c g) / (1 - alpha (u + c g))

This is derived from the definitions above rather than taken from a later paper, several of which use
inequivalent rearrangements. It is integrated along an applied ``H(t)`` path with classical RK4 on each
monotone segment; the step error is measured in the tests. …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Radial-flux machine with surface permanent magnets (or none: a reluctance rotor), 2D A_z FEM.

The cross-section is meshed with :func:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.mesh.polar_mesh`:
rotor rings turn with the rotor and a one-layer moving band in the middle of the air gap is
re-triangulated for each rotor angle, so rotor and stator elements keep their indices and shapes at
every angle (smooth co-energy, rotor-frame quantities for losses, a fixed design-variable set for
topology optimization). Slots, teeth and magnets are resolved on the polar grid (their edges snap to
the nearest grid line); ``n_theta`` sets the angular resolution.

    from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machine import SPMMachine
    m = SPMMachine()                                   # 4 poles, 24 slots, illustrative data
    sol = m.solve(theta=0.0, currents=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0))  # no load
    T = m.torque(sol)                                  # Maxwell stress (Arkkio), N m
    Tc = m.torque_coenergy(0.01, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0))      # virtual work, N m
    psi = m.flux_linkage(sol)                          # Wb-turn per phase

Conventions: angles in radians, rotor angle ``theta`` counter-clockwise, torque on the rotor positive
counter-clockwise; ``currents`` are the instantaneous phase currents (A). Phase ``k`` of a balanced
supply is ``I cos(p theta + phi0 + pi/2 + gamma - 2 pi k / 3)``, where ``phi0`` is the electrical angle
of the magnet flux linkage at ``theta = 0`` (from …

Rotor design of the V-magnet IPM machine with the design-study core of :mod:`pinneapple_design.design_optimizer`:
the FEA as a reference evaluator, a Gaussian-process surrogate with active learning, NSGA-II, re-verification of
every Pareto design by FEA, and the FEA calls this saves against a GA that calls the FEA directly.

* :func:`rotor_evaluator` (an ``IPMRotorEvaluator``) -- design vector (magnet width ``W4``, thickness ``H3``, V depth ``H0``, opening ``W0``,
  bridge ``H1`` of :class:`~.geometry.VRotor`) to mean torque and torque ripple at a fixed current (FEA) and magnet
  mass (exact). Designs whose polygons cross or leave the pole (:func:`~.geometry.geometry_errors`) are returned as
  invalid, without a solve.
* :func:`rotor_design_problem` -- maximise torque, minimise magnet mass, ripple below a limit.
* :func:`hybrid_vs_fea_only` -- surrogate-assisted NSGA-II (LHS start, rounds of GP fit, NSGA-II on the GP, FEA on
  points along its front) against NSGA-II on the FEA itself; the hypervolume of the FEA-verified front of each,
  and how many FEA calls the FEA-only GA needs to reach the hybrid's hypervolume.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Drive model of a synchronous machine: dq steady state, MTPA and flux weakening under inverter limits,
efficiency map and drive-cycle energy.

The machine enters as a *flux map*, any object with ``psi(i_d, i_q) -> (psi_d, psi_q)``, ``torque(i_d, i_q)`` and
``core_loss(i_d, i_q, f_e)`` (vectorised over arrays):

* :class:`LinearDQ` -- constant ``L_d``, ``L_q``, ``psi_m``: ``T = 1.5 p (psi_m i_q + (L_d - L_q) i_d i_q)``; its MTPA,
  base speed and flux-weakening torque have closed forms (:meth:`LinearDQ.mtpa_closed_form`,
  :meth:`LinearDQ.max_torque_closed_form`) that verify the numerical optimiser.
* :class:`FluxMap` -- tables of the FEA (:meth:`FluxMap.from_fea` on an :class:`~.pmsm.IPMMachine`): mean torque and dq
  flux linkages on an ``(i_d, i_q)`` grid (saturation and cross-saturation included), and per grid point the
  frequency-free iron-loss sums and the magnet-loss coefficient (:meth:`~.pmsm.IPMMachine.loss_components`), so the
  core loss at any speed is ``k_h f^alpha S_h + k_c f^2 S_c + k_e f^1.5 S_e + c_m f^2``.

Steady state (amplitude-invariant dq, peak values): ``v_d = R i_d - w_e psi_q``, ``v_q = R i_q + w_e psi_d``, phase
current amplitude ``|i| <= I_max``, phase voltage amplitude ``|v| <= V_max`` (``V_dc / sqrt 3`` for space-vector PWM
in its linear range, :func:`v_max_svpwm`). :class:`Drive` picks for a requested torque and speed the feasible current

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
End windings: resistance and leakage inductance of the coil ends, outside the 2-D cross-section.

Each coil end is a thin conductor on the cylinder at the mean slot radius ``r_c``: axially out of the stack by the
overhang ``e``, then a half circle (in the developed cylinder surface) over the coil span, then back. Its length per
coil side, ``e + pi s / 4`` with ``s`` the developed coil span (half of ``2 e + pi s / 2`` per coil end), is the
end-turn length used by :func:`~.drive.prius_phase_resistance`, so resistance and inductance share one geometry.

:func:`end_winding_inductance` integrates the phase inductances of these conductors (Neumann's formula with the
thin-wire kernel, :func:`~..statics.filament_inductance`), both ends, with the coil bundle as a round conductor of
the slot's copper area, in air and with the stator end face as an infinitely permeable mirror; the two bound the
real laminated end face. The dq leakage inductance of a balanced three-phase winding is ``L_aa - M_ab``; it adds to
L_d and L_q (``Drive(..., L_end=...)``).

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Parametric cross-sections of radial-flux machines: V-shaped interior magnets and round-bottom slots.

A machine is described per *sector*: one rotor pole and one stator slot pitch, each a list of named closed
polygons inside an annular sector (straight edges; arcs are discretised by :func:`arc`). The mesher
(:mod:`.mesher`) meshes one sector with every polygon edge as a mesh edge and copies it around the circle,
so the regions of the mesh are the polygons exactly, and every pole and every slot has the same mesh.

Parametrisations (lengths in metres, angles in radians):

* :class:`VRotor` -- a lamination with one V of two rectangular magnets per pole, the parametrisation of
  pyleecan's ``HoleM50`` (Apache-2.0; P. Bonneel, E. Devillers et al.): opening ``W0`` and depth ``H0`` of the
  V, tangential-bridge thickness ``H1``, magnet thickness ``H3`` and width ``W4``, inter-pole rib ``W3``,
  centre-post width ``W1``. The V angle follows from them (:attr:`VRotor.v_angle`).
* :class:`RoundBottomSlots` -- open trapezoidal slots with a round bottom (pyleecan ``SlotW11``): opening
  ``W0`` x ``H0``, wedge ``H1``, body width ``W1`` at the top and ``W2`` at the bottom, depth ``H2``,
  bottom fillet radius ``R1``.

:func:`prius_2004` returns the 2004 Toyota Prius traction motor with the dimensions of pyleecan's
``Toyota_Prius.json`` (48 slots, 8 poles, 83.82 mm stack).

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Independent cross-check of the machine FEA with gmsh (mesh) and GetDP (solver).

gmsh (https://gmsh.info) and GetDP (https://getdp.info) are GPL programs used here as external executables only
(``gmsh`` and ``getdp`` on the path; no code of theirs is copied or linked). For one rotor angle and one set of
phase currents, :func:`solve` writes

* a gmsh geometry (``.geo``, built-in kernel) of the full cross-section from the same polygons as the mesher of
  :mod:`.mesher` (:func:`write_geo`): every region is a plane surface bounded by shared lines, iron regions with
  the pole and slot holes as inner loops; the rotor is turned by ``theta``, so each angle has its own unstructured
  mesh (no moving band);
* a GetDP problem (``.pro``, :func:`write_pro`): A_z magnetostatics in ``H(curl)`` with perpendicular edge
  (nodal) functions, nonlinear iron from the B-H table (Akima interpolation of ``nu(b^2)``, Newton-Raphson with the
  ``JacNL`` tangent term), linear magnets with remanence, coil current densities, ``A = 0`` on the shaft and outer
  circles; post-processing in GetDP of the Arkkio torque over the air gap and of the three phase flux linkages,

runs both programs and returns their numbers. Nothing of this package's own mesher, solver or post-processing is
used for the result, so the agreement with :class:`~.pmsm.IPMMachine` measures discretisation and implementation
differences between two independent codes on identical geometry and material data.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Conforming Delaunay meshes of machine sectors and their assembly into a rotating machine mesh.

:func:`mesh_sector` triangulates one annular sector (:class:`~.geometry.SectorGeometry`) so that every edge
of every polygon, both arcs and both radial sides are edges of the mesh: boundary points are placed at the
local size ``h``, interior points on a staggered polar lattice, and any boundary segment whose diametral
circle contains another point is split (or the interior point removed) until every segment is a Gabriel edge,
which a Delaunay triangulation always contains. Elements are then named by the polygon that contains their
centroid, so the regions are the polygons exactly.

:class:`MachineMesh` copies the rotor-pole sector and the stator-slot sector around the circle (identical
elements in every pole and slot, so cogging and ripple carry no mesh noise of their own) and joins them
through the air gap with three ring layers: rotor air, moving band, stator air. Turning the rotor moves the
rotor nodes rigidly and re-triangulates only the band (:func:`~..mesh.zipper`), so rotor and stator
elements keep their indices at every angle.

Interior permanent-magnet synchronous machine: 2-D nonlinear A_z FEA and its post-processing.

    from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines import IPMMachine, prius_2004
    m = IPMMachine(prius_2004(), n_gap=960)
    op = m.operating_point(I_peak=250.0, gamma=math.radians(50))  # torque, psi_d, psi_q over rotor positions
    T, psi_d, psi_q = op["torque_mean"], op["psi_d"], op["psi_q"]

Conventions. Rotor angle ``theta`` counter-clockwise (mechanical radians), torque on the rotor counter-clockwise
positive. The d-axis is the axis of the magnet flux linkage (found from a no-load solution,
:meth:`IPMMachine.pm_flux_angle`); the amplitude-invariant Park transform ``x_d + j x_q = (2/3)(x_a + a x_b +
a^2 x_c) e^{-j theta_e}`` with ``theta_e = p theta + phi0`` gives ``psi_d``, ``psi_q``, and phase currents
``i_k = I cos(theta_e + pi/2 + gamma - 2 pi k / 3)`` put ``i_d = -I sin(gamma)``, ``i_q = I cos(gamma)``
(``gamma = 0`` on the q-axis, ``gamma > 0`` towards -d; pyleecan's current angle ``Phi0`` is ``gamma + 90 deg``).
Electromagnetic torque from the flux linkages: ``T = 1.5 p (psi_d i_q - psi_q i_d)``; from the field:
Arkkio's Maxwell-stress torque averaged over the rotor-side and stator-side air layers.

Materials: rotor and stator iron follow a nonlinear B-H curve (stacking factor applied), magnets are linear
(``mu_r``, ``Br`` at a temperature), pockets, slot openings and slots are air for the field. The shaft is outside
the model (A = 0 on the rotor's inner …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Step skew, manufacturing tolerances and a 3-D view of the field of an IPM machine.

Step skew (multi-slice 2-D): a rotor of ``K`` axial segments, segment ``k`` turned by ``delta_k = s (k - (K-1)/2)``
(step ``s``, total skew ``(K-1) s``). Each segment is a 2-D slice of the same stator with the same phase currents,
so the torque at rotor angle ``theta`` is ``(1/K) sum_k T_2D(theta + delta_k; i_abc(theta))`` and the flux linkage
the mean of the slices (end effects and the inter-segment axial flux are neglected, as in every multi-slice model).
For a quantity with a harmonic of order ``h`` per period ``lam`` the mean over the slices multiplies that harmonic by
the step-skew factor ``|sin(K h pi s / lam) / (K sin(h pi s / lam))|`` (:func:`step_skew_factor`).

Tolerances: :func:`tolerance_model` maps samples of (remanence scale, magnet thickness, magnet width, air gap) to the
FEA mean torque and ripple; with :func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate` (JCGM 101 Monte Carlo,
Wilson interval of the yield) it gives the output distributions directly from the FEA or from a surrogate trained on
it.

3-D view: :func:`skewed_field_3d` extrudes the 2-D solution of every segment into prisms (wedges) along the stack,
each segment turned by its skew angle; :func:`~.export.write_vtu` writes it for ParaView.

Catalogue electrical steel and magnet data for machine models, with their sources.

``M400_50A``: non-oriented electrical steel grade M400-50A (EN 10106; 0.50 mm, at most 4.00 W/kg at 1.5 T,
50 Hz): the B-H curve (44 points, 0 to 2.3 T) and the specific-loss table (W/kg at 50, 100, 200, 400, 1000 and
2500 Hz, 0.1 to 1.8 T) of pyleecan's material library (``pyleecan/Data/Material/M400-50A.json``, pyleecan 1.4.2,
Apache-2.0), resistivity 4.6e-7 Ohm m, density 7650 kg/m^3. These are the data of a supplier datasheet for the
grade, not of one coil: a design should use its own supplier's curve.

``MAGNET_PRIUS``: sintered NdFeB of pyleecan's ``MagnetPrius.json``: Br = 1.24 T at 20 degC, mu_r = 1.05,

table and returns the fit's errors; :class:`TableIronLoss` interpolates the table itself (log-log), so it
reproduces the catalogue exactly at its points.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Lumped thermal network of a radial-flux machine, and the demagnetisation check of its magnets.

:class:`ThermalNetwork` is a general network of isothermal nodes: heat capacities ``C`` (J/K), conductances ``G``
(W/K) between nodes and to fixed-temperature boundaries, heat sources ``P`` (W). Steady state solves
``(L + G_b) T = P + G_b T_b`` (``L`` the conductance Laplacian); transients use backward Euler or the trapezoidal
rule (A-stable, orders 1 and 2), with time-dependent sources.

:func:`machine_network` builds the classic seven-node model of a water-jacketed machine (stator yoke, teeth,
winding in the slots, end windings, rotor, magnets, shaft/bearing path) from the cross-section and stated material and
contact data: conduction through cylindrical shells ``G = 2 pi k L / ln(r2/r1)``, through the slot insulation
(equivalent conductivity of the winding), axially along the conductors to the end windings, and convection across the
air gap and at the end windings with given heat-transfer coefficients. The coefficients are inputs, not
correlations fitted here: a validated model needs them from measurements or a CFD study of the actual machine.

:func:`demagnetisation_margin` evaluates the FEA field inside every magnet element: the field opposing the
magnetisation, ``H_rev = -(B . m - Br) / (mu0 mu_r)``, against the intrinsic coercivity ``Hcj(T)`` of the grade (the
knee of a square-loop NdFeB magnet); margin < 0 marks elements that would demagnetise irreversibly.

``run(quick=...)`` returns :class:`~..verification.CaseResult` rows (the same table format as the
electromagnetics suite); ``examples/electrodynamics/10_pmsm_prius.py --write-docs`` writes them into
docs/guides/electromagnetics.md. Published reference: torque against current angle of the 2004 Toyota Prius
motor at 250 A peak (Z. Yang, M. Krishnamurthy, I. P. Brown, "Electromagnetic and vibrational characteristic of
IPM over full torque-speed range", IEEE IEMDC 2013, pp. 295-302), values as tabulated in pyleecan's test suite
(``Tests/Validation/Electrical/test_EEC_PMSM.py``, Apache-2.0).
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc1: Verification of the machine FEA: closed forms for the mesher and solver, internal consistency of the torque, flux-linkage and inductance post-processing, and a cross-check against a published benchmark machine.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Magnetic materials for 2D A_z magnetostatics: linear media, permanent magnets and nonlinear B-H curves.

A nonlinear material is described by its reluctivity as a function of ``s = |B|^2``: ``nu(s)`` with
``H = nu(s) B``, the derivative ``dnu/ds`` (for the Newton tangent ``dH/dB = nu I + 2 nu' B B^T``) and the
energy density ``w(s) = int_0^|B| H db = 0.5 int_0^s nu(t) dt`` (for the energy functional, the line
search and the co-energy torque). Both curve classes below are single-valued (no hysteresis).

``BHCurve`` interpolates measured (B, H) points with a monotone cubic (PCHIP), so H(B) stays increasing
and the energy stays convex; beyond the last point it continues with the vacuum slope ``1/mu0``.
``BrauerCurve`` is the closed form ``nu(s) = k1 exp(k2 s) + k3`` (J. R. Brauer, IEEE Trans. Magn. 11(1),
1975). ``illustrative_steel()`` is a smooth, saturating curve generated from a formula: it is NOT a
measured grade; use a supplier's data for design work.
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc1: Magnetic materials for 2D A_z magnetostatics: linear media, permanent magnets and nonlinear B-H curves.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Electric and magnetic media for wave problems: linear, anisotropic and dispersive (Drude, Lorentz, Debye).

Time convention. Phasors are ``Re[X exp(+j omega t)]`` throughout this package (the engineering convention of
Taflove & Hagness, Pozar and scikit-rf, and of :mod:`.eddy`), so a lossy medium has ``Im(eps_r) < 0`` and a
wave travelling towards ``+z`` is ``exp(-j k z)``. Physics texts (Jackson, Bohren & Huffman) use
``exp(-i omega t)``: their ``eps`` is the complex conjugate of the one here.

Dispersion models, relative permittivity ``eps_r(omega) = eps_inf + sum_k chi_k(omega) + sigma / (j omega eps0)``
(Taflove & Hagness, *Computational Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed., ch. 9):

* :class:`Drude` ``chi = -omega_p^2 / (omega^2 - j omega gamma)`` -- free electrons (metals, plasmas);
* :class:`Lorentz` ``chi = delta_eps omega_0^2 / (omega_0^2 + 2 j omega delta - omega^2)`` -- bound resonances;
* :class:`Debye` ``chi = delta_eps / (1 + j omega tau)`` -- orientational relaxation (water, tissue).

Each pole carries the coefficients of its auxiliary differential equation (ADE) for the FDTD solver, a
second-order accurate discretisation of the polarisation current ``J_p = dP/dt``.

:class:`Anisotropic` holds 3x3 tensors ``eps_r``, ``mu_r`` and ``sigma`` and returns the refractive indices
of a plane wave along a direction (Fresnel's equation of wave normals as a generalised eigenproblem).

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Triangle meshes for 2D magnetostatics: a polar ring mesher with a moving band, and a gmsh importer.

The polar mesher builds a mesh from concentric rings of nodes. Two consecutive rings are joined by a
"zipper" triangulation that works for any node counts and any angular offsets, so the same routine
gives quad-like layers (equal counts), coarsening towards the centre (fewer nodes inside), a fan to a
centre node, and the sliding (moving) band of a rotating machine: the rotor rings carry an angular
offset ``theta``, the stator rings do not, and only the band layer between them is re-triangulated
when the rotor turns. Rotor and stator elements keep their indices and shapes for every angle.

Geometry is resolved on the polar grid (a "staircase" in angle), so boundaries of slots, teeth and
magnets should fall on ring radii and on multiples of the angular step of their rings.

    from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.mesh import Ring, polar_mesh
    rings = [Ring(0.0, 1), Ring(0.01, 32), Ring(0.02, 64), Ring(0.03, 64)]
    mesh = polar_mesh(rings, classify=lambda layer, r, th: "air")

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.m.doc:
Mie scattering of a plane wave by a homogeneous sphere (and a perfectly conducting one).

Implementation of the series of C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, *Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small
Particles* (1983), sec. 4.4 and appendix A (BHMIE), with the logarithmic derivative ``D_n(m x)`` by downward
recurrence and the series length of W. J. Wiscombe, *Improved Mie scattering algorithms*, Appl. Opt. 19 (1980)
1505, ``n_max = x + 4 x^{1/3} + 2``.

Convention: Bohren & Huffman use ``exp(-i omega t)``, so absorbing media have ``Im(m) > 0`` there. This package
uses ``exp(+j omega t)`` (``Im(eps) < 0`` for loss); :func:`mie` accepts the relative index in this package's
convention and conjugates it internally. Efficiencies are real and convention-free.

``x = 2 pi n_medium a / lambda`` is the size parameter, ``m = n_sphere / n_medium`` the relative index.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.p.doc:
Periodic structures (infinite arrays, FSS) in unit-cell Floquet runs, and the campaigns built on them.

* :mod:`.tcda` -- a generic tightly coupled dipole array cell for EMerge (Floquet port, periodic boundaries with the
  scan phase): active reflection over frequency and scan angle; a CLI the runner starts;
* :mod:`.benchmark` -- DOE campaigns of cells, the (frequency x scan) dataset, an FNO from the cell parameters to
  the whole map with held-out error, and the equal-budget comparison of FNO + optimiser against Bayesian
  optimisation on the solver.

Guide: docs/guides/unit_cell_benchmark.md.
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.p.doc1: Periodic structures (infinite arrays, FSS) in unit-cell Floquet runs, and the campaigns built on them.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.p.doc:
Unit-cell campaigns and the equal-budget benchmark of an operator surrogate against Bayesian optimisation.

* :func:`cell_simulator` -- a :class:`~..antenna.runner.CLISimulator` on :mod:`.tcda` (one process per cell, every
  frequency and scan angle in it, SuperLU), with the peak memory and wall time of each run;
* :func:`campaign` -- a space-filling DOE of cells (:data:`CELL_RANGES`, generic) run through it;
* :func:`to_arrays` -- the (design, frequency, scan) table as ``X (n, d)`` and ``Y (n, n_f, n_scan)`` (active
  reflection in dB);
* :func:`fit_fno` -- an FNO from the design parameters to the whole (frequency x scan) map, trained with
  :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.surrogate` (its FNO candidate, budget-limited Adam, best validation checkpoint), and
  :func:`heldout` its error on cells it never saw;
* :func:`equal_budget` -- the same number of solver calls for two strategies on the worst-case active reflection
  over the band and the scan range: (a) DOE of ``budget - n_verify`` cells, an FNO, an optimiser on the FNO and the
  solver on its ``n_verify`` best candidates; (b) Bayesian optimisation calling the solver directly
  (:mod:`pinneapple_design.design_optimizer`, ``"bayesian"``). The best value is always the solver's, never the
  surrogate's. The DOE alone is reported too (random search with ``budget - n_verify`` calls).

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.p.doc:
A generic tightly coupled dipole array (TCDA) unit cell for EMerge Floquet runs, written from scratch.

The cell (millimetres; infinite array in the x-y plane, E-plane = x-z): a square cell of side ``a``; the ground
plane at z = 0 (the bottom face of the cell, PEC); a dipole strip of width ``w`` along x at height ``h``, fed across
a gap ``s`` at the centre by a lumped port of ``z_port`` ohms; its arms stop ``g / 2`` from the cell edge, so
neighbouring dipoles couple capacitively across a gap ``g`` (the "tight coupling"); an optional dielectric
superstrate (``er_s``, thickness ``t_s``) at ``d_s`` above the dipole; air up to half a wavelength (at the lowest
frequency) above everything, closed by a Floquet port. Periodic boundary conditions with the phase of the scan
angle (theta, phi) close the sides.

Per scan angle and frequency the run returns the active reflection coefficient at the lumped port
(``S11`` with every element excited with the scan phase). One mesh serves every scan angle of a cell (the scan only
changes the boundary phases and the Floquet port), so a cell at several angles costs one mesh and one solve per
angle. EMerge (GPL-2.0, ``pip install emerge``) is imported only to solve; this module is called, never copies it.
SuperLU is used (PARDISO can die with SIGBUS without MKL).

``python tcda.py --params '{"h": 9}' --freq 3 4 5 6 --scan 0 30 45 --out run/`` writes ``result.json`` (the
:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.antenna.runner` format); it has …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.p.doc:
Post-processing of A_z solutions: torque, flux linkage, back-EMF, iron losses, magnet eddy losses.

Torque
------
* :func:`torque_maxwell_stress` -- Maxwell stress tensor averaged over an air annulus
  ``r1 < r < r2`` (Arkkio's method, M. Arkkio, Acta Polytechnica Scandinavica EE-59, 1987)::

      T = L / (mu0 (r2 - r1)) * int_annulus r B_r B_phi dS

  Averaging the stress over the annulus instead of taking one circle removes most of the mesh noise.
* :func:`torque_coenergy` -- virtual work: ``T = dW'/dtheta`` at constant currents, by central finite
  differences of the co-energy of two solutions at ``theta +- delta`` (the caller supplies a function
  that solves at a given angle). Agreement of the two methods is a check of the whole chain.

Flux linkage and EMF
--------------------
A coil side with ``N`` turns in a region of area ``S`` and orientation ``+-1`` links
``psi = L N / S * (+-1) * int A dS``; a phase sums its coil sides (divide by parallel paths).
``e = dpsi/dt = omega_m dpsi/dtheta`` (sign convention: generator EMF is ``-e``).

Iron loss
---------
Per element, the flux density over one electrical period (stator elements in the stator frame,
rotor elements in the rotor frame) is split into Fourier harmonics; each harmonic ``n`` traces an
ellipse whose major and minor axes are treated as two alternating fields (a common engineering
approximation for rotational loss). Each alternating component of amplitude ``B`` at ``f`` adds
``k_h f^alpha B^beta + k_c f^2 B^2 + …

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.r.doc:
Closed forms that check the physical-optics code of :mod:`.po`.

* :func:`disk_on_axis` -- the exact field on the axis of a flat PEC disk carrying the PO current of a normally
  incident plane wave (``J = 2 E0 / eta`` uniform). With ``A_x = mu J (e^{-jkz} - e^{-jkR_a}) / (2 j k)``,
  ``R_a = sqrt(z^2 + a^2)``, and ``d^2 A_x / dx^2 = -(k^2 A_x + d^2 A_x / dz^2) / 2`` on the axis (Helmholtz and
  symmetry)::

      E_x(z) = -j k eta J g / 2  +  eta J a^2 e^{-jkR_a} (k^2 / R_a^2 - j k / R_a^3) / (4 j k (j k))

  with ``g = (e^{-jkz} - e^{-jkR_a}) / (j k)``, which simplifies to
  ``E_x = -E0 [e^{-jkz} - (1 + z^2 / R_a^2 + j a^2 / (k R_a^3)) e^{-jkR_a} / 2]``: the wave reflected by the plane
  plus the edge ring, whose weight tends to ``(1 + cos theta_e) / 2`` and does not vanish for a large disk (unlike
  the obliquity factor of scalar Kirchhoff diffraction). This checks the quadrature and the near-field Green's function of :func:`.po.radiate`.
* :func:`go_aperture_taper_db` -- geometrical optics of a paraboloid fed at its focus by a ``cos^q`` feed: a ray
  leaving the focus at angle ``psi`` from the feed axis reaches the aperture plane with relative amplitude
  ``sqrt(D(psi)) / rho``, ``rho = F + z`` the focus-to-surface distance (feed pattern times the space attenuation
  of the spherical wave; C. A. Balanis, *Antenna Theory*, 4th ed., ch. 15, the aperture distribution of a
  paraboloid). In a compact range the
  collimated field keeps this taper along the rays, so it is the …

:class:`CompactRange` holds the design (frequency, :class:`~.geometry.OffsetReflector`, a ``cos^q`` feed of a given

the reflector, computes the PO current and the exact near field on the quiet-zone plane (and wider, to find the
usable size) and returns the :func:`~.qz.qz_metrics` with the cost. :func:`scaled` changes the section size keeping
the clearance below it (the feed stays out of the collimated beam) and the quiet zone on the section's centre line.
:func:`sweep` runs a grid of feed gains, section sizes and roll radii into a :class:`~..antenna.runner.ResultTable`.

The default parameters are a generic example (3 GHz, F = 1.5 m, a 1.2 m section), not any particular range.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.r.doc:
Offset paraboloid reflectors with optional rolled edges, as triangle meshes for :mod:`.po`.

The paraboloid is ``z = (x^2 + y^2) / (4F)`` (vertex at the origin, focus at ``(0, 0, F)``, reflected rays along
+z). The section is the part whose projection on the aperture plane lies inside a superellipse centred at
``(0, centre_y)`` with half sizes ``half_x``, ``half_y`` and exponent ``n`` (``n = 2``: an ellipse; large ``n``: a
rectangle with rounded corners). Past this junction contour an optional rolled edge continues the surface in each
vertical plane through the section centre: the profile leaves the paraboloid tangentially and with its curvature,
blends (``sin^2`` over the first ``blend`` fraction of the roll) to a constant curvature ``-1 / roll`` turning away
from the quiet zone, and stops when its tangent has turned to ``end_angle`` degrees (from the outward horizontal;
-90 = pointing straight back). ``roll_aspect`` stretches the roll's departure from the junction tangent line along
z (the tangent stays continuous): 1 gives the circular roll, larger values a deeper, elliptic-like one. This is a blended rolled edge in the spirit of Gupta and Burnside; the exact
profile of a given range (ellipse ratio, blending function) is a parameter, not built in.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.r.doc:
Physical optics on a triangulated PEC surface: feed fields, PO currents and their exact radiated field.

* :func:`cosq_feed` -- an ideal ``cos^q`` feed (Ludwig-3 co-polarisation, no back radiation), normalised to 1 W
  radiated: ``|E| r = sqrt(eta D(psi) / (2 pi))`` with ``D(psi) = 2 (2q + 1) cos^(2q) psi`` for ``psi < 90 deg``;
  :func:`q_from_gain` / :func:`gain_from_q` convert between ``q`` and the feed gain;
* :func:`po_currents` -- ``J = 2 n x H_inc`` on the lit triangles (normal facing the source), zero in shadow;
* :func:`radiate` -- the field of surface currents at any point, near or far, with the complete free-space dyadic
  Green's function (no far-field approximation)::

      E(r) = -j k eta / (4 pi) sum_i A_i e^{-jkR}/R [ (1 - j/(kR) - 1/(kR)^2) J_i
                                                      - (1 - 3j/(kR) - 3/(kR)^2) (J_i . R^) R^ ]

  one-point (centroid) quadrature per triangle, so triangles of lambda/8 or smaller; computed in chunks.

``exp(+j omega t)`` convention, SI units. PO neglects the fringe (non-uniform) edge currents (PTD) and multiple
reflections; the edge diffraction it does contain is that of the truncated PO current.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.r.doc:
A compact-range study that plans itself: problem -> which checks and sweeps to run -> results -> datasheet.

Given a :class:`Problem` (frequency, focal length, section, rolled edge, feed, quiet zone and, optionally, a
measured or simulated reference table and a band) this module

1. **plans** the study from the geometry alone (:func:`plan`) -- the steps, and the reason each one is there:
   a Fresnel number below two means the quiet zone is in the near field of the section and a size sweep is
   called for; a rolled edge shorter than three wavelengths means the edge diffraction needs its own sweep; a
   reference table means a comparison and a rolled-edge calibration; a spec the baseline misses means an
   optimisation at equal solver budget; no band means no bandwidth step, and the plan says so;
2. **runs** it (:func:`run`), writing every number to JSON so the document can be regenerated without solving;
3. **renders** it as a technical datasheet (:func:`report`), by number, table and figure.

No language model is involved anywhere: the steps come from thresholds on dimensionless numbers computed from
the geometry, and the sentences come from the numbers themselves.

    python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report --out cr_study
    python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report --freq 3 --focal 1.5 --section 1.2 \
        --offset 0.9 --roll 0.15 --qz 0.6 --qz-distance 3 --gain 12 --band 2 4

The datasheet of a compact-range study: every sentence is computed from the study's numbers.

The narrative rules are fixed here and take no model: the verdict compares the usable diameter with the
specification at the declared tolerance; the near-field remark is the Fresnel number against two; the
cut-versus-disk remark is the ratio of the two computed peak-to-peak values; the reference comparison
reports the signed differences of the rows it was given.  When a step was not run or a number is missing
the sentence says so instead of being written anyway.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.s.doc:
Electrostatics and magnetostatics in closed form, and Biot-Savart integration of filamentary currents.

References: J. D. Jackson, *Classical Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed. (1999), ch. 1-5; D. J. Griffiths,
*Introduction to Electrodynamics*, 4th ed. (2017), ch. 2-5; the off-axis field of a circular loop in
complete elliptic integrals is Jackson's eq. 5.37 rewritten for ``B`` (Simpson et al., NASA TM 2001-210720
give the same expressions in Cartesian form).

All functions are SI and vectorised over field points.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.u.doc:
SI dimensions of electromagnetic quantities and a dimensional check of Maxwell's equations.

Every field, source and material parameter of this package is in SI. :data:`QUANTITIES` gives the SI unit of
each named quantity (parsed by :mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`, dimension vector over
``(m, kg, s, K, A, mol)``); :data:`EQUATIONS` writes each law as a list of terms, each a product of quantities
and derivative operators, and :func:`check_equations` verifies that all terms of every law have the same
dimension. :func:`check_units` checks user-declared units of fields against the table, so a field stored in
``V/cm`` or a permeability given in ``H/m`` mislabelled as ``T`` is caught before any residual is computed.

pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.v.doc:
Verification suite of the electromagnetics package: each case runs a solver or a reference implementation
against an independent result (closed form, a published value, another library, a limit) and reports the
measured error and, where a mesh or step is refined, the measured order of convergence.

``run()`` returns :class:`CaseResult` objects; ``to_markdown()`` renders the table of
docs/guides/electromagnetics.md, which is produced by ``examples/electrodynamics/07_em_verification.py``, so every
number in that table comes from a run. ``tests/test_em_verification.py`` asserts each case's tolerance.

Cases are registered with :func:`case`; later modules (FDTD, edge elements, particles, ...) add theirs.

functions.name: skin_depth

functions.doc1: Surface impedance of a good conductor, ``Zs = (1 + j) / (sigma delta) = (1 + j) sqrt(omega mu / (2 sigma))``.

functions.name: rect_waveguide_modes
functions.doc1: The lowest ``n_modes`` modes as ``(f_c, "TE"/"TM", m, n)`` sorted by cut-off. TE needs ``m + n > 0``, TM needs ``m, n >= 1``.

functions.doc1: Transverse profile of TE_mn in an ``a x b`` guide (unnormalised): ``Hz = cos(m pi x/a) cos(n pi y/b)``, ``E_t`` proportional to ``(n/b cos(m pi x/a) sin(n pi y/b), -m/a sin(m pi x/a) cos(n pi y/b))``.

functions.name: circular_waveguide_cutoff
functions.doc1: Cut-off (Hz) of TE_mn (``n``-th zero of ``J_m'``) or TM_mn (``n``-th zero of ``J_m``) of a circular guide.

functions.name: propagation_constant

functions.name: rect_cavity_resonance
functions.sig: (m, n, p, a, b, d, eps_r=1.0, mu_r=1.0) -> float
functions.doc1: Resonance (Hz) of mode (m, n, p) of an ``a x b x d`` PEC box: ``f = c / (2 sqrt(eps_r mu_r)) sqrt((m/a)^2 + (n/b)^2 + (p/d)^2)``.

functions.name: rect_cavity_modes
functions.doc1: Lowest resonances of a PEC box with multiplicity: ``(f, [labels])``. A mode exists as TE_mnp (relative to z) if ``(m or n) and p >= 1`` and as TM_mnp if ``m, n >= 1``; at least two indices must be non-zero.

functions.doc1: Conductor-loss Q of the TE101 mode (Pozar eq. 6.46): ``Qc = (k a d)^3 b eta / (2 pi^2 Rs) / (2 a^3 b + 2 b d^3 + a^3 d + a d^3)``.

functions.name: hertzian_dipole_fields
functions.doc1: Complete fields ``(E_r, E_theta, H_phi)`` of a z-directed Hertzian dipole with moment ``I l`` (A m) at the origin (Balanis eqs. 4-8a..c, ``exp(+j omega t)``)::

functions.name: hertzian_dipole_power
functions.doc1: Time-averaged radiated power ``eta k^2 |I l|^2 / (12 pi)`` (W, peak phasor).

functions.name: hertzian_dipole_radiation_resistance
functions.doc1: ``R = (2 pi / 3) eta (l / lambda)^2`` = ``80 pi^2 (l/lambda)^2`` ohm with ``eta = 120 pi``.

functions.name: dipole_pattern
functions.doc1: Far-field E_theta pattern of a thin centre-fed dipole of length ``L`` with sinusoidal current (Balanis eq. 4-58a): ``[cos(k L/2 cos t) - cos(k L/2)] / sin t`` (unnormalised). ``L = lambda/2`` gives ``cos(pi/2 cos t) / sin t``.

functions.name: cylinder_tm_coefficients
functions.doc1: Coefficients ``(n, a_n, b_n)`` of the TM_z scattering by a cylinder of radius ``a`` (``ka = k0 a``): scattered ``Ez = E0 sum j^-n a_n H_n^(2)(k rho) e^{j n phi}``, inside ``E0 sum j^-n b_n J_n(k1 rho) e^{j n phi}`` for the incident ``E0 exp(-j k x)``. ``eps_r=None`` is a perfect conductor (``a_n = …

functions.name: cylinder_scattering_tm
functions.sig: (x, y, k0, radius, eps_r, E0=1.0, total=True)
functions.doc1: Phasor ``Ez`` at points ``(x, y)`` for a plane wave ``E0 exp(-j k0 x)`` (``exp(+j omega t)``) on a circular cylinder centred at the origin (``eps_r=None``: PEC). ``total=False`` returns the scattered field outside (and the total field inside).

functions.name: half_wave_dipole_radiation_resistance
functions.doc1: ``R = eta / (4 pi) Cin(2 pi)`` with ``Cin(x) = gamma + ln x - Ci(x)`` (Balanis eq. 4-93): 73.08 ohm in free space (input resistance of an infinitely thin lambda/2 dipole).

functions.name: spp_wavenumber
functions.doc1: Surface plasmon polariton on a flat interface: ``k_sp = (omega/c) sqrt(eps_m eps_d / (eps_m + eps_d))`` (Maier eq. 2.14), with ``Im(k_sp) <= 0`` for a lossy metal under ``exp(+j omega t)``.

functions.name: plasma_dispersion_omega
functions.doc1: Transverse waves in a collisionless plasma: ``omega^2 = omega_p^2 + c^2 k^2``.

pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.doc:
External tool integrations for PINNeAPPle.

Subpackages
-----------
openfoam  — case staging, execution, field sampling, and UPD packaging
matlab    — MATLAB Engine API wrapper, subprocess runner, .mat I/O
modelica  — FMU simulation (fmpy) and OpenModelica (OMPython)
fenics    — workflow layer on top of pinneapple_solvers.fenics_bridge
mujoco    — MuJoCo (google-deepmind/mujoco) trajectory collection + MJX parallel rollouts
genesis   — Genesis AI (Genesis-Embodied-AI/Genesis) multi-physics robotics simulation
newton_physics — NVIDIA Newton rigid-body solvers (XPBD, Featherstone, MuJoCo-Warp) with analytic checks

All subpackages use lazy / optional imports so that the base package remains
importable even when a specific external tool is not installed.

pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.a.doc:
ANSYS Fluent live-solver coupling: launches a real ``fluent`` batch-mode
process (journal-file driven, ``fluent <precision> -g -i run.jou``) and
drives an actual simulation, then hands the result off to the existing
``cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader`` UPD bridge.

This is distinct from -- and complements -- ``cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader``,
which only reads ``.msh``/``.cas`` files Fluent has already produced and
has no live-solver coupling of its own. See ``runner.py``'s module
docstring for the honesty note on what could and couldn't be tested
locally (no licensed Fluent installation is available in this
environment).
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.a.doc1: ANSYS Fluent live-solver coupling: launches a real ``fluent`` batch-mode process (journal-file driven, ``fluent <precision> -g -i run.jou``) and drives an actual simulation, then hands the result off to the existing ``cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader`` UPD bridge.

pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.a.doc:
ANSYS Fluent batch-mode journal (``.jou``) generation.

Fluent has no Python/REST scripting surface used here -- like every other
"drive a real external solver" integration in this repository
(``external_solvers/openfoam/runner.py`` shells out to real OpenFOAM
executables), the only way to actually run it non-interactively is its
documented Text User Interface (TUI), invoked in batch mode with a journal
file of TUI commands (``fluent 3ddp -g -i run.jou``). The TUI command set
used below (``/file/read-case``, ``/solve/initialize/initialize-flow``,
``/solve/iterate``, ``/solve/dual-time-iterate``,
``/file/write-case-data``, ``/file/binary-files``, ``exit``) is Fluent's
own public, documented command-line interface -- the same commands that
appear throughout ANSYS's own Fluent Text Command List documentation and
in essentially every publicly published Fluent journal-file tutorial. This
is knowledge of a standard tool's documented CLI (like knowing ``git
commit -m``), not anything reverse-engineered or proprietary.

Confidence level, command by command
-------------------------------------
High confidence (these are the commands used by virtually every public
Fluent journal example and have been stable across Fluent versions for
decades):
  - ``/file/read-case <path>``
  - ``/file/binary-files no`` (ASCII/text I/O toggle)
  - ``/solve/initialize/initialize-flow``
  - ``/solve/iterate <n>``
  - ``/file/write-case-data <path>``
  - ``exit`` / ``yes``

Medium confidence …

ANSYS Fluent live-solver coupling: launches a real ``fluent`` batch-mode
process against a generated journal file and drives an actual solve, then
hands the result off to the existing ``cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader``
UPD bridge.

Mirrors ``external_solvers/openfoam/runner.py``'s shape (a frozen

Fluent's batch-mode command line (``fluent <precision> -g -i

syntax -- ``-g`` (no GUI), ``-i <journal>`` (run a journal file
non-interactively), ``-t<n>`` (processor count) are all in ANSYS's own
Fluent User's Guide / Text Command List documentation and used throughout
publicly published Fluent batch-run tutorials and HPC cluster job
scripts.

tested in this repository, along two paths:

     fully real logic, fully testable with no Fluent install.
  2. The "executable not found" error path here -- also fully real and
     testable, and it is the actual path a caller hits in this
     …
