pinneapple_systems.time_series.enso.data.doc:
Openly licensed ENSO observations, downloaded once, reduced to monthly tropical-Pacific products and cached with
the SHA-256 of every source file.

Sources (all without credentials; NOAA data are public domain, ERA5 is under the Copernicus licence):

* **SST** -- NOAA OISST v2.1 (AVHRR-only, daily, 0.25 deg; Huang et al. 2021, J. Climate 34:2923; Reynolds et al.
  2007, J. Climate 20:5473) from the NOAA Open Data Dissemination bucket on AWS
  (``noaa-cdr-sea-surface-temp-optimum-interpolation-pds``). :func:`oisst_monthly` averages every final (not
  preliminary) daily file of a month into 1 deg cells over the tropical Pacific. The Nino indices are cos-latitude
  weighted box means of that field (:data:`NINO_BOXES`).
* **Thermocline** -- 20 deg C isotherm depth (D20) from the moored-buoy (TAO/TRITON) and, optionally, XBT profiles
  of the World Ocean Database (Boyer et al. 2018, NOAA Atlas NESDIS 87; AWS bucket ``noaa-wod-pds``).
  :func:`wod_d20_casts` interpolates D20 in every quality-controlled cast; :func:`d20_monthly` bins them into
  monthly longitude bins. The warm-water-volume proxy is the zonal mean D20 anomaly over 5S-5N, 120E-80W (the
  region of Meinen & McPhaden 2000, J. Climate 13:3551).
* **Atmosphere** -- ERA5 (Hersbach et al. 2020, QJRMS 146:1999) 6-hourly 10 m wind, mean sea-level pressure and SST
  on the 64 x 32 (5.625 deg) grid of WeatherBench 2 (Rasp et al. 2024, JAMES 16:e2023MS004019; bucket
  ``gs://weatherbench2``), 1959-01 to 2023-01: …

ENSO forecasters with the :class:`~pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.Forecaster` interface, so the
forecast_lab protocol (purged walk-forward tuning, untouched test period, DM tests) applies to them unchanged.

They read the monthly indices from ``data.obs`` (columns named in ``data.meta["columns"]``, see

pinneapple_systems.time_series.enso.inte.doc:
An intermediate coupled model of the tropical Pacific in the spirit of Zebiak & Cane (1987, Mon. Wea. Rev.
115:2262), simplified, and the checks that every component is solved correctly.

* :class:`ShallowWaterOcean` -- linear reduced-gravity (first baroclinic mode) ocean on the equatorial beta-plane,
  Arakawa C-grid, closed basin 120E-80W (walls east and west, sponge layers north and south), Rayleigh friction
  and Newtonian damping r, wind-stress forcing tau / (rho H), RK4 in time. Free waves: the equatorial Kelvin wave
  at c = sqrt(g' H) and long Rossby waves at c / (2n + 1) (Matsuno 1966, J. Met. Soc. Japan 44:25), which reflect at
  the boundaries -- the delayed-oscillator memory of the ocean.
* :class:`GillAtmosphere` -- the steady damped long-wave response to a heating Q (Gill 1980, QJRMS 106:447) solved
  exactly per meridional mode: Q is projected on parabolic-cylinder (Hermite) functions; the Kelvin mode
  (eps + d/dx) q0 = -Q0 and the Rossby modes ((2n + 1) eps - d/dx) q_{n+1} = -(Q_{n-1} + 2n Q_{n+1}) / 2 are solved
  by FFT on a periodic longitude circle; u = (q - r) / 2, p = (q + r) / 2 with r_n = 2 (n + 2) q_{n+2}.
  :func:`gill_analytic` is the closed-form solution for Q = F(x) exp(-y^2 / 2) by periodic Green's functions.
* :func:`sst_tendency` -- the SST anomaly equation dT/dt = -eps_T T + gamma(x) S(y) h + kappa(x) S(y) tau_x (local
  damping, thermocline feedback, Ekman-upwelling / wind feedback), coefficients per longitude estimated from data.
* …

**Recharge oscillator** (Jin 1997, J. Atmos. Sci. 54:811; the linear stochastic form of Burgers et al. 2005, GRL
32:L13706 and Jin et al. 2020, in *El Nino Southern Oscillation in a Changing Climate*, AGU), with T the eastern
Pacific SST anomaly [K] and h the warm-water-volume / thermocline-depth anomaly [m], t in months::

    dT/dt = R(s) T + F1(s) h + sigma_T (1 + B T) xi_T
    dh/dt = -F2(s) T - eps(s) h + sigma_h xi_h

Each coefficient may carry an annual cycle c(s) = c0 + c1 cos(2 pi s / 12) + c2 sin(2 pi s / 12) of the calendar
month s (0 = January); the seasonal growth rate R(s) is the textbook origin of the spring predictability barrier
(Stein et al. 2014, J. Climate 27:4985). B != 0 is multiplicative (state-dependent) noise (Levine & Jin 2017, Clim.
Dyn. 48:3241 discuss its role in ENSO asymmetry). The constant-coefficient system has eigenvalues
``lambda = (R - eps) / 2 +- sqrt((R + eps)^2 / 4 - F1 F2)`` (:func:`ro_eigen`): growth rate (R - eps) / 2 and,
when F1 F2 > (R + eps)^2 / 4, period 2 pi / sqrt(F1 F2 - (R + eps)^2 / 4).

Parameters are estimated (:func:`fit_recharge`) by least squares of the centred monthly tendencies on the state
(times the annual harmonics), the method of the extended recharge oscillator of Zhao et al. (2024, Nature 630:891);
the noise amplitudes from the residuals, B by maximum likelihood of the T residuals.

**Delayed oscillator** (Suarez & Schopf 1988, J. …

:func:`slab_scene` builds a cut-away slab of the basin: the sea surface coloured by SST from 2S to 20N, a vertical

:func:`encode_video` writes an H.264 MP4 with ffmpeg.

pinneapple_systems.time_series.enso.stud.doc:
The ENSO forecasting study: the protocol, the model zoo, and one call per model (so the zoo runs in parallel
processes and is merged by :func:`~pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.study.merge_zoo`).

* :func:`protocol` -- horizons 1-12, 15, 18, 21, 24 months; the test period starts at ``test_start`` (default
  2012-01) and is untouched until the final scoring; the last 15 % of the development period is the validation
  block; purged walk-forward tuning on the rest (forecast_lab rules).
* :func:`zoo` -- the specs by family: baselines, data-driven (GBM, MLP, LSTM, TCN, transformer, LIM, CNN),
  data + physics (CNN pre-trained on the intermediate model, PINN-identified recharge oscillator with and without a
  learned closure, PINN extrapolation, MLP with a recharge-oscillator residual loss, GBM with physics features),
  physical (recharge oscillator deterministic / stochastic / seasonal with multiplicative noise, the RO fitted by
  multiple shooting, the delayed oscillator, the intermediate model with SST nudging), hybrid (RO + GBM residual,
  UDE closure of the RO, the intermediate model with EnKF, a multi-model ensemble).
* :func:`run_model` -- tune / fit / score one spec; also the forecasts from the case-study origins.
* :func:`event_hindcast` -- refit a spec on data that end before an event (1997/98) and forecast it.

pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_.doc:
Common interface of the forecasters in :mod:`pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab`.

A forecaster sees a :class:`SeriesData` (the observed array, which column is the target, the sampling step) and
makes direct multi-horizon forecasts from *origins*: a forecast from origin ``t`` may use ``obs[: t + 1]`` only and
predicts the target at ``t + h`` for every ``h`` in ``horizons``.

``fit(data, train_origins, val_origins, horizons)`` receives the origins of the training samples and of the
validation block. The labels of a training origin reach ``t + max(horizons)``, so the data a forecaster may use for
fitting end at ``train_end(train_origins, horizons)``; models fitted on a contiguous segment (physical models,
ARIMA, filters) use exactly that segment, window models use the samples. The validation block is used for early
stopping and to calibrate the predictive spread (:meth:`Forecaster.calibrate`): a point forecaster gets a Gaussian
predictive distribution whose standard deviation at each horizon is the root-mean-square error on the validation
block. Nothing after the validation block is ever passed to ``fit``.

pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_.doc:
Hybrid forecasters: a physical model plus something learned.

* :class:`ResidualCorrectionForecaster` -- physics forecast + statistical error correction: a gradient-boosting
  model (or MLP) learns y_{t+h} - physics_{t+h} from the lagged observations and the physical forecast itself.
* :class:`UDEForecaster` -- universal differential equation (Rackauckas et al. 2020, arXiv:2001.04385):
  dx/dt = f_known(x; theta) + g_NN(x), with theta estimated first by an :class:`ODEForecaster` on the training data
  and the neural closure g trained through the RK4 integrator on short windows of the training trajectory
  (multiple shooting). The SDE counterpart (drift closure) is
  :class:`~pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_lab.physical.SDEDriftForecaster` with ``closure=...``.

Data-driven direct forecasters on lagged windows: gradient boosting and neural networks (MLP, LSTM, TCN,
transformer), with optional physics-derived input features and, for the MLP, a physics residual penalty.

All of them predict the change of the target from the origin, y_{t+h} - y_t, standardised per horizon, from a
window of the last ``n_lags`` observations (every ``lag_step`` samples) of the observed columns. Predicting the
change keeps persistence as the zero output, so an untrained or over-regularised model falls back to the random-
walk forecast instead of to a constant.

Neural networks are trained with :class:`pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer` (Adam, weight decay), early stopping on
the validation block with the best weights restored, and an optional ensemble of ``n_members`` seeds whose mean
is the forecast.

pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_.doc:
Physical forecasters: the governing equations with parameters estimated from the training data only.

* :class:`ODEForecaster` -- an ODE whose state is fully observed; parameters by least squares on short
  (multiple-shooting) predictions from the observed training states; forecasts integrate from the observed state
  at the origin. Pass a wrong vector field to measure a misspecified model.
* :class:`DelayODEForecaster` -- a delay differential equation dx/dt = f(x, x(t - tau)) of a scalar series
  (Mackey-Glass), integrated by the method of steps from the interpolated observed history.
* :class:`LinearSSMForecaster` -- linear stochastic models sampled exactly: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process and the
  noise-driven damped oscillator, with observation noise. Parameters by maximum likelihood through the Kalman
  filter; forecasts are the exact Gaussian predictive distribution from the filtered state at the origin (data
  assimilation of a linear model).
* :class:`SDEDriftForecaster` -- dx = f(x) dt + sigma dW with f in a polynomial basis, estimated by regressing the
  increments on the basis (first Kramers-Moyal coefficient; Friedrich et al. 2011, Phys. Rep. 506:87);
  Euler-Maruyama ensemble forecasts. An optional neural closure of the drift makes it a hybrid.
* :class:`EnKFForecaster` -- ensemble Kalman filter (:class:`pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman.
  EnsembleKalmanFilter`) with a fitted :class:`ODEForecaster` as the model; forecast ensembles start from the
  …

pinneapple_systems.time_series.forecast_.doc:
The evaluation protocol: fix the test period first, tune on purged walk-forward folds of the rest, fit once,
score once on the untouched test period, and test the differences.

* :class:`Protocol` -- the split: the last ``test_frac`` of the series is the test period, chosen before any
  tuning; the development part ends with a validation block (early stopping, spread calibration, choosing a
  family's representative). Training labels never reach into the validation block (purge = largest horizon by
  construction), validation labels never reach into the test period.
* :func:`tune` -- the same configuration budget for every model, scored by purged walk-forward cross-validation
  on the development part (each fold with its own purged inner early-stopping block).
* :func:`evaluate` -- MAE, RMSE, CRPS, central-interval coverage and PIT per horizon.
* :func:`run_zoo` -- all of it for a list of :class:`ModelSpec`, plus skill against persistence and climatology,
  Diebold-Mariano tests against persistence and against the best baseline on the validation block, Holm (per
  horizon, across the zoo) and Benjamini-Hochberg (all model x horizon tests) adjustments, and for each family the
  last horizon with significant skill.
* :func:`overfitting_study` -- train / cross-validation / test errors of training variants under several
  cross-validation schemes (shuffled k-fold, walk-forward without purge, purged walk-forward, purged k-fold with
  embargo), so the train-test gap and each …

pinneapple_systems.time_series.foundatio.doc:
Pretrained time-series *foundation model* forecasters.

Everywhere else in this repo, forecasters are architectures you train
yourself: ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.transformers`` has
Informer/Autoformer/FEDformer/TFT/TimesNet trained from scratch on your
data, ``pinneapple_systems.time_series.classical_ts`` has ARIMA/Kalman/VAR/
TCN fit on your series, and ``pinneapple_systems.time_series.baselines``
has the simple ``NaiveForecaster`` family. This module is different: it
wraps REAL, openly published, **pre-trained** checkpoints that a research
lab trained on large heterogeneous time-series corpora and released on the
HuggingFace Hub, so a forecast can be produced zero-shot -- with little or
no fitting on the series at hand.

Wrapped models
---------------
* :class:`ChronosForecaster` -- Amazon's Chronos, a T5-based pretrained
  probabilistic time-series forecaster:

      Ansari, A. F. et al. "Chronos: Learning the Language of Time
      Series." arXiv:2403.07815 (2024).

  Backed by the real ``chronos-forecasting`` PyPI package
  (``pip install chronos-forecasting``) and real checkpoints published at
  https://huggingface.co/amazon (e.g. ``amazon/chronos-t5-tiny``, ~8M
  params -- the smallest real variant, used here for testability).

* :class:`TimesFMForecaster` -- Google's TimesFM, a decoder-only pretrained
  foundation model for time-series forecasting:

      Das, A. et al. "A decoder-only foundation model for time-series
      forecasting." arXiv:2310.10688 …

pinneapple_systems.time_series.metrics_e.doc:
Comparing forecasts: skill scores, the Diebold-Mariano test and multiple-comparison control.

* :func:`skill_score` -- 1 - score / score_reference (positive: better than the reference).
* :func:`diebold_mariano` -- equal predictive accuracy of two forecasts of the same targets (Diebold & Mariano
  1995, J. Bus. Econ. Stat. 13:253) with the small-sample correction of Harvey, Leybourne & Newbold (1997, Int. J.
  Forecast. 13:281). An h-step forecast error is serially correlated up to lag h - 1, so the variance of the mean
  loss difference uses the autocovariances up to that lag.
* :func:`holm` (Holm 1979, Scand. J. Stat. 6:65, family-wise error) and :func:`benjamini_hochberg` (Benjamini &
  Hochberg 1995, JRSS B 57:289, false discovery rate) adjust a family of p-values.

pinneapple_systems.time_series.predictab.doc:
Is there anything to predict? Measures of predictability to compute before fitting any forecaster.

* :func:`fit_ar` -- least-squares AR(p) with the order chosen by AIC or BIC, and its one-step R^2.
* :func:`permutation_entropy` -- Bandt & Pompe (2002), Phys. Rev. Lett. 88:174102; 1 for an i.i.d. series.
* :func:`sample_entropy` -- Richman & Moorman (2000), Am. J. Physiol. 278:H2039.
* :func:`rosenstein_lyapunov` -- largest Lyapunov exponent from a scalar series (Rosenstein, Collins & De Luca
  1993, Physica D 65:117). It returns a positive slope for noise too; read it only next to the surrogate test.
* :func:`iaaft_surrogate`, :func:`phase_randomized_surrogate`, :func:`shuffle_surrogate` -- surrogate data
  (Theiler et al. 1992, Physica D 58:77; Schreiber & Schmitz 1996, Phys. Rev. Lett. 77:635).
* :func:`nonlinear_prediction_error`, :func:`time_reversal_asymmetry` -- discriminating statistics.
* :func:`surrogate_test` -- rank test of a statistic against surrogates: does the series have more structure than
  an i.i.d. process (shuffle) or a linear Gaussian process seen through a static monotone transform (IAAFT)?
* :func:`predictability_report` -- all of the above for one series, with the persistence and climatology errors.
pinneapple_systems.time_series.predictab.doc1: Is there anything to predict? Measures of predictability to compute before fitting any forecaster.

pinneapple_systems.time_series.solar_cyc.doc:
Solar-cycle envelope from the daily sunspot number: (E)EMD, the IMF nearest 11 years, its Hilbert amplitude, and
a fit of that amplitude by an extreme learning machine (ELM) with the end-point equality f(0) = f(1) built into the
basis (a constrained expression of the Theory of Functional Connections), then extended past the data.

Data. :func:`fetch_silso_daily` downloads SILSO's daily total sunspot number V2.0 (``SN_d_tot_V2.0.csv``,
Royal Observatory of Belgium, Brussels; licence CC BY-NC 4.0: cite "SILSO data/image, Royal Observatory of
Belgium, Brussels" and do not use it commercially). Nothing from SILSO is shipped here; :func:`synthetic_daily`
makes a series of the same shape for tests and offline demos.

Method.
1. Min-max scale to [0, 1] on a normalised time axis t in [0, 1].
2. Decompose with EMD or EEMD (``PyEMD`` from the ``EMD-signal`` package, Apache-2.0, when installed; otherwise
   :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.eemd`, whose IMFs plus the returned residue also sum to the
   signal). IMFs run from high to low frequency, and which index lands near 11 years depends on the series length
   and ``max_imf``: on a 2005-2025 SILSO slice the source app measured IMF 0 at ~3.6 days and the ~10-year
   component last. :func:`closest_to_schwabe_cycle` therefore picks the IMF whose measured period (median Hilbert
   instantaneous frequency) is nearest 11 years and warns when even that one is more than 40 % off.
3. Hilbert amplitude of that IMF …

pinneapple_systems.time_series.synthetic.doc:
Synthetic time series with known ground truth, for forecasting studies.

Every generator returns a :class:`SyntheticSeries`: the clean state, the noisy observation that a forecaster sees,
the true parameters, and (for the chaotic systems) the largest Lyapunov exponent computed from the equations with
:func:`largest_lyapunov_benettin`, so a forecast horizon can be stated in Lyapunov times.

Systems
-------
* Lorenz-63 (Lorenz 1963, J. Atmos. Sci. 20:130), sigma=10, rho=28, beta=8/3.
* Lorenz-96 (Lorenz 1996, ECMWF Seminar on Predictability), cyclic, forcing F.
* Mackey-Glass delay equation (Mackey & Glass 1977, Science 197:287), dx/dt = beta x_tau / (1 + x_tau^n) - gamma x.
* Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process dx = -theta x dt + sigma dW, sampled exactly (an AR(1)).
* Stochastically forced damped oscillator x'' + 2 zeta omega x' + omega^2 x = sigma xi(t), sampled exactly
  (matrix exponential and Van Loan's integral for the process-noise covariance).
* Double-well Langevin equation dx = (x - x^3) dt + sigma dW: noise-driven switching between two regimes.
* White noise and a Gaussian random walk (controls where nothing can beat the baseline).

The vector fields (:func:`lorenz63_rhs`, :func:`lorenz96_rhs`, :func:`mackey_glass_rhs`, :func:`double_well_drift`)
accept NumPy arrays or torch tensors of shape (..., d), so the same definition drives data generation, the fitted
physical models, and the known part of a universal differential equation.

pinneapple_tools.aero_coefficients.doc:
Shared aerodynamic-coefficient utilities (Cp, surface-force integration, CL/CD/CM).

Plain numpy in / numpy out -- no framework lock-in, so both PINN surrogates
(which typically hand back predictions as numpy arrays after `.detach()
.cpu().numpy()`) and non-PINN solvers (analytical, LBM, panel methods, ...)
can share one implementation instead of every example re-deriving the same
algebra inline.

Sign / axis conventions
------------------------
The pressure-coefficient definition (``Cp = (p - p_inf) / q_inf``) is the
standard aerodynamics convention and matches the inline computation in
``examples/benchmark_suite/15_naca0012_aerodynamic_surrogate.py`` (which uses
the incompressible Bernoulli special case ``Cp = 1 - |V|^2 / U_inf^2``, i.e.
``p - p_inf = q_inf * (1 - |V/U_inf|^2)``).

The wind-axis rotation used by :func:`force_to_coefficients` mirrors the
normal/axial -> lift/drag transform in
``examples/use_cases/missile_aero/missile_aero_pipeline.py``
(see the module docstring there, and lines ~262-267 of
``solve_aero()``)::

    CN = normal-force coefficient   (body axis, perpendicular to axis of symmetry)
    CA = axial-force coefficient    (body axis, along axis of symmetry)
    CL = CN * cos(alpha) - CA * sin(alpha)
    CD = CN * sin(alpha) + CA * cos(alpha)

That pipeline works in a single meridional plane, so "normal" and "axial"
map directly onto two coordinate axes. This module generalizes the same
rotation to a full 3D force vector by picking a 2D "aero plane" out …

pinneapple_tools.automation.doc:
Engineering GUI agent: run a task in engineering software and deliver the files plus the evidence of what
happened ("Selenium for computational engineering").

* :mod:`.workflow`: the structured workflow (inputs with bounds, steps, preconditions, expected artifacts,
  confirmations, acceptance criteria), loaded from YAML/JSON.
* :mod:`.interpret`: a task (sentence or structured) to a committed workflow and its inputs; Ollama optional.
* :mod:`.adapters`: one adapter per application: FreeCAD and CfdOF (Python API inside the FreeCAD GUI), OpenFOAM
  (command line), ParaView (pvpython), ``verify`` (acceptance criteria with ``pinneapple_check``), ``web``
  (Playwright).
* :mod:`.display`: Xvfb virtual display, screenshots, GUI drivers (xdotool; Playwright; pywinauto for Windows).
* :mod:`.runner`: executes the steps, stops on failure or when a step needs a person's confirmation, records every
  command, log, artifact (SHA-256), screenshot and check.
* :mod:`.report`: self-contained HTML evidence report and the StudyResult JSON.

    from pinneapple_tools.automation import Runner, catalog, interpret
    it = interpret("channel with a 55 mm obstacle at 20 mm/s", catalog())
    run = Runner(it.workflow, "runs/r1", inputs=it.inputs).run(approve=["solve"], approver="me")
    print(run.state, run.message)          # report.html and study_result.json are in runs/r1

pinneapple_tools.automation.adapters.bas.doc:
What every adapter implements, and the context a step runs in.

An adapter wraps one application (FreeCAD, OpenFOAM, ParaView, a web UI) and offers named actions. Each action
receives its rendered ``params`` and a :class:`StepContext`, does the work, preferably through the application's own
API or command line, and returns an :class:`ActionResult`: outputs for later steps, the files it produced, the
images of what happened and the checks it ran on its own artifacts.

Executors of other runners (the Simulation Workflow Runner) can call the same adapters: ``get_adapter(name)``,
``adapter.available()``, ``adapter.run(action, params, ctx)``.

FreeCAD and the CfdOF workbench.

Actions run a Python script **inside the FreeCAD GUI** on the run's virtual display (CfdOF needs ``FreeCADGui``;
the GUI also gives real screenshots): the script works through FreeCAD's own API, then the adapter finds the FreeCAD
window with xdotool, captures the screen (``screen`` evidence) and the 3D view region of it (``window`` evidence),
and lets FreeCAD exit.

* ``freecad.open``: open a document, list its objects and spreadsheet parameters, measure a solid.
* ``freecad.macro``: run a macro (``.FCMacro`` / ``.py``) with arguments; the macro gets ``ARGS`` and fills ``RESULT``.
* ``cfdof.setup``: build a CfdOF analysis (laminar steady incompressible, velocity inlet, pressure outlet, walls,
  gmsh mesh) on a solid and write the mesh case and the OpenFOAM case.

pinneapple_tools.automation.adapters.ope.doc:
OpenFOAM through its command line: run the mesh script and the solver script of a case (CfdOF's ``Allmesh`` and
``Allrun``, or any command list), then read what happened from the logs with
:func:`pinneapple_data.simulation_metadata.openfoam.parse_log` (end reached, fatal errors, residual history,
convergence message, checkMesh quality).

* ``openfoam.mesh``: ``Allmesh`` in the mesh case, then ``checkMesh``. Checks: a polyMesh exists, checkMesh says
  "Mesh OK".
* ``openfoam.prepare`` / ``openfoam.post``: the case and the post-processing of the FreeCAD -> OpenFOAM pipeline
  (:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.pipelines.freecad_openfoam`).
* ``openfoam.solve``: ``Allrun`` (or ``commands``) in the case. Checks: the solver reached ``End`` without a fatal
  error or floating-point exception, and either OpenFOAM's residual control stopped it ("SIMPLE solution converged")
  or every initial residual of the last iteration is below ``residual_tol``. Evidence: the residual history plot.

Compatibility with OpenFOAM v1912 (the Ubuntu 24.04 ``openfoam`` package; CfdOF targets newer releases), each
edit recorded as an action of the step:

* CfdOF picks the ``transformPoints`` syntax from ``FOAM_API``, which v1912 does not set, so the mesh would stay in
  millimetres: :func:`patch_cfdof_allmesh` adds the v-numbered (ESI) case to the test in ``Allmesh``.
* CfdOF's velocity inlet (``fixedNormalInletOutletVelocity``) did not hold the prescribed flux on v1912:
  :func:`patch_cfdof_inlet` writes it …

Adapters of the FreeCAD -> OpenFOAM pipeline (:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.pipelines.freecad_openfoam`):

* ``freecadcmd.export``: FreeCAD **headless** (``freecadcmd``, no display) sets the document's spreadsheet
  parameters, recomputes, exports STEP and the faces; the patches are named by rule and written to a multi-region
  STL. ``backend: fake`` uses the NumPy stand-in (tests, machines without FreeCAD).

and, on the ``openfoam`` adapter (:mod:`.openfoam`), through :func:`pipeline_call`:

* ``openfoam.prepare``: mesh dictionaries and case (internal: blockMesh + snappyHexMesh / cfMesh, simpleFoam /
  pimpleFoam; external: ``ExternalFlow``), with ``Allmesh`` and ``Allrun`` for ``openfoam.mesh`` / ``openfoam.solve``.
* ``openfoam.post``: measured quantities, figures, derived quantities and reference errors.

pinneapple_tools.automation.display.doc:
The screen GUI applications run on: a virtual X display (Xvfb) on a Linux server or container, screenshots of it,
and the three ways of driving a GUI when an application has no usable API.

* :class:`VirtualDisplay` starts Xvfb on a free display number and captures the whole screen with Pillow
  (``ImageGrab.grab(xdisplay=...)``), so no screenshot utility is needed.
* :class:`XdotoolDriver` finds, raises and types into X11 windows with ``xdotool``.
* :class:`PlaywrightDriver` drives a web UI (a solver's web front end, a licence portal) with Playwright.
* :class:`PywinautoDriver` is the interface for Windows desktop applications (Ansys Workbench, Abaqus/CAE, ...)
  through ``pywinauto``. It runs only on Windows: in the Linux container it reports itself unavailable.

API control (the application's own Python, the solver's command line) always comes first; these drivers are the
fallback and the observer.

pinneapple_tools.automation.interpret.doc:
From a task to a structured workflow.

A task is either a workflow already (a dict, or JSON/YAML text: it is validated and used as is) or a sentence
such as "run the channel case with a 55 mm obstacle". A sentence is matched against a **catalog of committed
workflows**: the words of the task pick the workflow and the numbers next to an input's words set its value (with
unit conversion), then the inputs are checked against their bounds. Nothing in a sentence can add steps or run
code: it only chooses among workflows someone reviewed, and sets their inputs.

An LLM is optional. With ``llm=OllamaClient(...)`` (``pinneapple_data.formfill.llm``; the Ollama service of the
deploy stack) the model answers in a JSON schema with the workflow id and input values, and its answer goes
through the same validation; if the server is not reachable, or the answer is invalid, the rule-based reading is
used and the reason is kept in ``notes``.
pinneapple_tools.automation.interpret.doc1: From a task to a structured workflow.

pinneapple_tools.automation.record.doc:
What a run leaves behind: one :class:`StepRecord` per step (state, commands, logs, artifacts with their SHA-256,
screenshots, checks, outputs, error) and the :class:`RunRecord` around them, saved as ``run.json`` in the run folder.

A step is ``passed`` only if its action ran, every check it produced held and every artifact it was expected to
leave exists; nothing else may be reported as passed.

The evidence of a run, for people and for other tools.

* :func:`write_report`: one self-contained HTML file (images embedded) with the inputs, the tools and versions, a
  timeline of the steps (state, duration, commands, actions, checks, artifacts with SHA-256, logs, screenshots),
  the acceptance criteria and the errors. Print it to PDF from a browser for a PDF.
* :func:`to_study_result` / :func:`write_study_result`: the same facts as a ``pinneapple_data.contracts.StudyResult``
  (the contract the apps share, read by the Evidence Report app): checks, criteria, metrics, files with SHA-256,
  limits and provenance; inputs, decision, step states and images in ``metadata``.

Nothing is inferred: a step is shown as passed only if its record says so, and an image's kind (screen, window,
render, plot) is shown next to it.

pinneapple_tools.automation.runner.doc:
Run a :class:`~pinneapple_tools.automation.workflow.Workflow` step by step, observe each step and stop on the
first failure or on the first step that needs a human decision.

For every step, in order:

1. skip it if an earlier run already passed it (a run folder can be resumed);
2. block if a step named in ``after`` has not passed, or if the application it needs is not installed;
3. stop with ``awaiting_confirmation`` if the step falls into a confirmation category (``expensive``,
   ``overwrite``, ``destructive``, ``external``) and was not approved: a step whose expected files already exist
   is an overwrite even if the workflow does not say so;
4. run the action through its adapter, with a virtual display if it drives a GUI;
5. check the artifacts it was expected to leave, hash every file it produced, keep its logs, commands, screenshots
   and outputs; the step passes only if the action returned and every check held.

``run.json`` in the run folder is rewritten after every change, so a UI can follow a run while it executes; when
the run stops, the evidence report (``report.html``) and the StudyResult (``study_result.json``) are written.

    from pinneapple_tools.automation import Runner, Workflow, example_workflow
    wf = Workflow.load(example_workflow("channel_obstacle"))
    run = Runner(wf, "runs/demo", inputs={"obstacle_height_mm": 50}).run()
    if run.state == "awaiting_confirmation":         # the solver step is "expensive"
        run = Runner(wf, …

pinneapple_tools.automation.runner_step.doc:
The GUI agent as a step of the Simulation Workflow Runner (``pinneapple_core.workflows``).

``register()`` adds the step kind ``guiagent``: one step of a runner workflow runs a whole automation workflow
(FreeCAD, CfdOF, OpenFOAM, ParaView, ...) in the step's directory and returns its verdict as outputs, so a runner DAG
can mesh and solve a CAD variant per case and use the acceptance criteria downstream::

    from pinneapple_core.workflows import Step, Workflow, WorkflowRunner
    from pinneapple_tools.automation.runner_step import register
    register()
    wf = Workflow(name="channel sweep", steps=[
        Step(id="h55", kind="guiagent", params={"workflow": "channel_obstacle",
                                                "inputs": {"obstacle_height_mm": 55}, "approve": ["solve"]})])
    WorkflowRunner("work/runner").run(wf)

Step parameters: ``workflow`` (id of a committed workflow, see :func:`~pinneapple_tools.automation.catalog`),
``inputs`` (checked against the workflow's bounds), ``approve`` (ids of the steps the workflow asks to confirm; whoever
writes the runner workflow approves them, and the record says so). A run that stops for a confirmation that was not
given, fails or is blocked makes the runner step fail with the agent's message. Outputs: ``state``, ``message``,
``passed`` (every acceptance criterion met), ``criteria`` (name -> met), ``metrics`` (the numbers of the
StudyResult), ``report`` and ``study_result`` (paths in the step directory).

Cancelling …

pinneapple_tools.automation.verify.doc:
Acceptance criteria on a finished run, computed from the produced files with PINNeAPPle's checks.

=================  ==========================================================================================
kind               what is computed
=================  ==========================================================================================
``mass_balance``   volume flux through every boundary patch of the OpenFOAM result (``pinneapple_check``'s
                   finite-volume reader and :func:`pinneapple_check.fv.fv_mass_balance`, from ``phi`` when written);
                   passes when |inlet + outlet| / |inlet| <= ``tol``
``inflow``         the volume flow through the inlet patch equals ``velocity`` x the patch area of the mesh within
                   ``tol`` (the boundary condition the case asked for was actually applied)
``pressure_drop``  area-weighted mean static pressure on the inlet minus the outlet, times ``density`` for
                   incompressible solvers (kinematic p); passes when ``min_pa`` <= dp <= ``max_pa``

``artifact``       a file or folder of the run exists and is not empty
``metric``         a numeric ``output`` of a passed ``step`` lies within [``min``, ``max``] (either may be omitted),
                   e.g. a reference error or the largest Courant number
``physics_lint``   ``pinneapple check`` on the case (conservation, divergence, …

pinneapple_tools.automation.workflow.doc:
The structured workflow an automation run executes: inputs with bounds, steps with preconditions, the artifacts
each step must produce, the confirmations it needs, and the acceptance criteria of the result.

A workflow is plain data (YAML or JSON), so it can be written by hand, produced by :func:`interpret` from a sentence,
reviewed in a pull request and replayed later::

    id: channel_obstacle
    title: Channel with an obstacle, pressure drop vs obstacle height
    inputs:
      obstacle_height_mm: {default: 40, min: 10, max: 80, unit: mm, description: height of the obstacle}
    steps:
      - id: open_project
        action: freecad.open
        params: {document: "{example}/channel_obstacle.FCStd"}
        expects: [{path: "open_project/project.json"}]
      - id: solve
        action: openfoam.solve
        after: [mesh]
        confirm: [expensive]
        params: {case: "{steps.setup.case}"}

Values in ``params`` and ``expects`` are templates: ``{inputs.<name>}``, ``{steps.<id>.<output>}``, ``{workdir}``
(the run directory) and ``{example}`` (the folder of the workflow file). A template that is a whole value keeps the
type of what it refers to (a number stays a number).

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.api.doc:
Arena — high-level API for running PINNeAPPle resolution pipelines.

This module bridges the problem design phase (``ProblemSpec``) with the
resolution pipeline (dataset generation → training → metrics).

Three entry points
------------------
1. From a ProblemSpec (built with ProblemBuilder)::

       from pinneapple_physics.pde_environment import ProblemBuilder
       from pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite import Arena

       spec = ProblemBuilder("heat_1d").domain(x=(0,1), t=(0,1)) ...build()
       result = Arena.from_spec(spec).run(model="VanillaPINN", epochs=5000)

2. From a registered preset::

       result = Arena.from_preset("burgers_1d", nu=0.01).run(...)

3. From a YAML config (existing workflow)::

       result = Arena.from_yaml("configs/experiment_burgers_1d.yaml").run()

Output contract
---------------
All ``.run()`` / ``.compare()`` calls return an ``ArenaResult`` dataclass with:
- ``spec``     : ProblemSpec used
- ``model``    : trained nn.Module
- ``history``  : list of loss dicts per epoch
- ``metrics``  : final evaluation metrics dict
- ``artifacts``: dict of paths to saved files

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.crossfr.doc:
The one evaluator of the cross-framework benchmark, and the statistics over seeds.

Every runner exports plain arrays (predictions on the shared test points, on the residual stencil, the identified
parameter of an inverse run, the operator predictions on the test split); this module turns them into metrics. A
framework's own reported error is never used.

Metrics (float64):

* ``rel_l2``: ``||u_pred - u_ref||_2 / ||u_ref||_2`` over the test points (:func:`pinneapple_physics.metrics.relative_l2`).
* ``max_abs``: ``max |u_pred - u_ref|`` over the test points.
* ``residual_rms``: root mean square of the PDE residual at fresh interior points, from second-order central
  differences of the exported stencil values (:func:`.problems.residual_from_stencil`); the same formula and step
  for every framework, so it measures the trained function, not the framework's autograd.
* inverse runs: ``nu_rel_err = |nu_hat - nu| / nu`` and the field ``rel_l2``.
* operator runs: mean per-sample relative L2 over the test split (the metric of Li et al. 2021).

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.crossfr.doc:
The forward and inverse PINN problems of the cross-framework benchmark, with their references.

Every framework gets the same problem definition from here: domain, coefficients, source terms, the exact or
reference solution, the shared training point sets, the test points and the fresh residual points. Nothing in this
module depends on a competitor framework.

Problems (``benchmarks/vs_frameworks/PROTOCOL.md``):

* ``burgers``: ``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx`` on ``x in [-1, 1]``, ``t in [0, 1]``, ``nu = 0.01 / pi``,
  ``u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x)``, ``u(+-1, t) = 0`` (Raissi, Perdikaris, Karniadakis 2019). Reference: the Cole-Hopf
  solution by Gauss-Hermite quadrature, :func:`pinneapple_physics.closed_form.burgers.burgers_sine_exact`.
* ``poisson``: ``u_xx + u_yy = f`` on the unit square, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, manufactured
  ``u = sin(pi x) sin(pi y)``, ``f = -2 pi^2 u``.
* ``helmholtz``: ``u_xx + u_yy + k^2 u = q`` on ``[-1, 1]^2``, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, manufactured
  ``u = sin(a1 pi x) sin(a2 pi y)`` with ``a1 = 1``, ``a2 = 4``, ``k = 1`` (Wang, Teng, Perdikaris 2021, SIAM J. Sci.
  Comput. 43(5), A3055), ``q = (k^2 - (a1 pi)^2 - (a2 pi)^2) u``.
* ``allen_cahn``: ``u_t = d u_xx + 5 u - 5 u^3`` on ``x in [-1, 1]`` periodic, ``t in [0, 1]``, ``d = 1e-4``,
  ``u(x, 0) = x^2 cos(pi x)`` (Raissi et al. 2019, the discrete-time example's data set). Reference:
  :func:`allen_cahn_reference`, Fourier pseudo-spectral in space and ETDRK4 in time
  …

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.deepone.doc:
The four canonical operator-learning ground-truth solvers from Lu, Jin &
Karniadakis 2019 (DeepONet), arXiv:1910.03193, Section 4: given a GRF-sampled
input function u(x) (`pinneapple_data.grf_sampler.GRFDraw`), each solver
computes the TRUE solution of a different dynamical system driven by u.
Standard, widely-used ground truth for benchmarking any operator-learning
architecture (DeepONet, FNO, or otherwise) — not tied to a specific dataset
or application. Each solver takes a GRFDraw plus query points and operates
on ONE case at a time; a dataset-generation loop over many draws assembles
whatever operator-learning training format the caller needs (e.g. sensor
values + query point + solution at that query point).

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.meta_be.doc:
Meta-Learning Benchmark for PINNs.

Trains MAML and Reptile meta-models on PDE parameter families (e.g. Burgers
with varying viscosity nu), then evaluates K-shot adaptation against
from-scratch training with the same number of gradient steps.

The central result is a **K-shot error curve**: how quickly each approach
reaches low relative L2 error as K (adaptation steps) grows.

Algorithms
----------
MAML (FOMAML)
    Bi-level: inner loop adapts a copy for K steps on support set, outer loop
    minimises query-set loss w.r.t. the meta-initialization.  First-order
    approximation (FOMAML) is used — gradients through the inner update are
    detached, which scales to deep networks without higher-order overhead.

Reptile
    Per-task: deep-copy model, run K SGD steps, then interpolate meta-weights
    toward task weights by step size epsilon.  Simpler than MAML and often
    competitive in practice.

Scratch baseline
    Start from random Kaiming initialization, run K gradient steps.  Same
    optimizer (Adam) and same data as the meta-adapted models.

Full-scratch oracle
    Train from scratch for the same TOTAL gradient steps as meta-training
    (n_meta_epochs x n_tasks_per_batch x n_inner_steps).  Upper bound on
    what dedicated per-task training can achieve.

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.physics.doc:
PhysicsPipeline — standard 6-step PINNeAPPle physics pipeline.

Standard flow
-------------
  Step 1 – Problem selection   : preset registry, built-in list, or custom ProblemSpec
  Step 2 – Geometry & mesh     : GeometrySpec / MeshData / STL / None (use domain bounds)
  Step 3 – Auto-generate       : physics losses compiled + collocation + mesh sampling
  Step 4 – Solver selection    : auto-picks best numerical solver → synthetic reference data
  Step 5 – Models              : user list + physics loss auto-attached per architecture
  Step 6 – Train & export      : auto-metrics, train, visualize, checkpoint (.pt), rank table

Uses:
  - pinneapple_environment.presets  (get_preset, list_presets → ProblemSpec)
  - pinneapple_pinn                 (compile_problem, LossWeights → loss_fn)
  - pinneapple_models               (ModelRegistry.build → any registered model)
  - pinneapple_train.metrics        (MSE, MAE, RMSE, R2, RelL2, MaxError)
  - pinneapple_geom                 (GeometrySpec, MeshData → mesh-based sampling)
  - pinneapple_solvers              (SolverCatalog → numerical reference data)

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite import PhysicsPipeline

    pipeline = PhysicsPipeline(
        problem = "burgers_1d",
        models  = ["vanilla_pinn", "siren", "modified_mlp"],
        epochs  = 3000,
    )
    report = pipeline.run()
    report.save("outputs/burgers_report.json")

    # Show available problems
    PhysicsPipeline.list_problems()

# …

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.runner..doc:
End-to-end pipeline: geometry → solver → dataset → train → predict → report.

Orchestrates the complete workflow:
  1. Load or generate geometry (pinneapple_geom)
  2. Generate mesh (mesher_2d or gmsh)
  3. Run physical solver (OpenFOAM or FEniCS) to generate ground truth
  4. Build training dataset from solver output
  5. Train surrogate model (PINN, GNN, DeepONet, etc.)
  6. Run inference and compute error metrics
  7. Generate report: error plots, field comparisons, loss curves
  8. Save model + all logs + HTML/JSON report

YAML config example
-------------------
pipeline:
  name: my_experiment
  out_dir: results/my_experiment

geometry:
  type: rectangle         # rectangle | sdf | gmsh | mesh_file
  params:
    xlim: [0, 1]
    ylim: [0, 1]
    obstacle: {type: circle, center: [0.3, 0.5], radius: 0.05}

solver:
  backend: openfoam       # openfoam | fenics | builtin
  params:
    solver: simpleFoam
    n_iterations: 500
    n_cores: 4

problem:
  id: ns_incompressible_2d
  params:
    nu: 0.001
    Re: 100

dataset:
  n_collocation: 10000
  n_boundary: 4000
  strategy: lhs           # uniform | lhs | sobol | adaptive

models:
  - id: pinn_mlp
    type: VanillaPINN
    params:
      hidden: [128, 128, 128, 128]
      activation: tanh
    train:
      epochs: 2000
      lr: 1e-3
      device: cuda
      amp: true
      grad_clip: 1.0
      compile: true       # torch.compile()
      grad_accum_steps: 4
    physics_weights:
      pde: 1.0
      bc: 10.0
      data: 5.0

  …

Navier-Stokes 2D Taylor-Green Vortex benchmark task.

       u_x + v_y = 0  (continuity)

Domain: (x,y) in [0, 2*pi]^2,  t in [0, 1]
Fields: (u, v, p)  (3 outputs)

Exact Taylor-Green Vortex solution:
  u(x,y,t) = -cos(x)*sin(y)*exp(-2*nu*t)
  v(x,y,t) =  sin(x)*cos(y)*exp(-2*nu*t)
  p(x,y,t) = -1/4*(cos(2*x) + cos(2*y))*exp(-4*nu*t)

nu   : 0.01 (default)

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.tasks.p.doc:
Poisson 2D benchmark task.

PDE  : -u_xx - u_yy = f(x,y),  (x,y) in [0,1]^2
f    : 2*pi^2 * sin(pi*x) * sin(pi*y)
BC   : u = 0 on all boundaries
Exact: u(x,y) = sin(pi*x) * sin(pi*y)

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.tasks.w.doc:
Wave equation 1D benchmark task.

PDE  : u_tt = c^2 * u_xx,  x in [0,1], t in [0,1]
IC   : u(x,0) = sin(pi*x),  u_t(x,0) = 0
BC   : u(0,t) = u(1,t) = 0
Exact: u(x,t) = cos(c*pi*t) * sin(pi*x)
c    : 1.0 (default)

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.timeser.doc:
TimeSeriesBenchmarkSpec — declarative time-series benchmark pipeline.

Uses exclusively existing PINNeAPPle modules — nothing built from scratch:

  pinneapple_timeseries.datasets.windowed  WindowedTimeSeriesDataset (sliding windows)
  pinneapple_timeseries.spec               TimeSeriesSpec
  pinneapple_train.trainer                 Trainer, TrainConfig  (training loop)
  pinneapple_train.losses                  CombinedLoss, SupervisedLoss
  pinneapple_train.normalizers             StandardScaler
  pinneapple_train.metrics                 MetricBundle + individual metric classes
  pinneapple_data.datasets                 load_dataset  (data loading)
  pinneapple_models / TSModelCatalog       model registry fallback

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite import TimeSeriesBenchmarkSpec

    spec = TimeSeriesBenchmarkSpec(
        source   = "lorenz63",
        models   = ["lstm", "nbeats", "tcn"],
        metrics  = ["mse", "mae", "rmse"],
        horizon  = 50,
        lookback = 100,
        plots    = True,
    )
    report = spec.run()
    report.save("outputs/ts_benchmark.json")

pinneapple_tools.benchmark_suite.transfe.doc:
Transfer Learning Benchmark for PINNs.

Trains a source model from scratch, then fine-tunes it to a family of target
problems using different strategies from ``pinneapple_transfer``.  Compares
each transfer approach against two from-scratch baselines.

Strategies
----------
scratch_budget : train from scratch with same epoch budget as fine-tuning
scratch_full   : train from scratch with source + fine-tune epochs (total budget)
finetune       : transfer all layers, low LR (TransferTrainer strategy="finetune")
partial_freeze : freeze first half of linear layers, fine-tune rest
feature_extract: freeze all except last linear layer
progressive    : frozen backbone for warmup_epochs, then full unfreeze

Key metrics
-----------
rel_l2            : relative L2 error vs exact/reference solution
speedup_factor    : steps_to_threshold(scratch_budget) / steps_to_threshold(transfer)
trainable_ratio   : trainable params / total params
convergence_epoch : first epoch where pde_residual < threshold

pinneapple_tools.compute_backends.doc:
Multi-backend support for PINNeAPPle: PyTorch (default) + JAX.

Provides a backend abstraction layer so PINN code can run on PyTorch or JAX
without modification.  JAX gives ``vmap``/``jit`` speedups on CPU/TPU; the
default PyTorch backend requires no extra dependencies.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_tools.compute_backends import set_backend, get_backend, JAXBackend

    # Switch to JAX (requires: pip install jax jaxlib)
    set_backend("jax")
    print(get_backend())  # "jax"

    # JIT-compile a PINN. residual_fn receives (u_fn, x), where u_fn is
    # model_fn bound to params (x -> u(x)), so it can take derivatives via
    # jax.grad/jax.hessian -- not a precomputed value, which JAX cannot
    # differentiate.
    compiled = JAXBackend.jit_pinn(model_fn, residual_fn)

    # Vectorise a single-point residual over a batch of collocation points
    batched = JAXBackend.vmap_residual(single_pt_residual)

    # Convert between PyTorch and JAX
    jax_x = JAXBackend.torch_to_jax(torch_tensor)
    torch_x = JAXBackend.jax_to_torch(jax_array)

pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality.doc:
pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality — dataset quality assessment.

Two independent ways to vet a dataset before training on it:

``checks``
    Generic, statistical/heuristic checks over a plain ``(coords,
    fields)`` point-cloud representation: completeness (NaN fraction),
    cross-field shape/monotonicity consistency, distribution summaries,
    IsolationForest outlier detection, physical-range issues. No
    framework dependency, no model involved.

``vlm_curation``
    Vision-language-model curation: run a VLM over a short clip of each
    sequence and use its label/confidence judgment (parsed from real
    generated text, never fabricated) to filter a raw dataset down to a
    curated one before training. Ported and generalized from the
    downstream ``physcurator`` project. Requires the ``vlm_curation``
    extra to actually run a model; the parsing/filtering logic itself has
    no heavy dependency.

pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality.checks.doc:
Generic dataset quality-assessment checks.

Operates on a plain `(coords, fields)` representation of a point-cloud
dataset (`coords`: (N, d) array of sample locations; `fields`: {name: array}
of per-point field values, each array's leading dimension of length N) — the
same shape any PDE/PINN dataset naturally takes, independent of where it came
from. No framework dependency (no orchestration/task-runner coupling).

This is intentionally generic/heuristic — …

Useful for evaluating a differentiable PDE-residual function against static point-cloud data when no trained model is available — the …

pinneapple_tools.dataset_quality.vlm_cur.doc:
Vision-language-model dataset curation.

Generic engine for curating a synthetic training dataset by running a
vision-language model (VLM) over a short video clip of each sequence and
using its judgment of physical plausibility to filter a raw dataset down
to a "curated" one before training on it.

Ported and generalized from a downstream project (``physcurator``), which
used this exact approach -- clip -> VLM judgment -> JSON label/confidence
-> filter -- to screen synthetic 2D heat-diffusion sequences for
physically-implausible injected anomalies, against a fixed model
(``nvidia/Cosmos-Reason2-2B``) and a hardcoded heat-diffusion prompt.
Nothing in this module is heat2d-specific or Cosmos-specific: the VLM
model name/class, the prompt template (via a caller-supplied physics
description), and the raw-sequence -> clip-path lookup are all parameters
here. ``physcurator`` itself now calls into this module rather than
duplicating the logic locally.

Design, stated plainly (same "no fabricated results" stance as the rest of
this package): this module never invents a curation judgment. Every
label/confidence/reason returned by :func:`curate_sequence` /
:func:`curate_dataset` comes from parsing the VLM's own generated text
(via :func:`extract_json`); a response that is missing or isn't valid,
parseable JSON degrades to a neutral fallback label at confidence 0.5, it
is never silently promoted to a "consistent"/"passed" judgment. Running
:func:`curate_dataset` end to end against a …

pinneapple_tools.model_services.doc:
PINNeAPPle Model Services: ready-made PINNeAPPle models as local microservices with the shape of NVIDIA NIM.

Each service is a model with a card (task, inputs, outputs, validity range, measured metrics, references) and a
trust function; every answer carries PINNeAPPle's trust report (decision APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT with its checks),
and a query outside the validity range says so. The HTTP routes follow NIM's: ``GET /v1/health/ready``,
``GET /v1/health/live``, ``GET /v1/models`` (OpenAI list format), ``POST /v1/infer`` (``{"model", "inputs"}``) and,
for language services, ``POST /v1/chat/completions`` (OpenAI format, with ``nvext.guided_json``).

    from pinneapple_tools.model_services import default_registry, serve_in_thread, ModelServiceClient
    server, url = serve_in_thread(default_registry())
    c = ModelServiceClient(url)
    c.models(); c.infer("airfoil_cst_rans_mlp", {...})        # outputs + trust
    ModelServiceClient("https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1", api_key=os.environ["NVIDIA_API_KEY"]).chat(...)

``python -m pinneapple_tools.model_services serve --port 8000`` runs the server; ``docker/model_services`` has a
Dockerfile and a compose file. Built-in services: every model of the PINNeAPPle zoo (``pp.zoo``, trust from
``pp.zoo.validate``), physics checks of any field (``pp.trust_card``), and ``pinneapple-intent``, the deterministic
specification extractor of ``pinneapple_design.intent`` behind the chat route (no network, no key: every value it
returns …

pinneapple_tools.nvidia.doc:
pinneapple_tools.nvidia -- PINNeAPPle with the NVIDIA stack (PhysicsNeMo, Omniverse / OpenUSD, Isaac Sim,
Cosmos, NIM).

PINNeAPPle's part is the physics: the problem, the reference solvers and the checks every result must pass before
anyone uses it. The NVIDIA part trains (PhysicsNeMo), shows and simulates (Omniverse, Isaac Sim), generates
(Cosmos) or answers (NIM). This package holds the glue so the examples in ``examples/nvidia`` stay thin:

``diagram``     architecture figures of a pipeline (who does what; which steps need a GPU or an API key)
``omniverse``   results as OpenUSD stages with fields as primvars, a stage validator and a read-back preview
``isaac``       Isaac Sim-ready articulations (``UsdPhysics``), their checks, and the Isaac Sim runner script
``nim``         a client for NIM microservices (OpenAI-compatible, ``nvext.guided_json``) and a physics guard
``cosmos``      clients for Cosmos world foundation models (``/v1/infer``) and Cosmos Reason, and physics
                checks of a video (ballistic fit, conservation of the tracked object)
``physicsnemo`` small PhysicsNeMo surrogates (``FullyConnected``) trained and checked the PINNeAPPle way; grid
                operators (FNO, MeshGraphNet) are in ``pinneapple_neural.physicsnemo_bridge``
``testing``     a local fake server speaking the NIM / Cosmos HTTP contracts, for tests without a key or GPU
``runinfo``     versions, hardware and timings of a run, and which NVIDIA components ran
``figures``     field …
pinneapple_tools.nvidia.doc1: pinneapple_tools.nvidia -- PINNeAPPle with the NVIDIA stack (PhysicsNeMo, Omniverse / OpenUSD, Isaac Sim, Cosmos, NIM).

pinneapple_tools.nvidia._brep_worker.doc:
USD BRep worker: builds a part from a recipe and measures it. Standalone (usd_brep + numpy + stdlib only), so it
runs in whichever interpreter has ``usd-brep`` (its wheel is CPython 3.12):

    python _brep_worker.py request.json result.npz

The request is ``{"recipe": {"ops": [...], "result": name}, "options": {...}}`` (see ``pinneapple_tools.nvidia.brep``).

pinneapple_tools.nvidia.brep.doc:
Exact geometry with NVIDIA USD BRep (the SMLib NURBS B-rep kernel, ``pip install usd-brep``), measured for
PINNeAPPle: mass properties of the exact solid, curvature of every face, tessellations at several chord tolerances
with their measured deviation from the exact surfaces, and B-rep USD export.

    part = PartRecipe().box("plate", (0, 0, 0), (0.1, 0.06, 0.01)) \
                       .cylinder("hole", (0.05, 0.03, -0.005), 0.01, 0.02).difference("bracket", "plate", "hole")
    rep = evaluate_part(part, chord_tolerances=[1e-4, 1e-5], density=2700.0, usd_brep_path="bracket_brep.usda")
    rep.volume, rep.min_radius, rep.tessellations[-1]["max_deviation"], rep.mesh(-1)   # (V, F) of the finest mesh

A part is a recipe (a list of operations on named solids), so it is data: it can be stored with a result,
regenerated, varied by a design study, or written by a model service. The kernel runs in a worker process
(:mod:`pinneapple_tools.nvidia._brep_worker`) in whichever interpreter has ``usd_brep``: the current one if it
imports, else ``$PINNEAPPLE_BREP_PYTHON`` (the ``usd-brep`` wheel is built for CPython 3.12 only:
``python3.12 -m venv /opt/brep && /opt/brep/bin/pip install usd-brep numpy`` and point the variable at
``/opt/brep/bin/python``).

Checks it gives a trust report: the solid is manifold; mesh volume and area converge to the exact ones; the
largest distance from a mesh triangle to the exact surface (chord error) is below the tolerance asked; the mesh
size resolves …
pinneapple_tools.nvidia.brep.doc1: Exact geometry with NVIDIA USD BRep (the SMLib NURBS B-rep kernel, ``pip install usd-brep``), measured for PINNeAPPle: mass properties of the exact solid, curvature of every face, tessellations at several chord tolerances with their measured deviation from the exact surfaces, and B-rep USD export.

functions.doc1: Build ``recipe`` with USD BRep and measure it (see the module docstring). ``vertex_curvature``: the exact surface curvature at every vertex of the finest mesh (``rep.vertex_curvature``, 1/m) and the B-rep face each vertex lies on (``rep.vertex_face``).

pinneapple_tools.nvidia.diagram.doc:
Architecture diagrams of a PINNeAPPle + NVIDIA pipeline, drawn by code (matplotlib only, no graphviz).

    from pinneapple_tools.nvidia.diagram import Block, architecture_diagram

    blocks = [Block("data", "Darcy solver\n(finite volumes)", "pinneapple", col=0),
              Block("fno", "FNO\nphysicsnemo.models.fno", "physicsnemo", col=1),
              Block("usd", "USD stage\n(OpenUSD, usd-core)", "omniverse", col=2),
              Block("kit", "Omniverse Kit / RTX", "omniverse", col=3, ran=False)]
    architecture_diagram("Cold plate", blocks, [("data", "fno", "a, T pairs"), ("fno", "usd", "T field")], "arch.png")

Each block has an owner (``pinneapple``, an NVIDIA product: ``physicsnemo``, ``omniverse``, ``brep``, ``isaac``,
``cosmos``, ``nim``, or a PINNeAPPle stack: ``robotsim``, ``services``, ``worldmodel``) that sets its colour, a column (left to right is the data flow) and an optional row. ``ran=False`` draws a
dashed, hatched block: the step needs a GPU, an API key or a download and was not executed where the figure was made.

pinneapple_tools.nvidia.isaac.doc:
Isaac Sim-ready robots in OpenUSD (``UsdPhysics``), their checks, and the Isaac Sim script that replays a motion.

Isaac Sim simulates articulations described with the ``UsdPhysics`` schemas (rigid bodies with mass properties,
colliders, revolute joints with drives, an articulation root, a physics scene). This module writes those from a
plain description, so the masses and inertias Isaac Sim uses are the ones PINNeAPPle computed with:

``Link`` / ``Joint`` / ``ArticulationSpec`` (from :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.spec`)
    links as boxes or cylinders (visual + collider) with mass, centre of mass and principal inertia; revolute
    joints with an anchor point, axis, limits and an angular drive (position or effort).
``author_articulation(stage, spec)``
    adds the robot under ``/World/<name>`` of a :class:`pinneapple_tools.nvidia.omniverse.FieldStage` (or any
    ``Usd.Stage``) with a ``PhysicsScene``, a ground plane, a fixed joint to the world for a fixed base, and the
    articulation root on the robot prim.
``validate_physics(path)``
    :func:`omniverse.validate_stage` plus the physics a simulator will read: ``UsdPhysics.LoadUsdPhysicsFromRange``
    (the USD physics parser) finds every body, joint and articulation; masses positive; inertias physical
    (triangle inequality); every joint between rigid bodies; a gravity direction and magnitude.
``isaac_replay_script(...)``
    a standalone Isaac Sim script (``isaacsim.SimulationApp``, …

pinneapple_tools.nvidia.omniverse.doc:
PINNeAPPle results as OpenUSD stages for NVIDIA Omniverse (authored and checked with ``usd-core``).

Omniverse apps (USD Composer, Kit, Isaac Sim) open OpenUSD files. This module writes a result as a USD stage with the
physics fields kept as data, not only as colours, and checks the file before anyone opens it:

``FieldStage``
    ``/World`` (Z up, metres) with meshes (``add_mesh``), curves (``add_curves``, pipes, streamlines) and points
    (``add_points``, sensors). Every field is a ``primvars:<name>`` float array (vertex interpolation) with its unit
    in ``pinneapple:unit:<name>``; one field per prim is also baked into ``primvars:displayColor`` so any USD viewer
    shows it. ``add_time_samples`` keys a field (and its colours) over time, so the Omniverse timeline plays a
    transient result. ``set_trust`` stores a trust decision and its checks on a prim (``pinneapple:trust:*``), so the
    scene carries the verdict of the numbers it shows.
``validate_stage``
    re-opens the file and checks it: it opens, up axis and units, every mesh has consistent topology (indices inside
    the points, counts summing to the indices), every vertex primvar has one finite value per point (per time
    sample), extents are set, and the ``UsdUtils.ComplianceChecker`` result.
``render_stage_png``
    a preview: the meshes and curves read back from the file, drawn with matplotlib in their ``displayColor``. It is
    a check that the file holds what was written, not an Omniverse RTX …

pinneapple_tools.nvidia.physicsnemo.doc:
Small PhysicsNeMo surrogates for tabular physics (a few inputs -> a few outputs), trained and checked the
PINNeAPPle way. Grid operators (FNO, MeshGraphNet) are in :mod:`pinneapple_neural.physicsnemo_bridge`.

``MLPSurrogate.fit(X, Y, budget)``
    ``physicsnemo.models.mlp.FullyConnected`` with inputs and outputs scaled to [-1, 1] by the training box, Adam
    with a cosine learning rate, mini-batches, run until a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget.ComputeBudget`
    is spent (``train_within_budget``, so two models with the same budget got the same compute).
``predict(X)``, ``in_box(X)``, ``save`` / ``load``
    NumPy in and out; the training box is kept so a caller can count extrapolated queries.
``sign_violations(f, grid, axis, output, sign)``
    a physics check on any model: the fraction of grid cells where ``d output / d input[axis]`` has the wrong sign
    (e.g. a wheel's load must grow with sinkage), by finite differences on the grid.
``relative_errors(pred, ref)``
    per-output relative RMS errors.

pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.doc:
rea_bridge -- study reference implementations with REA, under a license gate.

`REA <https://github.com/morluto/rea>`_ (Reverse Engineer Anything, MIT) is a
Node.js CLI/MCP server that inspects software without its source and returns
Evidence JSON. Within PINNeAPPle it is a third source for the research
pipeline (:mod:`pinneapple_tools.hpo_experiments`): arXiv gives papers,
GitHub gives repositories, REA gives *how a feature is actually built*,
with the artifact's SHA-256 and REA's stated limitations attached.

Modules
-------
client      run the ``rea`` CLI and parse its JSON (no Python dependency)
licenses    license detection and the adapt / clean_room / reference_only gate
evidence    JavaScript Evidence -> compact feature map; keyword ``locate``
harvest     JSON ledger of studied projects and findings, gate-enforced
tools       registration on :class:`pinneapple_worldmodel.PhysicsToolRegistry`

See ``docs/dev/REA_INTEGRATION.md`` for setup and the harvest workflow.
pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.doc1: rea_bridge -- study reference implementations with REA, under a license gate.

pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.client.doc:
Thin, honest wrapper around the REA command-line tool.

REA ("Reverse Engineer Anything", https://github.com/morluto/rea, MIT) is a
Node.js CLI / MCP server that inspects software *without its source code* --
JavaScript/Electron bundles, websites, native binaries (through Hopper,
Ghidra or IDA), .NET assemblies, WASM, Android packages -- and returns
**Evidence JSON**: every finding carries the artifact's SHA-256, the
operation that produced it, its confidence/authority and its limitations.

This module only runs that CLI and parses what it prints. It never
interprets, completes or "fixes" REA's results: whatever REA did not
observe stays absent. That matches the rule used by
:mod:`pinneapple_llm.research` (results trace back to a real tool output,
never to an LLM's recall).

Resolution of the executable, in order:

1. ``PINNEAPPLE_REA_BIN`` -- an explicit path (or a command line, split on
   whitespace, e.g. ``"npx -y rea-agents@6.4.0"``);
2. ``rea`` on ``PATH`` (``npm install --global rea-agents``);
3. ``npx -y rea-agents@<PINNED_VERSION>`` if ``npx`` is on ``PATH``.

Nothing is installed implicitly beyond what ``npx`` itself caches.
pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.client.doc1: Thin, honest wrapper around the REA command-line tool.

pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.evidence.doc:
Turn REA's JavaScript application Evidence into a compact feature map.

``rea analyze-javascript-application`` returns a large (often tens of MB)
Evidence JSON whose ``normalized_result.semantic_graph`` holds every
function, call site, binding and relation REA recovered from the code, each
with an exact source range. This module keeps only what is useful for
studying *how a feature is implemented*:

- named functions per module with their line ranges;
- the resolved static call graph between them (``calls`` relations from a
  call site to a function, attributed to the call site's enclosing function);
- timers and storage mechanisms the app uses;
- REA's own limitations, copied verbatim.

:func:`locate` then answers "where is feature X?" by matching keywords
against function names and the source lines inside each function's range,
and expands the hits one level along the call graph. Every hit points back to
a file, a line range and the Evidence id, so a finding can always be checked
against the original.

Nothing here infers semantics REA did not record: an unresolved call stays
unresolved, an anonymous function stays anonymous.

pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.harvest.doc:
Harvest ledger: what was studied, under which license, and what came of it.

Each :class:`HarvestEntry` records one studied project (URL, commit, license
policy, the REA Evidence id/SHA-256 when REA was used) and its
:class:`Finding` items -- an idea, a technique or a feature, where it lives in
the original, and what PINNeAPPle did with it.

``Finding.status`` values:

``idea``           noted, nothing implemented yet
``adapted``        PINNeAPPle code derived from the original code (needs ``adapt``)
``reimplemented``  written from the published method / observed behaviour
``exists``         PINNeAPPle already had it; the finding only cross-checks
``rejected``       studied and not taken (``note`` says why)

The ledger enforces the license gate: an ``adapted`` finding under a
``clean_room`` or ``reference_only`` policy is refused at construction time,
so the rule cannot be bypassed by editing a JSON file and reloading it.

pinneapple_tools.rea_bridge.licenses.doc:
License gate for anything harvested from another project into PINNeAPPle.

PINNeAPPle is Apache-2.0. What may flow from a studied project into this
repository depends on that project's license, so every harvest is tagged
with one of three policies -- the same "a missing license means all rights
reserved" stance as :mod:`pinneapple_catalog.resources`:

``adapt``
    Permissive and Apache-2.0-compatible (MIT, BSD, Apache-2.0, ISC, Zlib,
    CC-BY-4.0, CC0, Unlicense). Code may be adapted; the original notice
    must be kept (``attribution_required``) -- recorded in the harvest
    ledger and, for copied code, in ``NOTICE``.
``clean_room``
    Copyleft (GPL, LGPL, AGPL, MPL, EPL). Only *behaviour* may be taken:
    equations, algorithms as published in papers, interfaces, observed
    input/output. The PINNeAPPle implementation is written from the
    published method, never from the code, and the ledger refuses an entry
    marked ``adapted`` under this policy.
``reference_only``
    No license, unrecognised license, or a non-commercial / no-derivatives
    term. Read for orientation; nothing is reused.

Detection is deliberately conservative: when a repository carries several
licenses (e.g. VisualPDE: MIT for code, CC-BY-4.0 for HTML/CSS) the most
restrictive one decides, and anything not positively recognised is
``reference_only``.

pinneapple_tools.reporting.datasheet.doc:
A technical datasheet: the engineering record of a study, laid out from data -- no LLM anywhere.

A study produces numbers and figures; this module turns them into one self-contained document in the
shape a hardware datasheet has and a review meeting reads:

* a strip of headline numbers (the question the study answers, in six cells);
* numbered sections, each a table beside its figure, every figure captioned with what it shows and
  what to read from it;
* a cost table (how long each step took, on what), a run plan (done / running / queued, with the reason
  each step exists), the items to confirm, and a limitations block.

Nothing here decides content: every string, table and figure is passed in by the study.  The module
owns only layout, so a report can be regenerated from stored results without re-solving.

    from pinneapple_tools.reporting.datasheet import Datasheet, Figure, KPI, Step, Table

    d = Datasheet("3 GHz compact range", subtitle="quiet zone by physical optics", eyebrow="EM / reflector")
    d.kpis([KPI("Focal length", "1.50", "m"), KPI("Quiet zone", "0.60", "m @ 3 m")])
    s = d.section("Reflector geometry", lede="The section and its rolled edge, as modelled.")
    s.row(Table([["Focal length", "1.50 m"], ["Section", "1.20 m square"]], header=["quantity", "value"],
                caption="As modelled."),
          Figure("side.png", "Side section with the rays."))
    d.plan(done=[Step("Geometry", "built from Problem", "done", "0 s")])
    …

pinneapple_tools.reporting.paperkit.doc:
Figure style and PDF paper builder for PINNeAPPle technical reports.

Figures: one fixed categorical colour order (never cycled past its 8 entries in a single plot), a
single-hue sequential blue ramp (``SEQ``, registered as ``"seq_blue"``), a blue/red diverging ramp with
a neutral grey midpoint (``DIV``, registered as ``"div_blue_red"``), recessive axes and no top/right
spines. Call :func:`setup_mpl` once, then save each figure with :func:`savefig`.

PDF: :class:`Paper` builds an A4 report with reportlab/platypus in the STIX serif shipped with
matplotlib (full Greek and math glyphs): title block, abstract, numbered sections, equations,
figures, tables with captions, references and page numbers. reportlab is optional and is imported
only when a :class:`Paper` (or :func:`para`) is created::

    pip install "pinneapple[veriphysics]"

Example::

    from pinneapple_tools.reporting.paperkit import CAT, Paper, fmt, savefig, setup_mpl

    setup_mpl()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 3))
    ax.plot(x, y, color=CAT[0])
    png = savefig(fig, "out/fig1.png")

    paper = Paper("Heat conduction in a slab", subtitle="PINN vs. FEM")
    paper.abstract("We compare ...", keywords=["PINN", "FEM"])
    paper.section("Results")
    paper.figure(png, "Temperature along the slab.")
    paper.table([["Method", "rel. L2"], ["FEM", fmt(1.2e-4)]], "Errors against the exact solution.")
    paper.build("out/report.pdf")

Matplotlib's backend is left alone; scripts that run headless and want …

scripts out-of-process with best-effort resource limits.

See ``custom_solver_runner`` for the (important, honest) limits of what
this actually protects against -- it is process-level resource limiting,
not a real sandbox.

pinneapple_tools.sandbox.custom_solver_r.doc:
Run an untrusted, user-supplied Python solver script out-of-process,
with best-effort resource limits.

SECURITY WARNING -- read this before using this module for anything
------------------------------------------------------------------------
``run_custom_solver`` isolates a script into a *separate OS process* and
applies POSIX resource limits (``resource.setrlimit``) plus a wall-clock
``subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)``. That is **process-level resource
limiting, not a sandbox**, and it does NOT provide a security boundary:

  * No filesystem restriction. The script can read, write, or delete any
    file the calling OS user can touch.
  * No network restriction. The script can open sockets, make HTTP
    requests, exfiltrate data, etc.
  * No syscall/capability restriction of any kind (no seccomp, no
    namespaces, no chroot). It can spawn further subprocesses, load
    arbitrary shared libraries, etc.
  * ``RLIMIT_AS`` bounds *virtual address space*, not resident physical
    memory -- it stops a script that tries to allocate a huge array, but
    is not a general memory-abuse defense (e.g. many small long-lived
    allocations that never trip a single large allocation), and some
    platforms/allocators don't enforce it as tightly as Linux glibc does.
  * ``RLIMIT_CPU`` bounds *CPU time*, not wall-clock time -- a script that
    sleeps, blocks on I/O, or spins a busy network wait can run
    indefinitely without touching its CPU budget. That's why this module
    …
pinneapple_tools.sandbox.custom_solver_r.doc1: Run an untrusted, user-supplied Python solver script out-of-process, with best-effort resource limits.

functions.name: run_custom_solver
functions.doc1: Run ``script_path``'s ``solve(params)`` in a separate, resource- limited subprocess. See the module docstring's SECURITY WARNING for exactly what protection this does (and does not) provide.

pinneapple_tools.surrogate_policy.doc:
pinneapple_tools.surrogate_policy — measured-runtime "does this problem
need a trained surrogate, or can we just call its solver directly?"
policy.

Deliberately measurement-driven, not a dimension-based guess: a 3D solve
is not always slower than a 2D one (a closed-form/analytic 3D solver can
run in microseconds while an iterative 2D CFD solve takes seconds), so a
"3D = always needs a surrogate" heuristic is wrong often enough to be
worth avoiding entirely. The caller supplies a zero-argument thunk that
runs one real solve; this module only handles timing, a small JSON cache
so the same problem isn't re-timed every call, and thresholding.

Animation-centred dashboards for any simulation: an animation in the middle, charts synced to its time cursor,
KPI tiles, a parameter panel and a colour bar; exported as interactive HTML (scrubbing a chart moves the

    import pinneapple as pp

                   charts=[Chart("Angle", "angle [deg]", "time [s]", [Series("theta", theta_deg)], slot="right")],
                   tiles=[Tile("Energy", E, "J")], params=[Param("Length", 1.0, "m")])
    db.to_html("pendulum.html"); db.to_png("pendulum.png"); db.to_video(gif="pendulum.gif", mp4="pendulum.mp4")

Bridges from PINNeAPPle results to other 3-D viewers.

pinneapple_tools.visualization.molecular.doc:
Molecular visualisation: proteins and molecules, alone or adsorbed on metal surfaces, rendered as stills, MP4
trajectories, 3-D scenes (glTF for the PINNeAPPle web viewer) and MD dashboards.

The visual side of a protein-on-metal MD pipeline (the kind RoyalMD Gold runs with OpenMM), with nothing of an MD
engine in it: anything that gives atom positions can be shown (a PDB file, an OpenMM or mdtraj trajectory, the
torch MD of ``pinneapple_simulation``).

* :class:`Molecule`: atoms read from PDB (multi-MODEL files give the frames), element and residue chemistry,
  CA backbone trace, per-residue class (hydrophobic, polar, positive, negative, special);
* :func:`fcc_slab`: an fcc metal slab (Au, Ag, Cu, Pt, Pd, Ni, Al, Pb) with a (111), (100) or (110) top facet, sized
  in whole lattice repeats so a periodic box does not strain it; :func:`slab_for_footprint` sizes it from a
  molecule's footprint plus padding;
* :func:`orient_on_surface`: principal axes of the molecule, the thinnest direction along the surface normal (the
  broadest face down), an optional active site turned away from the surface, and a set gap above the slab;
* :func:`render`: a still with pyvista (off-screen): atoms as spheres coloured by residue class, element, chain or
  height, a backbone tube, the slab with a metallic material, three-point lighting;
* :func:`render_frames` / :func:`encode_mp4`: a trajectory as PNG frames and an H.264 MP4 (imageio-ffmpeg), and
  …

pinneapple_tools.visualization.pyvista_b.doc:
PyVista bridge: turn PINNeAPPle meshes and fields into publication-quality 3-D images.

Everything that builds a mesh (``calculix_grid``, ``scene_to_multiblock``, ``grid_from_arrays``) is
plain NumPy + PyVista and runs on any machine. Rendering (``render_png``, ``render_gif``) needs an
OpenGL context: a desktop session, or ``xvfb-run`` / OSMesa / EGL on a headless server. Because VTK
**segfaults** (kills the whole Python process) when no context exists, ``can_render`` probes in a
subprocess first and the render functions raise a ``RuntimeError`` with the fix instead.

Install: ``pip install "pinneapple[pyvista]"``. Headless Linux: ``xvfb-run -a python your_script.py``.

PINNeAPPle studio: realistic 3D visualisation of any geometry and its physics.

    import pinneapple as pp
    sc = pp.viz.Scene.from_file("result.frd")          # or an STL, an OpenFOAM case, arrays, a CFD result
    sc.save("result.glb")                               # glTF with the fields, also .usda (Omniverse) and .stl
    pp.viz.render(sc, "stress.jpg", field="STRESS")     # Blender Cycles, jet colour scale, colour bar
    pp.viz.web_viewer(sc, "viewer/")                    # interactive three.js page: surfaces, streamlines, slices
    pp.viz.LIGHTING_PRESETS["lunar_south_pole"]         # black sky, low hard Sun (also: studio, lunar_low_sun, ...)
    pp.viz.field_view(mesh, fields, deform=..., markers=...)   # fields, errors and deformed shapes for the apps' views

pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.an.doc:
Time animation of a :class:`~.scene.Scene`: rigid bodies moving along a trajectory, per-frame arrows, trails,
per-vertex fields and head-up numbers, for the browser viewer (:mod:`.web`) and Blender (:mod:`.blender`).

    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio import Scene, Surface
    from pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.animation import Animation
    sc = Scene([Surface("runway", Vr, Fr, "concrete"), Surface("body", Vb, Fb, "paint", group="body")])
    anim = Animation(t)                                   # times (T,) in seconds
    anim.add_track("body", positions, quaternions)        # (T, 3), (T, 4) [w, x, y, z]; body vertices in body frame
    anim.add_vectors("forces", origins, vectors, values=mag, attach="body", label="Force [N]")
    anim.add_trail("path", positions)
    anim.add_hud("V", speed, "Speed", "m/s")
    sc.animation = anim.resample(200)                     # scene.json stays small
    web_viewer(sc, "viewer/")                             # play / pause, time slider, follow camera

The animated axis need not be time: ``Animation(f_ghz, time_label="f", time_unit="GHz", interpolate=False)`` steps
through solved frequencies (the viewer shows only those frames, never a blend), and
``add_surface_shape(surface, vertices)`` moves a surface's vertices frame by frame (a radiation pattern that changes
shape with frequency, a deforming body).

Every array is in the scene's axes (``Scene.axes``, e.g. ``"z_up"``). A track moves the surfaces …
